PREFACE. 


A GREAT deal of pains has been taken to preserve 
in printed records, some account of the labours 
and success of those men, whom God has honoured by 
putting them into the ministry ; while many females, 
whose praise was in all the churches while they lived, 
have been suffered to drop into oblivion, and their pre- 
eminent labours, and success in the conversion of 
souls to remain as destitute of any public record, as 
though they had never existed; or if any account of 
their exemplary piety is preserved, their public labours 
are either suppressed, or passed over in silence. - It is 
very easy to account for this, the great majority of 
Biographers and Editors of Magazines, are enemies to 
female preaching, so that we have very little concern- 


‘ing their labours, except what is found among the 


Friends, or people called Quakers ; among whom, the 
ministry of women, has received a regular establish- 
ment. It is true, there have been raised up of late, 


_ several religious communities, who by their rules and re- 


gulations, publicly allow and encourage such a ministry. 


Such were the high church principles, and the 
prejudice of education, of that eminent servant of 
Jesus Christ, the Rev. Joan Westey, that for a season, 
he could scarcely give the right hand of fellowship, to 


any Labourers in the Lord’s Vineyard, that had not

received Episcopal Ordination. But when he was 
fully convinced, that God had owned the labours of 
pious laymen in his community, he encouraged them 
to proceed. And he never molested any pious female, 
who was subject to decipline and order, in his Societies 
for calling sinners to repentance ; but when fully satis- 
fied that God had owned their labours, he gave them 
encouragement. This is evident in his conduct 
towards Mrs. Gilbert, Mrs. Johnson, Miss Bosanquet, 
Miss Mallet, Mrs. Crosby, Miss Hurrel, and some 
ethers. Indeed he could» not-have done otherwise 
according to his own reasoning in his Sermon “against 
Bigotry”? His argument throughout that Sermon is, 
that the conversion of sinners is the work of God, and 
whoever is the instrument of doing this work, is the 
servant of God. And we must not forbid such a one. 
His words are (Mark ix. 38, 39) “Is there full proof, 
1. That a person before us was a gross, open sinner ? 
2, That he is not so now, that he has broke off his 
sins, and lives a Christian life? and 3. That this 
change was wrought by hearing this man preach ? If 
these three points be plain and undeniable, then forbid 
him not. Beware how you attempt to hinder him, 
either by your authority, or arguments, or persuasion. 
But what if he be only a layman, who casts out devils? 
Ought I not to forbid him then? Is the fact allowed ? 
Is there reasonable proof, that this man has or does 
cast out devils? If there is, forbid him not; no 
not at the peril of your soul. Shall not God work by 
whom he will work? No man can do these works 
unless God be with him; unless God hath sent him 
for this very thing. But if God hath sent him, will 
you call him back? Will you forbid him to go? 
But I do not know that’ he is sent of God, “Now 
herein is a marvellous thing,” (may any of the seals 
of his mission say, any. whom he hath brought from 
Satan to God) “that ye know not whence this man. 
is, and, behold he hath opened mine eyes! If this 
man were not of God, he could do nothing.” If you 
doubt the fact, send for the parents of the man: send

for his brethren, friends, acquaintance. But if you 
cannot doubt this, you must needs acknowledge, “that 
a notable miracle hath been wrought,” then with what 
conscience, with what face, can you charge him whom 
God hath sent, “not to speak any more in his name.’ 


Apply this, to those pious females who think it 
their duty to call sinners to repentance. Let them 
be judged by this rule. Mr. Wesley knew. that it 
made no difference whether the servant of God who 
performed these miricles was male or female, This 
does not alter the facts. On this principle he answerd 
a certain person who said to him, “ Mr. Wesley, how 
is it, that you encourage certain females in preaching P? 
« Because (said he) God owns them in the conversion 
of sinners, and who am 1 that I should withstand God.’’ 


1t is worthy of remark that those females that are 


- most-active in the church, are in general those of the 


highest order in religious attainments, especially in 
communion with God, and conformity to him. If 
they did wrong in calling sinners to repentance, is it 
not strange, that the persons who live nearest to God, 
and are most like him, should be most guilty here? 
And is it not equally strange; that true repentance 
should never be afforded them; but as they draw 
nearer eternity, and as the prospect brightens before 
them into the eternal world, they should the more 
abundantly rejoice in what they have done. 


With respect to the impropriety of pious females 
addressing mixt. companies of men and women, there 
would be some weight in this objection, if we lived in 
a country, where women were secluded from the society 
of men, and where in their religious assemblies they 
worshiped God in separate apartments; but this 
argument amounts to nothing in a country where 
they always mix in society, and where females are 
allowed to address companies of men and women in 
the public theatres, markets, fields, and shops; and if

they are allowed to address the other sex in the way 
of trade and business, and to get money; surely, they 
may be allowed to address them, upon the subjects 
which regard the soul, and eternity ; provided they 
have piety, and the other qualifications suitable for the 
important work. 


As to the argument that the call of women to 
preach, must be a Quakers’ call, as it has been said; I 
would reply, that all the arguments which go to prove 
that women should only preach by immediate inspiration 
from heaven, will go to prove that men should preach 
only when so inspired. But providing we were to 
admit this, then the objection to their addressing mixt 
companies falls to the ground. For supposing a female 
to be inspired of God to prophesy or preach in his 
name, while sitting in a large congregation of men, 
and women, how is she to know, that what she has 
gotton to say, may not apply to the men equally with 
the women? Mr. Wesley in his Notes on 1 Cor. xiv. 
34, 35, allows that woman are to teach when inspired, 
but he does not so much as hint, that it was impro- 
per for them to address men, as well as women. ‘The 
Notes were written in the year 1753. It is very evident 
however, by his Letters, and subsequent conduct, that 
he entertained more favourable views on this subject 
afterwards. The Letters published in this volume 
were written in 1788, and 1790, about thirty-six or 
thirty-eight yeurs after he wrote the Notes. And his 
Letter to Miss Bosanquet, in which he approves of her 
call, was written June 13, 1771, about eighteen years 
after his Notes; and from these Letters, and his con- 
duct towards these, and uther female preachers, it is 
evident, that he fully approved of their conduct. 
More especially as it respects Miss Mallet, for he and 
the Brethren assembled with him in the Conference, 
held in Manchester, in the year 1787, designates, 
authorizes, and so to speak, ordains her as a preacher 
in his connexion. And if he thus approved of these

labours; and where the same doctrines are preached, 
and in a great measure, the same discipline enforced, 
as among the Wesleyan Methodists. 


I believe the ordinary call of God to the ministry 
is to men, and the extraordinary call to females. But 
in this extraordinary call I do not consider any female 
strictly and fully called to the pastoral office ; or to be 
the regular pastor of the Church of Christ, but I do 
believe that the Lord calls some females to be fellow- 
labourers with the pastors, or helpers, or as we shonld 
call them Local Preachers, and I think we should help, 
or encourage those women, who thus help us in the 
Gospel. Mr. Wesley did so; more especially during 
the latter part of his life. The great Apostle St. Paul 
did so,—and he wished others to encourage them too. 
Mr. Wesley “in his Letters to Miss Bosanquet, and to 
Mrs. Crosby, says “I think the strength of the cause 
rests here, in your having an extraordinary call ;” St. 
Paul’s ordinary rule was, “I permit not a woman to 
speak in the congregation, yet in extraordinary cases, 
he made a few exceptions at Corinth, in particular. 


From the pages of History. we learn that women 
have moved in the most exalted spheres, and achieved 
the most astonishing exploits. They have worn the crown 
of royalty, occupied the bench of civil magistracy, and 
and sat at the head of all ecelestiastical dignity. They 
have led victorious armies to the valley of decision, 
conducted them to the honours of conquest, and 
celebrated their triumphs in exalted strains of poetic 
eloquence. Women have been divinely inspired with 
the spirit of prophecy, and resided in the college of the 
prophets. They have signalized themselves by learn- 
ing and piety, and manefested as extensive capacites 
as persons of the other sex. Women have been called 
to publish the glad tidings of redeeming mercy, and 
through their instrumentality many have been brought 
to the enjoyment of divine regard. They have even 
been sent to instruct the the teachers of mankind, and

most important offices with propriety and honour ; 
and if in these last days the great Head of the Church 
has called a few of that sex, to warn sinners to “ flee 
from the wrath to come,” and to point them to “the 
Lamb of God that taketh away the sins of the world,” 
who are we that we should withstand God, or say unto 
him, what doest thou ?

x PREFACE. 


The opinion of another divine ; perhaps as learned 
and as pious, as any that ever wrote upon the Serip- 
tures, is found in the following comment upon Romans 
xvi, 12... ** Salute Triphkena and Tryphosa, who labour- 
ed in the Lord. Salute the beloved Persis, who labour- 
ed much in the Lord.’ “Two holy women, says he, 
« who were assistants to the apostle in’ his work, pro- 
babiy by exhorting, visiting the sick, &c. Persis was 
another woman, who it seems, excelled the preceding 5 
for of her it. issaid,; she laboured much in the Lord. 
We learn from this that Christian women, as well as 
men, laboured in the ministry of the word. In those 
times of simplicity, all persons, whether men, or 
women, who had received the knowledge of the truth, 
believed it to be their duty to propogate it to the utter- 
most of their power. Many have spent much useless 
labour in endeavouring to prove that these women did 
not preach. That there were some prophetesses, as 
well as prophets, in the Christian Church, we learn ; 
and that a woman might pray or prophesy, provided 
she had her head covered, we know ; and that whoever 
prophesied, spoke unto others to edification, exhorta- 
tion, and comfort, St. Paul declares, 1 Cor, xiv, 3. 
And that no preacher can do more, every person must 
acknowledge; because, to edify, exhort, and comfort, 
are the prime ends of the gospel ministry. If women 
thus prophesied, then women preached. There is 
however, much more than this implied in the chris- 
tian ministry ; of which men only, and men called of 
God, are capable? Dr. Adam Clarke. 


A Female ministry, in some extraordinary cases, is

of Miss Mallet, Miss Bosanquet, Mrs. Crosby, Mrs. 
Gilbert, Miss Barritt, and others, to call sinners to re- 
pentance ; and that they sinned not against God in 
so doing. And if God called them, surely he can, and 
perhaps he will, call others to the same work. All 
who admit this, will think with me that a female

ministry in extraordinary cases should be fully recog- 
nized and encouraged. 


To offer a little encouragement to such is my de- 
sign in publishing these Biographical Sketches,—and 
Ihave no doubt through the blessing of Almighty 
God, without which nothing is wise, nothing strong, 
this design will in- some decree, be. accomplished. 
Many a pious female whom God has called to active 
labour in his Church, will read her own experience in 
the convictions, deliverances, and success, of some 
character here recorded» And in this record of the heart 
and life, the views, and feelings, the experience and 
conduct, the labours and. success of those that have gone 
before them from tribulation to heaven, through. the 
cross to the crown, will find a powerful support in trial, 
and a stimulus to duty. I want neither honour, nor 
profit, but have written this chiefly to put honour 
upon, and to encourage those, whom God delighteth 
to honour, in making them his instruments in forward- 
ing and accomplishing his work, and glory in the 
world. 


Perhaps some may think I should not have brought 
into notice, any characters that are now living. I 
have been very sparing in this, but while public cha- 
racters are considered a kind of public property, and 
the subjects of public opinion, we must submit to the 
expression of that opinion, especially in this land of 
freedom, where, ministers of religion, and ministers of 
state; members of parliament, and even the King 
himself, are subject to this ordeal. It is hardly pos- 
sible to take up a catalogue of books, but living cha- 
racters are exhibited. Mr. Wesley was in the constant 
habit of publishing Biogragphical Sketches of the life, 
experience, and labours of the ministers in his con- 
nexion. He also published great numbers of those 
Letters of friendship, which he received from his nu- 
merous correspondents. His great object was useful- 
ness, and front whatever source this object could be

Mrs. SUSANNAH WESLEY,* 


«Tue mother of the late Mr. John Wesley, was the 
youngest daughter of Dr. Samuel Annesley, and a few 
years younger than her husband. Being educated in 
avery religious family, she early imbibed a reverence 
for religion; but having a strong understanding, and 


a E E R TE a a 


* The Character of Mrs. Wesley with which these Sketches 
commence, may appear to some to be out of place; as she gene- 
rally read tothe people, her call to minister in holy things, 
will perhaps on that ground be disputed. But who will take upon 
him to affirm, that none who read their sermons are divinely 
called to the sacred office. Ifsinners are awakened and converted 
to God through their instrumentality ; itis, at least, a presump- 
tive evidence that the Almighty approves of their labours of love, 
and though they may not be so ewfensively useful as those who 
preach extempore, yet they are doing something towards helping 
on the Ark of the Lord. Hence I have been induced to place 
Mrs. Wesley amongst these female preachers, more especially as 
Mr. Wesiey says of her, “ that even she, as well as her Father and 
Grand-father, her Husband and three Sons, had been, in her 


measure a preacher of righteousness,” and T feel a peculiar pleasure ` 


in having such a character at the head of my little work.— Ep.

« About the year 1700, she made a resolution to 
spend one hour, morning and evening, in private de- 
votion, in prayer and meditation, and she religiously 
kept it ever after, unless sickness hindered, or some 
absolutely necessary business of her family obliged her 
to shorten the time. If opportunity offered, she spent 
some timeat noon in this religious and profitable emi- 
ployment. She generally wrote ‘down her thoughts 
on different subjects at these times, and great numbers 
of her meditations have been preserved in her own 
hand-writing. We shall select afew, because they 
shew us this excellent woman in her most private re- 
tirement, conversing without disguise with him who 
knows the heart.

« Mr. Wesley observes of his mother, that even she, 
as well as her father and grand-father, her husband and 
three sons, had beenin her measure, a preacher of righte- 
ousness. And this is a remarkable circumstance in

Her husband usually attended the sittings of convo- 
cation ; and on these occasions was obliged to reside 
in London, for a length of time that was often injuri- 
ous to his parish ; and at an expense that was incon- 
venient to himself and his family. It was on this 
business, it appears, that he spent so much time in 
London in the beginning of the year 1712. During his 
absence, Mrs. Wesley formed a little meeting at her 
house on a Sunday evening, when she read a sermon, 
prayed, and conversed with the people who came for 
this purpose. She acquainted her husband of their 
meeting, who, on account of the newness and singu- 
larity of the thing, made some objections against it. 
Her answer is dated the 6th of February, 1712, in 
which she says, “ I heartily thank you for dealing so 
plainly and faithfully with me, in a matter of no com- 
mon concern. The main of ‘your objections against 
our Sunday evening meetings, are, first, that it will 
look particular; secondly, my sex; and lastly, your 
being at present in a public station and character; to 
all which I shall answer briefly,

so does almost every thing that is serious, or that may 
in any degree advance the glory of God, or the salva- 
tion of souls, if it be performed out of a pulpit, or in 
the way of common conversation ; because in our cor- 
rupt age, the utmost care and diligence. have been used 
to banish all discourse of God, or spiritual concerns, 
out of society ; as if religion were neyer to appear out

much as, of professing ourselves to be Christians. 
eieko yaur second, I reply, that, as I am a woman, 
so I am also mistress of a large family. And though 
the superior churge of the souls contained in it lies 
upon you, as head of the family, and as their minister, 
yet in your absence I cannot but look upon every soul 
you leave under my care, as a talent committed to me 
under atrust, by the great Lord of all the families of 
heaven and earth; and if I am unfaithful to him or to 
you, in neglecting to improve these talents, how shall 
Lanswer unto him, when he shall command me to 
render.an account of my stewardship. ; 

« As these, and other such like thoughts, made me 
at first take a more than urdinary care of the souls of 
my children and servants; so knowing that our most 
holy religion requires a strict observation of the Lord’s 
day, and not thinking that we fully answered the end

likewise we were obliged to fill up the intermediate 
spaces of that sacred time by other acts of piety and 
devotion ;*I thought it my daty to spend some part. of 
the day in reading to, and instructing my family 5 
especially in your absence, when, having no afternoon 
service, we have so much Jeisure for such exercises ; 
and such time I esteemed spent in a way more accept- 
able to God, than if I had retired to my own private 
devotions.

« With those few neighbours who then came to me, 
I discoursed more freely and affectionately than before; 
I chose the best and most awakening sermons we had, 
and I spent more time with them in such exercises. 
Since this, our company has increased every night; 
for I dare deny none who ask admittance. Last 

Sunday I believe we had above two hundred, and yet 
many went away for want of room. 

«c Your third objection I leave to be answered by your 
own judgment. We meet not upon any worldly design. 
We banish all temporal concerns from our society ; 
none is suffered to mingle any discourse about them 
with our reading or singing: we keep close to the 

_ business of the day, and as soon as it is over they all 
go home. And where is the harm of this? If I and 
my children went a visiting on Sunday nights, or if we 
admitted of impertinent visits, as too many do who 
think themselves good Christians, perhaps it would be 
thought no scandalous practice, though in truth it 
‘would be so; therefore why any should reflect upon 
you, let your station be what it will, because your wife 
‘endeavours to draw people to church, and to restrain 
them by reading and other persuasions, from their 
profanation of God’s most holy day, I cannot conceive. 
But if any should be so mad as to do it, I wish you 
would not regard it. For my part, I value no censure 
on this account: I have long since shook hands with 
the world, and I heartily wish I had never given theim 
more reason to speak against me.” 

Mrs. Wesley continued to discharge the duties of a 
wife and parent with the greatest diligence and punc- 
tuality. The letters she wrote to her sons when at 
Oxford, and after they left it, shew her in the most 
amiable light, both for knowledge and piety. ln 1735, 
she lost her husband, and afterwards divided her time 
between her children, till about the year 1739; after 
which, she resided chiefly in London.

Mr. Wesley gives the following account of his 
mother’s death':* «I left Bristol, in the evening of 
Sunday the 18th, (July, 1742,) and on Tuesday came 
to London. 1 found my mother on the borders of 
eternity. But she had no doubt or fear; nor any de- 
sire, but as soon as God should call; to depart and be 
with Christ. t 

« Friday, the 23d, about three in the afternoon, I 
went to my mother, and found her change was near. 
She was in her last conflict, unable to speak, but, 1 
believe, quite sensible. Her look was calm and serene, 
and her eyes fixed upward, while we commended her 
soul to God. From three to four, the silver cord was 
loosing, and the wheel breaking at the cistern ; and 
then, without any struggle, or sigh, or groan, the soul 
was set at liberty! We stood round the bed, and ful- 
filled her last request, uttered a little before she lost 
her speech ; ‘ Children as soon as l am released, sing 
a psalm of praise to God? 

«Sanday, August Ist. Almost an innumerable 
company of people being gathered together, about five 
in the afternoon, I committed to the earth the body of 
my mother, to sleep with her fathers. The portion of 
scripture from which 1 afterwards spoke, was, “ T saw 
a great white throne and him that sat on it; from whose 
face the earth and the heaven fled away, and there was 
found no place for them. And I saw the dead, small and 
great, standing before God, and the books were opened ; 
and the dead were judged out of those things which were 
written in the hooks, according to their works.” Tt was 
one of the most solemn assemblies I ever saw, or ex- 
pect to see on this side eternity. 

« We set up a plain stone at the head of her grave, 
inscribed with the following words :— 

«Here lies the body of Mrs. Susannah Wesley, the 
youngest and last surviving daughter of Dr. Sam. 
Annesley.

With Christian love to your partner,

Your affectionate Sister in the Lord, 


MARY FLETCHER.” 


This cminent female preacher, was born Sept. 1, 
1739, at Laytonstone, in Essex. At five years of age, 
she was powerfully wrought upon by the Holy Spirit 
of God, and much concerned about finding out and 
walking in the way to Heaven. When she was be- 
tween seven and eight years of age, she appears to have 
possessed saving faith, and to have “ tasted of the 
powers of the world to come.” Mrs. Le Fevre, was of 
great use to her, aud also a religious servant they had 
in the family. When about sixteen, she had a heavy 
cross to take up. Being brought up in high life, in all 
the gaities, and amusements of the fashionable world 
which she saw were sinful, and being determined by 
divine grace to renounce them altogether, and form her 
life by the written word of God, when requested by. her 
Father to go to the Play, she begged to be left at home, 
and laid open her whole mind to Him on this subject. 
At twenty-two, she was cast out of her Father’s kouse, 
and took Lodgings in London. In the year 1761 and 
1762, a great revival in the Methodist Society, in 
London, (of which she was a member,) took place. 
A wonderful outpouring of the Spirit of God upon 
both preachers and people was experienced, and many 
simple persons both men and women, as she informs us, 
were lively arbingers of, the approaching pentecost, 
and cried aloud, ‘ the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.” 
When about twenty-three years of age, she removed 
to Laytonstone, toa house of her own. Here she began 


to exhort, and to read, and expound the scriptures. 


About 1768, she removed into Yorkshire. 

In the year 1771, she wrote a long Letter to Mr. 
Wesley, dated Cross-Hall, near Leeds, of which the 
following is a short extract :— 


22 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Very dear and honoured Sir, 


Various bave been my bindrances in writing, 
but none sufficient to have kept me so long silent to 
you, had L not been at a loss on one particular subject. 
I want your advice and direction in an important point, 
and to know if you approve my light in it. 

When we first settled at Laytonstone, sister Ryan 
and I began with little kind of prayer meetings, &c. 
and they were productive of a blessing. Afterwards 
on coming into Yorkshire, sister Crosby and I did 
the same. God was with us, and made it known by 
the effects in many places—but several object to this : 

First Objection. 2 Tim. ii, 12. “ Let the women 
learn in silence,’ &e. I understand that text to mean 
no more than that a woman shall not take authority 
over her husband, but be in subjection, neither shall 
she teach at all by usurping authority, she shall not 
meddle with church discipline, neither order nor regu- 
late any thing in which men are concerned in the matters 
of the church; but I do not apprehend it means she 
shall not entreat sinners to come to Jesus, nor say, 
« Come and I will tell you what God hath done for 
my soul,” 

Sccond Objection. Nay, but the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 
xiv. 34, “ Let your women keep silence,” &c. I answer 
was not that spoke in reference to a time of dispute 
and contention? So that his saying, “ they are not 
permitted to speak,” here seems to me to imply no 
no more than the other, she is not to meddle with 
Church government. 

Third Objection. Nay, but it means literally not to 
speak by way of edification, while in the church, or 
company of promiscuous worshippers. Answer, Then 
why is it said, 1 Cor. xi. 5, “ Every woman that prayeth 
or prophesicth with her head uncovered, dishonoureth her 
head.” Can she prophesy without a peters | ? or ought 
she to speak, but not to edification ! 

Fourth Oljection. She may now and then, if under 
a peculiar impulse, but never else. Answer. But 
how often is she to feel this impulse? Perhaps you

will say, two or three times in her life. Perhaps 
God will say, two or three times in a week, or day ; and 
where shall we find the rule fur this ? 

Fifth Objection, But it is inconsistent with that 
modesty the Christian religion requires in women pro- 
fessing godliness, Answer. It may be and is, painful 
to it, but I do not see it inconsistent with it; and that 
for this reason, does not Christian modesty stand in 
these two particulars—purity and humility. First, I 
apprehend it consists in cutting off every act, word, and 
thought, which in the least infringes on the purity 
Ged delights in.—Second, In cutting off every act, 
word, and thought, which in the least infringes on 
humility; knowing throughly our own place, and 
tendering to every one their due ; endeavouring to be 
little, and unknown, as far as the order of God will 
permit, and simply following that order, leaving the 
the event to God. Now I do not apprehend Mary sin- 


ned againrt either of these heads, or could in the least . 


be accused of tmmodesty, when she carried the joyful 
news of the LORD’s resurrection, and in that sense 
taught the teachers of mankind. Neither was the 
woman of Samaria to be accused of immodesty, when 
she invited the whole city to come to CHRIST. 
Neither do I think the women mentioned 2 Sam. 
xx, could be said to sin against modesty, though she 
called to the general of the opposite army to converse 
with her, and then went to all the people to give them 
her advice, and by it the city was saved. Neither do 
1 suppose Deborah did wrong in publicly declaring the

Letter from Mrs. Fletcher to Mr. and Mrs. Taft. 


« Madeley, Oct. 30, 1809. 
My dear Friends, 


I am thankful you are so agreeably settled, and 
that all the difficulty you feared has so well passed 
over. For my part, I never had much uneasiness 
about it,—if it were not of God I was very willing to 
give it up; and if it were, I well knew what is of God 
shall stand, ner can men or devils overrule his designs. 
My health is at present tolerably well, but last 
winter I was confined some weeks. All is right 
that our dear Father sees good to order, and if 
his Providence should choose to bring you back 
this way, l shall be glad to see and hear you both, 
if able to go out of the house. O what gracious pri- 
viliges hath the adorable Jesus purchased for us! 
How is it we can let one thought be careless and dull 
in seeking after him? Lord enable us not only to 
creep, but to run our race; throwing away. every 
weight, and constantly sinking deeper into God. 

` May all the blessings of the new covenant rest on 
you and yours. wi 
Lamy, „ai 


Your affectionate Friend and Sister, 


MARY FLETCHER.” |

and that the smile of the Almighty hath been on your 
endeavours since. When you were here, the light of 
God shone on you both. ‘The Sermon Mr. Taft preach-

-ed in my room, was blest to a great many, and while

case, I am in the pit and must be brought out, or T shall

and grow deeper. A man also seems to have felt anew, 
from the time when Mrs. Taft was speaking at Coal-

come forward, and some fresh ones have been called 
within these three or four weeks; I trast they will 
stand, and some are sinking deeper into God. 

If we live till next summer, we shall be glad to see 
you. You know we have one bed at your service, 
devoted to the preachers of the gospel, and I trust and 
doubt not but the Lord will be with you. I have 
reason to praise the Lord, my health has been very 
tolerable this summer, and though we have had a good 
deal of fatigue, both Miss Tooth and myself have been 
comfortably brought through. Poor Mr. Furness is 


in a trying situation, his wife came with him ten days 


ago, as far as the Dale, where she was seized with a 
very painful disorder. She is confined to her bed, 
unable to stir or to be moved without very great pain; 
we found her much on our minds in prayer, join us in 
her behalf. O how well it is for us to have a wise and 
tender. Father to rely upon, yes, infinite wisdom, and in- 
finite power are boih engaged on our side, then let us 
rejoice evermore, for final salvation is nearer than when 
we first believed. : Just now I have a glimpse of such a 
great and mighty salvation purchased for us, as I cannot 
express. O for faith and heavenly vigour to stretch 
after all the fulness of God. Lord enlarge our hearts, 
and fill them with thyself. The two Miss Tooths, 
and many others, desire to be remembered to you 
both, wishing you every blessing for time and eternity. 


I remain, my dear Friends, 


Your affectionate Sister in Jesus, 


M. FLETCHER.”

From the same to Mrs. Taft. 


« Madeley, June 3, 1811. — 


My dear Sister, 


We were thankful to hear from you, and that 
the Lord appeared in your behalf, and gave you success. 
And may you still be owned and preserved under the 
shadow of the Almighty. The account you give of 
your daughter’s sight and dream is particular; but 
your mother, I doubt not, knew all about you before 
she told her of . We are surrounded with the 
innumerable company, ‘‘ Millions of heavenly creatures 
walk the earth unseen, both when we wake and when 
we sleep ;”? and he hath given bis Angels charge con- 
cerning us, to keep us in all our ways. It seems the 
Lord sees good to try his children in the furnace, for 
you are permitted many exercises by the illness of that 
child; but this is our comfort, all shall work together 
for good; we are safe in the hand of our Almighty Redee- 
mer. We have cause to praise God, several have-of late 
been brought in. Some young people, in whom there is a 
wonderful change indeed; and a few have received an 
inheritance in the rest of peace and love. I see eternity 
is near, and feel the importance of the present moment ; 
blessed be God, faith grows stronger, and I think I 
may say, divine unction doth increase. O for a deeper 
draught of the pure fountain. My health is tolerable, 
1 am enabled to keep with the dear people, though in 
much weakness. Miss Tooth has her heart in the 
work more and more, and desires her kind remem- 
brance to you both. 


l am, 
Your affectionate Friend and Sister in the Lord,

The following short account of the closing scene of 
this mother in our Israel is taken from Miss Tooth’s 
letter to the inhabitants of Madeley and its vicinity. 

« Knowing that it is your desire to hear something 
respecting the close of the life of my invaluable friend 
Mrs. Fletcher, now in glory, and being assured that 
none but myself can undertake the work, as I alone 
was her constant companion, being separated scarcely 
a day, for more than fifteen years, I have endeavoured 
to set down a few circumstances relative to the close 
of alife surpassing in usefulness most of her fellow- mor- 
tals. For the last month of her life, her breath was more 


- oppressed than usual: it had been much affected 


for years, upon motion ; yet when she sat still or laid 


herself down at night, she could breath quite easy; but 


the-middle of November last, her breathing was affect- 
ed both while she sat still and when she was laid down. 
She had also a troublesome cough, that disturbed her 
rest at night ; and when this was the case. her strength 
quickly declined. Yet with all that she-went through, 
how did she labour for the good of souls! Many 
times she has gone to speak to the people, when she 
has said, “ It is like as if every meeting would take 
away my life, but Pll speak to them as long as I can ; 
while ve any breath, and power to get out, Ill not 
spare myself.’ And truly she did not. as will be 
readily testified by many hundreds who have been in 
the habit of attending her meetings. 

‘«-T aminclinedto think the24th of last July will not be 
forgotten by a large proportion of the great numbers 
who crowded to hear her: she explained the twenty- 
fifth chapter of Matthew’s Gospel. It was the last 
Monday night she was able to speak to a listening 
crowd of attentive hearers, some of whom had come 
many miles, but did not think much of the pains they 
took, because of the Spiritual good they derived from 
the opportunity. I remember she spoke in a peculiar- 
ly striking manner on the necessity of being born again. 
When she came to the thirteenth verse, “‘ Watch there- 


32 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


fore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein 
the Son of Man cometh,” and from the following verses. 
respecting the talents, she enlarged much ; powerfully 
insisting upon the right use of the understanding, will, 
mind, or memory, with every affection ; the right ap- 
plication of time, with every penny of money ; and the 
watching over the tongue, which she observed might 
enjoy the honour of being God’s advocate, but for 
want of watchfulness was, as the Apostle expresses it, 
«set on fire of hell.” 

«But it is in vain for me to attempt to repeat any 
part of what at that time was felt in many hearts; she 
continued to meet her classes occassionally, as she had 
strength for it, until the middle of October. Her two 
o'clock sabbath-day meeting she spoke at on the last 
sabbath of September: this was her last public engage- 
ment. 
` « Many striking proofs we have had that her labours 
of love in this way were not in vain, for it is certain 
many souls were brought to God through her.— Some 
circumstances occurring last summer, which brought 
to her recollection afresh, the solemn season of the 
opening of the room, (the Vickerage barn,) twenty- 
seven years before, she took the paper, (read on that 
occasion,) and read it to the people; and there is good 
reason to believe, that our heavenly Father was pleased 
to make this also, such a season of refreshing to some 
then present, that they will ever remember ib with 
gratitude; indeed, all her labours of love were, in a 
peculiar manner, blest of God. Six years after the 
opening of her room, the old Charch was taken down, 
and the Church Service was performed in it, till t 
new one was erected. 

«« Amongst the numerous company that will have to 
ascribe glory to our God, for the good received through 
her instrumentality under that roof, I cannot forbear 
saying, my hope is, that I shall stand among the ran- 
somed of the Lord, and say, “I was born there.’’ 
Yes, my friends, 1 must say, the good Lord, made her. 


HOLY WOMEN. 33 


the means of the awakening, conversion, and deepening 
the work of grace in my soul: and while I give all the 
glory to my God for the grace received, I cannot but 
feel much love to the channel through which* that 
grace was communicated. Nor are my feelings in this 
peculiar, they are the feelings of a number of lively. 
souls, who bless God that the sound of her voice ever 
reached their ears; and in whose affections she will 
long live, and though dead, yet speak. Thus did she 
whether sick or well labour for the increase of spirituality 
in the hearts of the people: her eyes were always heaven- 
ward, and whether at home or abroad, she was ever 
endeavouring to draw souls to a closer walk with God. 
She was often reminding us who were about her, of 
the fulness that was to be obtained. I shall not 
exceed the truth, If I say that none more fully 
possessed the happy art of leading souls into a 
close internal walk with God, than she did; being 
hérself so experimentally acquainted with the path of 
righteousness, she was well qualified to conduct others 
therein: and as to her own soul, she was contiually 
drinking more and more into the spirit of her Lord. 
Her capacious soul was always panting after deeper 
and deeper draughts of the living water,—and whatever 
duty she enforced upon the’ minds of others, she was 
exemplary in practising herself. It was always her 
custom, (unless some providential call prevented,) to 
go from secret prayer to the class, and from the class 
to prayer: thus did she habitually draw fresh supplies 
of light and life from above ; and when the seed was sown, 
her unwearied supplications followed it. Indeed she was 
a great lover of prayer, and often continued in that exer- 
cise on her knees for such a length of timc, (while her 
streneth would admit of it,) that I have sametimes 
gone into her chamber to remind her how long she 
had been, fearing she would injure her body ; but on 
such occassions she has sweetly smiled and said, “1 shall 
be none the worse for prayer; come, kneel down by me, 
and let us pray together.” At another of these times, 


34 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF — 


she has said, “ No, not leave off praying yet; my dear 
husband used to say, let me wrestle till I die. can’t 
leave off yet, but come and join me ; great things are 
promised where two agree to ask in the name of Jesus.” 
Many of these times have become seasons of peculiar 
advantage: my soul has eause to praise the Lord both 
for her private, social, and public exercises. —One day, 
I think the 6th of December, when waking out of a 
doze, she said, “ I am drawing near to glory y? and 
soon after, “ there is my house and portion fair ;? and” 
again, ‘ Jesus come, my hope of glory :” and, after a 
short pause, “ He lifts his hands, and shews that I am 
graven there.” On the 7th of December, taking my 
hand in her’s, she said, “ My precious, my invaluable 
friend, I have prayed that light and wisdom may guide — 
you in all, in every difficulty and it will be so, I know 
it will; my prayer for thee is heard, my choice friend.” 
The day following, the Sth, was as the day before, a 
day of praise for fulness of blessing.—All this day her 
breathing was exceedingly difficult : but through all, 
her mouth was full of the loving kindness of the Lord. 
We always prayed together before we went into the 
chamber, her breath being so greatly oppressed ; she 
prayed very sweetly, but short, and then said, “ Now 
you call upon the Lord; I can enjoy your. prayer, 
though not able to speak;” 1 did so, and found an 
uncommon degree of liberty, while pleading the graci- 
ous promises made to the people of God. When I had 
ended, she said it had been to her soul a peculiar 
time of enjoyment, while I was calling upon the Lord; 
and concluded saying, “O this has done me good,” 
When we were ready to go into the chamber, and it 
was after ten, I got her into the chair, but she was now 
weaker than at noon; however, I wheeled her to the 
bed side, and could not but look upon her as dying; 
and indeed so she considered herself, for when got into 
bed, she said, ‘My love, this is the last time I shall 
get into bed; it has been hard work to get in, but it is 
work J shall do no more; this oppression upon my

‘increasing his work among you. May his rich blessing 
be poured on you both, and many, very many souls be 
given to your labours. ‘There are several here who do 
remember you with love, We have cause to praise 
the Lord, fresh ones are frequently added, and several 
have been blest; but I have not strength to write 
many particulars, as writing affects my head: but, one 
circumstance I will name,—an old man, who met a 
little time with me in the meeting on Tuesday night, 
appeared very sincere, though always rather cast down; 
afterwards he joined Coalport class, but working almost 
night and day, he could seldom attend, and hada 
carnal persecuting wife; the other day Miss Tooth 
heard he was ill, and desired brother M. to call upon 
him, he found him very full of pain, and very earnest 
for his soul, the poor man cried out, “O if I had 
but such a hope as John had, (his son who lately died) 
‘IT would not mind all my pain;” B. M. replied, «why 


you may have it, Jesus isa thousand times more ready , 


to bless you, than you are to be blest, expect it now;”’ 
that word struck him much, and he left him encour- 
aged : next day he went again, and found him happy ; 
he said, “ after you were gone, as I lay on this bed in 
prayer, my wife being below, I heard the most delight- 
ful music, such as I never heard before! I looked up, 
and saw a most glorious place, with many appearances 
so beautiful as you cannot conceive.” 

Another answer to prayer we have had, a very wick- 
ed young man brought in, and died happy—he saw

My dear Friends, 


Your letter gave me pleasure to hear how the 
Lord had favoured and prospered you, and that your 
brother and you, and your children were yet in health. 
Should you by the order of our divine Master, be 
thrown this way once more, I shall be glad to see you. 
Our time is short, and eternity appears to me very near ; 
though at present Lam better than I have been for 
some time. ‘The work of the Lord I trust goes on, 
but we have been stripped of some of our dear people, 
for the trade here is much interrupted, and some are 
forced to seek it elsewhere; yet, «the wall is built in 
those troublesome times,” and I have no doubt, but 
all will work together for good. Blessed be the Lord, 
Į feel his presence draws nearer and nearer! O fora full 
plunge into God; the promises seem to me of late, to 
rest on such a sure foundation, as is a great help.to 
faith. It is just now applied to my heart, “If thou 
canst believe, all things are possible to him that 
believeth ;” in short, the constant look brings all; 
«he that seeth him, sinneth not; he that sinneth, 
sees him not.” Nothing can be more strong and 
clear, while we look we are kept, while we abide in 
our centre, as the snail in her shell, we rest secure:

The words of Mr. Henry Moore, the Biographer of 
‘this extraordinary character, are so excellent, and so 
fully accord with my views on this subject, that I 
cannot forbear reciting them :— 

«The question of the lawfulness, or even of the 
expediency of Female Preaching, will recur to every 
_ sensible and pious reader.—But I cannot but think 
» that much that has been said on this question, especi- 
ally since the days of George Fox, (when the ministry 
-of Females received a regular establishment in his 
community,) may be spared on this occassion. Mrs. 
Fletcher has spoken on this subject, (see page 110) 
and every candid reader has, I believe felt the modesty, 
E2 


40 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


and simplicity of that short statement. In truth her 
preaching was but an enlargement of her daily and 
hourly conversation. Her family—her visitors, might 
be said to be her constant congregation. And as she 
never, in her more public efforts, meddled with the 
_ government of the church,—usurped authority over the 
man, or made any display of a regular authorita- 
tive commission, but merely strove to win souls, by 
pureness, by knowledge, by long-suffering, by kindness, 
by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned, by the word of 
truth, by the power of God ;—while she was herself 
the least, and the servant of all: may not every pious 
Churchman and Methodist unite and say, “ Would to 
God that all the Lord’s people were such Prophets and 
Prophetesses”’? Amen. * Another writer gives the 
following character of Mrs. Fletcher, “She was alto- 
gether an extraordinary person; endowed with a strong 
understanding, great decision of character, and simpli- 
city of mind, heroic zeal, and unbounded benevolence ; 
in the Apostolic age, she would have been a Priscilla, 
and have taken her rank among the Presbyteresses, 
or female confessors of the primitive church. She _ 
had all the spirit of a Martyr. Had she been born 
within the Romish communion, she would probably 
have been enrolled among the Saints of the Calendar. 
In this country, the community to which she attached 
herself, alone afforded a sphere suited to the energies 
of her character, which might otherwise have remained 
dormant, because, under ordinary circumstances, zeal 
such as hers could hardly have been developed. 
Among Prostestants, enthusiasm like hers is apt to be 
regarded as the worst of heresies.” (Burder’s Memoirs 
of Pious Women, vol. iii, page 366.)

Miss SARAH LAWRENCE, 


: (The adopted daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Fletcher.) 


- For an account of this very excellent and useful 
person, I refer to a little tract written by Mrs. Fletcher 
and published and sold at the Methodist Book-room, 
price threepence. 

In this account (and for very obvious reasons) Mrs. 
Fletcher kept back what chiefly related to the public 
ministry of this excellent woman, nevertheless, she 


bears ample testimony in this memoir, and in the jour-, 


nal of her own life, that God abundantly owned the 
piety, zeal, faith, prayer, and labours of Sarah Law- 
rance. A few extracts from Mrs. Fletcher’s account 
shall compose this character. 

« Sarah Lawrence was the neice of my friend Sarah 
Ryan. Providence cast her into our hands, when 
a little child... As she increased in reason, we observed 
aremarkably upright, obedient spirit in her, and a 
great attachment to us. When very young, she would 
often ery to the Lord, with great earnestness, that she 
might never be separated from me. Before she was 
eight years old, she was often under strong convictions 
of sin. When she was about ten years of age, she found 
a strong desire to be devoted to God ; and when she 
heard us read in the family, of the sufferings of our 
Lord, or of the martyrs, it would kindle in her Lreast 
an intense desire to suffer something for Him who had 
borne so much for her; and she used to do many 
actions, according to her childish idea, to satisfy that 
desire—such as tying her hands behind her all night,

Here I did indeed see the spirit of my dear Mr. Fletcher 
seem to reston her; and like him, she begun a meet- 
ing in a very hardened part of the parish with a bell in 
her hand. 

Madeley Town is a hardened spot; I do not know 
that I ever found more discouragement in speaking 
any where than there; and she was brought to shed 
tears over them many times, when going from door 
to door she entreated them to come, and in return met 
with only reproach and rudeness. But that was no- 
thing to her, who sought no honour but from God. 
Sometimes Satan would represent, how ridiculous she 
appeared in their eyes; and when carnal strangers 
passed by in carriages, &c. that they would think her 
mad. But as these means she knew had been instru- 
mental in calling some, and had been blest to many, 
as well as prevented much sin, she rejoiced to have 
the honour of being thought a fool for Christ. And 
such an intense love did she feel towards them, at the 
very time they were ridiculing her, that she has told 
me, “ It seemed, she could with pleasure, submit to 
be bound to a stake and burned, if it might but draw 
these souls to choose the way of life.” 

One night passing by a public house, where they 
were dancing, she looked to the Lord for power, and 
going in among them, began to plead for them, and 
in a very moving tender manner, to express the love 
and concern she felt for their souls. And glory be to 
God, we have some in Heaven who dated their first 
conviction from that hour. Indeed her whole soul 
seemed to be drawn out after the salvation of all 
around her. She began meetings in different places, 
on which numbers attended. Her method was, after 
singing and prayer, to read some life, experience, or 
some awakening author, stopping now and then, to 
explain and apply it as the Lord gave her utterance. 
And several, who are now lively believers in our connex- 
ion, were brought in through that means. But in every 
step, she enquired of the Lord, fearing much to take 
one out of his order. She has mentioned to me a

HOLY WOMEN 


Mrs. ANN GILBERT, 
(Aunt to William Carne, Esquire.) 


Has been a very distinguished woman. Her 
piety was of a most meek and amiable kind. She was 
a class leader at Gwinear, near Redruth, in Corn- 
wall, and usually paid an annual visit to the prin- 
cipal towns in Cornwall West. She had a most per- 
suasive and engaging address, and was sure in the end 
to bring tears from the greater part of her auditors. 
It appears that the Lord ordained this eminent female 
to the work of the ministry in the year 1771. And it 
is a fact that she was favoured with many seals to her 
ministry. Once she consulted Mr. Wesley on the 
subject of her labouring in public. He gave her his 
hand after hearing her statement, and said “Sister do 
all the good you can? Her experience is printed in 
the Methodist Magazine for 1795, page 42. It was 
written by Mr. Joseph Sutcliffe, and recommended 
by Mr. Taylor, who had long known her, She 
appears to have been awakened in the year 1743 when 
but a child, under the preaching of Mr. Williams, one 
of the first itnerant preachers who visited Cornwall ; a 
man-whose ministry abounded with seals. The con- 
victions she then received were partially lost. In the 
year 1760, the preachers visited the parish where she 
lived, she again heard the word, her former convictions 
returned, and she soon found the pearl of great price. 
Some time after, when in her class she received the 
perfect love of God, and she seems to have lived in the 
enjoyment of this liberty, for some time before she 
heard a single sermon on tbe subject of christian per- 
fection. She writes “One blessed fruit of the work 
which God had wrought in me, was more than usual

concern for the salvation of poor sinners. T would 
have done and suffered any thing on their account, if 
I might have been the instrument of their conversion. 
I have poured out my soul both'in public and private 
on their behalf. In the year 1771 going one day to 
preaching in the adjoining village, the preacher hap- 
pened not to come; I therefore gave out a hymn and 
went to prayer according to. my usual custom ; I then 
told the people they need not be disappointed, for the 
Lord was present to bless them. Immediately I re- 
ceived such a manifestation of the love and power of 
God, that I was constrained to entreat and beseech 
hem to repent and turn to the Lord, All the people 
were melted into tears, and many were convinced of 
sin, some of whom continue steadfast to this day. I 
endeavoured to the utmost of my power to be diligent 
in every duty, both public and private, especially meet- 
ing my classes, visiting the sick, and attending the 
prayer-meetings. One Sunday I found my mind 
much pressed to go and meet afew back-sliders who 
had lately been joined in class at a neighbouring 
village. When I got into the meeting, the leader was 
reproving some young people for indecent behaviour, 
lie desired me to give out a hymn and go to prayer, 
which raving done, I admonished the young people, 
and while I was speaking to them, was so filled with 
the peace and love of God, that I could not Lut exhort 
and entreat them to repent. Presently their laughter 
was turned into weeping, and one person who had 
been a backslider fer twenty-three years, cried aloud 
for the disquictude of her soul, and the Lord healed her 
wounded mind before the conclusion of the meeting. 
These tokens for good so encouraged me, that I pro- 
mised the Lord, if he would give me strength, to use 
it to his glory; and blessed be his name, he has 
enabled me to continue to the present day. He gave 
me abundance of satisfaction, first, by restoring my 
health in a wonderful and unexpected manner ; second, 
by deepening his work in my soul; and third, by 
owning my poor labours in the conversion of many

sinners, [tis now about twenty-five years since I found 
the abiding Comforter. I do not know that I have 
lost the divine consolations for a single moment all 
this time; and although I have had abundance of 
temptations and sufferings, being deprived of many of 
my children by death, and exercised with various 
worldly trials and losses, yet in all these I have been 
so preserved, that the enemy has never been able to 
rob me of my confidence or comfort. I have always 
enjoyed a constant heaven; being enabled to rejoice 
_ evermore, to pray without ceasing, and in every thing

I live but a moment at a time, and that moment,— 
for eternity. But I cannot express in words what I 
enjoy ; for there is only a thin veil between Heaven 
and my soul; yet I never wanted Christ more than I 
donow. My strength is perfect weekness; and glory 
be to his name, I find him covering my infirmities, and 
presenting me blameless to his Father every moment.’

Mrs. BATHSHEBA HALL, 


OF the city of York, was one of the most eminent 
women of her time. She sought the truth, doing the 
will of the Father. She became famed for piety with- 
out intention or design. Possessed of a small fortune, 
she could devote all her leisure to religion, which was 
the warmest delight of her soul, She being thus de-. 
voted to God, and constantly attending the chureh, 
became acquainted with Mr. Nelson, Prebendary of 
Ripon, who had received much evangelical light from 
reading John Arndt’s True Christianity. When Mr. 
Wesley came to York, she presently embraced Metho- 
dism, but before that time ske had commenced the 
work of prayer, and of expounding the Holy Scriptures 
twice a week, as appears from Mr. Sutcliffe’s life of 
Mrs. Pawson. This she continued after she became a 
Methodist, and was often visited by Quaker ladies, and 
had good ministers of the Church when she could get 
them to take a breakfast with her, Mrs. Frances 
Pawson was among the many who received edification 
and comfort from her prayers and expositions. With 
Mr. Wesley she often corresponded, and her best letters 
are given in the earlier volumes of the Magazines. 


Miss GRACE REED, 


Was born at Holwell, in the parish of Buckland- 
Brewer, in the county of Devon, Sept. 30, 1802. She 


HOLY WOMEN. 53 


appears to have been naturally modest, industrious, 
and steady, conducting herself generally with propriety. 
But like all others of the human family fallen from 
God; she had a deceitful heart, which led her to seck 
happiness in the vanities of the world, Her parents 
being members of the established Church, endeavoured 
to bring up their children in the regular attendance 
upon its ordinances, and forms of religion. This ex- 
cellent young woman appears to have been brought 
to repentance and faith in Christ, through the instru- 
mentality of the Arminian Bible Christians, when 
about thirteen or fourteen years of age. “ November 
24, it pleased the Lord to work more powerfully upon 
her mind; and that night she felt the clear witness 
that God for Christ’s sake, had forgiven all her sins. 
There was a prayer-meeting held at her father’s house: 
‘atime which will be remembered by the family, to all 
eternity. When the prayer-meeting was concluded 
and the congregation was about to withdraw, her eld- 
est sister, who had for some time been seeking the 
Lord, began to feel very great distress of mind, and 
the friends were desired to pray again on her behalf. 
They began to pray again, and in a short time, the 
Lord began to work upon the congregation, insomuch 
that many were constrained to cry aloud for mercy ; 
and several professed to obtain peace with Goi, 
through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Grace ; joined that 
community and became an ornament to her christian 
profession, adorning the doctrine of God her Saviour 
in all things. Soon after she obtained a clear sense 
of the divine favour, she saw it her privilege to be 
cleansed from all unrighteousness. She sought this 
inestimable christian privilege with all diligence, and 
she did not seek’it in vain. She appears never to 
have lost the direct witness of this great salvation, and 
she was not backward when in the society of her 
christian friends, especially in the*class meetings, and 
loye-feasts, to declare that the blood of Christ Hap 
cleansed her from ALL sin. And it appears that the 
sincerity of her profession was never called in question

by any who knew her. Such was her circumspect 
walk before men, her humility, modesty, temperance, 
and self-denial, that she gained upon the esteem and 
affection of the pious, and even among those who 
were without, many were constrained to wonder and 
adinire the grace of God in her. 

From that ardent love she felt to God, and that 
strong desire for the salvation of others, she was 
sweetly constrained to seek the salvation of those 
around her. It was not a desire to rise above her sex— 
to be thought wise—to have the name of preacher— 
no! she knew, the contrary to this awaited her—some, 
perhaps many, would severely censure her conduct— 
call in question the purity of her motives, and charge 
her with vanity. Nevertheless she knew in whom she 
had believed—she knew the value of her own soul, and 
the worth of others—she had found the pearl of great 
price, others might attain it—and if she might be the 
honoured instrument of putting them in the way of 
attaining it, she would have an abundant recompense 
of reward. Hence she could say— 


“The love of Christ doth me constrain, 
To seek the wandering souls of men; 
With cries, entreaties, tears, to save, 

To snatch them from. the gaping grave.” 


It appezrs from her diary and letters, that she had 
felt the importance of the work in such a manner, that 
nothing but a full conviction in her own mind, that 
God required it at her hands would have supported 
her in the mighty undertaking. 

The Church of England requires all candidates for 
holy orders, previous to their being ordained by the 
Bishop, to declare that they are moved by the Holy 
Ghost, to take upon them this ministry. I am of 
opinion that there are but very few females, if any, 
who will take this office upon them, unless they believe 
they are moved by the Holy Ghost so to do. We

If they are deceived some great stretch of charity is 
due to their sincerity, and earnest concern to say, and 
do, however painful, what they believe the Lord re-

Thus this highly honoured saint soared, far above 
the experience of Christians generally, into the enjoy- 
` ments of the inhahitants of that land of rest and peace 
into which her happy spirit was to be soon translated. 
She seems to have partook of much of the sensibility, 
and tenderness, the affection, humility, and zeal, that 
was in her divine Lord and Saviour. And no wonder 
as she constantly denied herself, took up her cross, 
and followed him. She had consecrated her body— 
soul, talent, time, money, and all she had to the ser- 
vice of God. 

From the time of her conversion to God she was un- 
shaken in her attachment to the truth, and in her at- 
tendance upon the means of grace. 

What chiefly tended to this stability of conduct, was 
the intercourse and communion she had with God. 
This appears to be the sheet anchor of her soul. She 
was known to pray in private, seven. times a day, gene- 
rally ; and sometimes oftener. Indeed she prayed al- 
ways with all prayer. She lived in the habitual spirit 
of earnest prayer, and grateful praise.

her companion in gospel labours, will be acceptable 
and profitable.

From June 1820, her health continued to decline, 
but as she now and then. appeared better, hopes were 
entertained of her recovery. But the disease baffied 
the skill of the Physician, and the power of medi- 
cine. Though her disorder (a consumption) was of a 


HOLY WOMEN. 63 
lingering nature; yet, its termination was somewhat 
sudden: she was enabled to bear testimony in the 
prospect, and in the very jaws of death, that Ae had 
lost his sting. She felt perfectly resigned to the wiil 
of God, and had nothing to do with doubts and fears. 
The Lord graciously supported and comforted her 
now, because she had put her trust in him. 

About half an hour before she died, she desired her 
brother to call the people up stairs, and she said, 
“ T believe I am going,’ he asked her if she felt alarm-. 
ed? she answered “No.” As soon as the people came 
up she began to exhort them to be faithful. She said, 
“ Tell all to be in earnest—Tell all around that GOD 
IS LOVE!” And although she had not been heard 
to speak aloud for some time, she then said aloud, in 
her usual manner, “GLORY BE TO GOD.—Bless 
the Lord !” and then died without a struggle or a groan, 
a few hours after she had entered on the twentieth year 
of her age.” The Thursday following (we are inform- 
ed that) “a Sermon was preached at Holwell, on the 
occasion; and her remains were followed by some 
hundreds of people. The corpse was carried from the 
door by six preachers. We continued singing Hymns 
suitable to the occasion, the greater part of the way 
from Holwell to Lake; where her remains were com- 
mitted to the dust, in Ebenezer Chapel burying ground: 
In sure and certain hope of a glorious resurrection to 
eternal life—It was a day that will not soon be 
forgotten. The power of God rested upon the con- 
gregation; and I believe it drew forth from most that 
were present, the wish, “ Let me die the death of the 
righteous ; and let my last end be like His.”

HOLY WOMEN. 


Mrs. SARAH GRUBB, 


Was one of the people called Quakers, and an 
eminent minister in that community. - She was born 
in the year 1756, in the City of York, her maiden 
name was Tuke. She was early deprived of the foster- 
ing care of a tender mother, but this loss appears to 
have been in a good measure restored, and compen- 
sated by the maternal care, and affectionate regard of 
her mother-in-law. 

The religious instruction—the watchful care—the 
strict attention to religious ordinances, and the in- 
fluence of good example, with which the children of the 
Society of Friends, are generally favoured, was a means 
under the divine blessing of preserving the subject of 
this memoir from those corruptions and follies which 
abound in the world. 

In the days of her youth she appeared to have been 
greatly favoured with the teaching of the divine Spirit, 


and the powerful operations of his grace, so as to be- , 


come decidedly religious, and being possessed of superior 
attainments in knowledge and experience, and being 
amiable in her manners, and heavenly in her disposi- 
tion, she became an acceptable and useful companion 
to the pious youth of her acquaintance in that com- 
munity. f ; 
When about twenty years of age she began her public 
ministry, firmly believing that the Lord required it at 
her hands. Her public testimonies were generally re- 
ceived by the Friends who heard her, as having the 
divine sanction. And atthe age of twenty-three, she 
was recognized, and acknowledged in that community

as an able minister of the New Testament. “ For this 
awful service (says her Biographer) she had been pre-

humbling baptisms of the Spirit. But as she continued 
patient and faithful, under this proving dispensation,

She travelled and preached throughout most of the 
counties of this kingdom—also through Ireland, Scot- 
land, and a great part of Holland, Germany, and France. 
In 1782 she married Robert Grubb, of Clonmel, 
Ireland. Abouttwo weeks after this event she entere 
on a religious visit to friends in Scotland, accompanied 
by another female preacher (Mary Proud,) having pre- 
viously obtained a certificate of concurrence from the 
Monthly Meeting. 

Of her journey to Dunkirk, she writes as follows : 
“We were at Rochester on the first day, at the 
Monthly Meeting, at Canterbury on third, and got to 
Dover that evening ; from whence we dalled next day 
for Dankirk, and had a fair but slow passage, being on 
the water sixteen hours. The day we arrived was their 
week day meeting; and it may with thankfulness be 
acknowledged, that it was mercifully owned with divine 
refreshment; aid the communication of counsel from 
the living spring thereof. And what tended to heighten 
„our joy, on sitting down with the friends here, was the 
scene which we had beheld just before. W hat they 
call the host was carried about, with such a procession 
of the army, corporation, clergy, and little children, as 
I never saw before, or could have supposed ; there be- 
ing many thousands both of people and images ; and 
silver, pewter, and wood ; hundreds of candles near six 
feet long 3 abundance of rich silk, and other vestments ; 
bare-footed and shaven-headed friars ; music, drums, 
&c. cannon firing, and bells ringing. So that after all 
this stir; to sit down with our friends under our vines 
and fig-trees, and par take of substantial food was truly 
Joyous”? On this journey she and her companions

AMONGST the numerous congratulations await- 
ing thy accession to the Imperial Crown, accept, O 
King! our Christian good wishes and solicitude for 
thy present aud eternal well-being. We are conscious 
that we have no claim to the liberty of addressing thee, 
but from a belief that the Lord Almighty, who ruleth 
in the kingdoms of men, and giveth them to whomso- 
ever he will, hath inclined us to leave our habitations 
to visit some parts of this country, and now engages us 
in gospel love, to express our secret and united prayer, 
that thou mayest be an instrument in his holy hand, 
for the advancement of that glorious day, spoken of by 
the prophet. ‘ When swords shall be beaten into plough- 
shares, and spears into pruning-hooks, when nation-shall 
not lift up sword against nation ; neither shall they learn 
war any more. The great design of our universal Pa- 
rent, in sending his beloved Son, a light into the world, 
is for his own glory in the salvation of mankind ; and 
for this gracious end, he hath given to all men a mea- 
súre of his own eternal spirit. To co-operate with Him 
herein, dignifies human nature, and is particularly de- 
serving the most scrupulous attention of Princes. The 
smallest revelation of this heavenly gift in the believing 
soul, having a degree of omnipotence in it, brings into 
subjection the natural will and wisdom of man, and 
discovers to us the noble purposes of our creation; it 
diffuses that true benevolence which characterizes ve- 
nuine Christianity, and renders dear toa Prince the 
happiness of all, even the meanest of his subjects ; im- 
printing upon his mind the superior value of an immor- 
tal soui, to all worldly acquisitions. Through the neglect 
ofa principleso pure and important, how hath the ration- 
al part of God’s creation been sacrificed to the irregular 
passions of Sovercigns ; and many unprepared souls 
precepitated into an awful futurity! That the gospel

dispensation is intended to remedy these evils, and 
promote the government of the Prince of Peace ; that 
the Gentiles are to come to its light, and Kings to the 
brightness of its arising, are truths to which the sacred 
records, abundantly. testify. May this be thy happy 
experience, O King, that so the power thou art provi- 
dentially entrusted with, being subservient to divine 
wisdom, thy example may influence the minds of other 
Princes, who also beholding its excellency, may unite

purity and simplicity of the religion of Jesus. And

of Kings, and Lord of Lords, who lives and reigns for 
ever and ever.” 


This excellent woman, and her company arrived in 
London, in the year 1790. On her return to Freland, 
she visited York, Manchester, Ackworth, and Sheffield. 
When she arrived at Clonmel her strength was greatly 
exhausted. She shortly after attended a Quarterly 
Meeting in that neighbourhood, and spoke several 
times to the edification of many—at the close of the 
Meeting she was taken ill, and continued about ten 
days, during which time she was preserved in peace, 
and perfect resignation to the divine will.« She died 
in 1790, aged thirty-four years.

Monthly Meeting for the county of Tipperary, shall 
close this account. i 

“Qur minds being deeply affected by the recent 
great loss which the church hath sustained, in the re-

our friends William Tuke and his late wife Elizabeth,

testimony concerning her; for as the memory of the

just is blessed, so the remembrance of this dignified 
and eminently asefal member in the church militant, 
is precious to many; to whom she was a nursing 
mother. She was a woman of extraordinary natural 
abilities, strength of judgment, and clearness of dis- 
cernment, In ministry, she was sound and edifying, 
not only likethe scribe instructed to the kingdom, bring- 
ing forth out of her treasure things new and old, but 
qualified by pure wisdom, to bring them forth in the 
demonstration of the spirit and with power, in the autho- 
rity and becoming gravity of the gospel, being in her 
delivery an exampie to’ all concerned in bearing a 
public testimony for the Lord’s cause.” .

Friends, Mrs. Ruth Fallows, who lived in the neigh- 
bourhood (Castle Donnington). I never heard that 
Mrs. Jewett met with any opposition from her husband, 
or from the ministers or people with whom she enjoyed 
Christian fellowship. Her husband departed this life 
in the year 1786, and as old age and infirmities crowd- 
ed upon her, she declined standing before the public, 
She lived to a great age, and died in peace, greatly 
respected and sincerely lamented by all who knew her, 


Miss SARAH COX, 


Was born at Wishall, near Nottingham, March 
6, 1773. She was deprived of the care of her mother 
when about four years of age. During her juvenile 
years she frequently experienced the drawings of the 
divine Spirit; and through the influence of restraining 
grace was preserved from many of the follies of her 
day. At an early period she began to pray, and pious 
resolutions were formed in her breast, but they were 
generally of short continuance. She regularly attend- 
ed the Church of England, but was never fully aware 
of the latent depravity of her heart until she heard the — 
Methodist Preachers. Through their instrumentality 
new accessions of gospel light were brought to her 
mind, and while hearing Mr. Jas. Bogie, (one of the Me~- 


HOLY WOMEN. 71 


thodist Preachers then stationed in the Nottingham 

Circuit) preach she was deeply awakened from the sleep 

_ of sin, and became tremblingly alive to the concerns 
of her soul and eternity, She began to seek the Lord 
day*and night, with groans and cries, and many tears. 
Being of a reserved disposition, she concealed her dis- 
tress until it drank up her spirits, and overpowered her 
mortal frame. Her friends became alarmed on account 
of her declining health; and some thought that she 
was fast verging towards a state of mental derangement. 
While thus sinking beneath the pressure of unpardon- 
ed guilt, she was invited toa Methodist Class Meeting, 
and on complying with the invitation she was encou- 
raged in the ordinance. After having met two or three 
times in class, as she was on her knees before the 
Lord, he spake peace to her soul in these words, “ As 
ye have received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in 
him? She was immediately made “ free from the law 
of sin and death,” and was presently filled with love to 
God and all mankind ; and the language of her bound- 
ing heart was 


* O for a trumpet’s voice 
On all the world to call! 
To bid their hearts rejoice 
In Him who died for all !” 


This was about the latter end ofther nineteenth or 
the beginning of her twentieth year. Her experience 
was marked with precision. Prior to her enjoyment 
of the liberty of faith, her convictions were deep, and 
afterwards nothing could satisfy her anxious mind but 
the present possession of conscious pardon, No soon- 
er had the Lord blessed her with salvation, than she 
felt a concern for the safety of others; and in conse- 
quence began to pray in public, and in the family of 
which she was a member. She also visited those 
whom the Lord had bound with the cords of affliction, 
and while her labours were rendered beneficial to others,

was strengthened by a Sermon preached by Mr. John

received a deeper baptism of the hallowing Spirit. 
She then wished that every soul might become the 
happy recipient of the same blessing. With an in- 
crease of grace, her feeling for the souls of her fellow- 
creatures increased, and her zeal could be no longer 
confined within its accustomed limits. Such passages

“ Tet the dead bury their dead, but go thou and

convinced the impressions she felt were from God. 
She knew this because they were accompanied with

her religicus comforts were greatly diminished, and a

either divulge the secret of her mind to her female 
friend, or leave the room. She left the table but was

holy woman encouraged her to enter on the work of

in her mind against it, and for a long season resisted 
the powerful leadings and convictions of the Holy 
Spirit to this duty, till she found there was a necessity 
laid upon her, and a woe unto her if she obeyed not.

the unsearchable riches of Christ.” When first she 
stood before a congregation, she dared not to look 
them in the face, and when she repaired to the place 
of preaching, she generally did it as secretly as possi- 
ble; but she looked to the Lord and he saved her from 
the native timidity of her heart. Whatever difficulties 
she met with, as she had a single eye to God’s glory 
in the salvation of souls, there was always a door 
opened for her reception. Her constitution was deli- 
cate in the extreme, but according to her ability she 
laboured a few years in the ministration of the saving 
word. She preached through different parts of Leices- 
tershire and Nottinghamshire, with great acceptance 
and success. Her heart was in the work, and the 
«hand of the Lord” was with her. On the 15th of 
December, 1808, the breaking of a blood vessel, occa- 
sioned such an increase of affliction, as has rendered 
her incapable of strong exertions ever since. Her 
sufferings from that period have been great, but being 
possessed of “a soul inur’d to pain,” she is resigned to 
the will of God, under the most afflictive dispensations 
of His providence, and comforts herself with these 
words, “If we suffer with Him (Christ) we shall also 
reign with Him.” She is now living at Wishall, near 
Nottingham, in a very weak state, and has not eaten 
animal food for more than thirty years. We are crea- 
tures of habit, and habits of whatever kind are strength- 
ened by exercise and practice. The more congenial 
these habits are to our natural feelings, desires, and 
inclinations, the more easily they are confirmed, and 
the more difficult to be conquered and overcome. How 
necessary that we should enquire whether the habits 
we indulge and practise be sinful, or innocent, or use-. 
ful, We should not only abstain from all known sin, 
but we should hardly satisfy ourselves with any thing 
that is merely harmless. A good man will have an 
object in view, some usefulness to himself or others, 
the body or soul. No person was more rigidly tem- 
perate and self-denying than the subject of this memoir.
