Mrs. MARY HARRISON. 


Ir is generally allowed that ministers of Christ 
should be made partakers of those blessings which 
they hold forth unto others; that they should feel the 
importance as well as understand the nature of those 


doctrines and precepts which they teach and recom- 


mend ; for without this knowledge and experience of 
the truths they advance, it is not likely that their 
mission will be very successful, or that they will feel 
much interested in its prosperity. 


HOLY WOMEN. 77 


Mrs. Mary Harrison, the subject of this short me- 
moir, was a happy partaker of that salvation which she 
recommended to others ; she testified of the things she 
knew by happy and heartfelt experience. She was 
many years esteemed as a mother in Israel, by the pious 
of every persuasion, who had the happiness of a per- 
sonal acquaintance with her. She lived at Wishall, in 
the county of Nottingham, and was awakened to a 

sight of her sinful state, and to a sense of her danger 
under the ministry of the Rev. Samuel Davenport, who 
then preached the gospel with great energy, and con- 
siderable success in that neighbourhood. But this 
“ burning and shining light’? was soon removed from 
those parts. 

However our sister had received such strong convic- 
tions under his powerful and awakening sermons, that 
she could find no rest in her bones by reason of her 
sins. She, verily, groaned nnder her heavy burden, 
and mingled her drink with her weeping, and watered 
her couch with her tears. But, the minister being 
gone, and having no one in the village, nor in the whole 
circle of her acquaintance, who understood her case, or 
was capable of giving her suitable advice ; she concealed 
the various exercises of her mind from every huiman be- 
ing, and made the bosom of her Lord the repository of 
her fears, and cares, and sorrows. She sought his favour 
and salvation with many prayers, strong cries, and 
streams of tears, and did not seek in vain. But 
although she frequently derived a measure of comfort 
from God in prayer, and felt a degree of inexpressibic 
sweetness spring up in the midst of her sorrows, yet se- 
veral years elapsed before she had a satisfactory evidence 

_that God for Christ’s sake had blotted out her trausgres- 
sions. When she was fully satisfied on this. subjeci, 
She rejoiced “ with joy unspeakabie and full of glory.” 
She invited the Methodist Preachers io tie village at 
which she lived, and for many years eutertained the: 
in her own house. Sie went from douse to louse, to 
invite her neighiours to go and hear the gospel; aad 
whenever she perceived any aifecied uader tae word 

H 3 


78 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


or that anywise manifested a concern for their soul’s 
salvation, she invited them to meet her at a certain 
time and place, that she might have some conversation 
with them, and that some time might be spent in 
prayer to God for them. Thus she soon formeda class, 
and providentially became the leader of it. As the 
Lord had already opened her mouth to plead his cause, 
and given her words that her neighbours were not able 
to gainsay or resist, she unexpectedly obtained an in- 
fluence and repect among the people, which seemed to 
point out her call to speak to them more publicly on 
the concerns of their salvation. In the mean time, the 
Holy Spirit, and yearning bowels of love aud compas- 
sion for the souls of men, had been secretly but 
powerfully urging her to call sinners to repentance. 
In compliance with the heavenly calling, she began on 
the Sunday evenings to warn and exhort the people 
with great simplicity, deep humility, and much tender- 
ness and feeling. This greatly increased the number 
ofthe hearers, and some other visible effects were soon 
produced. The silent tear was seen trickling down the 
formerly hardened countenance of the sinner. A deep 
sigh, and not unfrequently a heavy groan, were heard 
from the breast of one deeply wounded by the arrows 
of conviction. These were pleasing discoveries to the 
mind of this holy woman, and indeed to all those who 
had tasted that the Lord was gracious. For the pious 
bearers of the gospel have ever been delighted when 
they have scen sinners affected under the word; when 
penitential tears have begun to flow, and callous hearts 
to feel the power of God. ~ To be unmoved at such a 
sight, would indicate an awful destitution of love and 
sympathy, and leave strong reason to suspect that we 
ourselves had never experienced the deep sorrows of 
sacred compunction, nor felt the pangs of the new 
birth; or else, that we had forgotten the hole of the pit, 
out of which we were digged, and the rock from which we 
were hewn. The returning of a sinner from “ the error 
of his way,” is an event that the angels look upon with 
pleasure, and which the God of both men and angels,

looks down through the shining ranks of Heaven to 


behold. <“ To this man will I look, even to him thatis — 


poor and ofa contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” 
This holy woman entered into all the feclings of those 
who sorrowed after a godly sort, and was well able to 
give them suitable counsel and encouragement. She 
sometimes read a chapter or a few verses, and explained 
and applied them as the Lord gave her utterance. She 
_ Was very weak in body, and did not travel much from 
home, but generally spoke jon Sunday evenings, 
to crowds of attentive hearers, many of whom will be 
the crown of her rejoicing in the day of the Lord J esus. 
Her last affliction was a very painful and lingering one, 
but she bore it with great fortitude, and perfect resig- 
nation, and all was peace, and quietness, and assurance 
for ever. She never once regretted having called sin- 
ners to repentance, nor ever intimated that she had 
taken astep too many, in striving to promote God’s 
glory in the salvation of immortal souls. She was never 
convinced that she had done a work which the Lord did 
not require at her hands. She fell asleep in Jesus, 
October the 19th, 1808, in the 56th year of her age. 
“ The memory of the just is blessed.”

From some manuscripts containing the experience

that time I was greatly concerned for the souls of 
others.—I prayed and wept in secret for them.—Soon

vision—respecting myself—my family—and many 
others.—I concealed this.—Three years after the 
Methodists came to the place—I heard and felt the 
trath. At thirteen I became a member of the Metho- 
dist Society, and the Lord made known to me what 
he would have me to do.— But Oh! how unfit did I see 
myself! From that time the word of God was an un- 
sealed book. It was my companion day and night. 
My love to God and souls increased.—I have been 
often led to cry out in the bitterness of my soul, O 
Lord I am a child, I cannot preach thy word. 
But the more deeply was it impressed on my mind 
« Woe is me if I preach not the gospel.” Till my dis- 
tress of soul almost destroyed my body.—In my 
twentieth year the Lord answered my prayer, ina great 
_ affliction—and made known to others as well as to myself 
the work he would have me to do,—and fitted me in the 
furnance for his use. From that time I began my public 
work. Mr. Wesley was to me a father and a faithful 
friend: The same Lord that opened my mouth,and endued 
me with power, and gave me courage to speak his word, 
bas through his grace enabled me to continue to the

I ANSWERED your Ictter long ago, and desired 
Mr. Whitfield to send my letter with the Magazines, 
which he was sending to Norwich, desiring withal that

that is within my power. Indeed I could not so well 
send the Notes on the Old Testament, as the edition is. 
nearly sold off, and we have very few of them left, 
which are reserved to make up full sets. But any other- 
books are at your service. I want to forward you in 
all useful knowledge, which indeed lies in a very 
narrow compass. You do not expect to go through 
life without crosses: and some will fall upon you on 
my account ; for my taking notice of you, may bring 
envy upon you. But in your patience possess your 
soul. Please God, and it is enough. Go steadily and 
quietly on, in the way wherein Providence leads you. 
And in every temptation He by His spirit will clear a 
way for you to escape. If any particular difficulty or 
trial comes upon you do not fail to let me know. 
None can be more ready to assist you than 


My dear Sally, 
Yours affectionately, 
J. WESLEY..

Near London, Dec. 13, 1790. 
Dear Sally, 


I am glad you put me in mind of the Books, 
Brother George Whitfield had quite forgotten them. 
1 will refresh his memory. Tell me of any thing you 
want, and I love you too well to let you want long. 
Some time ago it seems you had suffered that word to 
slip out of your mind, “ My child if thou wilt serve the 
Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” Particularly if 
thou wilt exhort others to serve Him : then expecta flood 
of temptation. That which you mention is common 
to man: but when Satan attacks us so violently, he 
provokes to jealousy one that his stronger than he. 
I am glad that you have been at and about Diss, and 
there is a good understanding between you and your 
Sister. Let that be the only contention between you, 
which shall be most zealous, and most humble. 1 was. 
well pleased when together to find that you could speak 
to me without reserve, so I trust you will always do. 


For has not God given me to you for a tender guard of 


your youth? And I believe you will find few that will 
watch over you more tenderly than 


Dear Sally, 
Yours affectionately, 
J. WESLEY.

HOLY WOMEN. 


Mrs. ELIZABETH REEVE. 


EuizaBeTa REEVE lived and died at Redgrove,, 
in Suffolk. She was one of the spiritual children which 
God gave to the public labours of Miss Mallet. She 
kept her brother’s house for many years. Soon after 
her conversion, her brother was brought to God. Miss 
Mallet went and preached in their house; and imme- 
diately after, the Methodist Travelling Preachers were 
invited, and came and had a comfortable home there 
for many years. Soon after Elizabeth had found the 
pearl of great price; she felt very desirous that her 
neighbours and acquaintance might obtain it too, and 
believing that they would seek it diligently if they knew 
its value; she took every opportunity of setting it before 
them in all the beauty and excellence of which she was 
capable ; and she begun to exhort diligently, at all 
opportunities, in private and in public; and the Lord 
amazingly increased both her gifts and grace. Miss. 
Mallet gave Mr. Wesley an account of the conversion 
and public labours of this young woman, on his last 
Visit to Norwich; he was much pleased with the 
relation, and requested Miss. Mallet to bring her to 
him at Diss, ona certain day which he named. She did 
so, he conversed with her upon her religious experience, 
and her views and feelings relative to her public exer- 
cises.; and being quite satisfied of the purity of her 
motives, and that God had called her to proclaim sal- 
vation in the name of Jesus, he encouraged her in her 
public work. This is the person referred to in Mr. 
Wesley’s letter to Miss Mallet, dated Bristol, July 3L.

1790. She continued to preach some years, and the 
Lord made her labours a blessing to many. She was 
instrumental in raising a little Society in the place 
where she lived.—Happy would it be for the world at 
large if every person, and every female, especially those 
who understand the plan of salvation, were to act ina 
similar way.—How would such a line of conduct tend 
to bring about the salvation of mankind. For although 
few women are so circumstanced as to go abroad in 
order to “Seek the wandering sons of men ;”’ yet all 
may do something towards helping on the work at 
home. Very much remains yet to be done in the 
immediate neighbourhood of every serious person ! 
and how many doors of usefulness stand wide open, 
and would certainly be entered did we, like this pious 
young woman, seriously consider the dangerous situ- 
ation of every unconverted sinner. She afterwards 
married, but died soon after of a consumption, in the 
full assurance of hope. Mr. Thomas Rogerson, who 
laboured then in the Diss Circuit, preached her funeral 
sermon—to a large and deeply attentive, and weeping 
congregation. She continued to preach as long as she 
could be helped into the pulpit, and was highly esteemed 
by all who knew her character and worth. 


Mrs. MARSH. 


_ Ir it is true, that adversity is more favourable 
toa religious course than prosperity, and that piety 
more frequently adorns the lower, than the higher — 


HOLY WOMEN. 93 


walks of life; it follows, that those who in affluent cir- 
cumstances devote themselves to God and his service, 
have the greatest sacrifices to make, and the most 
powerful temptations to resist, and are therefore de- 
serving of a more than ordinary share of our attention; 

Mrs. Marsh was a lady of small fortune, and conse- 
quently had the means of gratifying those unholy 
propensities, which are inseparable froin human natare 
in its unregenerate state; but of herself and all her 
substance, she made “ A free will offering unto the 
Lord.” . The Holy Spirit opened the eyes of her un- 
derstanding, and gave her to see that riches are not 
ouly unsatisfying, but often make themselves wings 
and flee away; and hence she set her affections on 
things above, not on things on the earth, She consider- 
ed not herself the proprietor, but the steward of her 
possessions, and therefore endeavoured to make such a 
use of them as to be able at all times to give an account 
of her stewardship. Aware of the shortness and uncer- 
certainty of time, she “So numbered her days as to 
apply her heart unto wisdom,” and laboured as one that 
would shortly be laid “ With the clods in the valley.”” 
She believed that the Lord never bestowed talents on 
any of his creatures but with a design and an expecta- 
tion that they should be improved, and on that 


ground judged it her indispensable duty to “ Stir up 


the gift that was in her,” by exhorting sinners to 
accept the mercy of their God, In so doing, perhaps. 
some would think she acted out of character, and as- 
sumed an office which was never intended for the 
female sex; but Mr. Wesley was not of this opinion ; 
for when on religious visits among her friends, she 
preached in his societies, and was never denied the use 
of his Chapels. This is a circumstance that will exalt 
the character of Mrs. Marsh, in the estimation of all 
who knew the discernment of that great and judicious. 
man : and from which we may reasonably infer that she 
preached the great doctrines of revelation, and gave 
visible proofs that she was sent of God,, 


94 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Had not this have been the case she would not have 
been allowed such a privilege. Mr. Wesley was well 
acquainted with her, and consequently had the means 
of judging of her piety and qualifications for the work 
of the Lord. And that he considered her a proper 
person to deliver God’s embassage of mercy to a sinful 
world, is evident from his conduct towards her- He 
gave her encouragement in all her efforts to do good. 

Her labours were much confined to London and 
Bristol, but she visited many of the towns and villages 
in the south of England; and as she acted from a prin- 
ciple of love to God and man, her labour would not be 
in vain in the Lord. 

I have not received any account of her latter end, 
but as she spent her life in striving to promote the in- 
terests of Zion, she is, without doubt, now before the 
throne of God. Some indeed, not considering the in- 
dissoluble connexion there is between a holy life and a 
glorious eternity, will scarcely believe that any one is 
gone to Heaven, except he was seen to triumph in the 
arms of death, and would tease a dying saint for fresh 
declarations of his acceptance every hour. But if a 
believer, through the influence of his disorder, were to 
leave the world in a state of wild delirium or raving 
madness, that circumstance of his departure would not 
at all affect the safety of his soul. What is called a 
triumphant death is very desirable, but all the truly 
pious are not favoured with holy raptures in their dying 
moments; and as a calm and easy exit is no sure evi- 
dence of salvation, so neither is a painful transition a 
sufficient proof of an ungodly state. But ifany person 
may expect an easy death, the Christian may; for 
the Psalmist tells us that the Lord will withold no good 
thing from them that walk uprightly. i 


WOMEN. 


Mrs. SIBYLL BEST, 


Or Brampton, near Carlisle, in Cumberland. 
When about nine or ten years of age, she felt the spirit 
of God powerfully opperating upon her tender mind, 
which led her to read and love the Scriptures, especi- 
ally the history of our Lord, and his sufferings and 
death.—And when she considered the design of his 
coming, she was drawn to love him with a degree of 
affection, which is beyond the power of language to 
express ; and she resolved, by the assistance of his 
grace, to live so as to please him, that she might live 
with him in Heaven for ever. In this state of mind she 
continued for sometime. In reading the new Testa- 
ment, frequently weeping over it ; and in secret prayer 
she spent many hours together; and on some occasions, 
nearly whole nights in this happy exercise. But having 
none to instruct her, or to encourage her by their ex- 
ample, and beginning to associate with young people, 
who were trifling and fond of play ; she gradually, and 
almost imperceptably, lost her enjoyments, and ina 
great measure her relish for secret duties. 

~ But the spirit of God did not wholly depart from her, 
bat frequently and in the most pungent manner re- 
proved her for her backslidings, so as to cause her to 
weep, and grieve before the Lord, so that, she knew the 
truth of that saying “ The heart knoweth its own bitter- 
ness,” as much as she had formerly known “ That a 
stranger intermeddleth not with itsjoy.’ Thus she con- 


_ tinued till the year 1809, when under a sermon preach- 


ed by the Rev. Mr. Blanshard, from “ Why stand ye 


96 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


here all the day idle,” she was aroused from her spiritual 
lethargy. This was in the Methodist Chapel, at 
Brampton, in Cumberland. The word came with 
inexpressible power to her heart. At that time, 
and for two years afterwards, the Lord gave her to 
drink deeply of the cup of repentance. Then she felt 
the bitter consequence of departing from the Lord. In 
the midst of the deepest anguish of spirit, and peniten- 
tial sorrow, she did not fear the punishment of the 
damned, so much as the displeasure of God, and the 
sin of grieving his Holy Spirit. She bitterly lamented 
her trifling, and the ingratitude by which it was so 
awfully aggravated, She was so covered with shame 
and confusion of face, so self condemned and self 
abhorred, that she dared not to open her mouth upon 
the subject of her distress to any one; and when com- 
fort was offered her, she refused to be comforted, and 
really thought none had ever sinned as she had done; 
nor could she suppose that there was a being upon the 
face of the earth in a similar state. She cried mightily 
to God through Christ for mercy, and felt perfectly wil- 
ling to endure any suffering or shame; but the divine 
terrors harrowed up her soul. 

She desired nothing but the favour of God, and 
nothing less could suffice. But in the midst of her 
extremity, God in his stupendous mercy vouchsafed to 
visit and deliver her. It was on October 10th, 1811, 
being in great agony of soul, and brought to the very 
brink of despair, when alone and prostrate at the foot- 
stool of divine mercy, the Lord appeared to relief, and 
set her soul at liberty. The peace and joy which fol-. 
lowed, were the very opposite to the guilt aud dis- 
tress which preceded. Now she did indeed praise the 
Lord with joyful lips, and with gladness. She felt the 
love of God shed abroad in her heart by the Holy 
Ghost given unto her. For sometime she was borne 
upon the wings of love. Her only desire was to please 
God, and enjoy his approving smile. Her language 
was similar to that of the Poet,

accepted this covenant on her part, and shone by his

In this way she has continued for several years, 
speaking to the people in the neighbourhood where 
she lives, as the Lord has opened her way. The effects 
produced in several places have fully satisfied her own 
mind ; and have been equally satisfactory to many others 
that she has not been deceived in this important 
matter. Her own words on this subject are as follows : 

“When I found the impression of God’s spirit, 
urging me to Preach the gospel, my heart was ready to 
sink within me, O how did I struggle with my own 
weakness. But at last I was as clear of my call by 
the spirit of God, as I was of my own conversion, that 
I must either preach or perish. And glory be to his holy 
name, he did bless my weak endeavours. Oh! the 
tender care the Lord takes of his followers. Blessed 
be his Holy Name he has brought me through much ; 
_ and in the midst of the fire, and the water, he has been 
with me, and made a way for my escape.” 


HOLY WOMEN. 99 


For several years she has continued to warn and 
exhort sinners, and to comfort and edify the Church of 
God. He has endowed her with very useful gifts, and 
with great zeal and feeling, and much power with God 
in prayer. But she has not been without her outward 
crosses, as well as her inward conflicts on the score of 
her public ministrations, but she has learned how to 
Jorgive. She finds her safety, and her comfort in 
imitating her divine Lord and Saviour, “ Who, 
when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he 
suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him 
that judgeth rightcously.’? The greatest cross she was 
ever called to endure of an outward nature, was from a 
Preacher, who took upon himself to talk to her, in her 
own house ; but not in the way of brotherly kindness, 
or of argument, but of redicule, insult, and abuse. 
The curious dialogue that took place on this occasion 
is written with pen and ink on paper, but I shall not 
offend the ear of delicacy, or grieve the heart of piety 
by transcribing it here. The pious reader will not be 
much surprised to hear that soon after this conversa- 
tion, a District Meeting was called, in which charges 
of immorality were preferred, and pon against this 
man, and he was forthwith suspended from his office, 
and requested to remove out of that neighbourhood. 
“ Verily there isa God that judgeth in the earth”? 

But I am happy in being able to say, that God hath 
given to him repentance unto life, and restored him to 
divine favour, to peace, and in some good degree to his 
former usefulness in the Church and the*world. Our 


Sister never entertained any malignity towards him, nor 


towards any of those who opposed her labouring in the 
vineyard of the Lord. But in all cases committed her 
cause into the hands of him who judgeth righteously. 
May he still protect—and preserve her till she with all 
the Lord hath given to her, be presented faultless be- 
fore his eternal throne.

Mrs. MARY HOLDER. 


Her maiden name was Woodhouse.—She was 
born at Whitby, in the North-Riding of Yorkshire. 
She was converted when very young ; and became an, 
active, zealous, and very useful member of the Metho- 
dist Society at that place. She soon beeame a leader 
of a class, and also met in band, with some young 
women which she had been instrumental in bringing into 
the good way. She becameearly and intimately acquain- 
ted with those eminent and useful females, Mrs Crosby, 
Miss Hurrel, Miss Rhodes, and Miss Richie ; which 
continued to the end of life ; as it respected those that 
are already gone, and no doubt will be resumed, per- 
petuated, and perhaps increased to all eternity. The 
bond of union which cements the members of the 
Christian Church together, is of such a nature, that 
no distance of place, alteration in circumstance, or 
ravage of time can dissolve it; but more especially when 
such kindred souls, as those named above, meet and 
become intimately acquainted with each other; such 
friendship being founded in the love of God, and mu- 
tually strengthened and increased by every interview, 
must be lasting as thesoul. Mary, the subject of this 
memoir, became united in the holy state of matrimony, 
to that man of God, Mr. George Holder, with whom. 
she has travelled, and laboured in the gospel for many 
years. She used very frequently to travel with her 
husband into the country parts of the circuit; and on 
these occasions generally gave an exhortation to the 
congregation, after Mr. Holder had finished his sermon; 


HOLY WOMEN. 101 


at other times she only engaged in prayer, and other- 
wise assisted as she saw occasion required, or felt moved 
by the spirit of God. On these occasions the Lord 
frequently made bare his arm, in the awakening and 
conversion of several souls. Sometimes the Lord gave 
a soul to one and sometimes to the other, of these his 
servants. The kind friends who „entertained them, 
never thought it a burden upon them to receive at the 
same time two such messengers of salvation, instead of 
one; they found an abundant recompence of reward in 
their own souls. As Iam favoured with Mrs. Holder’s 
Journal from the beginning, I shall make such extracts, 
as will leave her to speak for herself, fully assured that 
every pious reader will enter into her feelings, her joys 
and sorrows, as he travels with her through the way in 
which divine providence hath seen good to lead her. 
Perhaps it would have been better if she had borne a 


more ample testimony concerning her public labours 


and usefulness, in the great work in which she was en- 
gaged, but her great modesty and deep humility pre- 
vented this. It is well known that God has given her 
many souls for her hire.

“I was born in the year 1751, of parents that 
feared God, and strictly attended the ordinances of the 


‘Church of England, and was particularly attentive to 


the morals of their children. They were brought to 
the enjoyment of true religion by hearing the Methodist 
Preachers ; and lived and died witnessing the power of 


„the Lord to save in life and death. When about ten 
‘or eleven years of age, I attended the children’s mect- 


ing, kept by a poor good man, John Rogers by name; 
myself and some more were brought to enjoy the love 
of God at that early period, through his labours.—He 
met us in class while we continued steady ; but after 
some months, I, and some others, trifled and lost the 
knowledge of God: but such was the Lord’s mercy to 
my soul, that he followed me by the reprooss of his 


102 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


spirit from time to time. I was often grieved at my 
folly, and distressed at the thoughts of death and eter- 
nity, especially in the night season; the day I got 
over in various amusements, with a large family and 
trifling acquaintance ; but when evening came on my 
painful reflections increased, with the fear of dying in 
my present state; not daring to go to bed without 
prayer. I often asked the Almighty, with great sin- 
cerity and importunity, to spare me, thinking I would 
strive to be better; but when morning returned my 
best thoughts passed away like the early dew. 

Thus I went on till about the 16th year of my age. 
When waking one sabbath day morning, I was struck 
with the thought of often resolving in the evening to 
set out to seek the Lord.—But I now felt a desire to 
begin that morning in good earnest; I did so, and 
cried mightily to Heaven for help ; and He, who had 
long waited to give what I was unwilling or unpre- 
pared to receive, heard my ery, and increased my 
concern for salvation. 

As soon as opportunity offered, I went to the house 
of a poor woman, a zealous Methodist, who gladly 
received me, and prayed with and gave me the best 
advice; and soon after took me by the hand to the 
preacher, Mr. Wm. Brammah, who admitted me into 
the Methodist Society on trial. 1 think it was in the 
year 1767; from that time 1 was enabled to give up all 
my trifling acquaintance, and put off needless dress, 
and sought the Lord with sincerity of soul; but I did 
not feel that distress which many do. 

The Father of mercies dealt very tenderly with me. 
It was not long before I was enabled to believe that 
God, for Christ’s sake, had healed all by backslidings, 
pardoned my sins, and restored my soul to his favour. 
Soon after | was exhorted to seek after purity of heart, 
I soon felt the need of this, and resolved to seek after 
this inestimable blessing. One day I purposed to re- 
tire and plead at a throne of grace, until I obtained it 
—inany things hindered—towards evening I got into 
my room, and bowed my knees before the Father of 


HOLY WOMEN. 103 


mercies, and in my poor way—(and yet in the best 
way I could) poured out my complaints and wants into 
his compassionate ear, who seeth in secret.—Several 
times I inclined to rise, thinking I should not get the 
blessing I wanted; but I began again and again to 
plead—till the friend of sinners magnified his mercy by 
giving me power to believe in the accomplishment of 
his promises ; and I rose renewed in perfect love. 1 
have often been astonished at the condescension of the 
Almighty, for surely a more ignorant and unworthy 
creature never tasted of his love. But O since that 
period, how hath my unworthiness been increased by 
sins of omission and commission. After a few months 
enjoyment of the inestimable blessing of perfect love, 
by giving way to a light spirit, and by reasoning with 
the enemy, I lost the evidence of this blessing ; and I 
did it so frequently, that for some years I neither dared 
to say I had or had not the blessing of purity of heart. 
About the year 1775 or 1776, J. Blades came to Whit- 
by, and was made a great blessing to many in the 
revival of the work of sanctification.—At that time my 
soul was again set free, and for some time I was carried 
above all sin—temptation and fear; 1 was ready to 
say 


“JT cannot believe that I ever shall grieve, 
That I ever shall suffer again.” 


But since that period I may say— 


«O the infinite cares, temptations and snares, 
Thy hand hath conducted me through !” 


And how often have I held the shield of faith, and 
the blessings of salvation with a trembling hand. What 
heights and depths of the divine nature might I have 
enjoyed, had I been faithful to the grace given! And 
what great good might I have received, if I had im- 
proved, as I ought, a very painful dispensation of 
divine providence, in taking away, by a watery grave, 


104 BIOGRAPHIVAL SKETCHES OF 


an only brother ; and also in eutting off my expecta- 
tions, in taking to himself a faithful friend and com- 
panion! Had I been that obedient child 1 ought to 
have been, I might have been 1 mother in Israel years 
since, instead of being only a babe in Christ. And 
yet through rich grace and free mercy, I have cause to 
bless God that I am what I am. I trust I have been 
creeping on in the heavenly road, and I now rejoice in 
the God of my salvation. But when I view the advan- 
tages 1 have had—favoured with pious parents—and in 
enjoying the company of such holy men as Mr. Wesley 
—Coke—Nelson—Brammah—Hunter, &c. &c. under 
my father’s roof; and also—that mother in Israel, 
who was made a blessing to many, Mrs. Crosby. from 
Cross-Hall. Miss Bossanquet, (the late Mrs. Fletcher) 
was the first female that exercised in public among the 
Methodists in Whitby. She came from Scarborough 
to this place ; and spoke to the congregation after Mr. 
Taylor had preached.—There was a multitude of atten- 
tive hearers, and surely it was a most blessed time. 
After some months Mrs. Crosby came again, and 
Miss Hurrel came with her; and they were the means of 
many flocking to the house of God. Their labours 
publicly and privately were blest in town and country 
to numbers of precious souls. Mrs. Crosby, continued 
to come to Whitby several times for some years. She 
stayed with us in my father’s house many weeks, and 
was a pattern of holiness in all manner of conversation. 
Her life and labours of love were of great use to my 
soul, and I bless God that I ever saw her, although I was 
brought to the knowledge of the truth, before I be- 
came acquainted with her, yet her advice, reproof, in- 
struction, and example were rendered exceedingly 
useful, and might have been much more so, had I been 
more obedient to the spirit of God. She wrote to me 
many excellent letters—as also did that amiable woman 
Miss Richie, now Mrs. Mortimer, and many others ; 
such were the advantages for remembering my creator,in 
the days of my youth that I was favoured with the ac- 
quaintance and friendship, both of Preachers and 


HOLY WOMEN. 105 


people that I should never have known but for a reli- 
gious connection. When I look back on my singular 
advantages for spiritual improvement, Í see cause for 


- shame and great self abasement, But here I dare not 


stop, it would be likea quicksand, I should soon be 
like Peter sinking in the waves. But when I glance 
on the numberless mercies showered down upon me 
both temporal and spiritual from the Father of mercies 
through the Son of his love, 1 see my debt of gratitude 
inexpressible and it grows upon me daily. 


“ Oh to grace how great a debtor, 
Daily I’m constrained to be— ” 


1780, I have gone on heavily some time past, I often 
loose the evidence of the Lord’s purifying my heart, 
through evil reasoning, that Lam ashamed and afraid 
to profess what God hath done for my soul, though 
I feel nothing contrary to love. On Friday last, 
while lifting up my heart to God in prayer these words 
came with power “I am thy salvation.’ I was so pe- 
netrated with the love of God as I cannot express. 
Jesus the adorable Saviour was all in all. The lan- 
guage of my soul was— 


“ How shall I equal triumphs raise, 
Or sing my great deliverer’s praise.” 


I view the goodness of God towards an unworthy 
worm in giving me strong consolation, befure he called 
me to pass through any particular trial—such as giving 
up a friend whom he sees good to take to the blessed _ 
regions, where all is quietness and assurance for ever ; 
and their removal is a fresh call to my soul, to be quite 
ready.—My dear father has taken his flight, bearing a 
blessed testimony of the power of God to save. Aged 
sixty-seven. 

He exhorted his six daughters to be spiritually 
minded. My dear mother was enabled to bear the 
heavy stroke.—

The first thirty-five ycarsof my life was spent with my 
honoured praying parents, when I believe I was called 
of God to leave a tender mother, and all my relatives and 
friends, and unite with a servant of the most High, 
who was engaged in preaching the everlasting Gospel, 
as an Itenerant Preacher in connexion with Mr, 
Wesley. This was not done without much considera- 
tion and prayer. But the qualifications necessary for 
a Preacher’s wife—the going in, and out before the 
people—and setting an example worthy their imitation 
with a sight and sense of my wants for such a station 
affected me much. I was ready to repeat the ery, “ Lord 
help me. And blessed be his Holy Name he did so, 
I was enabled to cast my care upon him, believing he 
would fit me for whatever he called me to. I felt much 
at leaving a large class of young women, whom I had 
met ten years or more—with my band sisters. We 
were united in the bonds of love, ever glad to meet— 
but not very willing to part—though sure we still were 
one in heart. 

Blessed be God for the joyful hope of meeting where ` 
parting is not known.—My Husband’s first appoint- 
ment, after our marriage, was by the Rev. Mr. Wesley, 
to the Isle of Man. This was a trial to myself and 
friends, yet I believe I shall have to praise God for it 
to all eternity. . 

1788—August 17,—After spending some weeks at 
Whitby, and commending my dear mother, sister, and 
many friends and ourselves to God, we sailed for New- 
castle, and got safe into Shields the next ia The 
22nd we took coach, and arrived at Hexham about six 
in the evening ; a friend seeing Mr, Holder, and sup- 
posing him a Methodist Preacher, came to the Inn and 
asked him to preach, ‘The house was filled with atten- 
tive hearers, and the Lord blessed his word. On the 
23rd we arrived at Carlisle, 24th at Whitehaven.—On 
the 27th we sailed for the Island; and after a stormy 
passage of three days, landed safe at Douglas. We 
soon had many friends to welcome us. But ever 
thing was new and strange to me. The people—thew

meeting or Manx conference, so called.—Here the 
Manx Preachers are examined, and an exhortation 
given to them. On friday and saturday we had a

On Sunday we had a love feast here, as also on the 
Sunday following at Kirklonnon; but such times for 
Weeping, groaning, and crying aloud, I never witness-

would go into fits, with the heat and crowd of the 
people. I feel constant need of the blood of sprinkling,

794, Douglas, Isle of Man.—Before we left Scar-

of God would L sing and give thanks—his word is pre-

1800, May.—I was called with my other Sisters, 
to attend our dear Mother in her last sickness and death. 
It was a solemn time, a time of great affliction to her, 
and sorrow to us, though her mind was greatly sup- 
ported. She was strong in faith, giving glory to him 
that had bought and washed her in his precious blood, 
and kept her a witness of his power to save, for many 
years. It was a great privilege to attend so valuable 
a parent in her latest moments, after hills and seas had 
divided us. Though she suffered much, she was 
sweetly resigned to the divine will; while the pins of 
mortality loosened, her confidence in God strengthened. 
She had known and loved God for more than thirty 
years. Though Satan was permitted to buffet her 
once or twice sharply, yet the Lord lifted a standard 
against him. July 12, 1800, the happy spirit took its 
flight to regions of eternal day ——————__ 

1801. 1am still surrounded with blessings spiritual 
and temporal. The friends here both in town and 
country, are kind and we spend our days in peace, and 
the work of God prospers in different places in the 
Cireuit. Many are stirred up to seek the Lord, and 
some have found peace. A goodly company have been 
added to the society. I find class and band meetings 
exceedingly profitable. 

1807. We have once more returned to onr old friends

Whitby, Feb. 11, 1826. 
Mr Taft, 


Dear Sir, 


You requested me to give you some account 
of my religious experience, and public labours in the 
work ofthe Lord. I have given you some brief outlines 


_ of the Lord’s gracious dealings with my soul; and of 
‘pur various travels and success in the great work in 


which my dear husband has been called to labour ; you 
will easily perceive that I have studiously avoided 
speaking of my poor labours in the work of the Lord ; 
the reason of this is—I have done so little, that it is. 


‘not worth a name or place among those holy and use- 


ful females, who have laboured much in the Lord. I 
have no doubt there are some now, as well as in the 
Apostle’s day, that are called by the Lord to speak in 
his name. Mrs. Fletcher, Mrs. Crosby, Miss Hurrel, 
Mrs. Taft, and some others, have been eminent in 
their day for piety and usefulness, and many no doubt 
will be their crown of rejoicing in the day of the Lord. 
Mrs. Crosby I was well acquainted with; she often 
visited us at Whitby, and was made very useful both in 


her public and private labours here, and in the neighs.

ourhood. My method, as you know, was to give a 
word. of exhortation after my dear husband had finished 
his. sermon, or to pray, as 1 felt led by the spirit of God: 
and I must say, the Lord has owned and blessed my 
feeble efforts, ‘to the spiritual profit of some precious 
souls.—To God be the praise. Wishing you much 
success in all:your endeavours, for the glory of God. 
With love to Mrs. Taft, accept the same from A]

MADAME LA BARONNE DE KRUDENER. 


Tne ministerial labours and extensive usefulness, 
the deep piety and unbounded liberality of this woman, 
for upwards of sixteen years, has been the cause of 
pleasing astonishment, and unceasing thankfulness, 
to thousands of pious Christians of various denomina- 
tions. The great head of the church, whose way isin’ — 
the whirlwind, and his footsteps in the great deep; 


4 


whose prerogative it is to save souls from eternal death; 
and who is pleased to choose his own instruments 
accomplish his gracious and benevolent designs 5 | 
indubitable proofs, by clear and infallible signs folloy 
ing, that this greatly gifted, and highly exalted fe 

was his honoured instrament to do a great work int 
world. She was not disobedient to the divine » 

but entered the field of labour and-of conquest ; and she” — 
never quitted the post of duty, however dangerous or 
diffieult, until her divine master .said unto her “ftis 
enough, well done, thou good and faithful ser

enter thou into the poy of thy Lord?’ When we take 
into the account the country in which she was born, 
a land of darkness, and full of the habitations of cruel- 
ty; a land in which infidelity so lately almost univer- 
sally triumphed, with scarcely a ray of gospel light to 
clear the horrid gloom. The manner also in which she 
was educated, taught from reasons earliest dawn, to 
regard, as only essential, those light and vain accom- 
plishments, which were considered as absolutely neces~ 
sary, in order to move in those circles where God was 
dishonoured, and where his religion was constantly 
despised ; where every thing tended to feed the native 
pride of the human heart, and to strengthen all the bad 
propensities of the soul. And yet this extraordinary 
female became awakened to a sight and sense of her 
sin and danger, and sought and found divine merey 
through the blood of the everlasting covenant; and 
feeling an ardent, flaming, burning zeal, to save souls 
from death, was moved by the holy spirit of God to 
follow sinners— 


“With cries, entreaties, tears, to save— 
To snatch them from the gaping grave.” 


She not only actually engaged in the great work of 
preaching the gospel, but was made the honoured in 
strument in the hands of God, to awaken and convert 
to him, great numbers in those dark countries in which 
she laboured, and all this in such a manner as to con- 
vince all who are not blinded hy prejudice, that God 
hath granted unto some of the female sex a commission 
to preach unto the Gentiles, the unsearchable riches of 
Christ. The whole of her experience corresponds cir- 
cumstantially with the experience and call to the great 
work of the ministry, those who have been raised upin 
this highly favoured land. The public papers have 
announced the death of this holy woman; which event 
took place on Christmas day, 1824, at Karasubasar, in- 
the Crimea, after a painful illness, which she bore witi 
great resignation, supported by the full assurance of

“VETTER FROM MADAME LA BARONNE DE KRUDENER, TO 
MONSIEUR DE BERGHEIM, MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, AT 
CARLSRUHE. 


(At the close of last number, we mentioned an inte- 
resting letter from Madame de Krudener, to Monsieur 
Bergheim, Minister of the Interior, with a printed copy 
of which we had been favoured : and we now proceed 
to lay it before our readers. This lady is a native of 
Riga, and having in early life been endowed with 
beauty and talents, she figured away in all the gaity 
and dissipation of Paris. With the circumstances of 
her conversion, which took place about ten years ago 
we are not particularly acquainted. But from that 
period, she has been devoted, we are told, in soul, body, 
and spirit, to the service of her adorable Redeemer, 
whose cause she pleads with an energy that is almost 
irresistible. -We do not mean to deny that there is a 
portion of enthusiasm about her. She considers herself 
to be invested with a special Mission, and therefore, 
wherever she goes she points sinners to “ the Lamb of 
God, who taketh away the sin of the world.” Though 
privileged with a princely fortune, her liberality to the 
indigent is as extensive as her zeal—and her enemies 
say, her generosity exceeds what prudence would dic- 
tate. A character like hers cannot fail of exciting at- 
tention, and wherever she moves she is- surrounded 
with multitudes of the poorer classes of society, who 
listen to her teaching with great avidity. For the last 
three or four years she has been entreated to withdraw 
from almost every town in Switzerland : and the matter 
having been represented to the Diet, she has beem 
under the necessity of appealing to the public in her 
ewn behalf. The following letter was written and pub- 
lished with that view; and callous indeed must be the 
heart that can read it without emotion! Madame de 


HOLY WOMEN. 131 


Krudener is now upon the Continent, what George 
Whitfield, a century ago, was in Britain; and we look 
Sor similar effects from her ministry. She has been the 
successful instrument of arousing thousands from the 
sleep of death, and pointing them to the cross of 
Christ, as the only way to escape from impending des- 
truction. Some particulars in her letter have an illu- 
sion to the deplorable state of poverty and wr-tched- 
ness entailed on the Swiss and German peasantry by 
the late war.) EDITOR.

Sir, 


Prrcetvine myself publicly accused of having re- 
sisted the ruling powers, a thing repugnant to that spirit 
of peace and meekness I recommend to all, afid which 
ought to form the basis of my conduct, I feel myself 
compelled, for the first time, to break the silence I 
have hitherto invariably observed, notwithstanding all 
the injustice, outrages and persecutions to which I have 
been subjected, but which the Lord has given me grace 
to endure with patience, and often with joy. 1 there- 
fore declare, that I have never acted contrary to the 
ruling powers, except when they, by their measures 
have opposed commandments for which I ought to have 
a still higher respect, as coming from God, and to whieh 
it is my duty, even at the hazard of life itself to adhere. 
It is on this account, that notwithstanding the prohi- 
bition of the Bailiwick against affording to any dass of 
Pean an asylum, either at my own house, or rooms 

had hired in the vicinity, and where on the com- 
mencement of my stay in this country, I was allowed 
to shew hospitality, I could not, without criminality, 
on these occasions, have yielded to such injunctions. 
Did you, Sir, but know the calamities by which

with hunger and grief, casting their poor infants at my

could refuse them a shelter. At other times there were

than of man prevailed. 

At other times, (1 recite only facts) came sick per- 
sons, suffering acute pain, but knowing that, by the 
name of Jesus Christ, prayershould obtain them healing, 
At other times pilgrims in their way to Notre Dame 
des Hermits of so great an age, that had I been

sible to send away persons, who either came to me for 
relief, or who arriving at too late a period to persue their

sides, Sir, you already know that none are admitted into 
your country, unprovided with an express License, 
without the payment of a heavy fine. Whenever it 
was practicable and time allowed, I sent to procure such 
License, but distance oftentimes made it impossible to 
do so. Trepeatit, my conduct in any uncivilized re-

ready, Sir, to prove to you, that the actions which 
have drawn forth against me the apprehension of your 
government, were such as I could not avoid, unless I 
had renounced the religion in which I had been edu- 
cated, and which regulates my conduct, and I have too 
high an opinion, Sir, of your virtues, not to feel con-

vinced that you would, in similar circumstances, have

Another particular causing displeasure to the go- 
verament, is, that I did not send away to their pastors, 
such as came disclosing to me the anguish of their 
hearts, and desirous of prayer on their behalf. To 
which accusation I answer, that such persons frequent- 
ly came from a distant country. Sometimes they were 
sent by the pastors themselves ; they were afflicted and 
tormented by remorse, almost to the very brink of 
despair, At other times there were persons who had 
no religious instruction, wholly irregenerate, whilst 
others went not to church, poverty putting it out of 
their power to procure decent cloathing, an occurrence 
which more frequently happens than could be suppos- 
ed in Protestant Parishes. Besides the description of 
persons already noticed, there were also Jews who were 
struck with the excellency and beauty of the Gospel, 
and finally Priests and Pastors themselves, with whom 
I prayed. 

Accustomed for years to have people of every class 
opening to me the profoundest recesses of their hearts, 
and continually sending to Catholic Priests those who 
had lived long without confession, how could I have 
dared to send back the multitudes which I saw visit 
these districts. It was not I who called them. The 
Lord alone could communicate to them, power and 
grace. To him alone it belongs to perform the miracle 
of conversion ; he makes use of whatever instrument 
he pleases in this work. He has appointed none to 
be preachers, but has said, whoever pleases to be his 
disciple, let him forsake all, deny himself, take up his 


‘Cross and follow Him. Then shall he draw souls to 


his divine Master; he shall have the unction of the 
Holy Spirit, and be united to the true church, shall see 
miricles of conversion, and miracles of every kind; he 
shall be covered with opprobrium, with lics and ca- 
Jumnies, shall be hated of the world, and pray for kis 
blind persecutors. Then and not till then, may he be- 
come a Preacher. It is on this account St. Jerome has

He comes, himself, to resume the reins of govern-

He who sits above the Cherubim, and reduces to dust 
the insignificant being that would rise up against Him. 
For a long time he has had compassion on these blind 
people. He is patient because he is eternal, says St. 
Augustine. At length his forbearance comes to an end, 
the audacious mortal who resists him is swept from 
the earth, and the wind of destruction carries him 


_away to the dread tribunal. The time is also arrived 
when the kingdoms of the earth shall cry out, and 


shall be answered only in storms of divine vengeance. 
Yet it is his will, to save such as must be saved. Tt 

is then of himself, the Eternal, we must enquire, (were 

it lawful to do so) why he has still his chosen people, 


why he has still, in the midst of the tumults which 


agitate the world, messengers of peace; why that 
ancient mercy which desires not the death of the sin- 
ner, is still continued ; why, in the exercise of a love 
so vast, so superior to the grovelling conceptions of 
man, he still, as in this language addresses him from 
the Cross, “ My son, give me thine heart,’’ and suffer 
thyself to be snatched from the abyss. 

It is at the foot of that Cross, Sir, I have learnt to 


. smite upon my breast and to love Him. 1 have heard 


that voice which can make the sun grow pale, and which 
disdains not to address man. How could I resist it? I 
have wept over the crime of my ingratitude, in not 
having before loved that God, who called worlds and 


man into existence, only to be subservient to the 
- grand manifestation of his love. From that time forth 


l had no other thought thanchis glory. My only need 
was to love him. 

Hence the appeal, which has been evermore made 
to the hearts of such as are charged with this embassy 
of love, to look to’ heaven alone—to bear away, asa 
torrent, all the souls capable of one day enjoying

heaven—to cause them to renounce in the name of 
their God, the crimes of earth, to see placed in their 
forehead the seal of adoption and of happiness, and to 
leave to earth and hell their portion, consisting of 
hatred, mockery, and outrage. 

After this, let them feel indignant or not, that the 
Lord should have accomplished great things by a wo- 
man. Whether she be hated exceedingly, or accused 
of being too much beloved, is alike indifferent. She 
prays for those of whom it is said, that it were better 
for them that a mill-stone were about their necks, and 
that they were cast into the depths of the sea, than 
that they should distress one of these little ones that 
believe in Him, the Almighty. The love of Him she 
declares to be the great bulwark, which nothing shall 
eventually overturn, and that there is an insuperable 
energy in the faith of these words, “ All which ye shall 
ask in my name ye shall receive.” 

Yes, I have all, in possessing the favour of my God 
—withhold from me, if you can, by any human power, 
those who haye experienced that every prayer of this 
persecuted woman has met a gracious answer.— When, 
six months ago, I was desirous of obeying the orders of 
the government of Baden, which prohibited the re- 
union whereby different disciples of the Lord were held 
together under my protection, I used every effort to 
conceal myself on the days prescribed, in country 
houses ; multitudes of people found me out, notwith- 
standing the extreme desire I felt of enjoying a little 
respite from my labours. 

To the Lord, then, it belongs to command, and te 
the creature to obey. It is for him to explain why the 
feeble voice of a woman has been made to resound im 
the ears of the people, has made so many impious per- 
sons bend the knee in the name of Jesus Christ, has 
stayed the arm of the wicked, caused unfruitful despon- 
dency to dissolve in tears, has sought and obtained by 
prayer, means wherewith to nourish thousands of stary- 
ing persons as in the desert, and has announced in 
these countries alone to more than 25,C00 souls, the

i think I need not say more in the way of justifying

What avail us the so-called luminaries of our age,

or offer them the consolations of the Gospel. I know,

E have announced at his command the great cala- 
mities which will shortly overspread all Europe. 
Abundant testimony you may have to satisfy you of 
my having announced them in many countries, and 
that the disastrous events that has transpired, have 
confirmed the production. 

After what I have now said, you cannot doubt, E 
conceive for a moment, of my never having been led 
from any earthly consideration, to remain in your 
country. Common sense alone, Sir, is, I think, 
suficient, in order to see that men can neither impart 
to me, nor take away any thing, except it be that 
persecution which is the chief paradise of the Christian. 
And from my heart, 1 thank those who have employed 
it against me. It is the broad seal of my mission. 
Aad the Sacred books themselves declare to you that 
the Lord employs women as his mstruments, when he 
is bringing about the deliverance of his people. L 
have Leen resting on no human power. E complain 
not: I have endured outrage and calumny, praying 
and wecping for those who hated me. In following 
the footsteps of God, we have only to leve and suffer. 

I knew before hand all the plot that had been formed, 
in order to carry off the children and old men from 
under my protection. Defenceless indeed they were, 
as to human power, yet guarded by the Most Holy. 
I would on no account quit the post he had confi-

‘ded to me, and in spite of all these wicked machina- 
tions, the angels of the Most High being their guard- 
ians, they are still safe in the dwelling whence the 
Gazette has announced their expulsion. No human 

ower has been able to banish them from it, for the 
ord had sent them thither. True, indeed, a number 
of young people, and in general inhabitants of Switz- 
erland, who could produce every title to respectful 
treatment, were torn away with violence, not to say 
cruelty. They were not permitted to stop a day with 
me: they were driven away, yet not ignorant of the 
motives for their being persecuted ; and it was affecting 
to hear their young voices singing their songs, in the 
midst of the ruffian military which surrounded them. 
But though the Rhine were stopped, the inhabitants 
of the Alps, like the eagle lofty in its flight, have 
sought me out. They knew not even that I was on 
the territory of Switzerland. Thus have they exposed 
themselves to new dangers. 

I have further to remark, Sir, that it is a base false- 
hood, issued by the Newspapers, when they designate 
the multitude as idle vagabonds, at a period when 
none could find employment, when thousands sought 
it with groans, when all manufactures were brought to 
‘astand, by a series of misfortunes overtaking covet- 
ousness and selfishness, but which have taught the 
poor and industrious to seek the Lord, and confide in 
Him alone. For talking of thieves as these journals 
have done, the wonder is that the whole country was 
not over-run with highwaymen. 

Instead of encouraging idleness, Sir, I have de- 
clared it as a matter of reproach, to a city so populous 
as Basle, (the place where I am hated, and where these 
plots have been hatched, of which I have before spoken) 
‘that they have not been more attentive to the interests 
of the poor, and that employment has been diminished 
instead of being increased to them. But the poor are 
lef to. the care of the poor in villages, whilst the rich 
m Basle have the care of the rich. Dependance has 
been placed on certain charitable institutions, which,

in fact have quite extinguished any benevolent dis- 
position that may have existed before. Multitudes of 
needy persons came to ask bread from me, out ofthis 
same Basle, where provisions was said to have heen 
made for all their necessities. I very well knew it was 
quite impossible for any government to provide for all, 

at a crisis of general distress, and had I been intimi- 
dated by reproaches, the Rhine, which swept away 
dead bodies; the black forest which re-echoed the cry” 

_ of the needy, and so many despoiled Cantons, would 
have cited me before the tribunal of God, for having 
revered your authority more than His. a 

Yes, more than once have I wept with distressed 
mothers, have thrown myself on my knees with them, 
more than once prostrating myself before the God of 
the poor, and the God of my heart, have I said to him: 
weeping—Awake, awake, O my God, the dead, since 
the living refuse to obey, refuse to practise that virtue . 
of charity, of mercy, so pleasing in thy sight ! ee 

Where are the St. Vincent de Paule, St. Bernard, St. — 
Francois de Sales, St. Therese, all the souls who bene- 
fitted by such large institutions ? They would aid me 
—but no my God, thou who canst do all things, thou 
wilt aid me. And he does aid me. He alone could 
inspire me with courage not to quit my post. Out- — 
rages and insults, and the danger to which my life was. — 
exposed, affected me not. Faith supported me, but — 
I had to surmount oppression, and the Lord alone 
could give me power to stand firm, and grace to keep 
me from yielding, under so many fatigues, both men- 
tal and bodily. It is a miracle, my voice remains,- 2 | 
and indeed that I still exist, and that calamities so 
numerous have not entirely overcome me. But he 
who well knows whom he calls to his service, both — 
strengthens and fills them with heavenly joy. 

I conclude, Six. It only remains that I take my 
leave, and shake off the dust of my feet, for so hath- 
the Lord commanded.

contained within its walls, and for a long period near

After this, I think I need not defend myself against 
the reproachful insinuations of some, that I had been 
desirous of bribing one of the guards, not to obey the 
orders he had received. No, Sir, I told him to obey 
so far as concerned the sending away of the poor, but 
not to chase them away with violence, and beat them 
as had for a long time been practised around the house, 
nor to use them with a cruelty, which might call down 
upon every country the wrath of the Almighty. We 
‘told this man for the sake of his own welfare, for which 
we prayed, that he himself, if he repented not, would 
be smitten. It has come to pass. Though young 
and vigorous, the hand of God brought him low. - He 
has been seized with an illness, which has caused him 
to reflect seriously upon the state of his soul. 

I declare that in writing these papers, I have had no 
selfish ends in view. My only motive has been that the 
truth misht be known to the public, and that my ene- 

- mies might no longer by public reproaches bring my 
conduct into suspicion, ready as [ am to seal the doc- 

_trine I preach, at the expence of my life—a doctrine, 
consequently to which I owe fidelity in every particular. 
I desire to know nothing save Christ and him crucified, 
to the Jews a stumbling-block, and to the Grecks foolish- 

. ness, but eternal wisdom —eternal power, King of kings 
and of eternity. Iam happy in confessing him here, 
as I have ever done in the face of the people. 

I feel persuaded, Sir, that had the truth been known, 
these things would not have been committed, but 
blindness is nothing but the result of forgetting God, 
and it subjects cabinets, as wellas inferior associations, 
to the most disastrous results,

To the Editor of the Evangelical Magazine. 
Sir, 


I LATELY read in the New Evangelical Maga- 
zine, for February and March last, a letter written by 


the Baroness de Krudener, in her own defence, &c. &e. — 
It gave me a great deal of pleasure to read that letter, as — 
Ihave had the honour of visiting the Baroness fre- — 
quently, during her stay at Memel, in March, 1818, — 
Some parts of her history which I found in that letter, 


she related to me, and as I had always access to her, (ex~ 


cept one day, when the Police Officer refused me ad- — | 
mittance) I had much conversation with her. She was — 


a week at Memel, and left it on the 26th March, 1818, 


for Riga. Madame Krudener appears to me to be © 
truly pious and devoted to God. Humble and desirous ~

of the extension of the kingdom of the Redeemer ; and 
for this she was travelling. She experienced much op- 
position, and the Police attended her very strictly. I 
five seen seven or eight English Gentlemen and 
Ladies refused admittance to her apartments by the 
Police Officers. She met, t believe, much opposition 
from the Clergy, on account of her preaching, founded 
on | Tim. ii. 11, 12. However, I referred her to the 
message giyen te pious women who visited the sepulchre 
which they were to deliver to the Apostles, Matt. xxviii. 
7. Mark xvi. 7. John xx. 17. She immediately point- 
ed to Joel ii. 28, 29. In conversation, I told her that 
every minister that was called to preach the gospel, 
had an ordinary call by the Holy Spirit to that office; 
but that her’s, asa female, must be an extraordinary 
call. She said, “The Lord had pardoned her sins; 
cast them behind his back ; and washed her in the 
blood of Jesus Christ, and sent her on a great mission 
totell Emperors, Kings, Princes. and Governments, 
Rich and Poor, Jews and Gentiles, that Jesus is not 
asleep,” that is that he is risen from the dead, alluding 
to Matt. xxviii. 6, 7. In her exhortations, she speaks 
much of the necessity of the blood of Jesus, to cleanse 
us fromsin. She had a Chaplain with her, who con- 
ducted the worship, (viz.) gave out the Psalm or 
Hymn, and then prayed extempore, and then again 
sung a verse or two. He then begins to speak to the 
congregation by way of exhortation, and in a little 
time after, the Baroness would speak by way of exhor- 
tation only ; Z never knew her preach, but I have fre- 
quently heard her exhort the assembled congregations; 

Both her Chaplain and herself, in their exhortations,

Mrs. ELIZABETH EVANS. 


Tut following short Sketch of the Life and 
Ministry of this Holy Woman is abridged from a Memoir 
of her religious experience, written by her own hand, 
and which will be read with peculiar interest and feeling, 
especially by those females, who have been called to 
the same work, having received similar convictions of 
its being their duty, and who have been tried in the 
same farnace, and who have received from on high, a 
peculiar baptism of the Holy Spirit, to enable them 
toendure the fiery trial; and to rush in at every open- 
ing door, inorder to take the prey from the mighty, 
that the lawful captive may be delivered. But this 
Memoir, will also be read with peculiar emotions by 
hundreds in the Wesleyan Society, to whom the writer 
is personally known and highly esteemed. 

“For a long time Ihave felt it more or less my duty 
to write a short account of my unprofitable life, but 


it is with great dificulty that I make a begining. 
i o 


146 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


However, in the fear of the Lord, and, I trust, with an 
eye to his glory I at last submit to take up my pen. 

I was born at Newbold, in Leicestershire, in the 
Year of our Lord, 1776. My dear Mother, (of whom 


I must speak a little) died, before I was twelve months ~ 


old. She lived to God according to the light she had, 
and always believed that she must know her sins for- 
viven ; but never found the pearl of great price until 
a little before her death. On. the morning that she 
dicd, a Cousin of my Father’s who was in the Metho- 
dist connexion, felt a strong conviction to visit my 
Mother. He set out with all speed and when he ar- 
rived at my Father’s house, he found her as he thought 
dying, he spoke to her concerning her soul, she opened 
her eycs and said the Lord Jesus Christ has sent you 
hither, and she immediately found what she had so 
long been seeking, and almost in an instant expired. 
My dear Father’s name was Thomas Tomlinson, he 
professed himself to be a Churchman and for many 
years expected to be saved by the works of the Law, 
he used to instruct us to fear God and to be honest, 
&c. He could not bear the name of dishonesty or any 
thing that was dishonourable, but he knew very little of 


Gospel Faith, or the plan of salvation, until it pleased - 


the Lord in mercy to afflict him with (I believe) a 
paralytic stroke which confined him to his house for 
nearly two years; meanwhile our dear friends visited 
him very much, and 1 have reason to believe that be 
became soundly converted to God; his last and most 
earnest request was to be buried in the Methodist 
burying ground. Prier to this, prayer-meelings were 
Weld in his own house a year and a half. He was 
buried in the Griffy-Dam Chapel-yard, in the Ashby 
Circuit. ; 
But I must as proposed give some account of the 
dealings of God with my own soul. What Ihave suf 
fered throush the loss of my dear Mother, can only be 
explained in eternity, but ihe Lord’s ways are inthe 
whirlwind, and what we know not now, we shall know 
hereafter. E believe the kind hand of God has been

upon me all the days of my life. I believe the Lord di-

more than fourteen years old, I lived at Derby about 
seven years, with a family that knew very little more 
about religion than myself. We had plenty of prayer 
books, and saying of prayers, but very little heartteit 


religion. Previous to this time, the Lord blessed me’ 


with a little light when I was about seven years of age, 
He blessed me with clear light concerning the nature 
of preaching, I saw that reading was not preaching. I 
thought I could read a sermon and yet I could not 
preach, and it was not the way that God intended men 
to preach his Gospel to read it over like a school-boy 3; 
I was powerfully impressed with a sense of the short- 
ness of time and the awful consequences of dying in 
sin, from the sermons preached in the Methodist 
Chapel, the texts were “In hell he lifted up his eyes,” 
&e. and “ Here we have no continuing city but seek 
one to come.” The conviction never wore off to the 
day of my conversion to God, at this time I was very 
young. The Lord continued to strive with me and to 
keep me from falling into a many grevious sins which 
were both evil and bitter, 1 used to say many prayers 
and strictly examine myself by the law of Moses every 
night. I always felt condemned from these words, “ Thou 
shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain,” 
&c. I saw that he who offendeth in one point is 
guilty ofall. Those words were most powerfully im- 
pressed upon my mind, “Cursed is every one that 
continueth not in all things written in the book of the 
Law to do them,” what to do, I knew not. I wept 
and prayed, and longed to find the living way, though 
I was lost and confused; dark and blind. Oh! how 
1 longed for instruction, but had no one to take me by 
| the hand, or I believe at that time } should have been 
brought to the knowledge of the truth. Oh! how I 
prayed the publican’s prayer, “‘ God be merciful to me 
asinner,” l had some faint views of Christ coming 
into the world to save sinners, but how I was to be 
saved by him, I could not tell, 1 wandered in the dark,

sinning and repenting, for along time ; I removed to

believed if ever I was religious I would be one: but 
I had no acquaintance with any of them until I 
was more than twenty years of age, the tears I have 
shed on this account are known only unto the Lord, 
I had now left service and was at liberty to serve God, 
but I reasoned for a few weeks, with the enemy of my 
soul, I thought I never was happy, but I would be if 
possible; I sometimes went to the giddy dance, some- 
times to card-playing, shameful to tell, after such re- 
peated convictions for sin; but I could not find what I 
sought for, viz. happiness, I only grew more and more 
miserable until Easter Tuesday, which l believe was 
April 18th, 1797. 

The Rev. Geo. Smith was just returned from New- 
foundland, he preached in the Beck Barn, as our 
people were turned out of their Chapel, through Mr. 
Kilham’s division. He took for his text, ‘ Who art 
thou, great mountain, &c.”’ there was a great work 
among the people; many were crying out for mercy ; 
and the Lord’s people were earnestly engaged in prayer, 
and very often they broke out in singing, “ Praise God 
from whom all blessings flow ;’’ I saw no confusion in 
the matter, I concluded that sinners were repenting of 
their sins, as I ought to do; and the people of God 
were so anxious for them to be saved, and these things 
caused them to rejoice. I longed for repentance more 
than ever I did for any thing in my life, but I felt 
great hardness of heart; but while ] was looking to 
Christ, the mighty power of God fell upon me in an 
instant. I fell to the ground like one dead, I believe 
J lost my senses for a season, but when I recovered, 
the dear friends were praying with me, and I was 
trembling and weeping most bitterly. It pleased the 
Lord in about two hours to speak peace to my soul; I 
arose from my knees, and praised God for that oppor- 
tunity. Our dear friends omitted inviting me to a 
class, which might have proved hurtful, if the Lord

had not blessed me with courage, for I knew not one

speakable pleasure. 1 saw I could make a better use of 
my time and money, than to follow the fashions of a 
vain world. 

In a little time the Lord inclined me to read and pray 
much in private, on my knees. Oh! the precious 
seasons I experienced in this exercise. In a little 
more than one year after this, the Lord convinced me 
of the necessity of being sanctified, more sensibly 
than ever I was of being pardoned; 1 sought this 
blessing almost day and night, for even in sleep my 
mind was occupied with this subject. I had many 
fears. concerning it. I thought if I got the blessing 1 
should loose it again, besides 1 was not prepared for 
it, &c. But under the prayer of that man of God, Mr. 
Bramwell, I was enabled to lay hold on the blessing, 
and to sink into the purple flood. I held this blessing 
with atrembling hand, and was enabled to grow in 
the Grace wherein I stood, and to rejoice in hope of a 
greater glory ; still pressing after the fullness of God. 
For itis one thing to be emptied of sin, and to feel 
nothing contrary to love; and another to be filled with 
the fruits of righteousness ; I experienced many deep 
baptisms into the spirit of God. T saw it my duty to 
be wholly devoted to God, and to be set apart for the 
master’s use; and after many struggles, thousands of 
tears, and much prayer, with fastings, I did enter into 
a glorious liberty. 1 could truly say I am crucified with 
Christ; I live, yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. O 
the blessed deadness to the world, and to every thing

HOLY WOMEN. 


Mrs. SARAH STEVENS. 


as 


ts 


- Tue subject of this memoir was born at Bristol, 
in 1770. Her maiden name was Willis. Her parents 
were pious people, and members of the Methodist 
Society. She possessed an excellent spirit, and was . 
truly devoted to God and his work ; and endowed with 
talents and grace that would have been an honour to 
any christian, in the purest ages of the christan church. 
The line of public usefulness, in which she was led to 
occupy the talents God had given her, seems to have 
been in—leading classes, exercising in public prayer, 
and in exhortation ; in all of these she was eminently 
useful. Her husband being mach afflicted with the 
asthma, she was not only a great comfort, and an ex : 
cellent nurse to him, but also a peculiar helpmate in 
many important branches of his public calling—she 
laboured with him in the gospel, and sometimes laboured 
for him, when infirmities rendered him incapable of ex- 
ercising in the public functions of his ministry. She 
frequently travelled with her husband into the country 
part of the circuits ; and on these occasions, she fre- 
quently stood up after Mr. Stevens had finished his 
sermon ; and would give an exhortation with great judg- 
ment, and with much zeal, tenderness, and affection ; 
which seldom failed to produce visible, and in many ` 
cases lasting effects. Indeed some are now living, and 
no doubt many are gone to heaven, who were brought 
to God, through her instrumentality. There is a 

P2 


160 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


short memoir of the life of Mrs. S. published in the 
Methodist Magazine, for the year 1820, page 46, 127, 
chiefly extracted from her Journal.— She was admit- 
ted into the society,” says the writer, “April 9, 1786, by 
Mr. J. Brettell—Her talents in this early stage of her 
christian experience, were uscd for the benefit of others ; 
for she visited the sick, instructed the ignorant, and 
directed the wanderer in the right way. “God seemed, 

from the beginning, to have disciplined his servant, ii 
reference to the place she had to fill in society in future 
life. In the summer of 1788, Mr. Stevens visited 
Bristol. His object was to meet Dr. Coke, on Mission- 
ary business, and found Miss Willis actively engaged 
in doing good. She was then steward of a society of 
females, whom she had collected together; whose 
office it was to visit the sick in hospitals and prisons, 
with other distressed objects, principally confining 
themselves to women ; instructing, praying with, and 
relieving them from their little fund. On their first 
seeing each other, Mr. S. was struck with her person, 
(which was comely) but much more with her mind, 
which had been cast into the mould divine. A union 
of affection at that time took place; and after some 
time, were married.”’ 

In Mr. Steven’s journal we find the following sen- 
tence.—* Here,” (Isle of Guernsey) “it pleased God 
greatly to bless my dear wife, during her stay with this 
artless people ; she grew much in grace, and was made 
a blessing to many. Inthe Island ‘of Jersey she formed 
a society. for the relief of the sick and poor, which 
gave the visitors an opportunity of communicating re- 
ligious instructions to those in distress. With her 
little company she visited the hospital, the prisons, 
and the soldiers’ barracks; and some of the most 
wretched of the female characters she brought with her 
to the house of God.” 

Some little account of the part Mrs. Stevens took, 
and her usefulness in the work of God, is noticed in a 
Jetter from her husband to Dr. Coke.—They then 
travelled in the Oxford Circuit.

December 12, 1791. 


Rev. and dear Sir, 

_ I know your spirit exults in the prosperity of 
Zion; to our great joy God is visiting this city in a 
remarkable manner, by the out-pouring of his spirit 
upon the people. Yesterday Iadded nine to this long 
barren society. The Lord seems much to honour 
prayer meetings, which are established in diferent 
parts of the city ; the people flock to them with great 
earnestness, and are so remarkably affected as to 
cry aloud for mercy.—This condescension of our ado- 
rable Lord, appears to be in answer to the prayers of 
a few, my dear wife has collected together, at five. o’ 
clock in the morning, to wrestle with God for Zion’s 
prosperity. They hold prayer meetings in different 
parts of the city. The praying few being headed by 
a woman, excites the attention and curiosity of the 
people; and her soul being animated by the good 
done, and the prospect before her, has filled her with 
zeal and labour, which I am at times suspicious will 
considerably impair her constitution, if not end her 
days. The congregations are greatly increased, and 


the power of God is with us, 


Yours affectionately, 
2 es WM. STEVENS. 


At this time the travelling preachers were not at 


Oxford more than three or four nights in six weeks, 


so that very few of the pastoral duties could be attended 
toby him. In a society, such as that at Oxford was, 
with few leaders, and those without much life in their 
own souls, we see what a valuable helper Mrs. S. prov- 
ed, and how greatly the Lord owned and blessed her 
efforts to advance his glory among the people. She 
was also the means of establishing a select band, which 
was made a blessing to many.

In 1795, they removed to the Bridlington Circuit. 
On entering upon which, she, in union with her good 
husband, established a prayer-ineeting. In these meet- 
ings, she took a principal part. 

November 1, she writes in her diary in reference to 
these meetings: “ We had a very numerous congrega- 
tion this evening at our meeting for prayer: my soul 
was uncommonly drawn out for the salvation of their 
precious souls ; I found a great nearness to the throne of 
grace ; and hoped we should have had a great out pour- 
ing of the Spirit of God in the awakening and conver- 
sion of many souls; yet nothing particular appeared : 
thus the Lord exercised our faith and patience.” 

In every Circuit, she was active in establishing 
bath band and prayer-meetings at six o’clock in the 
mornings. 

February 6, 1796, she says, “ I bless God for his life 
and power in my own soul; the prosperity of Zion 
lies near my heart. The conversion of precious souls 
is that which I most long for. My heart is grateful to 
the Lord, that he has in any way used me for the 
benefit of others. The Lord is indeed doing a great 
work among us in this place: many souls have 
turned to the Lord, and obtained mercy. At present 
my hands are full with two classes, three bands, a
