BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


MADAME PERROTT, 


Was a Preacher of the Gospel for several 
years, and one of the first Methodists in the Jersey 
Island. From the information I have received, she was 
eminently pious, and also a pattern of christian meek- 
ness, sympathetic kindness, and fervent charity. She 
lived as every Christian ought to live, near the foun-. 
tain head of eternal felicity, and partook largely of the 
streams of that river which maketh glad the city of God. 

Being delivered from the fetters of unbelief, and from 
the galling yoke of sin; and enjoying the liberty of 
the children of God, she felt a strong desire that every 
son and daughter of Adam might be made free also. 
For this she prayed, and, so far as lay in her power, 
for the accomplishment of this, did she incessantly 
labour. She saw the “World laying in wickedness,” 
and well knew that “ The wages of sin is death.” She 
looked on the fields, already white for the harvest, and 
perceived thousands of precious souls dropping into 
eternity unprepared for the tremendous concerns of 
the world to come. And though she saw but few, ex- 
ceedingly few, who cared for these immortal souls, yet 
she could not look upon them and remain an idle spec- 
tator. She felt the constraining love of Christ to 
rescue these perishing im:aortal spirits from the way of 
destruction. Nor did she think that she could stand 
acquitted before the awful tribunal of Jehovah, unless 
she made an effort to. save sinners from the flames of 
an eternal Hell. She did so, and the word was made 
both quick and powerful, sharper than any two-edged 


s. @ em” ‘on ees em a 


a eee ee ma ee Eee ee 


HOLY WOMEN, 171 
sword. In the hands of God, she became a mighty 
opponent of the prince of darkness, and opposed with 
all her might his malignant and hellish desigus. 

It is not to be supposed however, that Satan would 
be a quiet spectator, and view this attempt to de- 
molish his kingdom, with indifference, although it 
was made by a weak and unusual instrument. No! he 
well knew that attempts like these, made out of the 
common way, are in general attended with very 
serious consequences to his cause and interest, and 
therefore demanded on his part the immediate adoption 
of such measures as should most effectually suppress 


these irregularities. 


The grand enemy therefore made a mighty effort to 
maintain his usurped authority over the hearts and 
lives of the people, by stirring up his servants to per- 
secute and abuse this pious woman in her great and be- 
nevolent work. But in the face of all opposition and 
danger, she pursued her way. 

Madame Perrott preached the word of life to all who 
would hear, in private houses, both in town and 
country ; and while thus engaged she was sometimes 
pelted with mud, and otherwise very roughly and 
cruelly treated. Once, if not oftener, she barely 
escaped with her life. If I am correctly informed, she 
once went into France for the express purpose of teach- 
ing sinners the way of salvation, and of inviting them 
to the marriage supper of the Lamb. In this visit, 
which she believed it wasthe will of God she should 
undertake, her pious labours were crowned with success 
and the Lord gave her a satisfactory evidence that she 
was not out of her place, but fulfilling his righteous 
will. She was the means of the conversion of an Inn- 
keeper and his wife, if not more during her short stay 
in that country. And were these the only fruits of 
her labours as a Preacher of the Gospel, she would re- 
ceive the glad word of “ Well done! good and faithful 
servant enter thou into the joy of thy Lord.” But she 
was made a great blessing to her relations, and even her 
grand-sons were some of her spiritual children. After

Miss MARTHA WILLIAMS. 


MartHa WiiiiaAmMs was born at Nottingham, 
and her parents died when she was very young. At 
an early period she became a subject of divine grace. 
She had a distinct recollection of the opperations of 
the holy spirit of God, when about four years of age ;

the chapel in Hallifax-Lane, Nottingham. Under the 
word her soul was deeply awakened, and she sought 
redemption in the blood of Christ. 

From the time of her conversion her mind became 
deeply impressed with the immense value of immortal 
souls ; and this impression led her to attempt to save 
her fellow mortals from the “ opening, the almost 
closing jaws of damnation.” 

Hence she took up her cross, and went from house 
to house, attended prayer meetings, visited the sick, 
entered workhouses, garrets, cellars, and prisons, in 
order to seek out the most desperate cases of human 

etchedness, and to make known the Saviour of sin- 
ners to such as were perishing for lack of knowledge. 
Nor did any outward circumstance delight her more 
than to see sinners awakened, and to hear them cry 
for mercy and salvation. 

In these humble and pious attempts to do good, 
she continued to exert herself for some years, when 
the great Lord of the harvest called her to a more en- 
larged sphere of action and usefulness. 

In the year 1814, a revival of religion broke out in 
Nottingham, under the ministry ofthat eminent servant 
of Christ, Mr. Gideon Ouseley, an Irish Missionary: 

In this revival many precious souls were freed from 
the fetters of sin, and from the way of destruction. 
The soul of M. Williams also received a deeper baptism 
of the Holy Spirit. So powerfully was the arm of the 
Lord revealed, and such was*the influence which at- 
tended his word, that she says, (in a letter which lies 
before me) “I was constrained to cry—Lord enlarge 
my heart, or my happy soul will break through its 
eumbrous clay, and take its flight to Glory.” “It 
was at that time,” she continues, “ and under that ine

The sacred ministry has for its object the conversion 
of sinaers, and when this object is thereby accomplish- 
ed, it is certainly the best proof which can be given, 
that the instruments employed are divinely authorized. 
Martha Williams saw this great end accomplished, and 
was encouraged to proceed, and to abound in the work 
of the Lord. 

Like most of her sex, however, who have acted in 
the same way, and from. similar convictions, she 
speaks of having to contend with opposition and dis- 
couragements. But the service in which she was 
engaged was the service of God ; and his all contrelling 
arm opened her way to a still wider range of usefulness 
aud labour. Since the year 1819, she has travelled 
through six or seven of the largest counties in Eng- 
land, proclaiming salvation in the name of Jesus; 
the“ Lord working with her, and confirming the word 
with signs following”? 

In every part where she has laboured, sinners have. 
been regenerated and made new creatures in Christ 
Jesus; and several of them have died in the faith, and 
their happy souls are now before the throne of the 
Eternal God.

Miss ELIZABETH HURREL. 
a 

Ir is much to be lamented that the Christian 
Church has not been favoured with an account of the 
experience and labours of this extraordinary female, 
She was one of those whom Mr. Wesley honoured with 
his correspondence and personal encouragement. She 
preached many years with his approbation and sanc- 
tion. Under the ministry of that servant of God, the 
Rev. Mr. Berridge, of Everton, she was awakened from 
the sleep of sin, and was soon after brought to an ex- 

perimental knowledge of the truth as it is in Jesus. 
_ Here we discover the nature of true repentance. Tt 
is achange of mind. Itis a revaulted sinner returning 
back from sin and Satan, from the world and self, to 
God his original happiness and rest. It is the prodi- 
gal coming back to his father’s housesand family. 
Hence, in the nature of things it implies Godly sorrow _ 
Jor sin, This sorrow and distress of soul is in propor- 


176 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


tion to the views and convictions we have concerning 
the perfections of God, our obligations to him, how - 
far, and how long we have wandered from him ; of the 
views we have of the sinfulness of sin, the aggravating 
nature of our guilt, impurity and danger. Of these 
things, the subject of this memoir had clear views, 
hence her repentance, was deep as well as sincere, 

Before she experienced the pardoning love of God, 
she partook largely of the bitter herbs of Godly sor- 
row and genuine repentance. Rest is sweet; more 
especially to the labouring man. It is a painful sense 
of the want of any blessing that enhances the value of 
it. A state of health is endeared to us, and valued by 
us in proportion to our afflictions. It is the hunted, 
parched, thirsty Hart, that desires the cooling, refresh-. 
ing water brooks; and it is the*burdened, weary, 
heavy-laden soul, that desires spiritual rest; and in 
proportion to our trouble and burden, is the sweetness 
and pleasure of our rest. When Miss Hurrel felt deli- 
vered of her burden of guilt and sin, she felt a joy and 
peace which passeth all understanding ; and with it an 
earnest,desire that others might partake of the joys of 
salvation. Having given herself to the Lord, she en- 
deavoured, from the overflowings of her benevolence, 
to bring others to him. She travelled through many 
counties in this kingdom, preaching the unsearchable 
riches of Christ; and the Lord was pleased to make 
known by her the riches of his grace, wherever she 
went. Many, very many, were, through her instru- 
mentality, brought to the knowledge of the truth. And 
not a few of these were afterwards called to fill up very 
honourable stations in the Methodist connexion, Some. 
were useful class-leaders—others local preachers—and 
several travelling preachers. Mr W. Warrener, who 
was the first missionary appointed by Mr. Wesley to 
labour in the West-Indies, and Mr. Henry Foster, who 
travelled seven years in our connexion, and died in the 
ies, were brought to God through her instrument- 
ality.

Mr. John Lancaster, who was a very acceptable and 

useful local preacher at Pickering, and afterwards at 
Burlington, was also converted under her ministry. 
These were brought to God nearly at the same time, 
and in the same neighbourhood.. This eminent female 
was rendered very useful in this part of Yorkshire, as 
also in Lancashire and Derbyshire. 
_ She was naturally of a cheerful and communicative 
disposition, and having improved and stored her mind 
by reading and study, she became a very desirable and 
useful companion to those whose spirit and temper 
were congenial with her own. Mr. Wesley, Miss 
Bosanquet, Mrs. Crosby, Mrs. Gilbert, Miss Rhodes, 
Mrs. Dobinson, Mrs. Mortimer, and many others of 
a similar stamp, found an agreeable companion and 
correspondent in Miss Hurrel. Nearly all these are 
now arrived— 


“ Where all the ship’s company meet, 
Who sail’d with the Saviour beneath.” 


But they being dead, yet speak ; their works follow 


them. And as these female worthies were preeminent, 


in the esteem of God and his church, on account of 
their privations and sacrifices, religious attainments, 
and glorious exploits ; and as their names are still dear 
to many, this feeble attempt to rescue from oblivion 
the sacred shreds of departed worth, will doubtless 
revive a pleasing recollection of former times and cha- 
yacters ; and perhaps prove a stimulus to those who 
are but babes in knowledge and experience, to emulate 
and copy their exccilencies. 

It is very much to be lamented, that she ever re- 
laxed, or in any’ measure buried that extraordinary 
talent God had committed to her; but such was the 
fact. The principal cause, or causes of this, are not 
known to the writer of this memoir. Some have attri- 
buted it to the influence some persons ‘of property had 
over her, who were opposed to her public labours, and 
that she gave it up to retain their confidence and friend-

ship; others have supposed that the loss of some con- 
siderable property at Whitby, and the effect it had 
upon her mind was the occasion ; while others suppose 
she sunk beneath the heavy cross connected with the 
public exercise of females, especially a female of such 
tender and delicate feelings as she possessed. Whether 
she turned aside from the path of duty to avoid suffering, 
to gain her friends, or through the power of temptation, 
or from whatever cause, she deeply lamented her un- 
faithfulness herein, when death and eternity stared her 
in the face. Indeed for some considerable time she 
was overwhelmed in anguish and distress, little short 
of black and dark despair. ‘* I am going to die,” said 
she, “I am entering the eternal world, but all is dark 
before me ; neither sun, moon, nor stars appear, O that 
1 had my time io live again, I would not bury my talent 
as I have done.” It pleased the Lord, however, before 
she departed hence, to lift upon her the light of his 
countenance. He saw the genuineness of her repent- 
ance, and he healed all her backslidings, and enabled 
her to bear ample testimony to his Almighty power to 
save to the uttermost. She died in London.

. Miss Hurrel was rather of a delicate frame of body, 
a woman of great simplicity, and integrity of mind ; 
she was warmly and invariably attached to the whole 
economy of Methodism. She possessed a wonderful 

` ability of conveying her ideas and feelings, with scrip- 
tural accuracy, and often manifested such strength of 
thought, and felicity of expression, as were irresisti- 
bly impressive. Her public labours were abundantly 
owned of God, and many will be her crown of rejoicing 
in the day of the Lord Jesus.

Miss ELIZABETH DICKINSON, 


_. Of Staveley, near Knaresbrough, in the West- 
Riding of Yorkshire, was a young woman of extraor- 
dinary character and genuine piety, from the time of 
her conversion to the day of her death. Her mother, 

R 


182 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


who was a pious woman, and died in the Lora ; during 
her life, and especially in her last affliction, gave to 
Elizabeth, who was then very young, such counsel as 
left deep impressions on her mind, but they were ‘as 
a morning cloud, and as the early dew” that goeth 
away. She soon gave place to: the vanities of the 
world, and sought for happiness in pleasurable amuse- 
ments, in dress, and trifling company: she became 
fond of cards and dancing, and being engaging in her 
appearance, and open in her disposition, many young 

ersons of both sexes sought her acquaintance. It 


pleased the Lord by his spirit powerfully to operate> 


upon her mind, and bring to her recollection the ious 
sayings and excellent advice of her mother, and her 
own vows and resolutions, insomuch that she became 
extremely unhappy. The arrows of the Lord began 
to stick fast in her soul. and to use her own language, 
« she began to think, Oh! what will be come of me! 
what a sad thing it would be if I should die and not go 
to heaven :” she then forsook all her companions, put 


off her unnecessary apparel, abandoned every thing 
that was evil, and retired into secret and betook herself 
to reading and prayer. The distress of her mind for 
several weeks was only known to God and her own 
soul. It pleased Him, however, in his infinite mercy, 
to set her soul at liberty, and she then rejoiced exceed- 
ingly in the God of her salvation. The distress of 


mind this young woman laboured under when convin- 
ced of sin, had greatly weakened her delicate frame, 
from which debility it appears she never fully recovered. 
After she was delivered from the bondage of sin, and 
brought into the liberty of the sons of God, she had 
some such wonderful revelations of the invisible and 
eternal world, that many will find it difficult to believe, 
but the following circumstances are related to convince 
any who may be inclined to doubt the truth of those 
things which were revealed to her. It was made’known 
to her, the time when she was to die, and it was fulfilled 
in that she died at, or near the time in which it had 
been revealed to her; when she set off) from home oR

“From the time this young woman was truly 
awakened and converted, to the time of her death, her 
spirit and temper, words and conduct, were becoming 
the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. As she thought 
it was her duty to preach, and exhort sinners to repent, 
and turn from their sins; and in doing this she fre- 
quently referred to her visions or trances; there were 
many who could not receive her testimony, and nota 
few who were truly pious, that thought she was under 
an awful delusion. But multitudes attended her ministry; 
for the wonderful story, was circulated far and wide ; 
and many came from a great distance to her, so that 
she could hardly get any rest day or night. She 
retired to several places for a little rest, but hundreds 
followed her, and heard the words by which they might 
be saved. During the short time of her ministry, 
many were converted through her instrumentality.” 
The writer of the above account says, “Her only 
motto was holiness to the Lord. She has often said

Mr, Bryan Proctor, of Pannel, a person well known 
and highly respected in the Methodist connexion for 
his piety, usefulness and stability, had one daughter 
awakened, and converted under the ministry of E. 
Dickinson. who was taken ill about a year after her 
death. Miss Proctor’s affliction was a consumption, 
during which she was very happy in God. The last 
night of her life Henry Cullingworth, a pious man 
and a class leader, who lived not far distant, was one 
that sat up with her. When he was returning home 
about four o’clock in the morning, with a lighted 
lantern, it being in the depth of winter: as he walked 
over Mr. Proctor’s meadow, suddenly a light shone 
around him, which eclipsed and seemed to put out the 
light derived from his lantern; he looked up and saw 
four angels, in company with Betty Dickinson, whose 
Jace he saw as clearly, and knew as perfectly, as he did 
while she was living, and she had a golden girdle about 
her loins. They were flying swiftly in the direction of 
Mr. Proctor’s house. The next morning he heard that 
Miss Proctor died soon after he left her, The whole 
of this account is certainly very extraordinary, and not 
a few will be ready to cry out in the language of the 
inspired Apostle, “ O the depth of the riches both of the 
wisdom and knowledye of God! how unsearchable are 
his judgments, and his ways past finding out.” 


BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Mrs. MARTHA ROUTH, 


Was one of the Society of Friends, commonly 
called Quakers. She was born at Stourbridge, in 
Worcestershire, the 25th of April, 1743. And died 
in London, on the 18th of July, 1817, at the house 
of one of the friends, of the name of Bailey ; and was 
interred in the friends’ burial ground, at Bunhill-Fields, 
aged 74 years, forty-five of which she ministered in 
holy things.—The following are extracts from her 
Biographer. 

“ It appears from her narrative, that as early as her 
fourteenth year, the mind of Martha Routh was awful- 
ly impressed, after many months of deep exercise, 
with a sense of duty, under the Divine requirings, to 
appear as a minister, and tell to others what the Lord 
had done for her soul; but giving way to fear, and to 
an apprehension that it was impossible for her, at so 
early an age, steadily to practice those things to which 
she would be required to exhort others, she lost ground 
through disobedience. 

‘About my twenty-sixth year,’ (she writes) ‘our 
dear and honoured father departed this life. He had 
been an approved Elder in the church many years.— 

It was not long before another deep and weightier 
exercise, the work of the ministry was again set 
before me. The necessary preparations and restric- 
tions were clearly presented, when I experienced in 
deed and in truth, that “ Strait was the gate, and nar- 
row the way that leads to life ;? and found I was still 
unwilling to enter on those terms; though any thing 
short thereof, I thougit I could be resigned to, even 
to be clothed in sack-cloth, if it was required. But 


HOLY WOMEN. 189 


this was not the sacrifice called for, My heavenly 
director saw meet to carry on his own work, and to 
lead me gently forward ; though I went heavily on my 
way; finding, at times, the exercise of my mind to be 
so great, that I seemed disqualified for the usual and 
proper attention to the children; (she keeping a board- 
ing school) but when school hours were over, I retired 
and poured out my soul in’ secret, with many tears, 
that my Alinighty helper would be pleased to show me 
with clearness, what I should do and what I should 
leave undune.—The spirit of prophecy was given 
both to servants and to handmaids: those who came 
from far, as well as those who were near, clearly pointed 
out ny state in public ministry ; and some of them 
told me afterwards, they could have laid their hands 
on my head; but I kept as close as it was possible 
from any discovery on my part, till my-health became 
so impaired, that I was not able to stand; and at 
length | was confined to my chamber and bed; a 
skilful Physician having done his utmost for me te 
little purpose, and those who kindly watched with me 
in the night season, thought I could not continue 
long. 

One night my sister sat up with me, and seeing her 
bathed in tears, I asked her why she was so sorrowful. 
She replied, “ How can I be otherwise, when I am 
likely to loose thee, and be left alone.’ Her tried 
state so much affected me, as to cause me to make 
some disclosure, for the first time. I then said to her, 
« My dear sister! my sickness is not designed, by the 
great Physician of value, for the death of the body ; 
if that would have been accepted as a peace offering, 
thankfully could I have resigned it: but resignation 
to the Divine will. in a way more trying to my nature, 
is what is required, and what I have been struggling 
under, till I am brought thus low.” Her tender so- 
licitude was such as might have been expected to be 
felt by une, so nearly interested in my welfare every 
way. Shesaid, she had been fully aware, with inany 
others of my friends, of the deep exercise I had long

been under ; but as I had never opened the subject to 
her, she was backward and fearful of mentioning her 
thoughts to me. 

Having afresh entered into covenant with a 
covenant keeping God, willing, through his Divine 
help, to do what he required of me, my recovery be- 
caine speedy, beyond all expectation. ————————— 

Many times did the current of ministry so flow 
towards me, in ‘an encouraging manner, that my soul 
at times seemed melted within me ; and I think through 
no instrument, more evidently pointed, or with more 
consolation, than through that worthy handmaid, 
Frances Dodshon. How had she to proclaim as on 
the house top, the secret sentiments of my heart, in 
offering up for- sacrifice, all but the one thing required ! 
but, in this, “ I pray thee have me excused?” She 
was, till then, an entire stranger to me, but after- 
wards became a near and intimate friend. ———— 

———-Our justly valued friends, Mary Ridgway and 
Jane Watson, being at Nottingham, on their way from 
the yearly meeting, both, but especially Mary, were 
so evidently led to open my state, and administer to 
it, that I was afraid all in the meeting would know 
who was meant. 1 think this proved the breaking up 
of my controversy; for I was.so brought down and 
humbled, in deep self-abasement, that when I got in- 
to my lodging room, I was constrained to fall on my 
knees, and to offer vocally the resignation of my will, 
to. the will of my Heavenly Father: that if He would 
be with me in the way I should go, and send me to 
“ say to the north, give up,’ and to “the south, keep 
not back,’ I would obey his holy commands. Seon 
after this offering, my bonds were broken, in the ninth 
month, and 29th year of my age, in our first day 
morning meeting ; though as little expected by me at 
that time, as at any preceeding one. 

-lI was soon again and again called upon, 
to bear further testimony to the Divine requirings, 
but my reluctance was yet so great, that I was plunged 
into unutterable distress ——-—-————— 


HOLY WOMEN. 191 


About a year after my first appearance in public 
ministry, the friends of our monthly meeting, united 
in receiving me as an approved minister, of which an 
elder was desired to inform me, and to request my at- 
tendance at the next select meeting. I often 
visited my dear and much tried friend, Ruth Fallow 
of Castle-Donnington, and sometimes accompanied 
her to a few neighbouring meetings. She was a true, 
living, gospel minister, and her company was helpful, 
encouraging, and edifying.” 

On the 7th of August, 1776, Martha Winter was 
married, in the Friends’ Meeting-House, at Notting- 
ham, to Mr. Richard Routh, of Manchester; and re- 
moved to his residence in that town. The Memoirs of 
her life and travels published at York, 1824, contains a 
long account of her labours and travels, with her com- 

nions, in different parts of this Kingdom, Ireland, 
Dunkirk, and several visits to America. A few more 
extracts will be given from her Journal. 

In 1795. We find her in America. She writes, 
“Qn third day morning I left Bedford, and, accom- 
panied by William Rotch and his wife, to attend the 
Yearly Meeting for New England, held on Rhode 
Island. Ata Tavern on the way, we had the satisfac- 
tion of meeting my endeared fellow labourers from Eng- 
land, Deborah Darby and Rebecca Young, which I 
believe was felt to bea solemnly effecting, season for a 
considerable time ; and much contrition spread among 
us; that I have scarcely known the like. What most 
deeply impressed my own feelings, was the renewed 
humbling sense that we poor females. were found 
worthy of being commissioned with such embassies to 
adistant land and to become fellow sufferers in. the 
bonds of the Gospel. In our united labours, through 
the various sittings of the Yearly Meeting, the strength 
of Israel being our hope, we were rendered a comfort 
to one another, and made at seasons joyful in the 
house of prayer, in fellowship, with the living members 
of the Church, in every rank of the family.

Second of Eighth Month, First day. Friends of 
Goosecreek were desired to meet at ten, to give us: 
time to attend another meeting in the evening, ten 
miles distant, which they readily complied with. When 
we got thither the house was so full, and many out of 
doors, that it was difficult to get in. A sense of the 
compassion of the Shepherd of Israel was soon feelingly 
raised in my soul, and gospel power renewed, to the in- 
formation and humbling, I believe, of many minds, 
with bodily strength to go through the exercise ; 
having to stand about an hour and a half, with the heat 
very great. To the Lord alone belongs the praise of: 
his own Works. 

Twelveth of Twelveth Month, First day. _(Charles- 
town.) The last meeting we sat, was in the evening and 
requested for the black people, and such of their em- 
ployers as chose to attend, in the City-Hall, a very 
large commodious room for the purpose, which was 
nearly filled. The instruction given to the Apostle 
Peter, * What God hath cleansed, call thou not common,” 
&c. impressing my feelings, with Gospel authority, I 
stood up, and humbly trust, spoke as the Spirit gaye 
utterance. A becoming attention appeared given to 
the illustration ; yet I seemed as if standing among 
scorpians, and when the subject turned in a few sym- 
pathetic expressions, towards the peculiar objects of 
that meeting, tending to draw their aitention to what 
might further open in the line of instruction to them, 
a person stood up, who appeared of high rank, and 
said, “ Madam! I am sorry to interrupt you; but as 
my office is the care of the police of this city, I must 
desire you to stop; for what you say is against it, and 
will not do.” 

I was favoured meekly, but with firmness to reply : 
“If thou wilt please to have patience, until I have dis- 
charged my duty, I believe thou wilt neither have cause. 
to be hurt, or to be sorry that thou hast done so.” 
He then remained silent, and the meeting ended in 
solemn supplication to that Almighty Being, who is 
no respector of persons.

Divine regard, was an open instructive opportunity. A

forgotten by her. ‘They were by profession Baptists. 

1796. Thirty-first of First Month, First day.. We

Many black people attended these meetings, to

designs against those who never belonged to them, in 
taking up, imprisoning and selling men, women and 
children, whom friends have set free, and settled on 
their own plantations, to work for themselves. The 
hearing of which with many aggravating circumstances, 
hath brought nature and spirit into deep mourning,

At eleven the Public Meeting for worship came on

had a short but living testimony to bear. On his clos-

gospel Truths to the different states of the people ;

two-edged sword, against the iniquitous traffic of 
buying, selling, and_ evil treating the sons and 
daughters of men. Through the arising of His 
power, who binds Leviathan, the crooked serpent, the 
spirits of such were chained, so as to make no opposi- 
tion ; though I was afterwards informed, that divers were 
present, who made it their particular business to buy 
and sell the black people. I humbly trust many minds 
were made thankful to the blessed Author of all good

I wished it might be mentioned, that my. concern was

which was accordingly inserted in my certificate.”

_ © Our beloved friend, Martha Routh, was born at 
Stourbridge, in Worcestershire, the 25th of fourth 
month, O. S. Her parents, Henry and Jane Winter, 
were steady religious friends, from whom she had the 
advantage of a guarded education; and, through the 
merciful visitation of our Heavenly Father’s love, religi- 
ous impressions were early made upon her tender mind. 
As she advanced in years, the same Divine power fol- 
Jowed her; by which she was preserved from a many 
evils which abound in the world; and as she subinit- 
ted tothe further discoveries of the Divine principle of 
light and grace in her own heart, she was made an ex- 
perimental witness of its cleansing and sanctifying 
operations. 

About the seventh year of her age, with the appro- 
bation of her father, her surviving parent, she removed 
to Nottingham ; where, first as an assistant, and after- 
wards as principal, in a boarding-schvol for Friends’ 
children, she manifested much concern and watchiul 
care for their preservation and religious improvement. 
= She had for several years been impressed with a view 
of being called to the work of the ministry ; and in the 
thirtieth year of her age, she first appeared in that 
service. In the year 1775, in company with that valu- 
able minister of the gospel, Ruth Fallow, she visited 

_the meetings of friends in some of the Northern Coun- 
ties, and Scotland. In the following year, she was 
married to Richard Routh of Manchester, and became 
a member of that meeting. After her settlement there, 
with the concurrence of friends she visited, at different 
times, the meetings in this Nation, Scotland, and 
Ireland, also those in the United States of North 
America,—labouring diligently in that couitry for three 
years ; and on her return, brought satifacitory certiti- 
cates of her services there. 

When at home, she was a diligent attender of meet- 
| ings for worship and discipline; and was therein fre- 
> quently engaged to labour for the promotion of truth 

and righteousness. Indeed, this our beloved friend, 
was eminently devoted to discharge whatever she be~

lieved to be required at her hands, whether at home’or 
abroad. . 

Unwearied in promoting the cause of truth, a: good 
example of plainness and christian moderation ‘in her 
manner of living, diligent in visiting the widow, the 
fatherless, and the afflicted, whether in body or mind; 
with whom she was a sincere sympathizer, having often, 
to such, communicated a word of comfort; also, ac- 
cording to her ability, she extended pecuniary assist- 
ance to those who were in need. 

During the winter in which she died, her bodily 
strength was on the decline; yet she continued to be 
diligent in attending meetings. Jn the fifth month she 
left home to attend the yearly meeting in’ London ; 
and was favoured to perform the journey without much 
apparent fatigue. Soon after her arrival there she be- 
came unwell, but was able to attend most of the sittings 
of the yearly meeting. Her illness increasing, she was 
confined at the house of our friend, Simon Bailey, in 
London. 

During the time of her confinement, which was about 
seven weeks, we are informed that she did not commu- 
nicate much, but sufficient to evince that she centred 
on the Rock of Ages; though at seasons under great 
conflict. Her utterance was very feeble and broken, so 
that it was difficult to preserve the connection in what 
she expressed; yet in substance it was strong and 
lively. Toafriend she said, her mind was fast anchored 
in the Beloved of souls ; at another time said, “ I want 
my fellow pilgrims to know, that there is a rest for thé 
people of God.” 

Alluding to her many and close provings by sea and 
land, she rejoicingly acknowledged, that she witnessed 
a state comparable to a morning without clouds. At 
another time she said, “I have known many plunges, 
I think the end cannot be far off.” And the repeated 
solemn request to those about her was, “ Crave the 
release of my spirit in the Divine will, and not other- 
wise.” Her departure was scarcely preceptible ; a short 
time previous to which there was a sweetness on her

countenance, and a prevailing solemnity, which was a 
support in that awful season, to those present; and we 
have no doubt that she has entered into that rest pre- 
yared for the righteous. 

= She departed this life, the 18th of the seventh month, 
1817, at the house of Simon Bailey aforesaid ; and 
interred in the Friends’ burial ground at Bunhill-Fields, 
‘on the 25th, after a solemn meeting at Devonshire- 
House ; aged 74, and a minister near 45 years.

God, her convictions for sin, and distress of mind con- 
tinued, yea, rather increased, partly on account of con- 
flicting passions, arising from a sense of duty to her 
parents on the one hand, and her obligations to God 
on the other: she felt her mind strongly drawn 
towards those means of grace and salvation, which had 
already been made the power of God to the awakening 
of her soul. After much prayer to God, and earnest 
entreaty she prevailed with her parents to permit her 
for one evening to go and hear a sermon, she esteemed 
this a great favour, and rejoiced as one having obtained 
great spoil. She went to the house ef God weeping; 
praying that the Lord would meet her in his ordinance ; 
in this she was was not disappointed. The preacher 
was led that evening to preach a sermon exactly suited 
to her state of mind, and while he was shewing the 
mercy of God to penitent believers, she was enabled to 
believe on Christ, as delivered for her offences, and: 
raised again for her justification : she returned home 
rejoicing in the God of her salvation. For some time 
she enjoyed that peace which passeth all understanding 
and experienced that joy which is unutterable and full 
of glory. But this was not of very long continuance ; 
for through unwatchfulness, evil reasoning, and the 
power of temptation, she lost her confidence ; and sunk 
into a state of unbelief—she lost her liberty, and fell 
into bondage—she lost her peace of mind, and again. 
laboured under guilt. She continued in this state for 
in weeks; but no words can describe the anguish and 
distress of mind she suffered during this time; she 
knew the value of that salvation she had Jost, and she 
determined by divine grace never to rest until the Lord 
restored to her the joys of his salvation. She could 
scarcely either eat or drink, work or sleep : indeed for. 
the most part she was upon her knees, pouring out her 
soul to God in fervent prayer.—One day she took the 
Bible praying to the Lord for direction, and opened on. 
Isaiah, xli. 1, 10. which she was enabled to claim for 
berself as from the Lord. Immediately her former 
peace and joy were restored, and she again rejoiced im 


HOLY WOMEN. 201 


God her Saviour. Soon after this she opened her mind 
and related her religious experience to a Member of the 
Methodist Society, who invited her to meet in class ; she 
did so, and feeling her soul much blest in that means of 
instruction and edification; she soon after became a 
Member of that Society. 

In her eighteenth year she became leader of a class, 
andthe Lord was pleased greatly to bless her endea- 
yours; and feeling an increasing love for perishing 
sinners, and an earnest desire for their salvation, she 
yentured in public to give a word of exhortation, which 
the Lord owned with his blessing. She began to feel 
this more and more her duty : indeed the salvation of 
her own soul seemed closely connected with her striv- 
ing to save the souls of others; she becamé greatly 
alarmed at this, especially when she considered her 
want of judgement and ability ; on this ground she en- 
deavoured to excuse herself, and stifled those convic- 
tions, until the anguish of her soul became intolerable. 
In this state of mind, she passed through many 
wearisome days and sleepless nights. She had no 
peace until she consented to exhort sinners to repent 
and turn to God: so soon as she obeyed God in this, 
her peace returned. She is never so happy as when 
exercising in these labours of love, knowing that this is 
the will of God concerning her. Hitherto the Lord has 
owned her labours, hereby testifying that she is not de- 
ceived. She is now in hertwentieth year. 

While holy and zealous women of this description, 
who only live to glorify God, and to benefit their fel- 
low mortals on earth—who follow the openings of 
divine providence, the calls of the church, and the lead- 
ings of the holy spirit—into whose sacred breasts the 
design of making a trade of godliness never entered, 
looking for their reward only in heaven; and while the 
divine approbation is undeniably stamped on their 
pious efforts—Ought they not to meet the encourage- 
ment and support of every person who fears God and 
has love to man ? And ought we not to deprecate that 

power which would put a stop to, or silence them: and

Mrs. HANNAH HARRISON, 


Was a woman of an excellent spirit, of amiable 
manners, ardent piety, and burning zeal to promote the 
glory of God. From early life she was instructed in 


204 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


the doctrines, and precepts of our holy religion. Hav-

she willingly devoted. her talents to the duty of her 
holy calling, and it pleased the Great Head of the 
Church not only to qualify her for those duties, but to 
bless her with many seals to her ministry, For this she 
laboured, and for this she lived. The late Rev. John 
Atley was awakened under her ministry. She held 
many public meetings at Malton, and jn that neighbour- 
hood ; one of our aged and respectable friends, fre- 
quently speaks of the pleasure and profit, he and others 
derived from these opportunities. ‘There were very 
few persons in those days who made any profession of 
religion, and as there was considerable disgrace and 
persecution attached to all who met together for divine 
worship, in any place except the Church, it was not 
ikely, that her conduct could have been influenced by 
any other motive than that of sincerity and affection. 

The latter part of her life she spent in London, but 
was accustomed, during the summer season, to make 
excursions into the country, and her visits were accept- 
able and useful, till it pleased God to deprive her of her 
natural sight. The Lord raised her up many friends, 
some of these were in the highest walks of life, by whom 
a regular annuity was allowed her. The Rev. Mr. 
Wesley considered her, as possessing most exalted 
piety, and communion with God. In a letter to Miss 
A , he says, ‘Hannah Harrison is a blessed 
woman. I am glad you had an opportunity of con- 
versing with her; and why should not you enjoy the 
same blessing ? The Lord is at hand.”

Miss DOROTHY RIPLEY. 


Tuis extraordinary Female is a native of 
Whitby, in the North-Riding of Yorkshire, and has 
been engaged in preaching the Gospel, in this King- 
dom and in America for many years. Her manner of 
procedure is very singular, and if we admit that she 
is doing what the Lord requires at her hands, she 
must have received an extraordinary call from God. 
On this subject there will be a diversity of opinions, 
the author is inclined to believe that she is eminently 
pious and devoted to God; as her labours have been 
abundantly owned with His blessing. The following 
is a sketch of her religious experience and ministerial 
labours, with extracts from her correspondence, taken 
from a work published at Whitby, entitled “ The 
Bank of Faith and Works united, by Dorothy Ripley, 
citizen of this world, but going above to the New 
Jerusalem. second edition, 1822.” 
as My only motive for publishing these 
travels, is to disseminate the Gospel of our Lord Jesus 
Christ, and to do good among the indigent, where 
my lot is cast by the providence of God._—— 
. As I am nota member of any community, no society 
can answer for my irregular conduct; neither do [ 
wish to apoligize to the world for my procedure. 

Duty to my Maker excites me to faithfulness, know- 
ing that life is the time to work for God; that I may 
be counted worthy to reign with the Father, Son, and 
Holy Ghost, in “The city of the Living God, the 
Heavenly Jerusalem.’ 

It is twenty years since I became a citizen of this 
world ; travelling up and down, here and there, for 
the benefit of my fellow-creatures, whom I feel allied

Forty-three years have rolled into eternity since L 
bore the name of Christian, or in other words, witnes- 
sed the remission of sin, through the name of Jesus :

Wound ; a Cordial for my fears.’ 

Were it possible to settle now, I fecla disposition 
to indulge my friends, and also to free myseli from

to nation, and cities, towns, and villages around; but 
my Master Jesus leadeth me forth to gather souls for 
His Kingdom; and who dare say to Him, What doest 
thou? or, Whether goest thou ? 

In crossing the Atlantic eight times, God 
has been my supporter, preserver, and deliverer, there- 
fore my desire is, that all would follow on to believe 
in Him, that they may experience His boundless love, 
also to know Hg is their Father by the spirit of 
adoption, 

As many have lent me their helping hand in the 
time of extremity, so many have tried to degrade me 
by propagating falsehoods to my disadvantage: but L 
have looked upon them as being duped by Satan, and 
could say with my Master Jesus, ‘ Father forgive them: 
for they know not what they do’ 

I sum up the whole by saying, should this be the 
means of assisting any one to serve the Lord better, 
give Him the thanks: for He is the guide of my life, 
and hath directed me to speak forth His praise, to 
honour Him in my day and generation, which is fast 
passing away ; for I have dwelt in this state of muta- 
bility fi‘ty-five years; and am waiting for my change. 
It is good for me to be here: ‘ For me to live is Christ, 
and to die is gain.’

When the meeting was ended, my friend came up to

infinite love of the Father, not interfering concerning 
their doctrines of Universalism, as I was only to declare

Another dpportunity was given out for this day week,

As soon as I came from my labour of love, I crossed

Episcopal Church; worship beginning at six. It was 
a precious time to my soul; because | faithfully warn- 
ed the rich, by testifying ‘What shall it profit a man 
if he gain the whole world, and lose his own soul ?” 
‘The power of Jehovah was felt, and many went away

permit. —— ' 


New-York, sixth month, 1805. $. 


THis week I have spent in the alms-house, 
among. seven hundred men, women, and children. 
Five times I went there, and had three meetings with 
such as were able to collect together, where they have 
worship; and then I went from room to:room, consoling 
the blind, lame, deaf, and sick, who were rejoiced to, 
see me; while the lame and blind went after me, from, 
one place to another, till I was astonished at the love. 
they manifested. How good was my merciful Master, 
to furnish me with such power and strength, as was. 
communicated to my soul, through the medium of the. 
Holy Ghost. 

——_———_——— I feel satisfied with my labour of love: 
this day, having faithfully warned and encouraged all 
to come and wash in the cleansing blood of our Lord 
Jesus Christ, who hath saved millions of vile sinners, 
whose reiterated crimes must have doomed them to.

Great debility of body has rendered it impossible for

New-York State.—Vernon,

——— Every day brings me nearer the mansion of

in His sight! No cross, no suffering shall I decline,

His holy fire burns up the dross of sin. that remains

influence is poured forth all around this world, while

or devour.:

——— 14th eighth month, 1805. 


Samuel Kirkland, a Presbyterian Missionary to the 
Oneida Indians, called upon me this day, to give me 
an invitation to his residence. 

As l had made the best of it that I could, 
strength was given me to evidence to all present, that 
I feared none but the living God, saying in the midst 
of my subject, ‘Moe! be to me, if I preach not the Gos- 
pel, feeling as my day of suffering was, my inward 
peace and power abounded, which was a fresh manifes- 
tation of the Father’s love unto me, and a confirniation 
that I still moved in the line of my duty. When the 
meeling closed, six persons came unto me, to request 
f would go with them, each having a horse; but I was 

as much at a stand to know, how I should dispose of 
myself after meeting, as to comprehend how I should 
obtain admission among them.—One cried out, ‘ You 
must go with me,’ another, ‘She shall go with me; 
and my friend Samuel Kirkland, the Missionary, said, 
‘TI bave come six miles for her, and will not be excused 
from taking her to my house: therefore she must come 
with me; for J have promised to take her to Oneida 
next sabbath, as Skanando, the old Chief, will not be 
satis ied without her.’ 

The contest was finished, and I thought I was richly 
rewarded for my faithfulness, having exhorted them to 
be ready for the approach of the Bridegroom, who 
would come in such an hour as they thought not of. 
As I went home with S. K. we had a very solemn 
ride, and our tears flowed reciprocally y for the Lord 
our God had been with us in ten thousand dangers, 
where death threatened us in the most poignant man- 
ner. He said, ‘I have been a minister forty years, 
twenty of which have been spent amongst the Indians, 
living among them for their benefit. When my lot » 
was flret cast “there, I was fixed with the best man they 
had, who died a few days after ; which they attributed 
to me, and were determined to have revenge, life for 
life. I was commanded to fall asleep, and a fire was 


HOLY WOMEN. 213 


prepared ; bat while they were all round me, I kept 
singing hyms, trusting in God to deliver me; yet they 
often said, < Go to sleep, why do you sing? And at 
last one of the Chiefs was wrought on, and made an 
affecting speech, signifying—that, ‘ This brother had 
fallen down a few steps short of their forefathers, and 
because he had fallen short a few paces, were they 
to kill a white brother for it?” saying, ‘It will bring 
innocent blood upon our nation if we kill him : there- 
fore they hearkened unto this Chief, and I was marvel- 
ously delivered from the jaws of death.’ 
A large number assembled on the 17th 
for worship, who had come, from two to ten miles 
yound this neighbourhood; but having no other place 
better than a school-house—when it was full, the 
people came and requested me to go out in the open 
air, to accommodate those who had come so far. I 
therefore got into a cart, and lifted up my voice with 
authority, and said in the words of my Lord and 
Master, ‘Let your light so shine before men, that 
they may see your good works, and glorify your Father 
which isin Heaven.’ I was much favoured with the 
presence of God ; for this opportunity required great 
fortitude, as I never was before called to stand out in 
the open air, exposed to the burning sun, though I 
screened myself as well as I could.- 

A meeting was held again in Stockbridge, for the 
instruction of the poor Natives, who are dear to me. 
There are some of the Jersey Indians among this tribe, 
and the whole number here, is rising three hundred, 
which information I got from A. S. their minister. 
This day two of the Missionaries and a young Clergy- 
man were present, while my soul was earnestly engaged 
for the good of the Indians.” ———~ 


THE FOLLOWING IS AN ADDRESS 


From the Women of the Muhheconnuk Nation of 
Indians, written on their behalf, in their native 


214 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


language, and translated into English by Captain 
Hendrick, one of the Indian Chiefs, and presented 
to Dorothy Ripley, on her departure Jrom amongst 
them. 


Dear Sister, 


We, the poor women of the Muhheconnuk 
Nation, wish to speak a few words to you, to infornd 
you, that while our forefathers were sitting by the 
side of their ancient fire-place, about eighty years ago ; 
our father, the Rev. Mr. Sergeant’s father, came 
amongst them with the message of the Great and Good 
Spirit, which he then began to deliver'to them, He 
was the first Minister of the Gospel that ever preached 
to our fathers, and the Great and Good Spirit blessed 
his labours, by which means many of our poor Natives 
were turned from darkness to light. 

Our ancestors loved their Minister, wlom they 
looked upon as a father, because he was willing to 
live and die with them, 

Sister, we will also inform you, that since our father, 
Mr. Sergeant’s father died, he began to manifest a 
compassionate feeling towards our dismal situation; 
he in the first place began to teach us to read and write, 
‘this he did several years; after this he then began to 
deliver the word of the Good Spirit, and his labours 
have been blessed, by which means we who are com- 
monly called by the white people, Squaws, are en- 
quiring the way to Zion. l 

Sister, while we were sitting by the side of our fire- 
place here, we saw you coming, and when you opened 
your mouth, we believed you were sent by the Great 
and Good Spirit to visit us poor of this Island. We 
feel thankful to Him that He has put such a iove in 
your heart, that you were willing to deliver His mes- 
sage tous. We thank the Great Good Spirit that He 
has protected you on the way, and that you arrived 
here in safety, 


215 


HOLY WOMEN. 


Sister, in behalf of the rest of our women, we now 
heartily thank you for your kindness, and for the pains 
you have taken in visiting us. 

- We hope, by the help of the Great Good Spirit, we 
shall ever remember you, and the good words which 
you delivered to us. Although we do not expect ever 
to see you again, yet we believe that the Lord Jesus is 
able to help us, that we may hold out unto the end, 
that we may see you among His sheep on His right 
hand, where we shall never be parted again. May the 
Good Spirit protect you on your way, “that you may 
have a pleasant journey unto the end, farewell.

Vernon, July 26, 180°. 


A Lavy from England, by the name of Dorothy 
Ripley, was introduced to me by a gentleman, who 
came passenger with her in the mail stage, for the 
purpose of preaching to the Oneida, and the neigh- 
bouring Indians. On Sunday, the 28th, I had ihe 
pleasure of introducing her to a part of the Oneida 
‘Tribe, called the Pagan Party, who believe not in 
the Christian Religion, but in worshiping the Great 
and Good Spirit, by sacrificing and dancing. Iin- 
formed the Great Chief that she had come a great way 
to preach to them. ‘This Chief is called Blacksmith, 
and is a complete savage in every respect, and very

“fuvious to the white people; but in this instance

scemed well pleased with her visit, and expressed him-

A Letter from an Indian Squaw Woman, addressed to 
Dorothy Ripley, and received when in America. 


Dear Sister in the Lord, 


I BELIEVE that there is but one, the living 
and true God, and that He is the maker and preserver 
of our lives, and upholder of all things here below, 
and that He sent his only begotten Son into this 
world to be the Saviour of mankind, and that all 
those who believe and confess the Lord Jesus with 
their mouths, and believe in their hearts, that God 
the Father of our Lord Jesus did raise him up from 
the dead, shall be healed by His stripes, as thou hast 
very well observed to us; and I hope and pray to God ~ 
that thou mayest be the means of stiring up our strong 
hearts to turn unto Him, the living and the true God, 
and that the words which thou hast dropped among 
us may make deep impressions upon our hearts. 


HOLY WOMEN. 


t Sister, be pleased to pray for us, that we may 

_ be enabled through divine assistance to worship God 
in Spirit and in trath, I fully believe that thou art 
sent by the Great and Good Spirit into this part of 
the world to do good to thy fellow creatures, to preach 
_the gospel unto every kind of people; and although 
many are led to believe that it is not the duty: of a 
woman to preach, still I pray God that thou mayest 
not be discouraged, there being many infalible proofs 
in the Scriptures, of women Jabouring in the Gospel ; 
one great encouragement is, our Lord Jesus appeared 
to a woman first, after His resurrection. I hope, 
therefore, my dear sister, thou wilt keep on in thy 
gospel labour, and may that Great and Good Spirit, 
Who is able to protect thee by His Almighty Power, 
through all the changing scenes of this life, guide thee 
by His Word, and bless all thy endeavours—that thou 
mayest be preserved through all thy trials on this earth : 
and finally that we may meet when our day’s work 
is done here, at the right hand of God the Father, 
amongst the lambs of His fold, never to part again, 


which is the sincere prayer of thy sister in the Lord— 


CATHARINE QUACHEMUT.

Brother, enough has been said ; what is you wish ? 
tell us plainly! do you want money to repair the 


breach, and heal the wound made in your heart? or: 


do you prefer a confession from the young man, who 
thus insulted you, and a request for your forgiveness, 
promising before all the Chiefs, that he will never do 
the like again? and can you on these - conditions, 
freely, and from the heart, forgive him? if so, the 
Chiefs will be responsible for the young man.’ 

The latter proposition was accepted ; a notable and 
generous confession was made by the young Indian, 
and he received the full pardon of the white man, to 
the great joy of all present.” 


“I feel very languid with riding twenty-two miles in 
the stage, yet have appointed a meeting in the Pres- 
byterian Church, which I held to great satisfaction, 
many people attending through curiosity, which I hope 
will be profited, and my soul free from their blood.—— 

A person of the name of Alexander, who keeps store 
here, invited me to sup and lodge ; thus the Lord still 
follows me with earthly mercies, which makes me pass 
over many insults; and I had rather ten thousand 
pierced me by vile reports, as myself be found once in 
the practice of evil. 

A kind Quaker, who heard me in Agusta, gave me 
one dollar, which is the second I have received during 
five weeks, and. I have relieved three or four with it. 
This friend attended a meeting before, and spoke ad- 
mirably from the € Dry bones in Ezekiel,’ which after 
he had done, I arose and sanctioned it, as life and 
power were in the testimony.———I was induced to 
supplicate the Throne of Mercy, for preservation, and 
an increase of faith and love for each,—and then en- 
deavoured to conclude the meeting: but a Methodist 
Preacher requested I would permit him to say some- 
thing to the people, which I was free to do, and he, 
with tears, told all present, to treasure up what they 
had heard; for in Jesus Christ, male and female were

Letter from Abigacl Eames to Dorothy Ripley. 
New-York, September 3, 1805. 


Dear Dorothy, 


THe earnest solicitude which I at all times 
feel for your temporal, spritual, and eternal welfare, 
induces me again to make use of pen, ink, and paper, 


Å HOLY WOMEN. 223 


to manifest the real regard which I at all times feel for 
you; earnestly wishing that every dispensation of 
Providence, whether merciful or afflictive, might ter- 
minate in the furtherance of your faith in the Gospel 
of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ: therefore, my 
dear sister, let us go forth without the camp, bearing 
His reproach, knowing that we have here no continuing 
city, but we seek one to come; a city which hath 
foundations, whose builder and maker is God. O my 
dear sister! I do choose rather to “ suffer affliction 
with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasure of 
sin for a season”? And I am well persuaded this is 
your choice likewise, or you never would have laid 
down all that is near and dear, and become a stranger 
in a strange land; to endure hardness, and censure, 
and reproach, and pain, and weariness, and want, 
unless for Christ and the Gospel’s sake. But my 
precious friend, take the prophets and apostles, who 
have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example 
of suffering and of patience: behold! we count them 
happy which endure; therefore, do you endure, my 
dear, and that patiently, and a rich reward shall be 
given unto you ; for all your troubles and trials here, 
will only make you richer there, when you arrive at 
Home. 


But my dear, now it is that we have many 
painful sensations to pass through ; to part and meet, 
and meet and part: but by and by, if faithful unto 
death, we shall meet to part no more for ever; but 
spend a happy eternity in praising God together. 
And as the Poet sweetly sings,— 


“There on a green and flow’ry mount, 
Our weary souls shall sit ; 

And with transporting joys recount, 
The labours of our feet.” 


And though your unwearied diligence, and labour of 
love, and faithful obedience in the gospel vineyard of 
our Lord Jesus Christ, in travelling far and wide, to 


224 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


try to bring poor lost souls into the fold of Christ, 
may entitle you by promise, to a high mansion, in 
our Heavealy Father’s House; and I in my small way 
to a lower; yet humbly trust, that like Heavenly 
visitants, we shall often meet, and. sit and tell the 
wonders of His love; while new scenes of unthought 
of pleasures, will be for ever unfolding to our view.- 

I subscribe myself your constant real sympathizing 
friend, and well-wisher, 


ABIGAEL EAMES.

Letter from Dorothy Ripley to Abigael Eames. 


On board the Victory, “11th ninth month, 1805. 
My Dear Friend, 


Last night, when we came at the fort, three 
miles from Boston, the officers ordered us to return 
back to the Hospital for a pass, we being from New- 
York, and the fever having broke out since our 
departure. We felt it trying, to trace back through the 
water four miles, to ride quarantine, off at Rainsford’s 
Island, but, submission to the will of God must at all 
times be accomplished; yet how hard it is to say, on 
all occasions, ‘Thy will be done? As clay in the 
Great Potter’s Hand, I am laying soul and body, 
to fashion and form as He pleases; therefore I shall 
know what is His mind respecting me; for I dare not 
desire any thing contrary to His wisdom, or 1 am 
punished with my request, which I dread as much as 
His displeasure, 

Thou will be anxious for my return, sooner than it 
is possible for me to come, though I move as swiftly 
as I can that I may finish my work on earth by noon. 
These holy breathings are from His Spirit, who groans 


~

within me, for the Kingdom of Christ to come, with 
power, into the hearts of such who laugh at the idea 
of the Father giving His only Son to die for miserable 
sinners The death of Jesus Christ is mysterious to 
millions, because ‘No man can call Jesus Christ 
Lord, but by the Holy Ghost ;—let us then walk as 
the wise, not as fools, seeing our works shall be made 
manifest before all nations, when the Judge shall 
reveal every secret thing, which has not been brought 
to light, to the justification of the righteous and final 
condemnation of the wicked.—————— 
aa Thy midnight watches for three weeks, 
“and sympathetic tears on my account, (when exhausted 
with my. Gospel labours) demand my utmost solicitude 
for thy growth in the hidden life, which my efforts 
shall not be wanted to promote. - = 
— I pray the Father to sanctify us, soul, 
body, and spirit, that we may testify to the world, we 
are His adopted daughters, who through His might 
overcome all our combined foes, the world, flesh, and 
Satan’s host, who are watching the door, if happily 
they may gebt entrance, when we are supposing our- 
selves securely guarded by Prince Emmanuel, who 
requires us to wait at the door-post for directions, and 
keep from sin of every nature, seperating ourselves 
especially from the unholy, least they contaminate us 
with their pollutions, which they indulge themselves 
in, glorying in their shame, because their deeds are 
evil. I conclude with a hope of boundless bliss for 
us each, trusting in the Redeemer’s mercy to accom-

DOROTHY RIPLEY. 


Off Rainsford’s Island, on board the Victory, 
12th ninth month, 1805. 


_. An unexpected calm possesses my soul this 
day ! laying in the hands of the Almighty with resig- 
nation: He seeing meet to confine us here by His 


226 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Providence, to answer His purpose of shewing us, that 
all seasons are in His power, and that we can only 
move at His pleasure, or through His direction, hold- 
ing all His messengers of vengeance in subserviency, 
to do His offices of justice at any moment, when the‘ 
measure of their iniguities are filled up, as Jehovah 
hath wailed with long-suffering love for many years; 
that they might be their own accusers in the day of 
retribution. 

Submission to His divine authority I labour for with 
all my might, and I find a growing in the Lord. 

I long to live every moment for eternity, as it 
appears the grave waits to receive me, and this hand 
which my pen occupies, must become a feast for the 
worms, and the admirable bones crumble into dust, 
that they may-return into their original state; that 
God may form an immortal structure like unto His 
body, which being glorious, did not see corruption, 
because it was begotten through the power of God, of 
incorruptable seed, and appointed to be the first fruits 
of them who are fallen asleep. Roll on ye fleeting 
moments which hasten my departure from a scene of 
sorrow, to the transcendent joys of yonder bright 
world, where glorified spirits reside, worshipping their 
Maker with incessant praises, which they learn from 
the Angelic Throng, who have reverentially adored 
the Author of their spiritual existence, from the bles- 
sed era when they first were fashioned by His wisdom, 
for His praise. ; 

A bliss like yours, suits my immortal spirit, that 
seems like a spark of celestial glory, derived from His 
immense divinity who quickens all with animal life, 
as well as with divine. The uninterapted peace will 
come, then silent sorrow shall be rewarded with life- 
everlasting, and a long holy-day of pleasure, will 
compensate for scorn, poverty, reproach, and a variety 
of sufferings, which a christian’s life is surrounded 
with, while in this state of mutability. In full and 
certain hope of this ecstatic joy I close the day; 
looking for immortality by the spirit of Jesus Christ, 


HOLY WOMEN. 227 
whose I am, and whom I have revered from the dawn 

of life, in this terrestrial globe, which shall be dissolved 
"by fire, at the coming of my God, when the Heavens 
and Earth shall pass away with His refulgent beams.”

Dear Friend, 


i How pleasant is the thought of dwelling 
with Jesus our merciful Redeemer. Dear friend, an 
evidence was given me lately, that we should stand 
firm in the Lord, abounding in His knowledge ; patient- 
ly waiting before Him, to worship Him acceptably with 
‘spiritual obedience. I long for an increase of His Holy 
Zeal, to possess the soul of my precious fiiend, whom 

“Fieel cemented to, by the attracting charms of the 
love of the Father.——— 

Come hither with me continually ; wash 
in the fountain, that there may not appear any spot 
on our raiment henceforward ; then we sbail join hand 
in hand, urging our way to our eternal rest, that 
awaits us when we put off this corruptible robe, the 
covering of the soul. Perhaps one will outstrip the 
other, and gain the reward first, which the Father 
dispenses to every welcome guest, my race is not fin- 
ished, though I long to stand unclothed before Him, 
whom | love with intense desire, such as one would sup- 

= pose a mortal creature could not possess. Many times 

>. say, Iam ripening for eternity, and shall soon receive 

“from Him, “ Well done good and faithful servant, thou 
hast been faithful over a few things; enter thou into 
the joy of thy Lord ;? but at other seasons it appears 
that my work is only begun, though I wish my sun to

I believe I am an heir of life ; and often hear 
the songs of the spirits of the just, who once like us 
were pressured with flesh and blood, which they have 
left behind. Ten years ago, or more, an intimate of 
mine addressed me thus, “ If I go home to Glory first, 
I will visit you, if God permit,” and as she determined, 
so she has many times performed her promise in vocal 
music, or on a stringed intrument, but not such as we, 
(in that day) were delighted by ; and with astonish- 
ment I have silently revered the Maker of us both, for 
His condescension to me a worm. In justice to my 
aged friend, I say, if ever there was a spotless bride, 
I believe she was one, when her spirit returned back 
to God, which was three months after our engagement 
was fixed, she died suddenly, by a lethargic disease, 
that had grieved her Heaven-born soul many years, 
being cumbered with her fleshly house, and blind for 
fifty years: yet how fine her sentiments were !—how 
quick her penetration !—noble and generous her heart, 
that was touched with every woe! every new calamity 
that was abroad in the world at large !—angelic in her 
visage, that won my soul, and allied it to her’s, as 
though one mould would fashion us in close communion 
to our God for ever! Every thought of her heart she 
could tell to me; and unburden her soul unto a friend, | 
that admired her mind, richly fraught with useful 
knowledge, that led her to meditate upon Jehovah’s 
vast design, in reinstating man to his Divine favour 
once more. Many years her peace was made with 
God, and as an angel of the highest order, I view her 
now: for her spirit was so divine, that she was not fit 
to dwell with mortals longer ; and very few could pen- 
etrate into her wisdom, it was so sublime. Ah me! 
I am left behind to point poor sinners the way to Cal- 
vary! while she is viewing the beatitudes of the 
lowly Jesus, clothed with His Royal Vesture, as the — 
Sovereign of the world, preparing for battle against 
Gog and Magog; who shall close the year of jubilee, 
when the Saint’s number is complete, and Zion’s 
children are all gathered in from east to west. —-———=

New York, 14th tenth month, 1805. 


«A desire hath arisen in my soul this week, 
that I might clear myself of this city ; accordingly 
it was proposed by a friend, to gather me the inhabi- 
tants together near the Manbattan Well. 

It was asolemn and an awful time.- My text was 
“If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted È and 
if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.’—I sap- 
pose there were present eighteen hundred people, 
notwithstanding all the thousands who were absent on 
account of the fever. I stood and preached for my 
Master two hours.—Retiring into J. E’s house, many 
followed me thither, and would not go home, begging 
for another meeting the same evening, which they 
waited two hours for, standing all-around the windows 
and doors. My strength being a little revived, I was 
willing to stand up again, and had a very precious 
opportunity, with the most solemn part of them, who

‘supply with His grace, and glory, with His life, and

The Author, thus far, has given the foregoing out- 
lines of this distinguished female, and will leave them 
to the reader to mark the end of a life so spent in the 
service of God. 

She has crossed the Atlantic Ocean ten times; and 
is now in America, scattering the seed of eternal life. 

She is well received by professing Christians of 
almost every persuasion, having nearly lived down the 
calumnies of evil tongues. May the Lord preserve her 
as in the hollow of his hand, and if it seem good in 
his pleasure, bring her to her native land, and to the 
bosom of her friends ; and when she has done the will 
of God on earth, may she be gathered home to her 
fathers, with the multitudes of the redeemed of every 
name and colour, whom she has been the instrument 
of gathering into the fold of Christ. 


BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Mrs; MARTHA GREGSON. 

Sue lives at Saham, near Swaffham, in Norfolk. 
Her mother was a pious woman, but died when Martha 
was very young. She was married in the year 1799, 
and it appears was very desirous at that time to obtain 
true religion. She read Law’s Serious Call, and some 
other religious books. In 1817, the Methodist Maga- 
zines were lent her by a friend: she was much affected 
with an account of the pious characters therein record- 
ed, particularly with their happy and triumphant 
deaths. She prayed sincerely to the Lord for direction 
from his word and spirit, respecting her future conduci, 
and especially whether she'should join the Methodist 
Society. She read the word of God for direction, and 
immediately opened on Isaiah Iviii. 8. which appeared 
to her a promise, that grace and glory from the Lord 
would follow such a step. She prayed that the mes- 
sengers of salvation might be sent to the village where 
she lived; and not many months after, they came, 
and she was one of the first who joined the society. 
She received a note of admission on trial, from Mr. 
Moses Dunn, in Jan. 1818.—Since which time the 
Lord has kept her in the good way. 

She soon afterwards felt much affected with the 
awful view she had of the miserable condition of sinners. 
For them she interceded with God in mighty prayer, 
ihat he would convert them to himself. Sometimes it 
was powerfully impressed on her mind to warn her 
fellow sinners of their danger ;—she treated these im- 
pressions, for a season, as so many devices of the 
enemy :—her being a female—her great ignorance— 
and the important character which her husband sus- 
tained—were arguments by which she endeavoured to 
satisfy her mind; and remove these powerful convic- 


HOLY WOMEN. 243 


tions. But the more she strove to resist the secret 
impulse, the stronger were her convictions—of its 
being her indispensible duty to call sinners to repentance. 
The first year, she began to exhort a little, when no 
preacher came. The people being pleased and profit- 
ted, and her own soul being blessed in the work, she 
continued. She has a most useful talent for the work, 
and is very generally received as a messenger of good 
tidings, sent by the Lord. The Preachers also have 
encouraged her to go on in the good work. Her name 
appears in the printed plan for the Swaffham Circuit, 
and likewise in that of the Attleborough Circuit.—She 
has one or more classes committed to her care, In the 
experience of this excellent woman, of which I have 
only given a brief outline, we find that a religious and 
faithful use of our present knowledge, is the sure way 
to increase it unto full salvation, and to be directed in 
that way in which the Lord would have usto go. This 
was the case with the Ethiopian Nobleman; with 
Cornelius; and with Nathaniel. This was the case 
-with the Founder of Methodism :—he was sincere in 
all his researches after truth, and was providentially 
Jed to take those steps, and form those plans which 
have been so wonderfully owned of God. Similar to 
‘those was the case of hundreds, when Methodism arose ; 
they felt the want of rest for their souls, but knew not 
where to find it. They read Burkitt, Henry, Russell’s 
Sermons, the Duty of Man, &c. but found it not. 
To these, the Methodists were the messengers of 
God for good; who formed part of their first Societies. 
So in the case of sister Gregson, the Lord saw her 
sincerity, heard her prayer, and lead her in the right 
way. May she prove faithful unto death.
