BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Miss JULIANA WHITE, 


Or Ipswich, appears to have been brought toa 
saving knowledge of the truth, in the year 1809-1810, 
under the preaching of Mr. Padman ; the Lord applied 
His word, by His Spirit, and deeply wouaded her 
conscience, or as she expressess it, the Lord sent her 
home bleeding with anguish ; and for a fortnight “ the 
arrows of the Almighty stuck fast in. her soul, and 
His hand pressed her sore;”? so that she could not 
forget the wormwood and the gall. But the hand that 
wounded applied the sovereign baim. After she anited 
‘with the Methodists, she went to the class one evening 
in deep anguish of mind, where she disclosed her 
heart, prayer was made for her: and not in vain, the 
Lord heard and answered; the burden was removed 
and hope with some degree of peace sprung up in her 
soul. She hastened home to her chamber, and there 
she gave full vent to the feelings and desires of her heart, 
and throwing herself upon the divine mercy, she felt 
that she was the happy subject of it; encompassed in 
the cloud of the Divine Presence she saw by faith the 
Bleeding Lamb, and heard the soft whisper in her 
soul, “ Thy sins which are many are all forgiven, go in 
peace and sin no more.’ She observes, “ Long was I, 
as it were, rivetted to the sacred spot, bound there 
by inexpressible emotions of gratitude, love, and. praise. 
During a month I continued almost in an extacy, 
carried far above all earthly things; but at the expira- 
tion of which, I was made sensible I had to engage with 
the three-fold enemy, and enter upon a warfare. Soon 
the storm began to beat upon me, whose ruthless 
winds are not yet wholly hushed to rest.’ About 
1810-1811, she began to exercise her talents in public. 


HOLY WOMEN 


- Many providential occurrences, and very extraordinary 
manifestations from the Lord prepared her mind to 
' do His will. 
‘She saw multitudes of her fellow-creatures enveloped 
in sin, ignorance, and unbelief, without God, and any 
saving hope of future glory, and therefore in danger of 
' being eternally lost; she felt great love and pity for 
_them, and ceased not day and night to pour out her 
soul to God in earnest prayer for their salvation. But 
‘she could not be satisfied with this, the Lord require 
something more at her hands, an increasing conviction 
rested upon her mind, that it was her duty to warn 
sinners of their danger, and invite them to “ Behold the 
Lamb of God, which taketh away the sins ofthe World.”’ 

In her first attempts to speak, the Lord gave her 
several seals to her ministry. Since then she has 
been fully employed. The word of the Lord was as 
fire in her bones, a dispensation of the Gospel was 
committed to her; and the ministry of reconciliation. 

- The preachers of the Wesleyan connexion did well to 
give her employment under their direction, otherwise 
she must have united to some other church in which a 
female ministry is sanctioned. . 

In that sphere of action and usefulness, in which 
Divine Providence has called her to move, may she 
long continue to shine, till gathered to the church of 
the first born in Heaven, where she will reap the fruits 
of her labour. 


Miss SAVAGE, 


OF Hornsea, in the East-Ridine of Yorkshire, 
was eminently useful in the Mcthodist conucxion, 
about thirty years ago. Of her first religious impres- 

X3 


246 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


sions, and the early stages of her christian experience, 

I have not been able to obtain any information; but 

as she lived many years in the enjoyment of true 

religion, it is of littke consequence what were the 

peculiarities of her conversion. Such was the ardency 

of her affection for God, that she openly espeused his 
cause, and diligently sought the promotion of his 
glory. And the deep concern she felt for the welfare 

of those who were ‘ignorant and out of the way,” 
led her to the adoption of every measure, which she 

believed was calculated to promote the salvation of their 
souls. In the prosecution of her designs she was not 

over-awed by a mortal’s frown ; but despised the sneers. 
of ungodly men, and followed her Lord through 

honour and dishonour, through evil as well as guod 

report. With an intention to enlarge and establish the 

kingdom of the Reedeemer, she occasionally visited 

the neighbouring villages ; but she did not travel much, 
especially during the latter part of her life. Her labours 
were confined chiefly to the place of her residence, 

where, in a small chapel belonging to the Methodists, 

she generally spoke on sunday evenings, to a crowd of 
attentive hearers: She seldom took a text, but some- 

times said, that such a passage had struck her mind, 
and then made a few remarks upon it. She for the 
most part gave an exhortation, without referring to 

any particular part of God’s word; and it seems she 

aimed more at being useful to her congregations, than 

at the orderly distribution of the various parts of her 

discourses. 

Perhaps the most remarkable trait in the character 
of this pious woman, was her steadfast cenfidence in 
the providential care of her Heavenly Father. Like 
many of God’s dear people, she possessed but little of 
this world’s good ; but she cast her care upon Him, to 
whom she had made an unreserved dedication of all 
her powers. And from an inward persuasion of her 
interest in his favour, she was enabled to say with the 
Psalmist, “The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not 
want.” Confiding in the supplies of an ever-watchful 


HOLY WOMEN. 


_ Providence, she could calmly sing,——- 


Tho’ troubles assail, and dangers affright, 
Tho’ friends should all fail, and foes all unite,— 
. Yet one thing secures us, whatever betide,— 
The promise assures us—the Lord will provide. 


The birds without barn or store-house are fed, - 
From them let us learn to trust for our bread : 
His saints what is fitting shall ne’er be deny’d, 
Solong as °tis written—the Lord will provide,” 


_ And why should we be surprised at finding a soul 
that is wholly devoted to God, expecting from him 
every needful blessing, for both body and soul, for ` 
time and eternity. Those who honour God by relying 
on his promises, shall be honoured of him by a bounti- 
ful supply of all their necessities. None ever trusted 
in him and were confounded. The expectations of 
Miss Savage were fixed on too great and good a Being 
to be cut off. The Lord provided for this child of 
his in a singular manner. When she had little or 
nothing to depend on, but the promises of Jehovah, a 
benevolent lady, with whom she had been acquainted, 
died, and left her twenty pounds a year, for a certain 
term of years; and this legacy, together with the 
assistance of her friends, rendered her circumstances. 
easy, and made her very comfortable. But still there 
was room for faith in God, and reliance on the divine 
- care, for the lady who bequeathed to her the aforesaid 
legacy, could only, on some account, leave it to her 
fora certain length of time. And as the time speci- 
fied, was not beyond the probable extent of her life, 
there was a possibility of her out-living the annuity, 
and thus be left without the means of support. But 
she was a woman who was “ careful for nothing, but 
in every thing by prayer and supplication, with thanks- 
giving, made known her requests unto God.” - She 
often prayed, that, if it were the will of God, she might 


248 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


die before the expiration of her income, and frequently 
expressed a strong confidenee that the Lord had heard 
her prayer. And the event proved that she was not 
deceived ; for, according to her wish, she received the 
last payment, and died before it was expended, leaving 
just enough to defray the expenses of her interment, 
Truly “the eyes of the Lord are over the righteous, 
and his ears are open to their prayer.” 

How strange that so many who profess to have 
committed the keeping of their souls to God, should 
nevertheless be continually disquieted with tormenting 
tears, respecting the maintenance of their comparative- 
ly worthless, and short enduring bodies. 

Miss Savage was a woman of good understanding, 
and possessed more than ordinary abilities. Her piety 
was deep, and her usefulness extensive. She was 
much beloved while living, and greatly lamented when 
dead. She departed this life “ in the comforts of the 
Holy Ghost,” and went to her rest, at an advanced 
age, about the year of our Lord, 1810, May we 
follow her as she followed Christ.

Miss SARAH DRURY, 


A young lady well known at Doncaster, was 
the offspring of an opulent family in that place, She 
‘received an education suitable to her rank, and proffered 
to figure in the fashionable world; but through the 
Divine interposition, her prospects of worldly glory 
were beclouded, and a different scene of things was 
opened to her view. When about sixteen years of age, 
the Lord was pleased to afflict her with a disease in 
her face, which caused her ever afterwards to wear a 


HOLY WOMEN. 249 


green veil. It was doubtless this affliction that indu- 
ced her to abandon the society of the votaries of gaiety 
and fashion, who look on outward appearances only, 
and to associate with those who value persons and 
things according to their inward and real worth. 

She wasa woman of strong intellect, and amiable 
in her manner; and her mind was evidently inured 
to religious discipline, and brought under the correc- 
tive influence of the Divine Spirit. She became a 
member of the Methodist Society, at Doncaster, and 
during the time of her stay on earth, continued to 
walk worthy of her high vocation. It was soon dis- 
covered that she possessed more than ordinary talents, 
and was therefore appointed to the office of class- 
leader. To this appointment she could have no 
reasonable objection, for however meanly she might 
think of herself, she could not be unconscious of her 
‘abilities. But the desire she felt for the salvation of 
souls, was a sufficient inducement for her to embrace 
every opportunity of doing good. Divine love is 
always active, and where it does not operate, it cannot 
possibly exist. The knowledge she obtained of the 
things of God, she was desirous of imparting to as 
many as came within the hearing of her voice; and 
hence, soon after she was made a leader, she began to 
exhort sinners to turn to the Lord. This she always 
preferred doing, after some friendly preacher had 
ended his sermon, and would never take the pulpit 
when a preacher was present, but spake below or from 
the side of the gallery. 

She formed a connecting link between the higher 
and the lower orders in society, and on that account 
her usefulness was more extensive. Great numbers 
attended her exhortations, and were greatly benefitted 
by the gracious words which fell from her lips. But 
here envy began to strew her path with difficulties, and 
to hedge up the way of her success, But there was 
little need for opposition, for her race was nearly run, 
and Providence was rapidly preparing her for laurels 
of unfading glory. She made a blessed exit about 
the year 1807,

Mrs. HIDES, 


Late of Nottingham, was long a member of 
the Methodist Society, but spent the latter part of her 
life among the followers of R. Winfield. 

For many years she bad to struggle with the 
perplexing cares of a large family, and passed through 
many a gloomy dispensation of providence ; but she 
‘committed her way unto the Lord,’ and through 
divine grace her feeble mind was supported, and she 
was enabled to acquiesce in the disposals of Heaven, 
and to conduct herself as a woman ‘professing 
Godliness. In a revival of religion which took place 
at Nottingham about the year 1818 or 1819, she 
received a deeper baptism of the Holy Spirit, and was 
rendered very useful in promoting “the prosperity 
of Zion.” She was then convinced, that the Lord 
not only requires of every man something more than 
barely to get himself to Heaven, but also, that she 
had an extraordinary call to preach repentance unto 
sinners. Under this impression she entered into a 
sphere of “labours more abundant,” and therein met 
with, but little opposition, for she was amongst a 
people whose sentiments were accordant with her own. 
A flaming zeal for God’s glory, and a deep concern 
for human salvation, were visible throughout her de- 
portment. She visited the villages and hamlets for 
many miles round Nottingham, and became valiant 
for the truth and abundantly useful. 

She delighted herself in the Lord and in His work, 
and he gave her the desire of her heart, in the conver- 
tion of souls. In her last affliction, she evidenced an 
entire devotedness to God, and the possession of that 
inward purity, and full assurance of hope, which she had 
long professed to enjoy. To those who attended her in 


HOLY. WOMEN. . 251 


` her expiring moments, she manifested the most perfect 
resignation to the will of God, and expressed the 
strongest confidence in the divine regard, Her enjoy- 
ment at times seemed to border on holy rapture, but 
her peace continually ‘flowed as a river,’ and her 
death-bed was as “the gate of Heaven” to her soul, 
« Holiness to the Lord”? was written on every thing she 
saw; and she said that she felt as if already entered 
into a new world. She was a mother in Israel while 
she lived, and her end was truly glorious. 


Miss MARY BROWN, 


Was born at Nottingham, of industrious parents, 
who were constant hearers of the Methodists. Many 
of the family are now members of that community. 
Through the influence of religious instruction, good 
example, and restraining grace, Mary was preserved 
from those follies to which youth are particularly expo- 
sed, and into which many are most awfully plunged ; 
but it does not appear that she had any proper concern 
for the salvation of her soul, until about the eighteenth 
year of her age. She was brought to God by the 
labours of R. Winfield, who, about the year 1818-1819, 
preached many times in several of, the most public 
places in Nottingham. Great multitudes attended his 
ministry, and “the hand of the Lord” was with him; 
insomuch that many who went to hear out of mere 
curiosity, obtained “the knowledge of salvation, by 
the remission of their sins? Mary seems to have 
been one of this number, In exhibiting God’s saving 
truth, she was brought to a sense of her depravity, as 
a fallen creature, and led to a discovery of her danger

as a transgressor against the righteous law of a sin

shall find ; knock, and it shall be opened unto you; for

The same spirit that had set her sins in battle-array 
before her, and produced “the spirit of bondage to - 
fear,” presently assumed the office of comforter, and 
witnessed her adoption into the family of God. She 
was broken down before the Lord, and her spirit was 
deeply wounded, but through an application of the 
sovereign balm of saving grace, she was speedily heal- 
ed. By an instantaneous venture on the Redeemer, 
she suddenly “ passed from death unto life; and the 
evidence of what she then experienced, was as the sun 
shining in his meridian splendor. The wound was 
deep, and the healing was glorious. After her con- 
version to God, she became a member of R. Winfield’s 
society, and continued to ornament her holy profession 
with every christian grace and heavenly temper. And 
as she lived near to God, she enjoyed uninterrupted 
communion with him; and entered much into his 
gracious designs, in the salvation of sinful man. Her 
bowels yearned over sinners, and she longed to pro- 
mote their happiness. She knew, indeed, that nothing 
but the power of God, could raise a fallen spirit; but, 
she was equally conscious that the Almighty generally 
effected this work of mercy, through human instru- 
mentality. And seeing that he often made use of 
“the foolish things of the world,” to execute his bene- 
volent purposes, she was desirous of becoming an 
instrument of good to her fellow creatures. She 
trembled at the idea of engaging in a work of such 
publicity and importance, but was convinced that “a 
dispensation of the Gospel’? was committed unto her, 
and that it was her duty to make a tender of mercy, 
in the name of Christ, to perishing sinners. Through 
crowds of difficulties she made her way, and in the 


HOLY WOMEN, 253 


midst of opposition began to open the records of 
eternal life, and to declare God’s purposes of grace to 
“a rebel universe”? The Lord observing the purity of 
her motives, gave his sanction to her undertaking, and 
succeeded her efforts with his blessing. Several souls 
were soon awakened from sinful apathy, and some 
brought into the enjoyment of christian liberty. She 
has visited many places during the last eighteen 
months, but has resided chiefly in London and its 
vicinity, preaching the gospel in chapels, warehouses, 
and barns, in squares and in the fields, to hundreds, 
and sometimes to thousands of wondering hearers. 
She delivers her discourses with great humility and 
zeal, and generally takes such texts, as being plain 
and weighty in themselves, form a ground-work for 
the illustration, and application of some important 
doctrine, duty, or privilege. Her sermons, it is said, 
are methodical, and well supported by the sacred 
oracles, with which she seems to be very conyersant. 
She has a pleasing voice anda strong memory ; she 
speaks with peculiar pathos and much feeling, and 
through the accompaniment of divine influence, her 
word produces the happiest effect on those deeply 
attentive and crowded audiences which she addresses, 
It is not uncommon to see, while she is preaching, 
several hundreds melted into tears. Ministers of 
different persuasions have attended her ministrations, 
and many of the Gentry have gone in their carriages 
to hear her preach, some of whom have expressed 
their high satisfaction as they returned. She is ortho- 
dox in sentiment, and holy in deportment. Two classes 
are committed to her care, and she generally preaches 
four or five times during the week. She has often been 
noticed in the public papers, and generally in a way 
highly creditable to herself, and the community to 
which she belongs. She is about twenty five years of 
age, of the middle stature, and has rather a turn or 
cast with her eyes, but is comely in her appearance. 
She has been the instrument of the salvation of many 
souls. May she be “kept by the power of God

Mrs, M. SMITH, 
(Late of Cape Town, Cape of Good Hope.) 


Frw persons have done more than this illustri- 
ous female, towards ameliorating the condition of 
fallen man. She possessed extraordinaty powers, and 
every energy of both soul and body were in perpetual 
operation for the benefit of her fellow creatures. 
Christian principle had gained so complete an ascend- 
ency in her mind, that she rejoiced in the divine 
testimonies, and it was her meat and drink to do the 
will of her Heavenly Father. Her whole soul was 
brought under the influence of “the powers of the 
world to come,’’ and she made an eternal consecra- 
tion of all her possessions to God and to His cause. 
She considered her own happiness as being deeply 
involved in that of mankind at large; and her conduct 
was an exemplification of the Poets assertion— 


“ True bounty knows no bounds of time or place, 
But nobly feels fer all the human race.” 


The philanthrophy of her heart was as extensive as 
buman existence, and her hands contributed to the 
support of almost every institution that was founded 
in christian benevolence. Her ears were attentive to the 
cries of wretchedness ; -and the lips of thousands poured 
blessir gs on her name. Buther views did not termi- 
natem the temporal and social well-being of mankind ;

she aimed at the destruction of the infernal monarchy, 
the emancipation of human souls fromthe vassilage 
of hell, and the salvation of the world. And as she 
delighted herself in the Lord, he in a good degree, 
gave her the desire of her heart, Through her dever- 
sified and effective exertions, scores of precious souls 
were brought to the knowledge of God, and the enjoy- 
ment of His salvation. The most prominent trait in 
the eharacter of this distinguished female, was ‘her 
zeal for missionary efforts: 
“In addition to the circumstances generally con- 
nected with the lives of eminently pious females,” say 
‘the Conductors of the Evangelical Magazine, “the

religion in the town and colony of the Cape; and her 
journies and labours to-evangelize the degraded Hot- 
tentots and Bushmen, deserve the highest praise.’’* 
The Directors of the London Missionary: Society 
speak of her as being “ many years the zealous friend 
and efficient auxiliary of their Society, and recount 
her labours of love with the warmest approbation.” 
“Mrs. Smith,” say they, “is described by those who 
were well acquainted with her piety and various chris- 
tian excellences, as a-mother in Israel. To the interests 
of this Society, from the time of Dr. Vanderkemp’s 
` arrival in Africa, in. the year 1802, until her death, 
she was a most cordial, active, and constant friend, 
adding considerably to its funds by her zealous and 
persevermg exertions ; promoting the comforts of the 
Missionaries when they were at’ Cape Town, by her 
kindness and hospitality, aswell as-directing them by 
her counsel, and maintaining a useful correspondence 
with them, when employed at their:respective stations

igof the utmost importance to human life. Hardly

The following extract of a letter, from The Rev, 
John Campbell to the Editor of the Evangelical Maga- 
zine, contains much information respecting the charac- 
ter, labours, experience, and latter end of Mrs. Smith. 


« THe death of Mrs. Smith, which was announc- - 
ed in the last Number of your Magazine, will prove ~ 
a serious loss.to the Missionary Society. and to the 
cause of religion .in South-Africa. For many years - 
past Mrs. Smith took the lead in most of the plans 
adopted for doing good in that country, for she pos- 


sessed the happy art of setting all her friends to work | 
in one way or another. Her fluency of speech, the 
seriousness of her address, and the earnestness of her 
manner,. when recommending plans of usefulness, . 
generally prevailed. And so extensive were the good 
effects of her pious exhortations, that, on my first 
visit to the colony, wherever I met with persons of 
evangelical piety, I generally found that their first. 
impressions of serious religion were ascribed to Mrs. 
Smith, whose earnest addresses to them, on their 
annual or half-yearly visits to Cape Town for the 
purchase of goods, together with the books or tracts 
which she put into their hands, were eminently blessed 
of God. 

From the period of Dr. Vanderkemp’s arrival in 
Africa, to the time of her death, she was the cordial, 
active, steady friend of the Missionary cause. The 


+ Evangelical Magazine, tor 1803,—page 547, 548.

contributions made to: our Society’s funds, which were 
obtained chiefly through her instrumentality, were 
very considerable. Last year,.they amounted, I think, 
to five thousand rix-dollars,, (about £500: sterling.) 
The sums collected were not from Cape Town only, 
but from every drosdy (or district) in the colony, with 
the pious. people of which she maintained, for that 
purpose, a constant correspondence ; and the sums so 
subscribed, were regularly transmitted to her as the 
‘Treasurer. 

So well known and so highly esteemed was Mrs.. 
Smith, (universally called Mother Smith) that serious 
Christians. from. Europe, India, or America, who. 
touched at the Cape, soon found her out, and so deeply 
were they interested by her pious conversation and 
ingratiating manner, that they were generally anxious: 
to maintain a correspondence with her ever afterwards. 

(Tt will be recollected that at one period she joined 
the Mission at Bethelsdorp, and resided there for some 
time, being engaged in teaching the girls to. knit,. 
sew, &c.) 

In the year 1813, on my first visit to Africa, I had 
an opportunity of travelling with her for about a week,, 
on a journey to Paarl and Drakenstein, to promote 

_ Missionary exertions in that part of the colony. I 
had then the opportunity of witnessing the piety, the 
prudence, and the wisdom which marked her conduct 
on every occasion. 

She was in the habit of devoting much of her atten- 

_tion to the instruction of the rising generation. I have 
seen her standing up in the midst of a hundred young 
people, addressing them in the most simple, pious, 
and affectionate strains, engaging every eye and every 
ear, and afterwards, in the most solemn manner, com-. 
mending them by prayer to the blessing of God. 

During the last ten or twelve years. of her life, her 
constitution appeared to. be mueh enfeebled, and she 
was confined by violent pains in her head ;, but in 
these distressing circumstances she manifested great: 


patience and resignation to the will of her Heavenly 
Father.

The account of this truly valuable person shall be 
closed by the following poetic lines, which were writ- 
ten immediately after her death :— 


THERE is a season when the good must mourn, 
An hour when Piety herself must weep, 

When holiest ties oflove by death are torn, 
And saints in Israel pass away to sleep. 

True, ’tis a short farewell; and then to meet 
Where Sin, and Grief, and Death are known no more { 
There, sainted Mother Smith again shall greet 
Each happy pilgrim whom she lov’d before. 
Yet though at her arrival Heav’n is glad, 

And glory’s crown sits radiant on her head, 
Poor England, India, Africa are sad— 

For Mother Smith is number’d with the dead! 


Ye British Israel, mourn your helper here— 
Afric’s believers, your kind Mother’s gone— 
Your Friend, your Counsellor, your solace dear} 
Yet let a beam of comfort on you dawn 
That a bereaved heart would fain inspire, 

Your Jesus ev’ry need shall well supply, 

Though he remove his earthly servants higher: 
Ye, her to follow her dear children try. 

O! think how her ten talents she employ’d, 

And see her ruler over many things ; 

Walk with your God, enjoy what she enjoy’d, 

And serve, and praise, like her, the King of Kings,

Miss ANN WINFIELD, 
(Now Mrs. Johnson,) 


Gives the following account of her conversion 
and experience. ‘I was born,” says she, “at Amber- 
ston, near Derby, where I spent the early part of my 
life, but with little concern for my eternal welfare. 
But having a pious father, and a mother desirous of 
giving me every instruction, together with the means 
of grace in our own house, then it was that divine im- 
pressions were made on my mind ; but never set out 
for Heaven until I was nearly fifteen years of age: 
the Lord then gave me to see that I was-a sinner, 
| although so young in years. One night, while my 
~ father anda young woman were praying very earnestly 

for our family, I discovered that without converting 7 
_ grace, I should be lost for ever; I began to seek the

Lord with all my heart, but I had to go to a place 
where I could not well attend the meetings, which 
grieved me very much; thus I was debarred froin the 
divine ordinances nine weeks, bat, thank God, he did 
not leave me. My concern for my soul was great 
indeed ; 1 prayed and wept, and mourned both night 
and day. At a certain time, when my father had 
been preaching, he called to see me, and going with 
him a little way, he prayed with me by the river side, 
yet I fownd no peace for my soul. But on the Wednes- 
day night following, I went toa class-meeting at my 
father’s house, and there the Lord pardoned all my 
sins + after struggling a long time in prayer, he sent 
deliverance to my soul, ina moment my burden was 
removed, and the Lord filled me with peace and joy 
through believing; my sorrow was then turned inte 
joy, and my grief into praise and thanksgiving: I 
could then say with the Psalmist,—‘ Come and hear, 
all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath 
done for my soul” For nearly six years I have enjcy- 
ed this favour; but the Lord convinced me of the need 
of persevering after holiness of heart, and shewed me 
that the bloed of Christ cleanseth from all sin, l 
sought this blessing with diligence and prayer, and, 
through faith, happily obtained it at a class-meeting in | 
my father’s house, December, 1817. At that. time Í | 
experienced a second application of the blood of Christ 
to my heart. 1 had heard of the blessing of entire 
sanctification, and being convinced of the necessity of 
it, could not rest until I had received it. O what 
peace and joy dwell ina soul that is wholly set apart 
for God! It is a peace that flows as a river—a joy 
unspeakable—a Heaven below—a paradise in the wild- 
erness! © that my soul may ever breathe this balmy 
air, and live in this glorious liberty of the Gospel of 
Christ! «Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shail 
see God? < Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father 
which is in Heaven is perfect? O what a blessing is 
it to be made holy! ‘The more holy we are, the 
happier, even here, and the more glorious hereafter.

May the inestimable blessing of perfect love dwell in 
all our hearts on earth, that we may have an inherit. 
ance hereafter in glory ? 

- Soon after she obtained this fulf salvation, she took 
“a journey into Leicestershire, to pay a visit to her 
father. On her asrival, she found an extensive field 
for usefulness, and but few, comparatively, who were 
able and willing to labour. Feeling the love of God as 
a fire in her heart, she began with all her might to 
pray with souls in distress, and to exhort them to 
believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. The Lord was 
pleased to make her an instrument of great good to 
many ; and at the earnest entreaty of the people, she 
ventured to enlarge her sphere of action. In this also, 
God was pleased to vouchsafe his blessing, and many. 
sinners were awakened and converted. From that time 
to the present, she has continued to speak in the name 
of the Lord to her fellow-sinners and the- churches 
have been edified, and the name of God glorified. 
She has travelled through a great part of Derbyshire, 
Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Warwickshire, North- 
amptonshire, and in Norfolk, preaching the word of 
Jife; and the Lord has abundantly blessed her labours 
in the conversion of souls. Many, very many, are 
rejoicing that ever they heard her voice, and. saw her 
face. May they all be faithful unto death, and be the 
crown of her rejoicing in the day of the Lord!

Mrs. STEVENS. 


NOTHING is more common than for those who 
have found an interest in the divine mercy, to be 
deeply concerned for the salvation and happiness of 

Ba ' 


TN Gi 


EEPE p Er 


268 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


their fellow-creatures. And hence, in whatever sphere 
of life they may be placed, they endeavour according 
to their ability to promote the great object of their 
desires. . 

Mrs. Stevens, of Knaresborough, was providentially: 
led into her ministerial labours. Having established 
a school in the national church, a favourable oppor- 
tunity of inculcating religious truths presented itself 
unto her; and knowing that “the children of the 
present age are the hope of the age to come,” she 
delayed not to embrace it with all her might. 

An opportunity of doing a good action, was with 
her a suficient call to its performance. She began on 
Sunday evenings, to address the children with regard 
to their immortal interests, and to lay before them 
tthe vast concerns of an eternal world.” But she 
presently found that the field of labour into which she 
had entered, was far more extensive than she had ever 
anticipated. The ‘children’s parents and others soon 
incorporated themselves with the juvenile assembly, 
and observing that persons of riper years are frequently 
as defective in duty, and often as ignorant as children, 
she began to exhort them also, to harken to the voice 
of instruction. And it appears that her word was 
owned of God, for her congregations‘inereased that it 
became necessary to provide a place more convenient 
for her purpose. And if the Author is rightly informed, 
she has now a Chapel, in which she preaches to a large 
and deeply attentive auditory. We see as in her case 
that whom God raises up to “ declare his statutes,” he 
will not suffer long to want, either a chapel or a con- 
gregation: she is not connected with any body of 
dissenters, but closely adheres to the Church of Eng- 
land. The Author has not heard that she has extended 
her labours beyond the precincts of the town where 
she resides, but there she doubtless, has “ ample room 
and verge enough.” May her pious efforts be succeed- 
ed by the divine blessing ; and while she is striving to 
lead others to the great spring of unmixed felicity, 
may the Lord be unto her as “a place of broad rivers 
and streams.” i 


HOLY WOMEN. 


Miss ALICE CAMBRIDGE, 


‘ A LIVING character in Ireland, has long “ borne 
the burden and heat of the day,” and is now drawing 
near to her eternal rest. She formerly resided ‘at 
Kinsale, bat being convinced that souls were “ perish- 
ing for lack of knowledge” in other places as well as 
there, and believing that it was her duty to spread the 
savour of the Redeemer’s name as.far as. possible, she,. 
like him, ‘went about doing good ;” and in the course 
of her travels, she occasionally visited Cork, Bandon, 
Limerick, Dublin,.and many other towns and villages: 
indeed wherever she was invited by persons of respec- 
tability, she received the invitation as the call of God, 
and repaired thither to lift up the standard of the Cross. 
Daring the time of her bodily vigour, she was a stout 
woman, possessed of great. vocal powers, and not 
easily deterred from doing good.. She has sometimes 
preached to soldiers in barracks;. with considerable 
effect, being introduced. by the religious wives of the 
olficers ; flushed with zeal for the peaceful conquests of 
the Saviour, she unfurled the bloody flag of Calvary 
to their astonished view ; and exhorted them to join 
the armies of Jehovah,. and to: “war a good warfare” 
under the banners of Immanuel... If to this part of her 
conduct any should object, as being contrary to that 
humble diffidence which is so truly pleasing in the female 
character ;—we answer, if “true modesty is ashamed 
of every thing criminal,” and “ false modesty only of 
those things that are unfashionable,” she possessed the 
former and was free from the latter; for while she 
“ abstained from every appearance of evil,’’ she dared 
to be ‘singularly good.” 
She resided sometime with a lady of fortune in 
Dublin, but is now at Mallow, waiting for the coming.

Miss ANN LUTTON, 


A youne female, now living at Moria in Ireland, 
was brought to ‘the knowledge of the truth,” and 
numbered with the people of God, about the year 


1815. She is a woman of genuine piety and deep 
humility, and possesses talents for extensive usefulness 
in the vineyard of the Lord. She preaches to those of 
her own sex only ; and it seems the Lord has given 
her the hearts of many; for in her visits to the 
neighbouring towns and villages, she has frequently 
several hundreds of hearers. She is a member of the 
Methodist Society ; her character stands high, and her 
Jabours are well received in her own connexion. It 
does not appear that she has met with any opposition 
from the travelling Preachers who have laboured in 
those parts: they seemingly have appreciated her 
worth, fer concerning her piety, humility, and zeal, 
they speak in the highest terms of respect, and have 
ever encouraged her to proceed in her ‘labour of 
love.” ¥ 

If female labours had always been properly counte- 
nanced amongst the Wesleyan Methodists, it is likely, 
no other religious denomination would have produeed

Miss EMMA COTTLE. 


Bioerapuy has generally been considered a 
very interesting and useful part of History ; more 
especially to the pious mind, if its characters have 
been eminently holy, wise, and useful. 

As face answers to face in a glass, so in christian 
experience, we find a pleasing or a painful resemblance 
in our views and feelings, which through the divine 
blessing may be rendered a peculiar advantage in our 
christian warfare. The Holy Scriptures furnish us 
with a considerable portion of this kind of History. 
Here we have light and shade ; the virtues and failings 
of the characters delineated; and, no doubt each of 
these are recorded with the same gracious and benevo- 
lent design, viz. for the benefit of mankind. The 
virtues and excellencies of good men are left on record 
for our imitation and encouragement, and their failings 
and imperfections are handed down to us as so many 
beacons or way-marks, in order that we may guard 


272 BIOGRAPHICAL, SKETCHES OF 


against those temptations and sins by which they 
dishonoured God and injured their own souls. _ Hence 
we are commanded to “ Remember Lot’s wife.’ And 
why should we remember her, but in order that we 
may guard against that sin for which she was made a 
monument of Gad’s displeasure. We are also com- 
manded to remember the sufferings of the Patriarchs. 
and Prophets, Christ and his Apostles, that we may 
learn some useful lessons of suffering patience.— 
“ Take, my brethren, the Prophets who have spoken in 
the Name of the Lord, for an example of suffering 
affliction, and of patience.’—James v. 10. in the 
biographical sketches of those characters, which it hath 
pleased God to preserve and record in the sacred. 
writings, we have several. eminent females. A very. 
celebrated Divine, in his sermons on scripture charac- 
ters, observes—“ Hitherto we have seen only ‘holy. 
men of God speaking as they were moved by the Holy 
Ghost > but the great Jehovah is no respecter of 
persons or sexes: ‘the secret of the Lord is with them 
that fear him, and he sheweth unto them his holy 
covenant.” The simple dignity of this woman’s. 
(Deborah) unadorned, unassuming state is beautifully 
represented :— She dwelt under the palm-tree of 
Deborah, between Ramah and Bethal, in. Mount 
Ephraim ; and the children of Israel came up to her 
for judgment.’—Judges iv. 5. Behold a female mind 
exalted above the pageantry and pride of external 
appearance; a mind not deriving consequence from 
the splendour of her attire, the charms. of her person, 
or the number of her retinue, but from the affability of 
her manners, the purity of her character, the sacred- 
ness of her office, the impartiality of her conduct, the 
importance of her public services ; not. wandering from 
place to place, hunting after a little empty applause, 
bat sought unto of all Israel, for the eminency and. 
extensive utility of her talents and her virtues. Her 
canopy of state was the shade of the palm-tree ; her 
rule ofjudgment, the law and the testimony of the living 
God; her, motive, the inspiration of the Almighty; 


HOLY WOMEN. 273 


her-aim and end, the glory of God and the good of her 
people ; her reward, the testimony of a good con- 
science, the respect of a grateful nation, the admira- 
tion of future generations, the smiles of approving 
Heaven,’’. 

“ However weak and contemptible the instrument 
may be in itself, from the hand that wields it, it 
becomes mighty and respectable: and the history 
before us becomes, and that not darkly, a typical 
representation of the Gospel of Christ, which was ‘to 
the Jews a stumbling-block, and to the Greeks foolish- 
ness.” Pride and self-sufficiency smile at the idea of a 


_ female prophet, a female judge, a female poet, a female 


politician, a female warrior; and yet in truth women 
have filled ali those offices, with credit to themselves, 
and with satisfaction to ihe public. And ‘who hath 
made man’s mouth; or who maketh the dumb, or 
deaf, or the seeing, or the blind?’ In the honoured: 
list of those who ‘through faith subdued kingdoms, 
wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped 
the mouth of lions, quenched the violence of fire, 
escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were 
made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight’ 
the armies.of the aliens,’—female names stand record- 
ed with commendation and renown. ‘And what had 
thou, O man, but what thou hast first received?’ 
‘God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to 
confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak 
things of the world to confound the things which are 
mighty ; and base things. of the world, and things 
which are despised, hath God chosen; yea, and 
things which are not, to bring to nought things that 
are; that no flesh should glory in his presence.’ ”?*

«Emma Corrie was born at Brexworthy, in the par- 
ish of Bradworthy, in the county of Devon, on the 
10th day of June, 1792. She was naturally of a meek 
disposition, dutiful to her parents, kind and obhging 
to all around her; which procured her mach love from 
her parents, and esteem from her friends and neigh- 
bours. In the year 1803, she removed with her parents 
to Youlston, in the parish of Moorwmstow, in the 
county of Cornwall. When at school she was much 
Beloved for her pleasant disposition, and good conduct. 
Being piously inclmed, she was from her youth pre- 
served from the follies and vanities of the age: and 
though she had not the enjoyment of ehureh fellow- 
ship, or any one to take her by the hand 5 yet, it 
appears she sought the Lord in secret 5 being some- 
times observed to weep and sigh ; mourning in secret 
for something she felt the want of, but did net know 
how to attain. But that God who took compassion 
on Cornelius, had eompassion on her and brought her 
into the wealthy place, and spread His banner over 
her. Onthe 13th of February, 1816, I preached at a 
place called Brownspit, in the parish of Moorwinstow ; 
being the first time of my preaching in those parts, 
which was abont a mile and a half from Emma’s 
fathers. She was not there ner do I recollect seeing 
any of the family except her elder brother, who. after 
preaching, kindly. invited me to call at his father’s. 
house the next morning. I accepted the offer and 
went. This was the first time of my seeing this loving 
family. We continued the preaching at regular appoint- 
ed times, and soon the Lord began to work : seeing 
this I proposed to these who were piously inclined, to 
meet in class; several embraced the offer ;—Emma 
was one of the first. This was about the 23rd of 
March, 1816. After she came home her mother gave 
her to understand that she thought Emma had aeted 
injudiciously to join in that man’s society who she 
thought was sent to go all over the world to preach the 
Gospel, and who the mother thought must soon leave 
them. However it was not long before the father, 


HOLY WOMEN. 275 


mother, and four others of the family joined the society 
also. Her father boarded and lodged the preachers, 
and all the family seemed to be agreed to serve Gua 
and to unite in His worship. It was soon apparent 
that she knew how te impreve her privileges; light 
shined on her path ; she now saw the way to happiness, 
and walked therein. In a few weeks she could ‘Believe 
with her heart unto righteousness ; and with her lips she 
made confession unto salvation.’ The doctrine of holi- 
ness was preached and enferced,—she heard and 
believed,—sought, and found, the pearl of great price : 
“and maintained her confidence totheend. Ina short 
time she began to pray in public; and soon after to 
exhort in the meetings. She also filled up a useful 
place in the church, as a local preacher, holding meet- 
ings on Sunday and. week-day evenings, always 
embracing every epportunity of working for God.— 
She has walked many miles, (when she might have 
rode,) to publish the glad tidings of salvation: and 
would say that she chose te-do so, because she would 
“not indulge her body, as if she had been a lazy follower 
of Jesus, who Himself had travelled so many tedious 
journeys for the sake of poor sinners.—She would 
-sensibly feel from such considerations, when she had 
complied with her parents’ desire in taking a horse. 
When at home much of ker time wastaken up in leading 
classes, visiting the sick, and praying with those 
around her that were concerned for their spiritual 
welfare; being always ready to every good work. In 
‘May 1818, she had an appointment for-Michaelstow 
Circuit, as it is now called; and my eldest daughter 
Mary, (then about eleven years old, and had spoken a 


“Tittle in public,) went with her as a companion. They 


set out on their journey on Saturday, May 23rd, 1818. 


. Being about twe years after her conversion to God. 
She had accompanied one of our female speakers in 


Devonshire for a little while as a volunteer. But this 
was the first time she had an appointment to take a 
Circuit. As to her experience in travelling may be 
better known by her journal, or at least that part there- 
of which I have been able te obtain.

It begins with the date of her itinerancy, which | 
‘says, 1818, May 23rd. This day, I arrived at Michael- 
stow; and may say, I had a pleasant journey: I was 
enabled to come on praising God. And though con- 
sidering my own weakness for the work, I was about 
to be engaged in, yet I had a confidence that the Lord 
would give me grace to help, in every time of need. © 

24th. This morning I was rather tired : the enemy 
told me, that I should not be happy, and that it would 
be better had I not come away. I began to pray that 
I might be happy, and also to think on the evidence’ 
which I had the day before, that it was pleasing in the 
sight of God: Blessed be God, the tempter was forced 
to fly, and I had a blessed Sabbath. In the morning, 
in meeting the class, I found it good to be there,—I 
find where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.. 
We had a public meeting there in the afternoon, and 
at Helston, (near Camelford) in the evening, and a 
prayer meeting after. 

Monday 25th. This morning we came to Boscastle, 
and met with Sister B. Read; about noon she left us, 
and we took her plan. In the evening we went to 
Trefalgar, there I had a good season. 

Tuesday 26th. We returned to Boscastle, where 
we had a meeting ; I was much tried before the meeting 
began. Sister Mary began the meeting, and after a 
while she was taken unwell, and I had then to carry on 
the meeting myself, J found the Lord my present 
help in time of need ; and had a good meeting. . 

Wednesday 27th. In the morning I went to M, C. 
to prayer-meeting ; in the evening went to Treclago. 
I felt tried towards evening; but I was enabled to pat 
my whole trust in God, and did feel a good time ; the 
people seemed very serious, and some were happy. 

Thursday 28th. This evening we went to Trevie, 
and had a large congregation. Bless the Lord the 
more I am employed in His work, the more liberty I 
feel. This has been the best season that l have felt in 
speaking ; we could not get away from this place until 
Friday afternoon, the 29th; then we came to Teath,

a trial it was! To speak before so many old profes- 
sors; and having spoke around here to many of the 
same people. It seemed to be even offering my body 
to the stake: still I thought if I could but have hap- 
piness in my own soul, I care not what men may think. 
As soon as I came into the house, I felt hopes that 
I should have a good meeting. Bless the Lord I 
had. Here seems to be pious souls. 

Thursday 18th. This evening I went to Trencreek,

trial to meg but I determined to give it into the 
hands of the Lord, and not to be concerned about it,

Here I} met with a dear young woman, which did 
me good before meeting, in conversing with one 
which I have reason to believe is truly pious. Here 
was a great congregation, and I had a blessed time in 
speaking to them. 

Friday 19th. I had a meeting at Crantock, and felt

l have no account of her experience from Nov. Ith 
till the Feb. following. It it to be regretted that she 
did not leave some account of her journal or experi- 
ence in this time, it being an important period; or if 
she did, that it should not come to hand. In the ace 
count of her experience, the 8th of November, being 
then at home with her Father, she expresses a convic- 
tion of its being her duty to go forth again in the 
Name of the Lord, to warn sinners to flee from tle 
wrath to come. 

On the first of January following, she was at the 
opening of a preaching-house, at a place called Forda, 
in North-Petherwin, where I and my wife were also. 
The next day Emma parted from.us for a western cir- 
cuit, she being in good health. I did not think it 
was the last time that I should see her in this world; 
tho’ it fell out to be the case. How true it is—Jn the 
midst of life we are in death. However it is to be 
observed, Emma did not die in the field of battle; if 
she had, some of the ungodly, and lukewarm, perhaps, 
would have said, These maidens kill themselves with 
preaching ; yes, says another unbeliever; it is not 
work fit for them, you see they are not made and fit- 
ted for it, they cannot stand against, nor endure such 
exercise, it is killing work ; you see such a one has lost 
her life by it. This I say, is likely would have been 
the language of some unbelievers, who cannot be ex- 
pected to have much love for the cause of God, who 
have little or none for God Himself: but I am sorry 
that Emma had not so honourable a death as to die a 
martyr in preaching the Gospel; not that I believe 
she would have shunned her duty for fear of the labour 
and reproach, that might attend it: for 1 knew her to 
be devoted to God; and one who had every appearance 
of a christian. From the time 1 first knew her, (which 
was about the time she joined society, on the 23rd

that she never in one instance, knew her to disobey 
her parents; being of a meek disposition, and accus- 
tomed to obey, she obeyed this fatal command, and left

of “ leaving the word of God to serve tables.” 
While at Bundley February Ist. She writes thus: 
This day 1 know not where to begin to praise the Lord 
for His goodness. When | begin to take a view of 
my unfaithfulness, my cry is,—Lord make me more 
on stretch for thy kingdom. Oh! how precious time 
is, yet how little improved by one of the unworthiest 
of God’s creatures. As I am writing I can even view

‘ecordingly done. By this time she was very weak, 
she lay quiet having but little to say. Her mother 
asked her if she was happy ? She answered Yes. The 
standers by, perceived her lips to move, and some- 
times they could hear her articulate the name, Jesus ; 
and sometimes they said she was heard to mention 
my name: but it seems she was by this time too weak 
to deliver any message. AQ little before her death she 
said to those by, pray ;—she being so weak and low, 
they scrupled to pray vocally, but kneeled down and 
prayed in their hearts in silence. To their surprise 
Emma broke out in prayer ; her soul seemed to gather 
up fresh zeal, and make it’s last effort; and she prayed 
for a considerable time; (it was thought for near half 
an hour)—praying for each of the family ia particular, 
—for me, and for the cause in which I am engaged, 
that the Lord might prosper it, &c. until nature was 
nearly exhausted,—She ceased,—and lay quiet, ap- 
pearing by the moving of her lips still to be engaged 
in prayer; and in about half an hour, lying thus, she 
was heard to say—Jesus,—and the weary wheel of 
life stood still on the 2Ist of February, 1819, being 
in the 27th year of her age. 

On the day she was buried, and before the corpse 
was carried from the door, our Brother James Thorne 
preached a sermon on the occasion, from the fifth 
chapter of the second Epistle of Paul to the Corin- 
thians, and the eighth verse. A numerous‘ congre- 
gation attended on this solemn occasion, which with 
the energy accompaning the word, mutually wrought, 
to render it an affecting time, which will not soon be 
forgotten. After the sermon was concluded, the body’ 
was carried to the parish Church, so called, where 
her relatives had been buried; and committed to the 
dust; truly in sure and certain hope of the resurrection 
to eternal life, 

Her parents erected a stone at the grave, to her 
Memory, with an inscription thereon ; to which they 
wished a verse to be added, which is not altogether

Miss NEWMAM, 
(Afierwards Mrs. Jonathan Cousins) 


Kert a bookseller’s shop at Cheltenham in 
Gloucestershire. After her conversion to God, her 
conduct was somewhat similar to that of the Jewish 
exorcists, mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, who 
on their embracing christianity, burnt all their magical 
books, and thereby acknowledged the sinfulness of 
their former proceedings. She was determined to give 
circulation to nothing that was inimical to the interests 
ef that cause which she had espoused ; and therefore 
removed from her shelves all novels, plays, amd 
romances, with every other book that had a demoral- 
izing tendency, or was likely to lead mankind into

HOLY WOMEN 291 


forgetfulness of God. She united with the Methodists, 
and became a very active and useful member of their 
Society, and soon began to exhort in prayer meetings. 
She afterwards manifested her love to souls, by making 
occasional visits to Tewkesbury and the adjacent places, 
to publish the glad tidings of saving grace. Her reli- 
gious experience was clear, and included an acquaint- 
ance with the deep things of God. She was a woman 
of a strong understanding and amiable temper ; 
prudence and modesty were leading traits in her cha- 
racter. Mr. Wesley had an high opinion of her quali- 
fications and usefulness, and encouraged her in all her 
pious endeavours. She used. to exhort and preach 
occasionally, and the Lord owned her labours in the 
salvation of many souls. Among those who were 
brought to God through her instrumentality, was her 
own mother, and Mr. Cousins, who afterwards became 
her husband, being her son in the gospel. On this 
account he sometimes pleasantly observed that he 
married his mother. 

Mr. Cousins was a teachable christian, in conse- 
quence of which he arrived at more than ordinary 
attainments in religion. Having obtained the blessing 
of justification, he could not be satisfied with any 
thing less than a full renewal of his soul in righteous- 
ness, and the possession of all that mind, which was 
in Christ Jesus his Lord. In compassing the object of 
his desire, he was greatly assisted by Miss Newman, 
the subject of this memoir, and Mr. Samuel Wells, 
who was a zealous promoter of the cause of God in the 
neighbourhood of Cheltenham, and a warm advocate 
for the doctrine of entire sanctification : and hence on 
that train of providence, which led him to an acquaint- 
ance with these two deeply experienced christians, he 
acknowledged himself much indebted ; for the religious 
instruction and encouragement he received from Mr 
Wells, is evident from the following letter.

June Ist, 1777 A 


“ My dear Brother, 


I am glad that you have already experienced 
redemption in the blood of Jesus—the forgiveness of 
your sins; and 1 hope you are continually seeking 
that perfect Jove, which casts out fear and expels alk 
the carnal mind. Indeed, my dear brother, you -can= 
not expect it too soon ; for to every one who feels his 
need of it, “ Now is the accepted time, and now is the 
day of salvation.” Therefore you should, in the use 
of every mean of grace, be looking up and expecting, 
till God shall come and destroy all the works of the 
devil within you. 

«When you experience this degree of salvation, you 
will feel yourself calm in the presence of God: your 
soul will rejoice before him as a little child, possessed 
of unutterable simplicity and innocence of spirit ; while 
your heart will not-dare to move in his presence, but 
with full submission to his will. You will see the 
broad eye of God fixed upon your heart, while the 
loving obedient eye of your soul is fixed on the Lord. 
How sweet must be the communion which such a soul 
enjoys with God! My brother, look for this blessing 
to day. Strive to fix your wavering mind on God, as 
you would if you were at prayer... Endeavour to keep 
it to this point, recalling your heart to this simple —

SAMUEL WELLS.” 


Tt may not be amiss to inform the reader, that Mr. 
$. Wells was called to the itinerant work, in which he 
made a short, but a happy course. After travelling 


ten or eleven years, he was taken to his rest in the 
year 1780. The leading doctrine in this young man’s 
sermons, was that of christian perfection, He consi- 
dered the preaching of perfect love to God, so essential 
to the welfare of the Church of Christ, that he touched 
upon itin almost every sermon he preached. And 
was not Mr. Wesley ofthe same opinion? His senti- 
ments on this subject may be seen in the following 
extracts. 

« October 15, 1762.” he says in his journal, “The 
more I converse with the believers in Cornwall, the 
more I am convinced that they have sustained great 
loss, for want of hearing the doctrine of christian per- 
fection, clearly and strongly enforced. F see, where- 
ever this is not done, the believers grow dead and 
cold. Nor can this be prevented, but by keeping up 
in them an hourly expectation of being perfected in 
love. I say an hourly expectation, for to expect it 
at death, or some time hence, is much the same as not 
expecting it at all.”

« Aug. 14,1776,” he says, “I preached at Tiverton, 
and on Thursday went on to Launceston. Here I found 
the plain reason why the work of God had gained no 
ground in this circuit all the year.. The preachers had 
given up the Methodist testimony. Either they did 
not speak on perfection at all, (the peculiar doctrine 
commitied to our trust,) or they spoke of it only in 
general terms, without urging the believers, to go om 
to perfection, and to expect it every moment. And 
whenever this is not earnestly done, the work of God 
does not prosper.”

Mrs RACHEL BLACKBURN, 


Was born at Farndale, in the North Riding of York- 
shire, in the year 1777. - Her maiden name was Ware. 
When she was about seventeen years. of age, she was 
convinced of the depravity of her heart, and the sinful- 
. hess of her life, and by the grace of God was “ delivered 
from the power of darkness, and translated into the 
kingdom of his dear Son ; in whom she found redemp- 
tion through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins.” 
At that time she lived in servitude at Lastingham, and 
her religious privileges were very contracted. < This 
circumstance made her earnestly desirous of obtaining 
a situation more. favourable to a religious life: and 
knowing by“ personal experience, that the God whorn 
she served was a God that heard the requests of his 
people, she made her case the subject of importunate 
prayer; from a consciousness of the divine favour, she 
doubted not but the Lord would grant unto her the 
thing she asked at his hand; he gave abundant evi- 
dence that “the prayer of the upright is his delight.” 
Reader, “‘ commit thy way unto the Lord ; trust also in 
Him, and he shall bring it to pass.” Only a short time 
elapsed, before that eminent servant of Jesus Christ, 


296 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES OF 


Mr. Robert Venis,* of Fryupdale, came to enquire after 
her, and expressed a wish to hire her into his service. 
She looked upon him as the messenger of God, sent to 
fetch her from her iron bondage: and in serving this 
man of God, she spent two of the happiest years of 
her life. She afterwards removed into Glazedale, and 
continuing to live in communion with God, became an 
active and useful member of the Methodist Society. 
At twenty-three years of age she was married to Mr. 
William Blackburn, a pious young man, who wasa 
member of the same community. She did not take 
this very important step without first making it a 
matter of deep consideration, and much prayer. And 
that “a good man’s steps are ordered of the Lord” 
was verified to her in this instance. Sometime after 
their marriage they removed to East-Moor, but here 
she had to lament the loss of christian communion, 
and the benefit resulting from social intercourse with the 
people of God. Helmsley was then the nearest place at 
which she could attend divine worship, and being situa- 
ted from thence about five miles, she was soon led to 
discover the value of the means of grace, by being ina 
great measure deprived of the opportunity of attending - 
them; and in consequence of this privation, she lost 
some degree of that zeal for God, and love to souls, 
which she before possessed. If this holy woman who 
was providentially debarred from the advantage of 
christian communion, found it so difficult to maintain 
her ground in religious experience; how shall those 
who on every trivial occassion, optionally absent them- 
selves from it, preserve the life of God in their souls? 
Like King David of old, when he was deprived of his 
religious privileges, Rachel Blackburn “longed, yea 
fainted for the courts of the Lord: her heart and her 
flesh cried out for the living God.” Her language was 
“blessed are they that dwell in thy house, O Lord.” 
She wished for a settlement nearer to the divine ordin-

in vain. About the year 1817, her husband took a

dales; but having a large family and being frequently 
affiicted, she was not capable of much public service ; 
and meeting with some discouragement from a preacher

be her duty; but not without many a painful convic-

Miss MARY O’BRYAN. 


IT is a privilege of no ordinary kind to be born 
of parents who live in the fear of the Lord, and walk 
in the comforts of the Holy Ghost. Those who are 
working out their own salvation, endeavour to save 
the souls of all with whom they are connected. But 
pious parents feel a peculiar interest in the spiritual 
and eternal welfare of their own offspring. They con- 
sider that their children as well as themselves have 
souls which were redeemed not “with corruptible 
things, as silver and gold, but with the precious blood 
ef Christ,”’"—souls that will eternally exist, either im 


HOLY WOMEN. 299 


the immortal felicities of Heaven, or in the quenchless 
flames of penal fire. They look upon them as the 
Lord’s property, committed to their care for a little 
season, with an express command that they be trained 
upin the way that leads to Heaven. Aware of their 
awful responsibility, they admonish, reprove and in- 
struct their children; and to give effect to their labours, 
they set before them a pious example, and bring them 
before God without ceasing, in the arms of faith and 
prayer. 

Such were the advantages which this young woman 
enjoyed. Her father, mother, and grandmother, all 
knew the good way and walked unblamabiy before 
God, and their good instruction and holy deportment, 
through the divine blessing, had a good effect upon 
her tender heart. The Lord by His Spirt wrought 
powerfully upon her mind in her infancy. She loved 
to hear of the love of Christ, and of His sufferings for 
the redemption of fallen man. 

She saw and heard something in the life and experi- 
ence of her relatives, which she felt the want of herself. 
She was sweetly drawn to the throne of grace in sup- 
plication and prayer, and presently found such access 
to the mercy’s seat, and such intercourse with God, 
as made this exercise the delight of her soul. At the 
age of six or seven years, she felt the love of God shed 
abroad in her heart, though she hardly knew, at that 
time, from whence it came, or what to call it, she 
dared not to make it known. 

Being on a visit, soon after, to some relations, who 
instead of attending to prayer themselves, ridiculed 
her on account of it, she shrunk in some measure from 
the cross, and brought darkness upon her mind. As 
the consequence of thus grieving the Spirit of God, 
guilt and slavish fear succeeded that joy and peace 
which she formerly enjoyed. She continued in this 
state of perplexity, darkness, and misery, sometimes 
seeking the Lord with earnestness, at other times 
desparing of happiness and rest for her soul, until she 
was nine years of age. At that period, under a sermon,

objection.

was much blessed, and she and the people wept together.

a very pre-eminent degree. Her peculiar call from

ed in the method that is now practised, that is of 
selecting a text of Scripture, and then dividing, and

place, to impress the minds of the people with.a pow-

of the Church, and the Saviour of sinners was present, 
that He was in the midst, and that HE was there, to 
do the people good—to save souls. Having secured 
the serious attention of the people, she then in the: 
most simple, artless, and yet in the most powerful 
and awakening manner, preached the doctrines of 
human depravity; Christ’?s atonement and divinity ; 
the nature and necessity of repentance and faith in 
Christ, and holiness of heart and life-—She preached 
a free, a present, and a full salvation. And declared 
that Jesus Christ is able to save to the uttermost, 
all them that come unto God by him. 

And it is astonishing what effects were produced by 
her preaching. That God should condescend to perform 
so many miracles of grace and mercy, by an instrument 
so weak, and in appearance so insignificant, is as great a 
stumbling block to many, as the preaching of the cross 
of Christ was to the Jews, and equally as absurd and 
foolish as the doctrines which the Apostles taught, 
were to the learned Grecians, but it hath pleased God 
by a method, and by means which appears to many 
foolishness to save them that believe, “ that the excel- 
lency of the power may be evidently of God, and not 
of the instrument.”? Many dispensations of Divine 
Providence and grace, serve to shew that God is “ex- 
cellent in counsel and wonderful in working.”

of Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria,

The account of Ann Cutler, published by Mr. 
Bramwell, in the year 1796, is so excellent, that no 
apology need be made for its introduction in illustrating

« ANN CUTLER was born near Preston in Lanca- 
shire, in the year 1759. Till she was about twenty-six 
years of age she was very strict in her morals and 
serious in her deportment: but she never saw into the 
method of salvation by Jesus Christ till the local 
Methodist preachers visited that neighbourhood. Af- 
ter hearing one of these; she was convinced of sin; 
and; from that time, gave all diligence to obtain mercy. 
In a short time she received pardon, and her serious 
walking evidenced the power she enjoyed. It was not 
long before she hada clearer sight into her own heart; 
and, though she retained her confidence of pardon, 
was yet made deeply sensible of the need of perfect 
love. In hearing the doctrines of sanctification, and

that the blessing was to be received through faith,

mercy, 1785, the Lord said, “I will. Be thou clean.”

«Jesus, Thou knowest I love Thee with all my heart.’’ 
I would rather die than grieve Thy Spirit. Oh! I

tenance a smile of sweet composure ; it was noticed 
by many, as a reflection of the Divine Nature, and i 
increased to the time of ke: death. In a few months

nearly every time I saw her J was asked for instruction. 
She began to pray in meetings, and several were

HER FAITH IN GOD. 


Her manner was to search diligently the New 
Testament, to know what blessings were promised to 
her ; and if she could only satisfy herself from her own 
reading, or from the explanation of others, of what 
the promise contained, she instantly believed that 
the Lord would give it; and it appeared that she daily, 
through faith, increased in the work of God. I never 
remember hearing hersay she had received any bles- 
sing, but she added; “I see a great deal more for 
me in Jesus. ” 

When she was called upon to plead for others, her 
manner was, if possible, to know their state. For 
this she used every prudent means. If she was 
satisfied of what they then needed, she believed with 
all ber heart that the Lord would fulfil their desire. 
She was as confident for sanctification as justification 5 
yet she observed it required a greater exertion of faith 
in the person prayed for and the person pleading, te 
receive purity of heart than pardon. 

She lived by faith. I had evidence that, as she 
received she trusted in no grace, but looked through 
all to God. k 

In several places, when preachers and others had 
lost their hope of a revival, she has selected a few to 
assist her, and, to the astonishment of man. , bas 
prevailed with God.

HER CHRISTIAN LOVE. 


She often expressed herself thus: “It is all love ; 
nothing but love. God is love. I want more of this 
love. How do you think I may attain to more ? I feel 
nothing but pure love ; but God can enlarge my heart 
and give mea greater fulness. I feel my soul continually 
burn with love to Jesus.’ If ever any gave evidence of 
love, she did, according to the 13th chap. of I. Corinth- 
ians, “ believing all things, hoping all things, enduring 
all things.” 

Her love to sinners appeared in her frequent sighs, 
groans, tears, and strong crying to God in secret. What 
appeared the most like tautology in her petitions, was, 
« Jesus, save sinners! Thy blood was shed for them. 
Oh! save sinners |” 

Her love to real penitents was striking. Her soul 
travailed in birth till Christ was formed in them. She 
went through great sorrow, sympathizing with the 
broken in heart ; and she always seemed unwilling to 
‘leave them till they were comforted. Her love moved 
her to mourn with them that mourned ; and, when 
deliverance came, her soul rejoiced in God, her Saviour. 
She often said—“ None know the glory of pleading 
with souls but those who do it.” 

Whenever she found persons, to use her own ex- 
pression, «< quite devoted,” she showed uncommon 
respect for them ; and, in our conversation on the 
subject said—‘ [love to be with them; it helps me 
forwards. I see many things in them I want myself; 
but we shall soon be in heaven. f must do all I can 
for God every moment, and then I shall be near them 
in another world. Oh! it delights: my soul to see 
those that are not entangled with any thing below the 
sun!” Her love to the preachers and connexion was 
the strongest I ever saw in any person. 

She did “ cover a multitude of sins.” F never knew 
ber speak evil of any. She said—“ When I know any 
evil I tell the Lord; I can tell every thing to him.” 
She never would talk about the faults of others; any

HER HUMILITY. 
i$ 

Her friends sensibly feel, and all who have had a 
real knowledge of her character can testify, that this 
grace shone the most conspicuous. There appeared. 
nothing affected. What was seen proclaimed the senti- 
ments of her heart. I have often thought she did not 
know how to dissemble.—Whatever blessings she res 
ceived, she spent more time in thanksgiving than she 
did in the petition. «Glory be to Jesus V? was her cry, 
When she professed to receive an increase of grace, ` 
there appeared an increase of holy flame in all her 
conduct. She appeared sunk under the weight of love, 
with a soul full of gratitude. The image of the Son of 
God was then the most visible. Whenever she was 
answered in the salvation of others, which was exceed- 
ingly common, her mind was instantly turned to 
“Glory, glory to Thy name, oh! Jesus !” 

I saw it was not in her to be backward when called 
to work for God, or to let others act before her; but 
her. genuine humility was the acting instantly or not 
acting ; was the being nothing and feeling it; being 
any thing for God and and his glory ; a fool or wise, 
despised or esteemed, rejected or received.

HER GREAT PATIENCE. 


To see God in all things is the privilege of Chris- 
tians; and their happiness consists in acknowledging 
Him as their King, Judge, and Saviour. « Thy wilk 
be done,” was the language of Ann Cutler for eight 
years : “Thou canst not do wrong.” She met with the 
greatest opposition that I ever knew one person receive; 
and I never saw or heard of her being the least angry. 
She never complained of ill usage. She was sent for

HOLY WOMEN. 309 


by many, both rich and poor; and though she was 
exceedingly sensible of opposition, yet she would say, 
« {am not received at such a place; but the will of 
the Lord be done.” 

She bore the contradiction of sinners, and took 
patiently and joyfully the loss of her good name, willing 
to be nothing in order to possess all things. She said, 
«į want nothing, but to suffer all that Jesus will lay 
upon me, and for Him to fulfil His will in me every 
moment. I hope, through His assistance, to live as 
near to Him as any person in this world. I know He 
does all things well!” 


HER PRAYER, MANNER, &c. 


I never heard any thing spoken against Ann Cutler, 
except her manner of approaching the Lord. 1 hinted 
before that she prayed with great exertion of voice, 
and “in this she never lost her foes.” She was in our 
house several months at different times. It was her 
usual custom to arise at midnight, and pray and return 
God thanks for mercies received. Going to rest again, 
she slept till four, which was her regular hour of rising. 
She continued till about five, pleading for herself, our 
family, the society, the preachers, and the whole 
church. If we had no meeting at five, she retired into 
the chapel, and there continued in earnest prayer 
another hour. About six she went into her room, and 
read the scriptures with prayer. When she laboured 
with her hands, she would retire twelve or fourteen 
times in the day, and pray a few minutes at a time. 
She continued frequently very long in private, but was 
very short in public, and in general with a loud voice. 
Her plea for this was, “ I have tried to pray differently, 
but am always less confident, I would do any thing 
to please if it would not hurt my own soul; but I am 
in this way the most free from wanderings, and have 
the greatest confidence. I dare not strive against it 
any more,’’

She prayed without ceasing. Her life was a life of 
prayer, Ob! that I may follow her in this as she fol-

more earnestly.’ I have been in the chapel, when sud- 
denly the whole congregation have been deeply affec- 
ted in answer to her cries, For prayer, L never expect 
to see her equal again, 


HER MODESTY. 


Ann Cutler was often detained late in the evenings 
with people in distress, but would never return in coma 
pany with young men. She conducted herself in this 
respect to the glory of God, to the good of his people, 
and to the satisfaction of all. It appears from her 
journal that she laid a strong foundation for this mode 
of conduct: A short extract from which I shall here 
insert, 

“IT am Thine, blessed Jesus; I am wholly Thine, 
I will have none but Thee. Preserve Thou my soul 
and body pure in thy sight. Give me strength to shun 
every appearance of evil. In my looks keep me pure, 
in my words pure—a chaste virgin to Christ for ever: 
I promise Thee, upon my bended knees, that if Thou 
wilt be mine I will be Thine, and cleave to none other 
in this world, Amen, 


i 


ANN CUTLER? 


It appears, from difierent parts of her journal, 
that she had covenanted with God to live and die m 
this state; and she certainly was in a surprising 
manner kept from every stain in her conduct before 
men ; for both saints and sinners were constrained 
to say—“Nanny Cutler looks at nothing but heaven.” 


HER SELF-DENIAL. 


When with as she lived chiefly upon milk and herbs 
teas every thing strong she quietly but firmby rejected,

HOLY WOMEN. 3il 


When asked, she replied, «I dare not take it. I know 
what will grieve the Spirit. But though she was so ex- 
ceedingly temperate, she looked quite fresh and lively, 
I have often wondered that she went through so much 
labour with so little food, but she was in an extraordi- 
nary way supported. It never appeared that by any 
of her Jabours her life was shortened. Her manner 
was to see her call as clear as possible, to act in it with 
a single eye; and whatever extraordinary work the 
Lord called her to, she believed that He would support 
erin it. “She was crucified to the world and the 
world to her.” 
HER CONVERSATION. 


Many have entreated her to be more conversable : 
but her greatest gift was not argument, nor exhortation 
in public. She had uncommon sight into the people’s 
states either in leading class or in private. She was very | 
clear in her knowledge of repentance, faith, and holi- 
ness, “ but in this world knew little but herself? Her 
conversation was truly in Heaven. Ifany thing light 
or superficial was advanced when in company, she was 
uneasy, and would beg for a better subject, saying, “I 
am tired : I must talk about Christ or pray ; or I must 
retire.’ Thus she reproved many. I have often 
mourned that I was not so much in Heaven. 

Her words were few, “ seasoned with grace,” making 
a deep impression wherever she came. : With all this, 
she never had any gloom upon her countenance; but 
still presented the image of that sweet, that happy mind 
which was in Christ. I have seen her, when speaking 
of the glory of the world to come, stop suddenly, ap- 
parently filled with the spirit; and, when she could 
speak no more, she quietly sunk beneath the power of 
God, arose and retired under a holy shame.

make known bat to few. Yet it may not be wrong, as

Ann Cutler desired that I would declare my mind 
frecly concerning her call to different places, Two 
years before she entered into this way I persuaded 
her to the contrary, but at different times she believed 
it was her duty ; and when she went toa strange place 
her labours were much blessed. She came to see us 
at Dewsbury, where religion had been, and was then 
in a low state. In this circuit numbers had been de- 
stroyed through divisions, &c. I could not find a 
person that experienced sanctification, and but few 
who were clear in the knowledge of pardon. Our first 
year was a year of hard labour and much grief. The 
societies in some places increased, but active religion 
scarcely appeared. Nanny Cutler joined us in con- 
linual prayers to God for a revival of His work. As I 
was praying in my room, I received an answer from 
God in a particular way, and had the revival discovered 
to me in its manner and effects. I had no more doubt. 
All my grief was gone. I could say, the Lord will 
eome; I know He will come, and that suddenly. 

Nothing appeared very particular till under Nanny 
Cutler’s prayer, one soul received a clean heart. We 
were confident that the Lord would do the same for 
others. 

At a prayer-ineeting, two found peace with God: 
and the same week two more received the same bles- 
sing. On sunday morning we had a love-feast for tlre 
bands, then several were much concerned for sanctifi- 
eation. One young women received the blessing. On 
the Monday evening the bands met. A remarkable 
spirit of prayer was given to the people. Four persons 
received sanctification, and some were left in distress. 

Several, who were the most prejudiced, were sudden- 
ly struck, and in agonies groaned for deliverance, On 
the Thursday, one, who had been exceedingly pained 
for want of purity for a fortnight, was delivered. 

_ The work continued almost in every meeting; and 
sixty persons in and about Dewsbury received saneti- 
fication, and walked in that liberty. Our love-feasts 
began to be crowded, and people from every neighbour-
