ing circuit visited us. Great numbers found pardon, 
and some perfect love. They went home, and declared 
what God had done for them. , 

The more I consulted the Acts of the Apostles and 
church history, the more I was convinced that this 
was no new thing, either in its manner or effects ; but 
that in every great work of God similar things were 
produced. 1 consulted several of my, senior brethren, 
who exhorted me to use every means to support the 
revival. Satan began to use his agents in different 
ways. Some said one thing, and some another ; but 
no man, without the Spirit of God can properly judge 
of the matter. All must miss the mark, except those 
who are taught of Christ; and no greater mistakes 
can be made than they make who presume to say any 
thine of the work of God, and do not feel His love. 

The work, in a few weeks broke out at Great-land. 
Ann Cutler went over to Birstal, and was equally bles- . 
sed in her labours. She went to Leeds circuit, and, 
though vital religion had been very low, the Lord made 
use of her at the beginning of a revival, and the work 
spread nearly through the circuit. Very often ten or 
twenty, or more were saved in a meeting. 

She and a few more were equally blessed in some 
parts of Bradford circuit, and in Otley circnit. Where- 
ever she went there was an. amazing power of God | 
attending her prayers. This wes a very great trial to 
many of us: to sec the Lord make us of such simple | 
means, and our usefulness comparatively bat small. I 
used every means, in private, to prevent prejudice in 
the societies; but with many of my good elder brethren | 
it was impracticable. 

The Lord saw that, in Yorkshire, we were in too 
great-union with the world, which had certainly been | 
the case, for a number of years. He now drew the 
line: and to His name be ascribed the wisdom and 
gry. t

I FIND Jesus very precious. Ë hope you are

blessing. Every day some are brought to God. One. 
day twenty-five were justified; some sanctified. The 
Lord is carrying on His work. I think they have six- 
teen servants engaged in it. Three or four have received 
elean hearts. I never had a more blessed time than I 
have had here. I want to be more like Jesus. Let 
you and I give ourselves to God every moment, and 
seek in all things how to glorify Him. Pray for the 
preachers that you may receive them as from God. 
Whilst we live in the will of God, nothing can hurt us. 
No cross, no trial, need hinder our prospering, while 
we leave all and follow Christ. Watch against a light 
spirit, and all useless conversation; and let us pray 
every hour that God may save us from a mere forin of 
religion. May the power of God dwell in us!

seemed to be her daily custom to dedicate herself, body 
and soul, to God; to make that sacrifice which the 
Apostle recommends ;—when he says, “ I beseech you, 
brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your 
bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which 
is your reasonable service: She came to Macclesfield, 
on December 15, very poorly of a cold, being our 
preaching night. She had an earnest desire to have a 
prayer meeting ; but 1 told her, preaching beginning 
so late as eight o’clock, and classes to meet after, it 
would notbe convenient. Butshe was very importunate, 
and said, she could not be happy without one ; adding, 
«F shall not be long here, and L would buy up every 
opportunity of doing something for God, for time is 
short.” Knowing she had an uncommon talent for 
pleading for such souls as were coming to God, we 
got a few together, to whom she was made a blessing. 
Tuesday, the 16th, she was poorly, but used no less 
exercise in prayer, and would frequently say, “I. 
want to redeem time better, for L believe I shall not be 
in this world much longer;” and would lift up her eyes 
to heaven and say, “ O, blessed Jesus ! teach me to re- 
deem time better, that I may live more to Thee than I 
have ever done, that I may walk as Thou also walkedst 
here below.” At night we had our prayer meeting, 
in which she was very earnest in wrestling with the 
Lord for a present blessing for ‘every soul. Indeed, it 
was a blessed time to very many, a time in which much 
of the power of God came down. I believe it -was 
a season that will never be forgotten, After this meet- 
ing concluded, we went to another, where she exercised 
several times. I think it may be truly said, that she 
prayed with all prayer, and lived constantly in this 
spirit. On Wednesday the 17th, she complained of a 
soreness at her breast, and, for all this, did not abate 
of her usual exercise in prayer. The morning she 
employed in visiting sick persons, and many times 
prayed with and sweetly for them.—The afternoon she 
spent in praying with several friends. In the evening 
we had a public prayer meeting in the chapel. She

drawn out in prayer for them.

“Sunday the 28th, she was a little better, and was 
desirous of getting up, and did, whilst the bed was 
imade; but wished to lie down again immediately. 

After dinner she was worse, and complained of a pain 

inher breast. I asked her if I might send for the doctor; 

she said, I might, but added, “ He has done all he can: 
let us both be perfectly resigned to the will of God.” 

In the evening she was very restless, with a degree of 

delirium. 

_ About three o’clock on Monday morning, she began 

to ascribe glory to the ever blessed Trinity, and contin- 

ued saying, “Glory be to the Father, glory be to the 
| Son, and glory be to the Holy Ghost,” fora considerable © 
time. Afterwards she altered much for death. About 
seven o’clock, the doctor, with thoseabout her, thought 
she was just gone; but, to our great surprise, she con- 
tinued in this state till between ten and eleven o’clock 
in the forenoon. She then lifted herself up, and looked 
about her, and spoke just to be heard, and was very 
sensible: she seemed perfectly composed, but her 
strength hearly gone. About three o’clock she looked 
at her friends, and said, “I am going to die 7? and 
added, “Glory be to God and the Lamb for ever,” so 
loud as to be heard in any part of the house, till she 
was quite exhausted. About six o’clock I said, “Nanny 
how are you?” With a faint voice she said, “lam 
very ill.” I replied, “You are, but I trust your soul 
is perfectly happy.” She said, “ Yes it is, but I can- 
not so fully rejoice because of the weight of my aftlic- 
tion.” I said, “ Well, the Lord does not require it, or 

He would give strength.” “ Yes,” she said, “ He would, 
Glory be to God and the Lamb for ever |”? These were 
her last. words. Soon afterwards the spirit left this 
vale of misery. So died our dear and much valued 
friend, Ann Cutler. Obi 

The above are the particulars of her life during the 

time she was with us, and an account of her sickness 
on death, as far as 1 am able to recollect, 1 am yours,

© Miss SARAH WILSON, 


Was born near Atherstone in Warwickshire, and 
still resides at the place of her nativity. Her parents 
were strangers to religion, and had no saving acquaint- 
ance with the God of all their mercies. Sarah lived in 
the capacity of a servant, and was much respected in 
her situation. But being ignorant of the one thing 
needful, and unconscious of the value and state of her 
soul, she was careless about the salvation of the gospel. 
When Mr. R. Winfield visited Atherstone, he preached 
in the market-place ; and among the multitudes who 
went to hear him, she attended ; and the word of God 
was quick and powerful to the awakening of her con- 
science, and the alarming of her fears. She continued 
under the spirit of bondage, groaning for redemption, 
until, at a certain love-feast which she attended, she 
was freed from the remonstrances of a guilty conscience, 
and delivered of her load of sin, through faith in Jesus 
Christ. From that time she went on her way rejoicing 
in the God of her salvation, and in the inestimable 
treasure which she had found. But she was soon 
convinced that the carnally minded are at enmity with 
-God. Her friends’ and relatives, who were estranged 
from God through the ignorance that was in them, 
could not savour the power of godliness as manifested 
in her; and therefore endeavoured to shut up her way 
to the Kingdom. But none of these things moved her, 
for she knew the strength of that foundation on which 
she was building, and was fully assured that she had 
not followed a cunningly devised fable. She therefore 
remained diligent in the discharge of every christian 
duty, and delighted herself in the things pertaining to 
‘her peace.

Wherever religion exists it is manifest. The heart 


is the place whence words and actions proceed, anda — 
man’s deportment is always correspondent with those — 
principles by which his conduct is regulated. The — 


operations of divine grace are unseen by eyes.of flesh 
and blood; but a change wrought in the heart, gives 
an indubitable evidence : and while an unregener 
state is evidenced by the “ works of the flesh,” so is a 
state of salvation by the “ fruits of the spirit.” It must 
he so in the natare of things; “ Every good tree bringéth 
forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil 
fruit” 4 
This young woman had not long enjoyed. religion, 
before she began to be anxiously. concerned for the 
salvation of her family, friends, and neighbours. This- 
is the natural effect of regenerating grace. . The truly 


4 


pious are: not desirous of eating their morsel alone. — 


The grace of God expands the heart; and the benevo- 
lence of a good man, like that of bis. Heavenly Father, 


embraces the whole human family. Such. was the dis- _ 


position of Miss: Wilson, she longed for the salvation 
of souls, and prayed and laboured for the accomplish- 
ment of that which she desired. She began, in the 
fulness of ber heart, to preach to sinners, and to exhort 
them to behold the Lamb of God as. slain for a guilty 
world. In this work of mercy she is still engaged, and 
continues to visit the villages in the neighbourhood 
where she lives, “to. seek and to save that which is 
lost.” Her gifts are acceptable, and her fruit is visible 
and undeniable. She is highly esteemed in the con- 
nexion to which she belongs. t 


Miss MARY SEWELL, 


Was brought to God, and joined the Methodist | 
Society, when she was but young in years.. This was | 


HOLY WOMEN. 327 


at a period when the Church endured “a great fight of 
 affliction,”? and when God’s people were in little danger ~ 
- of falling under the curse contained in these words :— 
Woe unto you when all men shall speak well of you. 
_ Persecution rolled its malignant waves with infernal 
violence, and threatened to swallow up at once the 
harmless followers of the Holy Jesus ; and many a time 
- was this estimable young woman, like her suffering 
~ Lord, insulted and derided by the multitude. But 
_ with firm hold of the promises, and her eye fixed on 
_ the recompence of reward,” she 


“Stood as an iron pillar strong, 
And steadfast as a*wall of brass.” 


> 


Her attainments in religion were not of the ordinary 
kind. While she looked upon her interest in the divine 

mercy, as a blessing of incalculable worth, she had an 
astonishing apprehension of the, infinite fulness of the 
-renewing and sanctifying efficacy.of the blood of the 

me Redeemer. Imbibing the simplicity of faith, and 


plist | _ resigning her soul to the hidden teachings of the 
ine F) - eternal Spirit, she wasted.to.o discovery of the ama- 
o exho zing glory of the Gospel dispensation.. Her prayer 
a guiliy was—“ Let me thy witness live, when sin is all des- 
red, a troyed ;” and through faith in tbe hallowing grace of 
outho! the Father, and in the all cleansing blood of the Son, 
which b| E she obtained the desire of her heart. She was delivered 
svi] -- from all inordinate attachment to the world,Zand her 

whole soul leaned upon God. 
That such a person could be unconcerned about 
God’s glory, and man’s welfare, was impossible. Her 
love to souls was vigorous and constant; and her zeal 
for God was ardent and undaunted. She not unfre- 
quently hazarded her own life, in attempting to pro- 
mote the salvation of others, She suffered much from 
earth and hell, but she reckoned that the sufferings she 
endured, were not worthy to be compared with the glory 
which should be revealed. She laboured for the good 
ef her fellow-creatures, both “in season and out of

season.” and He who had called her to the work, was

minister of the Gospel wishes that his own household 
may be the first fruits of his ministry. Many places

her Heavenly Father. She has preached in Suffolk

strength. The ardour of her active spirit soon over- 
powered its earthly tenement, and taid it in the dust, 
While she lived she was a faithful witness for the Lord,

sion of the “ comforts of the Holy Ghost,” — 


“ Her eye she fix’d on the Eternal Throne,

PREFACE. 


Many and various have been the opinions of men 
„respecting a proper call to the christian ministry, and the 
-qualifications requisite for the right and successful discharge 

of that ministry. Some suppose that the call of a minister 
belongs to ministers, they being the most competent judges 
‘of thë talents and acquisitions necessary to the ministerial 
office; while others think he ought to receive it from the 
people among whom he is to labour. Some are of opinion 
‘that any person of ordinary abilities who has experienced 
the influence of divine truth on his own heart is qualified 
` to preach the gospel; but, others strenuously insist that no 
person is fit to minister in holy things unless he possess a 
critical knowledge of the languages in which the scriptures 
were originally written. * With regard to this last opinion, 


* As this last opinion is sanctioned by many divines of eminence 
and as it appears to me to be extremely erroneous and absurd, the 
reader will pardon me if I spend a little time in examining the grounds 

‘on which it rests. And first, let it be observed, that to be unqualified 

for the ministry, and uncalled to it, are as one; for the great Head of 

“thé church never makes choice of unqualified persons for that high 

‘office. But if ignorance of the dead languages disqualifies for the

we may observe, that while it is the interest of some men 
to represent the way to heaven as being very intricate, hard 
to find, and difficult to teach, we need not be surprised at 
finding it so described by them; for self-interest perverts 
the judgment and blinds the understanding. But whatever 
intricacies there may lie in the way which they teach, there 
are but few in God’s way, for it is spoken of as being so 


office, then the call of thousands of the most successful, yea, and the: 
most able ministers of the new testament, both living and dead, is 


at once disproved. 


If the bible was still buried in its original language, then indeed: 
an acquaintance with that language would be indispensable to every 
minister , but the real state of the case is very different. Possessing) 
as we do, a translation of the scriptures, which in the main, is consid- 
ered by all the learned, a faithful one ; and enjoying also the fruits: 
of the industry of a host of critics and commentators, whose integrity 
and learning can be relied upon, the necessity for this acquaintance 
disappears altogether. ge 


A person ignorant of other languages, may yet have a good 
knowledge of his own ; he may also have aready utterance, an inter- 
esting and impressive delivery, deep piety and zeal for God “according 
to knowledge, ” he may further have closely studied and obtained; 
tolerably correct views of the human character, and the great system 
of scriptural salvation ; together with so much of other sciences as 
are helpful in the illustration of divine subjects ; and, will any one 
say that such a man is not qualified for the ministry, or in other words! 
is not called to preach the gospel ! 


Suppose he knew so much of the original as to enable hin 
frequently to introduce critical remarks, &c. into his sermons, yet 
who will say how much this would help forward the great design o 
the gospel, viz. the salvation of souls? Who was ever converted b; 
literary disquisitions, the mere structure of sentences, or definin; 


of certain words?

PREFACE. ix 


_ Some persons have asserted that no one is justified in 
taking upon him the office of a minister without an over- 
whelming conviction that itis his duty; nay, it has been 
affirmed by some, that no man ought to begin to preach 
unless he is convinced he shall lose his soul if he do not. 
Now with regard to this sentiment, I would observe, that 
certainly no one ought to begin to preach without a per- 
suasion that God requires him to do so; but that this 
persuasion must in every case be overwhelming, I deny. 
Many thousands of useful ministers, whose subsequent 
eonduct, labours, and success, have proved them to be 
divinely commissioned, have begun to preach, not without 
a conviction of its being their duty,—but with a conviction 
which admitted of many scruples, and a great deal of 
uneasy suspicion as to its validity; and with -these 
suspicions they might be visited for some considerable 
time after they had entered upon their work. I allow that 
there should be the greatest caution where a man thinks he 
is moyed to preach the gospel, in order to ascertain that 
the movement really comes from the Holy Ghost and not 
from any other quarter; and to this end fervent prayer 
must be resorted to, together with the counsel and opinion 
of his religious friends ; but, that a person ought to resist 
the impression until the Holy Ghost is obliged to threaten 
him with damnation isa strange way of rendering him 
cheerful obedience. . That some men have felt such a convic- 
tion of its being their duty to preach we have known ; and 
that some WomEN have felt as powerful convictions of its 
being their duty. to call sinners to repentance,—-that God 
required it.at their hands,-—and that their salvation was at 


‘stake in case of disobedience, these SKETCHES will 


abundanily testify. And when it is remembered that no. 
female preaches for hire ; but that they. have to enter inte

x PREFACE. 


this field’ of labour, through much opposition from the 
counter-workings of their own mind, and the unchristian 
insinuations, and discountenance of hostile spirits ; it is not 
to be wondered at that many, perhaps most of those that 
have not had the above mentioned overwhelming convictions 
have shrunk from the cross and buried the talent which 
God gave them for public usefulness) A few however 
have in all ages of the christian church felt such a con- 
straining influence of the love of Christ, as ** Not to be 
awed by a mortal’s frown,” but at all hazards, ‘and at 


every expence t9 come boldly forward to snatch ** The: 
prey from the mighty, that the lawful captive may be) 


delivered.” But [am of opinion, that all those who have 


experienced the powerful energy of gospel truth on their: 


own minds, and believe themselves called to the work of the 


ministry; possessing at the same time a proper knowledge: 
of the scriptures, and the ability of expressing their ideas | 
with satisfaction to all sincere and reasonable hearers, are: 


divinely authorised to unfold the sacred treasures of redeem-. 
ing grace. And if in addition to this, they preach under a) 
divine influence, and sinners are converted through their 
instrumentality ; there is all the reason in the world in; 
acknowledging them the sanctioned heralds of the cross.

OF THE LIVES AND PUBLIC MINISTRY OF HOLY WOMEN, 


Hai noble worthies, ministers of grace, 

You holy females fir’d with zeal for God; 
Call’d to endure the scandal, shame, disgrace, 
To tread the thorny path your master trod. 


Fear not an arm of flesh, but rather féar 

His frown, who said to you go forth and preach ; 
That He hath bled,let ev’ry sinner hear ; 
The living way,—to ev’ry sinner teach. 


Let grave divines and learned doctors too, 
Dispute your call, forbid you to aspire, 

Say you invade their priestly rights, aad vow 
To keep you silent, and to quench your fire. 


Go forth ye veterans, fearlessly fulfil, 

That vast important task to you assigned ; 
Jehovah’s presence shall attend you still. 

Hence, stronger you than earth and hell combined, 


Approving heaven hath oft your labours crown’d, 
Living epistles doth your worth record: 
Pride and foul bigotry let this confound, 
That you are own’d and honoured by your Lord. 


Your names shall live, shall from oblivion rise, 
Transmitted down to ages yet unborn: 

A Tart is found eommission’d from the skies, 
To telt the world you rise above its scorn. 


LETTERS. 


Go on brave veteran, servant of the Lord, 
?Tis nobly done, and heaven approves the deed ; 
Be thine the task their virtues to record ; 

And smiling heaven will say, be thine the meed.

TO Mr. Z. TAFT. 


E’ER since by hell seduc’d ’mongst eden’s bow’rs, 
With vent’rous hand our hapless mother took 
The deadly fruit from the forbidden tree ; 

Her rude unblushing sons, with heart unkind, 
Have sadly torn her injur’d daughters’ name, 
And shut their eyes to all their godlike deeds, 
With Plautus bold, but few have roundly said, 
“Seek not a woman of virtuous rank to find, 

“Not one exists in nature’s wide domain ;” 

Or with the much admir’d licentious Pope, 
Declar’d each female is “a rake at heart. 

Yet, have philosophers and rhyming bards, 
Historians and divines in concert join’d 

To sing the name of women to its tomb. 

That joyless task be theirs. ‘To shew the world 
That female reputation ’still alive 

Has been reserv’d for you. Heaven bless the deed ! 
And with one eye full fix’d on human weal, 

And one straight on the glory of our God. 

Go on brave veteran! in the cause espous’d. 
Shroud from the pois’nous breath of envy’s lips 
Those plants of grace, which if with care preserv’d, 
Will vegetate, and teem with fruit divine. 

Woe to the man that impiously shall strive 

To quench those hallow’d fires, which mercy’s hand 
Throws down into our dungeon world, to guide 
Bewilder’d feet into the way of life. 

O Jesus! fan them to a living flame ! 

Direct them, blazing, through this lightless vale, 
To *illume dark souls, and frozen hearts to thaw:

FULL many a gem of purest ray serene, 

The dark unfathomed caves of ocean bear ; 

Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, 

And wastes its sweetness on the desert air. 
GRAY. 


So flows the elegiac minstrelsey of one 

Who sings of goodness modest,—hidden,—gone ! 
And has it always been? And shall it be? 

We turn to REASON, SCRIPTURE, and to THEE, 
Thou generous friend of slighted holy ones, 

But we appeal to those unfeeling stones — 

The marble hearted and the bigot eyed, 

Who scorn the gentle sex with bulky pride. 
First, then, we ask assuming REASON’S strain, 
Is MAN alone in dignity to reign? 

Is he to have no partner in his throne ? 

Or God decrees that he shall rule alone ? 

(Tis thus inquired: we pause to look around ; 
Perchance a queen for kingly man is found). 
Respondent words swell on the wondering ear: 
Let us attend: Jehovah’s self is neat. 

An help-mate for him, I will make, ordains 
The voice creative. Adam ne’er complains 
Altho’ alone,—companion of his heart—

Exert in public posts without controul ; 
Whilst they conform to laws in scripture given,

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES, &c. 


Mrs. SARAH CROSBY. 


THERE is some account of this eminently holy and 
useful woman published in the Methodist Magazine, but it 
has long been matter of wonder and regret, that a more 
lengthened memoir has not been laid before the christian 
public especially as she has left behind her three or four books 
in manuscript, each of them containing two or three hundred 
Closely written pages : and from an observation made at the 
end of one or two of these books, it evidently appears that 
She intended them for publication. She informs the reader 
that they were first written for her own profit, and for the 
perusal and edification of a few select friends, but having 
been earnestly solicited to suffer them to be made public 
_ by her most intimate and judicious friends, she has given 
_ her consent, and with an eye to this she has blotted out 
with her pen, or cut away, those particular parts of her 
journal which she could not consent to be made public. 
After the death of Mrs. Crosby, these journals fell into the 
hands of her intimate friend and companion, Mrs. Tripp, 
and from thence to Mrs. Mortimer, who had made a few 
extracts for the Methodist Magazine, but she did this very 
sparingly, as she knew but a small portion of that useful 
miscellany could be appropriated to such a purpose.

24 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


Mrs. Mortimer has expressed her high opinion of 
Mrs. Crosby, and of the subject matter of her journals in her 
introductory remarks to Mr. Benson; and to the writer of 
these ‘* Sketches,” she has expressed her long and earnest 
wish that Mrs, Crosby’s journals might bé given to the 
christian public. It will not be long, I hope, before the 
desire and expectation of the author and her confidential 
friends will be realized, and these documents receive that 
publicity, which their intrinsic excellence certainly 
merit. 


Having obtained the loan of part of these journals, I 
have made some very considerable extract in this Memoir, 
from which it will appear, that this apostolic woman was 
an itinerant, yea, a field preacher. She generally held a 
public meeting every morning at five o'clock, and also in 
the evening, and very frequently in the week-days, both 
in the forenoon and afternoon. On the sabbath she gen- 
erally went to the parish church, wherever she was, and 
held her meetings early in the morning,—at one o’clock,— 
and in the evening. She received the sacrament of the 
Lord’s Supper at the church at every convenient opportunity; 
and used fasting, or abstinence every friday. The vener- 
able Mr. John Wesley, whom she always calls her father in 
the gospel, highly approved of her conduct, believing that 
she was one of those females to whom the Lord had given 
a dispensation to publish the glad tidings of salvation by 
Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, he did not wish her, or any other ' 
female to assume the title and character ofa preacher, as he 
considered their call, not an ordinary, but an extraordinary 
one, and knowing the strong prejudice which prevailed 
in the minds of men in general, and of some in his own 
connexion against such a ministry, he gave such cautions 
to sister Crosby, and other female preachers with whom 
he corresponded, which, if attended to, he believed would 
be a means of softening the prejudices of his differing 
brethren, and yet increase and perpetuate the benefit which 
would accompany and follow their public ministrations.

To the Editor of the Methodist Magazine. 


Islington, Jan. 7, 1806. 
Dear Sir, 


Many have expressed a desire to see some account of 
that mother in our Israel, Mrs. Crosby. Her valuable papers, 
which would more than fill a jarge volume, have, by her 
“surviving friend Mrs. T, been put into my hands; from 
which I have selected a few of those parts that relate chiefly 
to her own experience. Her account of many of her labours 
and the difficulties she had to encounter while seeking 
| the good of precious souls, in that way to which she believed 
_ she had an extraordinary call, I have been obliged to omit, 
as too voluminous for your valuable publication ; but hope 
_ what is here transcribed will tend to quicken many to seek 
that degree of communion with God which she enjoyed. 


' Permit me to add, for near 36 years I have been 
favoured with the particular friendship of this- blessed 
woman, and for zeal for the glory of God, love to precious 
souls, manifested by unwearied labours, faithfulness in 
reproving what she thought wrong, and a happy facili- 
ty in encouraging souls to struggle up the hill of holi- 
ness, have found few to equal her; but her praise is in 
all the churches: she lives in the memory of thousands ; 
many who are gathézed home have cause to bless God they 
eyer knew her, as well as many who are still engaged in 
the glorious warfare. ‚But I will detain your readers no 
longer from a narrative, written by my dear friend, in a 
letter to Mr. Wesley, giving an account of her awakening,

London, August 17, 1757. 
Rev. and dear Sir, 


Your desire lays me under the blessed necessity of! 
recollecting past mercies. 


From my childhood I had desires to serve God, and! 
in particular to love Jesus Christ, and often wished that) 
I had lived when He was upon earth, that I might, like: 
Mary, have sat at his feet, and followed him whithersoever: 
he went. also often felt a painful wish that I might be: 
as good as ever any one was, and, on seeing funerals,. 
would often say, <‘ when I die, what will become of my | 
soul; if I were but sure of going to heaven I would noti 
care what became of my body.” Whenever I feared’ 
punishment for a fault, I prayed fervently against it, and | 
do not remember to have been blamed much, or corrected, . 
except when I forgot to pray.—Yet was I extremely rude: 
and heedless, so that some who knew me feared for me. 
But, O Lord! thy thoughts are not as our thoughts ! 


When I was about 14 years of age, I began seriously | 
to think I must not live as I had done. Accordingly I went’ 
to church on week days, learned forms of prayer, and did’ 
many things for a time, but was always subject to bondage! 
through fear of death, saying in my heart, “Ò ! that I might | 
never die, or that I knew God loved me!” Nevertheless, 
1 found in me a strong propensity to delight in singing, 
dancing, playing at cards, and all kinds of diversions ; but 


MRS. SARAH CROSBY. 27 


this I endeavoured to check from the beginning, not because 
I thought it sinful, but because I found the more I gave 
i way to these things, the more unhappy I became. 


About the age of 17, while sitting alone, I was struck, 
i as I thought, with death ; being seized with a cold trembling 
from head to foot, which, increasing, I directly fell on my 
knees, and prayed the Lord to forgive my sins, and save 
my soul. All that I knew to be sin was then placed before 
‘me; sothat I had but little hope of mercy. But while I 
laid myself down to die, my strength came to me again, for 
‘which I was very thankful, and made great promises to live 
to God; but did not begin to put them in practice till some 
‘months after, when reflecting on many things, I discerned 
in my soul an insatiable thirst for happiness. At first I 
thought it consisted in the abundance of things pertaining 
to this life; but was soon clearly convinced, if I possessed 
‘the whole universe, I should still be as far from happiness 
as ever. 


-~ A little after this I was providentially brought to hear 
Mr. Andrews, a dissenting minister, who preached from 
‘these words, Isaiah, lxii. 3, **Thou shalt also be a crown 
of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a-royal diadem in the 
hand of thy God; from which words he shewed, Ist, 
d that Christ was so, and 2ndly, every christian through 
‘Christ. I found my soul so drawn afier God at this time, 
that I determined to be a christian, at all events, and 
» to hear this minister at all opportunities; for I thought 
‘there was not such another man upon earth: I had many 
difficulties to break through; but was fixed to lose my 
i| dife rather than not hear him. 


I now began earnestly to strive against every thing 
that I knew tobe sin, and to practice all known duties : 
and I continued instant in prayer, for it was the very 
delight of my soul to pray at all times, and in all places. 
I also searched. the scriptures as I had time day and 
night; but the more I read, the more I was convinced 

Was not a christian; yet, I could not fear hell; for, 


23 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. ; 


although I knew I was not fit for heaven, I firmly believed 

I should not die till God made me fit. And whenever 
I was oppressed, these words were my support, I know 
that my Redeemer liveth. Hearing Mr. Andrews observe, 
that, without an interest in Christ we could not be saved, _ 
I believed him, but, thought I must make myself good, _ 
in order to come to Christ. Innumerable were my 
thoughts concerning God, myself, and the things ofi 
God, for upwards of two years. At the end of this time» 
finding myself worse, in my own apprehension, than» 
when I began this new course ; I was more distressed than i 
ever, and knew not what to do; till at length I resolved’ 
to ask Mr. Andrews how I might get an interest in Christ, - 
After asking me several questions, he told me that I had 
an interest in Christ, and that where God had begun a» 
good work, he would carry it on. F believed what hey 
said, and instantly felt my burden removed, and the- 
peace of God flow into my heart. For several days my» 
soul had felt an heavy burden, and I expected to hear») 
Mr. A. say, ‘you have done all that you can do, andi 
must now perish. I now praised God, and was amazed 1| 
that I should have an interest in Christ. What! sucha) 
wretch as I, be saved by grace !

diary and correspondence will very strikingly evince the: 
same truth; and also, that her self denying exertions in | 
the cause of Christ were of a most uncommon and praises: 
worthy description,

From Mr. Wesley to Mrs. Crosby. 
June 14, 1757. 


My dear Sister, 


I was concerned at not hearing from you for so longa I 
time, whereas I would not willingly passa fortnight without | 
it. Whenever you have leisure, write ; whether any one! 
else does or not. I shall be here near three weeks, and! 
then at York. It comforts me to hear that your love does i 
not decrease: I want it to increase daily. Is there notl 
height and depth in him with whom you haye to do, for: 
your love to raise infinitely higher, and sink infinitely | 
deeper into him than ever it has done yet? Are you fully | 
employed for him ? And yet so as to have some time daily, 
for reading and other. private exercises? If you should | 
grow cold, it would afflict me much. Rather let me always | 
rejoice over you. As for me I seem to be only just begin- 
ning to aim feebly at God: though I have found more 
liberty in the respect you mention lately, than of a long, 
season. Dear Sally, never forget to pray for 


Your affectionate Brother, 


JOHN WESLEY.

As this letter appears to be very different to Mr, 
Wesley’s letters in general, to this and other female; 
preachers ; there must have been at the time of his writing, 
some peculiar reason in his own mind for writing in the: 
way he did. Whether it arose from some exaggerated’ 
reports of the conduct of this eminent female, by which! 
he feared she had stepped, or was in great danger of stepping; 
over those boundaries, which modesty and christian pru-. 
dence would lay; or whether it arose from the opposition! 
he met with on account of his encouraging some females: 
in preaching, or from any other cause, does not appear.’ 
But that he believed, that some women had a divine call! 
to ministerial services in the church of God, none will! 
deny, who have read his letters, and observed his’ conduct’ 
to such in his connexion. Miss Bosanquet for many) 
years took a text, and explained and applied the passage: 
in the common method of preaching.. Mr. Moore, in his 
Memoirs of her life has given us several of her manuscript! 
Sermons, And she did nothing, as she informs us, buti 
what Mr. Wesley approved. ‘I think” says he to her,’ 
s< the strength of the cause rests here, in your having ani 
extraordinary call.” Miss Mallet preached for many years 
and Mr. Wesley’s letters to her were all intended to 
strengthen and encourage her to proceed in the same way. 
He says to her, ‘It gives me pleasure to hear thats 
prejudice dies away, and our preachers behave in a friend!

My. dear Sister, 


You oblige me much by speaking so freely, 

What an admirable teacher is experience! You haye | 
great reason to praise God for what he has taught you | 
hereby, and to expect that he will teach you all things. . 
But whatever you find now, beware you do not deny what | 
you had once received. 1 do not say ‘‘a divine assurance | 
that you should never sin, or sustain any spiritual loss,” ` 
I know not that ever you received this; but you certainly l 
were saved from sin; and that as clearly, and in as high | 
a degree as ever Sally Ryan was. And if you have sus- - 
tained any loss in this, believe, and be made whole. I | 
never doubted, but —— would recover her strength, though | 
‘she has long walked in a thorny way. . A general tempta- | 
tion now, is the denying what God had wrought. Guard | 
all whom you converse with from this; and from fancying | 
great grace can be preserved without great watchfulness | 
and self denial. 


I am Your affectionate Brother, 


JOHN WESLEY.

and as I said, the Lord guide us ; he answered inmy heart,

Thursday, July 14th, 1769. I unfeignedly thank my 
Lord for all the fatigue of body and mind his powerful 
hand-has helped me through, since I last recorded his 
mercies. Before we left Layton-Stone, we had a time of 
suffering, and our journey into Yorkshire was trying tothe 
flesh; but our Lord brought us safe hither, at the appointed 
time. Since we came to this place * it is impossible to 
describe our sorrows, or satan’s assaults ; yet hitherto hath 
the Lord helped us, and our confidence in him is greatly 
increased. From the first I always believed it was the 
will of God we should come and settle in Yorkshire; but 
never did I descern satan oppose any thing with more vio- 
lence and constancy, than he has done this. My prayer 


* Gildersome, about five miles from Leeds, in Yorkshire. Before 
this time she lived with Miss Bosanquet, at Layton-Stone, in Essex. 
For a particular account of Miss Bosanquet, her establishment at Lay- 
ton-Stone and ofher removalinto Yorkshire, I refer the reader to the 
life of Mrs. Mary Fletcher, written by Rey. Henry Moore, and sold at the 
Methodist Book Room, in London. She established a kind of Orphan- 
house, at Layton-Stone, (the place of her birth.) Mrs. Ryan, Miss 
Tripp,and Mrs. Crosby, were her assistants in this great work of chris- 
tian benevolence. ‘Fhese pious females, began more fully to enter into 
the work of the Lord, by holding public meetings for reading, exhor- 
tation, and prayer. Many attended, and much good was done. The 
first public meeting the Lord was eminently present, and two souls 
were set at liberty, Mr. Wesley was consulted, and applied to for 
counsel and assistance. He approved of their plan, and sent them 
a preacher, Mr. Murlin, and in a few weeks twenty-five joined in 
Society. Mr. Wesley’s opinion of this establishment at Layton-Stone 
may be found in his journal, (see his Works, Vol. 4.) he says 
“ Thursday, December 12, 1765. I rode over to Layton-Stone, and 
found one truly christian family. This is what that at Kingswood 
should be and would, ifit had such governors.” Again, “* Thursday, 
February 12, 1767, 1 preached at Layton-Stone, O what a house of 
Godis here! Not only for decency and order, but for the life and 

ower of religion, I am afraid there are very few such to be found 
in all the king’s dominions.” During the five years and three months 
Miss Bosanquet and her assistants and fellow labourers resided here, 
a very lively society of christian believers were raised up, and the 
general conduct, and behaviour of the people much improved, and 
several individuals died.in a very triumphant manner, Whether 
Miss Bosanquet did right in breaking up this establishment, is 
matter of doubt. Suffice it that she acted according to her best | 
judgment, and from the purest motives. Enprror.

Cross Hall, April 26, 1780, 


At my return from Halifax, J met with my good 
friend's truly simple letter, with which I was well pleasedy 
Notwithstanding all your complaints, I do charitably hope 
you have been gaining some strength, though, (as you 
observe) you are surrounded with trials, which you before 
knew little about, Tear not, only believe! cast not awa 
your confidence, which hath great reecompence of rewar 


Now learn experience by the things you have suffered —the 
insufficiency of men, or of books to establish your so in 
abiding peace, ** Verily” saith the Lord, ‘* if ye will nop 
believe ye shall not be established,” I rejoice im your 
determination to go onin the simple path, to be any thing 
or nothing: this is the way to true rest. I notice all yo 
say about preachers and people, and advise my dear friend 
to bear and suffer, say as little as you can to any ; but of 
Him whose love is for ever new. 1 think you have only 
lost the dross through your trials, and*trust you will be 
brought out of the fire, as gold that is purified. -Certainly 
you are not to expect a greater perfection than can be Obs: 
tained, but it is your privilege to “rejoice evermore, pray: 
without ceasing, and in every thing give thanks.” But if 
any man lack wisdom, let him ask of God.” As [trust 
you do, who will give liberally the wisdom, which sits by: 
his throne, and which is Ist. pure, 2nd. peaceable, ri 
3rd. easy to be entreated.’’ O what a blessing it i to 
be child-like and teachable! Many need no more kiah 
they have to make them truly great, (as one observes) bub 
to think themselves litle. Sink»down my soul, lie level 
with the dust. We truly rise by sinking. Glory be to 
my Lord! I find him to be the life-giving word, my pre- 
sent and eternal portion, You inquire about my com 
I have written to Mrs. Dobbinson to that effect, she will 
tell you. God bless you, and make your peace to flow like: 
Jordan’s swelling stream. Do all you can for God; andi 
remember me before the gracious throne, 

ht 


Your unworthy friend in Divine bonds, 


S. CROSBY.

From Miss Hurrel * to Mrs. Crosby. 


{ Derby, May 18, 1779. 
My dear friend, 


Your favours are generally the answer to prayer, 
and very acceptable. I have not forgotten former times, 
and therefore feel a great attachment to my good, old, tried 
miend; and while christianity has any seat in my_heart, 
Mrs. Crosby will be deservedly dear to me. I rejoice, to 
near that the Lord your keeper stands omnipotently. near. 
Í trust He. will ever give you to feel in all the changes of 
his fluctuating scene, beneath, and around you, are spread 
whe everlasting arms. I hope you have found a good time - 
at Scarborough, and that you are much blest to the Whitby 
ends, to whom present my love.—At length my dear, the 
snail hath left its shell, and here J arrived with God’s blessing 

n saturday week, where I have full employ, and here I 
believe it is the Lord’s will I should be for a season; but 
rest now satisfied, and wait the Lord’s direction. If nothing 
prevent, I intend going from hence to Sheffield, Doncaster, 
York, and to stop a little at Pocklington, Beverley, Driffield, 
and from thence to Scarborough, and then where the Lord 
pleases to appoint. ‘‘ I wait his guiding eye to feel.” —If 
you think any of my London friends have been whispering 
n my ear to stay among them, I must fully acquit them: 
I have many there who are truly concerned for my welfare, 
yet they do advise me to go, and be and doas the Lord 
points out. Here I am, and earnestly desire to be and do, 
what, and as God pleases ; all I ask is that I may not dis- 
grace the gospel, or cause the good way to be evil 
spoken of. Mrs. Dobinson joins in love to you. Pray 
for me. 

Tam 


Your affectionate friend, 
E. HURREL.

joy that is before, far overbalances these light afflictions, - 
I am thankful the Lord still makes you useful to others. [| 
wish he may continue to do so, for the reverse is quiet pain- - 
ful; and to be in society, as a wen upon a man’s face, is

what the Lord will enable me todo at Lynn, Walsingham, - 
Fakenham, Wells, Bury, &c. I-know a divine teacher

see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in ©

all that is within me, praise him for my daily mercies. I 
am fall of rheumatic pain in this nearly worn out body ; 
Lalso feel frequent pains of mind, in sympathizing with 
‘some dear friends, in illness, and other troubles, still believ-

andme. I have enjoyed many reviving seasons for these 
, last few months, blessed be my Lord. But I long for deeper 
manifestations of the divine nature. O, when shall I be 
overwhelmed with thy delightful presence.

January 21st, 1801. Glory be to God, I have great 
cause for thanksgiving this new year. O, that mercy may 
rejoice over judgment, and sinners humble themselves before 
God, from the king to the beggar. May we all become 
beggars at a throne of grace, and confess that our sins are 
the causes of all our national sufferings. It is painful te 
reflect that many are perishing for want of bread, on account 
of the high price of corn, notwithstanding the large contri- 
butions which have been made to help them. O! when 
wiit thou, O Lord, arise, and say, as thou once didst, ** I have 
seen, I have seen the affliction of my people, and am come 
down to deliver them?” Surely, because of swearingy 
wasteful living, and many other sins, our land mourneth. 
O Lord, send forth the spirit of repentance throughout the 
nation, that the spirit of faith may follow, and heal oun 
sinful wounds; that peace and plenty may cause the voice 


of thanksgiving and melody to be music for the king of (jet 


kings. On the first day of this year, while praying in my§ 
class, the Lord gave me such a manifestation of his loving 
presence, and such an assurance of his favour, as melted 
my soul intolove. My friends partook of the blessing, and) 
we praised our Lord together. On the sabbath day, I wasi 
too ill to attend publicly to renew my covenant with m 
Lord, among his people; but being alone, I offered myself $ 


afresh to him, who is the leader of his people.—He gra- fii: 


ciously shewed me, my present call was, patiently to suffer, 7 
with resignation, all the will of God; offering praise andi $ 
thanksgiving to him, who has poured a spirit of praise) 
into my soul. 5

Sunday, March 15th. Iwas much pleased and pro-

“gave us; dearness of provisions and scarcity of work, make 
“the times very trying. Afterwards as I was pouring out 
‘my soul in secret before the Lord, I was deeply affected 

with the wants of the poor, and the state of our nation. It 
‘seems as if all the powers of earth and hell were risen up 
against us, and as if it were impossible for us to escape their 
fury, or conquer so many nations now united against us, 
-andbent on our destruction; unless our gracious Lord will 
| appear for us ; and in answer to the prayers of his people, 
‘take the matter into his own hands, and fight our battles 
for us, by the winds or seas; or find a way to us unknown, 
| My very soul was poured out in pleading with the almighty 
for our king and nation, and while begging our adorable 
high priest to intercede for us, as a nation, upon which 
he had poured such multiplied mercies, and purged away 
the sins of so many of its inhabitants, by his own most pre- 
‘cious blood, my soul was divinely assured, and sweetly 
happy in believing, that the intercession of Jesus shall save 
the nation, my soul was sweetly filled with faith and love ; 
breaking forth in praise and thanksgivings, adoring the 
Godof my salvation. Glory, glory be unto his name for ever.

It is said that our departed friend Mrs. Crosby often ex-

that all faithful, useful ministers of Jesus Christ would stand,

he had given them in the world. Thus she understood

Several times in the week she said, if I die soon remember 
such and such things. Thursday and friday she met both the 
clases, as usual, relating to them a dream she had on the wed- 
nesday night, which is mentioned above. In one of the classes 
she said her time here would not be long, and repeated, 
who first shall be summoned away; my merciful God, is 
itl? Andsaid she found herself more allied to heaven 
than earth; for though she had many friends here, she 
had more in glory,—On saturday she wrote two letters, 
went to the select band in the evening, and bore a blessed 
testimony for her Lord, Though very poorly she rose on 
sunday morning, and went tothe preaching at seven, and 
said, she found her spirit sweetly refreshed under the word. 
At breakfast she began again the subject of dying soon, 
mentioned some little things she could like to have done, 
and some, concerning which it had given her pain, that 
she had not been able to accomplish them ; I think it was 
then she said, I have nothing that holds me here now, but 
you, my dear; but God will be with you. She wentagain 
to the preaching in the evening, and stayed the society 
meeting, but returned very ill, with a pain in her chest; 
we gave her something, which relieved her; but in the 
night, the pain returned again with violence, attended with 
shiverings, and cold sweats, as if she were dying. We 
sent for the doctor, who said she was very bad, although 
he hoped she would be brought through; but she said, 
without a change I cannot continue long ; and began pray- 
ing for her bands, classes, friends, and the church of God ; 
that they might all meet above. Being requested to spare 
herself, she said, my dear, if I go now, I have neither doubt, 
nor cloud; I know I am going to glory. I have been ask- 
ing my Lord for a promise, and he says, ‘<I will never 
leave thee.” Her weakness was such she could scarcely be 
kept from fainting, during the greater part of the day. 
Towards evening we conceived great hopes of her recovery. 
as the doctor said her pulse was good; and she began to

breathe with less difficulty. A little before she expired 
she said to one that was present, if I had strength how I 
could praise him. But at eight o’clock, without a groan, 
or struggle, she closed her own eyes and mouth, and sweet! 
fell asleep in Jesus. This was October 24th, 1804, on the 
eve of her spiritual birth-day, which was fifty fiye years 
ago, and she was aged seventy five, (within a,week*) So 
composed was her countenance, that when dead, not the 
least trace of death was discernible on it.

Mr. Taylor preached her funeral sermon to a crowded 
audience, from Rev. xxi. 4. a text. she had chosen for the 
purpose, soon after she was justified. To draw a just 
character of her would require a more able pen than mine; 
but after so many years close intimacy, and through know- 
ledge of her, 1 think it a tribute due to her memory to say, 
she was a sincere lover of truth, a pattern of christian 
simplicity ; and had such ardent love to Jesus, and zeal for 
his glory, as have been possessed by few. Being dead, she 
yet speaketh, and will live long in. the affections of those 
who had the happiness of her particular instructions and 
intimacy.

methodists, that we may imitate those that ate gone, im

his glory. Thus you see, my dear friend, I have endea- 
voured, though in.a very feeble and imperfect manner, to

loss 1 deeply feel; and whose memory I revere.. Much

_ Elizabeth Collet, (whose maiden name was Tonkin,) 
was born in the parish of Gwincar, in the county of Cornwall, 
| May 9th, 1762.. The Lord began to work on her soul at 
i an early age, and in various ways; sometimes drawing her 
i with the cords of love, and sometimes alarming her by ter- 
‘rors. Just after her mind became the subject of divine 
‘impressions, the Lord was pleased to encourage her by 
comfortable dreams; in which we cannot but admire his 
i goodness, in so adapting the comfort he afforded her, to 
i her age and circumstances. One night for instance, she 
| dreamed she was in a garden, were both Christ and Satan 
| were present with her; that Satan strove with all his might 
i to get at her, and hurt her, but could not move his foot, 
i and that Christ then said to her, ‘* wilt thou not now believe 
that thou art my child, seeing he cannot move to hurt 
thee?” At another time she dreamed tha$ she saw our 

Lord clothing his people with beautiful white robes, and 
| while standing at a distance with most intense desire, that 
she also might be thus clothed, he beckoned to her with 


118 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


his hand to come to him, which she gladly did, and wa; 
adorned like the others. Being thus blessed with a minc 
susceptible of the most serious feelings, whatever she heare 
or saw of a pious tendency, producing some lasting goue 
effect. Once, when her father set her this copy, “death i; 
in the old man’s face; but it may be at the young man’; 
back ;” it sunk into her heart, like a stone into the mighty 
waters. At another time, when in a neighbour’s house 
she saw the picture of St. Lawrence, roasting on a gridiron 
and saying, ‘‘this side is sufficiently roasted, turn me on the 
other side, that I may suffer for the Lord Jesus ;” she was 
so affected by the sight, as no language can describe. She 
now separated herself from all trifling company, having 
no relish for their communications ; and while her former 
youthful companions were employed in dissipating amuses 
ments, she was drawn to employ her leisure hours in acts 
of secret devotion, to which she was excited by the example 
of her mother, who conscientiously attended to closet duties, 
To these gentle drawings, strong terrors succeeded ; which 
were occasioned partly by deeper convictions of her need 
of salvation partly by alarming dreams respecting the 
misery of lost souls, and the end of time, and partly by 
powerful temptations to fear that she had committed the 
unpardonable sin, and that her day of grace was ee 
Under the influence of these feelings, she seemed to read: A | 
the sentence of death in every thing she saw; and would PA 
often retire to a solitary spot, to bewail her sad condition. 

While in this distressed state, she frequently repeated the f 
following lines of the xxxviii. Psalm, old version ; as she à 
thought them exactly adapted to her present situation, 


“Thy arrows do stick fast in me, 
Thy hand doth press me sore ; 

And in my flesh no health at all, 

Appeareth evermore, 

And all this, is, by reason of 
Thy wrath that I am in; 

Not any rest isin my bones, 
By reason of my sin. 

And I in fearful case am brought 
Into such great distress, 

That I go wailing all the day, 
In doleful heaviness,”

in which we have now seven societies, eight local preachers, and 
seven chapels, besides several other oceasional preaching places. 
Since the establishment of Methodism there, many have died happy in 
the Lord,—many, who were ornaments to civil and religious society, 
still remain,—and all visible opposition to the gospel has ceased. 
Never did Roseland so well become its name as now, when, through 
the influence of heavenly grace and truth, the desart blossoms as the 
rose,—when the inhal itants ‘see the glory of the Lord,--and their 
moral state so resembles the fertility of their soil.

The Rev. Jos. Taylor in a letter to my parents after 
their marriage, observes, “there seems to be a remarkable 
train of Providences in what you relate, and a literal fulfil- 
i ment of that promise, in all thy ways acknowledge God, 
and he will direct thy paths.” After my mother’s marriage, 
for nearly twenty years, she frequently held meetings in the 
“neighbouring places on the Lord’s-day, and sometimes on 
the working day evenings also; but never to the neglect 
of her domestic duties; for whenever she thus engaged, she 
ordered her family concerns so, that we were never deprived 
of one comfort on this account; and itis worthy of remark, 
that for the last thirty four years of her life, she was never 
one night absent from her family. es

_ Dear Sir,

| some years; except fora few months last past, in which I 
was ready to faint, and began to doubt of ever being cleansed

had to encounter dfficulties, similiar to those which she 
had surmounted at Philleigh; but conducting herself as 
she had formerly done, she at last succeeded in getting a 

place for divine worship established. But still she had three 
| miles to go to her class-meeting, from which she was very 

seldom absent; and in the work of ‘ refreshing the saints,”

my parents for some considerable time, stood almost alone ; 
by entertaining the preachers so that they might conveni- 
ently visit several places, where they could then find no 
accommodation but where they are now received with 
truly christian hospitality. Thus, amidst the increasing; 
cares and exercises occasioned by a growing family, and 
under much bodily affliction and infirmity, the love of 
Christ constrained my mother to continue all possible efforts 
in dependance on God for the spiritual welfare of her famil 
and neighbours, till she saw Zion in prosperity. But house 
a society was formed in Veryan, no convenient central place: 
for preaching could be obtained, for several years, On 
this account my mother ceased not to pray that a house 
might be built for the honour of God; and at last, amidst 
great opposition, a chapel was erected, chiefly through 
the instrumentality of my parents. 


In the year 1800, Providence opened our way to St. 
Erme, nearly ten miles from Veryan. About two or three 
years before this, Mr. Cornelius Philp, a respectable farmer) 
in St. Erme, was savingly converted to God; and being; 
deeply concerned for the salvation of his neighbours, he 
hired a house, and got both the travelling and local preachers 
to preach in it. A little after our arrival in that parish, my) 
mother, then not enjoying good health, nor expecting to 
live long, one night dreamt that she was in company with 
Mr. Philp, and told him, ** I am going home soon ;’? when: 
she thought he took her by the hand and replied, ‘no, not 
ou, but 1; for God sent you here; and so it proved, for 
he died in the faith, a few months after. The Lord was 
pleased to make use of my parents in carrying on the work! 
which he had begun by this good man ; for my mother took! 
his class, and my father built a chapel, in which preaching 
is still continued, ‘This was the second chapel, which my 
parents were the honoured instruments in erecting. It was) 
opened in April, 1804, and during the next month my 
mother held a meeting in it, which was the last time she 
ever spoke in public, Her health now declined, and she 
was unable to attend the means of grace, at any consider- 
able distance. A class was therefore appointed to meet at

I would fain so write as to be a comfort fo you, 
if I knew how. Well, I do ask of the Lord to shew me 
what to say.—Then I would observe, there are various 
paths in which the Lord sees good to lead his peoples 
Sometimes we are called to rejoice ; and at others to weep 
and bleed with our Lord in the garden. And at those 
times, I have often found satan accuse me, because I did 
not rejoice, when I was really called to weep. Now ] 
think this is a good deal your case. You are one who is 
called to drink of your Lord’s cup, and to be baptized with 
his baptism. ‘Therefore let all yvur exercise be, “ thy will

founded.” 


Mr. Wesley observes, ’tis probable our eternal enjoy- 
ment of God, will bear a proportion to our sufferings here ; 
because, if we endure our trials with resignation, looking to 
the things which are not seen, it has a great tendency to 
mould our hearts into his will. And therefore St. Paul 
says, our light afflictions which are but for a moment, work 
out for us a far more exceeding, and eternal weight of glory, 
than otherwise we should be capable of receiving. What 
an encouraging thought is this! Come my sister take 
courage, suffer, with the Lord to reign.

But amidst my mother’s diversified afflictions, she was 
greatly comforted not only by witnessing the ‘prosperity of 
Zion, in various instances, but also by the accomplishment 
of her soul’s most ardent desire, in behalf of her children. 
In the year 1806, the Lord began to work in my soul, 
being the eldest of the family, and the first that was brought 
into the good way. O! what happy seasons did I now enjoy 
with my mother, in conversing with her about heavenly 
things. I trust those days will never be erased from my 
‘memory. In the year 1813, the Lord caused her to rejoice 
anew, in seeing three more of her children joined to the 
lord, and his people; two of my brothers who are now 
local preachers, and my eldest sister. And a few years 
after, to her unspeakable joy, her other three children were 
also given to her prayers. In the year 1820; we removed 
from St. Erme. to Warliggan, where we now reside. On 
our arrival here, we found it necessary to divide the class ; 
and a part of it was appointed to meet at our house, being 
committed to the care of my mother, as the leader. About 
three months before her last illness, one day as she was 
waiting upon the Lord, she was favoured with one of the

To the proceeding memoir, much need not be added, 
| in delineating the character of its subject. That she was 
| always zealously affected in the good; cause of God, is evi» 
dent; but it should also be observed, that her prudence 
_ and modesty were no less ‘conspicuous than her zeal. It 
_ has already been seen, that no domestic duty was neglected 
through her compliance with what she considered a divine 
} call to more public exercises; and that she, had a dive 
| call to prophecy, or speak in the name»of Christ for the 
| edification, and comfort of his church, and the awakening 
i and conversion of sinners was the opinion of most, if not 

all those to whom she was intimately known, while living, 

and her memory is still precious to many. Whatever suc- 
| cess attended her labours, she uniformly ascribed to: God, 
_ being deeply impressed with the conviction that the good 
i which is done in the earth, the Lord. doeth it himself; and 
| at all times it appeared. her highest ambition to sit at the 
| feet of all, and to be the servant of all. 


_ Inconversing about the deep things of God, she greatly 
i excelled; being ever ready out of the good treasure of her 
| heart to bring forth good things. »But while her lips fed 
many, nothing like. ostentatious. display, ever appeared in 
her deportment. .When opportunities for speaking to the 
use of edifying, could not be obtaitied, she chose rather to 
| be thought singular, or unsociable, or-deficient in capacity, 
than to incur the guilt of speaking idly. 


Tn the practice of closet duties, she was conscientious, 
and abundant ; and walking humbly with God, she found 
it good to draw nigh unto him. To the comforts of christian 
communion, she was by no means insensible; for her 
delight was in those who excelled in piety. To domestic 

| happiness also, she was feelingly alive ; and enjoyed, while 
she dispensed sweet solace, in her beloved family circle. 
| But it was in secret intercourse with her heavenly Father, 
| and Redeemer, that she was favoured with the richest con- 
aolations. Here she found the clearest direction in ail 
difficulties, —the best, asylum, in every storm that either 
| frowned, or fell,—and the most exalted anticipations of

heavenly felicity. In-governing her family, and. rightly 
employing her influence on them,-she was exemplary, and 
successful. Amidst all the ‘vicissitudes which occurred) 
during the forty years “of her connubral. state, she ever 
acknowledged the hand of ‘God, and manifested the mosti 
serious concern to follow his direction. That all wader her 
tare might be at liberty to’ attend. the ordinances of God, 
and wait upon ‘him without ; distraction, she remembered) 
the sabbath day ‘to keep ‘it holy ; being always ¢areful toi 
make such preparation for ‘it, that nothing secular might bey 
done or said im it, but‘what was absolutely necessary. -Thati 
her children might learn’ what to°imitate and what to’shun,, 
she early stored their minds with records of the most’strik-. 
ing examples, and ends, both of good and bad characters: 
To preservethem from the influence of evil communications, 
she permitted them ‘to associate familiarly only with the 
wisest and best of those around them; ‘and she restramed!

The bible is the best source of instruction and) 
edification ; being nothing less, than the word of God,—. 
the production of His Spirit,—the Spirit of infinite wisdom, | 
knowledge, purity, and benevolence. There are however, | 
a variety of inferior and subordinate sources, of human: 
production ; which are only valuable in proportion as they: 
exhibit and recommend the pure and plain truth of God.| 
Among these faithful relations of christian experience, ' 
may be allowed to hold a distinguished place. Suchi 
documents, candidly and devoutly perused, afford much 
interesting and useful information. :; 


Ist. They serve to shew how sinners are savingly| 
brought to God,- viz; in the way of conviction for ‘sin,’ 
repentance towards God, and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ ; 
all which, are produced by the agency of the Holy Ghost; 
so that, though there may be a circumstantial diversity ini 
the conversion of sinners, as to the acuteness of their 
conyictions,—the pungency of their repentance,—the súbor- 
dinate means of their conversion.—and the degree of inward 
enjoyment, &c.—yet, the work, or thing itself, is always) 
one ;—always originating in conviction,—and comprising 
repentance, faith, and conscious freedom from the guilt and 
thraldom of sin. 


2nd. We learn also, how we are te proceed, in orderi 
io our retaining the pearl of great price, and in order to ii 
our increasing with the increase of God, viz; to be daily 
exercising faith in Christ,—watching unto prayer,—and 
striving to follow the leadings of Providence, as to our 
particular and proper sphere of action. 


MISS MARY HEWETT. 141 


3rd. They teach us likewise, that whatever may be our 
trials, our case is not peculiar; many having had to pass 
i through the like exercises, and some through much heavier. 
We are hereby taught the lesson which the word of God 
teaches us,—viz; that no temptation hath happened unto 
us but what is common to men; and that in every tempta- 
| tion, God will, if we continue faithful, make a way for our 
escape.

The following brief memoir, is an extract of the reli- 
gious experience of a young woman, written by herself. 


I was born on the 20th of the 12th mo. 1803. My 
“parents were regular attendants of the Friends’ meetings, 
and brought up their family in that discipline. The meetings 
which we attended were frequently held in silence ; though 
‘sometimes we were favoured with having the word of 
truth held forth amongst us. At such seasons, I have felt 
“a secret conviction that I was not what I ought to be. When 
in the eighth year of my age, I spent some time with a 
friend in Bristol, and once heard a young woman from 
_ America bear a public testimony to the truth, in the Friends’ 
meeting house; under which I was led to think, that there 
_was something in religion really desirable,—and to wish I 
could be a preacher. I delighted in reading the happy 
deaths of pious children, and have frequently wept. desiring 
to be like them ;—but I was a stranger to the knowledge 
of my fall in Adam, and the depravity of my heart,—nor 
did I know that I needed salvation through him, who 
alone could restore me to the favour of the Almighty. As 
I arrived to riper years, like too many, I loved gaiety and 
pleasure ;—and if I, in any wise, differed from them, it 
_ was not because I had not an inclination to the vanities of this 
‘wicked world, but because I was blessed with moral parents, 
who would sometimes curb me with the bridle of restraint.

MRS. MARY DUDLEY, 


Mrs. MARY DUDLEY. 


This pious and holy woman was born of respectable 
rents, who were members of the Church of England. 
Her mind was powerfully wrought upon by the operations 


of the divine spirit, when she was very young. And being 


Jed to hear the Methodists, she received further light, and 
conviction of the necessity of being fully devoted to God. 


She joined the Methodist Society, and became personally 


aid intimately acquainted with that great and good man, 
the Rey. John Wesley. How long she continued in his 
Society, does not appear, but her mind was not fully at rest ; 
and she seems to have been led by the secret, but powerful 
workings of her own heart, to attend the meetings of Friends, 
and finally to join that Society; Why she could not find 
rest, and pasturage in that community where so many holy 
and useful men and women have been-raised up, and pre- 
pared for mansions of glory, is not forme to say. If the 
reader be disposed to censure this part of her conduct, he 
must admire the purity of her motive. She appears to have 
been.a very eminent and useful woman inthe Society of 
Friends. . the following skETCH of her religious experience 
and labours, is taken from an Octavo Edition of her Life, 
lately published and edited by her daughter, Hannah Dudley. 


Mary Dudley was the daughter of Joseph and Mary 
Stokes, and born in the city of Bristol, the 8th of 6th mo. 
1750. Being of a delicate constitution, she was, during 
infancy and childhood, subject to frequent and severe indis- 
positions, yet she was early sent to school, and often 
mentioned, as a proof of serious thoughtfulness, her love of 
reading the Holy Scriptures, and that her partiality for the 
Prophecies of Isaiah was such, as to make her governess 
repeatedly inquire whether she had not yet got through that 


150 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES, 


book? Being of quick parts, and possessing facility at 

acquiring knowledge, she made rapid progress in learning ; 

and as she advanced to youth, the vanity whicl is inherent | 
in the human mind was much fed by the admiration of her 

relations and acquaintance ; yet, even at this early period, 

she was at times sensible of the humbling visitation of 
divine love. 


The following: are ‘her own words, -I am“ drawn to 
commemorate the gracious dealings of ‘a merciful Father 
and’ Creator in‘early visiting my mind,—Being educated in 
great strictness by my parents, ‘respecting the observance 
and ceremonies of the worship they professed, ‘(that of the 
Establishment;) I was a constant attendant: upon them from 
childhood, though with this, allowed to enter into most of | 
the vain amusements “of: the: world, to which my natural 
disposition greatly inclined ; while inthe midst of dissipa- 
tion, T often felt a dissatisfaction, and my mind was: visited 
hi with something so-awful, that I appeared to” others’ very 
grave, and havefrequently'been laughed at ‘for it.. I was 

fond of reading,-and found much:pleasure in yielding ‘to it; 
which, with a turn’for poetry, and the intimate acquaintance 
| of several sensible serious inclined persons, occupied much 
Ht of my time from seventeen to eighteen) years of age.—still 
my ‘mind was like a blank, waiting’ to befilled up, and 
prepared for the more extensive reception of the precious 
visitation, which, early in the twentieth year of my life, 
was sweetly vouchsafed ; so that all that was within me 
bowed in deep prostration, and yielded ’to the superior 
power of heavenly love. My mind being in the prepared 
state above described, it would be unsafe to date this change 
from the particular period of my attending the Methodist 
meetings; though in doing so, I certainly felt more of 
[hy divine impressions than at any previous season.—I conti- 
i nued to hear them, and was often sweetly affected and 
comforted ;. yet, even at such times, there was something 
within me craving the purity of an inward, ‘spiritual life. 
During these feelings, and consequent shakings from all 
visible things, I often went into Friends’ meetings, and 
there, especially in silence, did my spirit feed, as it also

The change which she felt it her duty to make, by 
leaving off ornaments, and wearing such attire as was 
consistent with her views of christian simplicity, being very 
‘mortifying to some of her nearest connexions, she suffered 

considerably on this account. ‘The peace, however, with

these trials ; and strength being mercifully proportioned to 
the occasion, she was enabled to persevere in the path of 
obedience, and has frequently been heard to say, that her 
company soon became as undesirable to her former gay asso- 
‘Gates, as theirs was to her; while her society and example 
proved the means of solid advantage to some of her cotem~ 
poraries, who continued, or sought her acquaintance. At

composition ; and the two following pieces are selected, as

Thus lay enwrapt my pow’rs, till merey spoke, 
And through the gloom a ray obedient broke. 
Amazing grace! through this I still survive, 
And boundless love has bid the rebel live :— 
Bids me, for once, with joy behold the day, 
That brought to light this animated clay. 
Since mercy deigns to smile,—hail welcome morn! 
For ever solemniz’d be thy return, 

On thee let pure devotion ever rise, 

And breathe to heav’n, unsullied sacrifice. 


A HYMN, 


WRITTEN IN THE TWENTY-FIRST YEAR OF HER AGE. 


How shall I tune a trembling lay, 
How touch the soften’d string ? 

Fain would I heav’nly love display,— 
The God of mercy sing. 


I would,—but Oh! how faint each power, 
How far too high the theme ;— 

Come, blessed spirit, aid restore, 
And raise the languid flame ! 


What wonderous grace! what boundless love! 
What soft compassion this, 

That calls my rebel heart to prove 
A never fading bliss ! 


Long have I sought the pleasing sound, — 
But sought, alas! in vain,—— 

Explor’d in pleasure’s mazy ground, 
In nature’s desart plain. 


What grace that I am not consum’d, 
Not hurl’d to endless night; 

Mercy has all her pow’r assum’d, 
And yields a cheering light. 


Tis mercy bids me seek the Lord ; 
Tis mercy bids me fly;

?Tis mercy speaks the balmy word, 
“ Repent, thy God is nigh.” 


Tis mercy fills my trembling heart, 
With agonizing pain, 

With keen distress and poignant smart,— 
Nor heave these sighs in vain, 


The tears that now in torrents flow, 
This mercy will repress ; 

Remove the load, a pardon show, 
And speak a healing peace. 


Then let me humbly wait the hour,— 
The hour of sweet release ; 

Incessant, saving grace implore, 
Iucessant, pant for peace. 


At thy blest feet my, LORD and Kine, 
Resigned let me lie, 

Till the glad peals of triumph sing, 
And faith behold thee nigh. 


Then shall the stammerer’s tongue proclaim 
The goodness of the Lorp ; 

In grateful strains rehearse his flame, 
In hymns his love record. 


Pll warble to each list’ning ear, 
The feeble song of praise ; 

My sweet employ while trav’lling here, 
To lisp redeeming grace!

the following extracts will be acceptable to the reader. 


May 10th, 1771. I have nothing my dear friend, to 
tell you, but of mercies,— nothing but unbounded love 
‘should be my theme. The Lorp is indeed gracious, and 
has lately given me to feel it. Oh! what sweet calls, what 
gentle admonitions has he indulged me with. The feeble 
‘structure of clay is impaired, but glory to my Gop, my soul

feels the invigorating influence of his grace; in some 
moments of retirement, lately, it has been ready to burst its 
barrier, and I have earnestly longed to be with my beloved; 
nor can I think it will be long first. Glorious prospect! 
Oh! my friend, if our next meeting should be around the 
throne! While I write, my heart feels unutterable desires, 
Pray for me, that the work of grace may be completed in 
my soul: I believe it will,—I feel I want every thing, and 
am fully confident Jesus will supply all that is lacking. In 
the eyes of some, this might appear as the wild excursion 
of enthusiasm ; to my friend it will wear a different aspecty 
and (I trust,) engage her in my behalf, at the throne 
of grace. 


November 5th, 1771. Do not you, do not I feel the 
need of just such an all-sufficient Redeemer as the compas- 
sionate Jesus? Blessed be his name, we cannot, we would 
not do without him, as our Prophet, Priest, and King, 
Here our poverty indeed is our greatest riches; we are 
content, yea, we rejoice, that our whole dependance is on, 
and our entire support derived from him, in whom all full- 
ness dwells; as having nothing, and yet possessing all 
things. Christ is indeed eyes to the blind, ears to the deaf}! 
feet to the lame, yea, all the sinner wants. For my own! 
part, I feel I am all weakness and helplessness, having) 
every thing to learn, but find the Lord Jesus to be that rock! 
whereunto I may always resort. I long to be more closely)

and intention, may be to live to his glory.— Surely infinite: 
love joins with infinite wisdom, and wills our peace. May) 
our language then, be ever this,

him, to which she replied, that not feeling at hberty to 
confer with flesh and blood, even by consulting her own) 
inclinations, she dared not to seek any human counsel, and 
was endeavouring to act in simple obedience’ tothe discov- 
eries of divine light in her own soul.. Upon leaving her, he:

_T now kept constantly to the meetings of Friends, and 
began to feel a settlement of mind in real peace, which my 
tossed state for several years had caused me only transiently 
‘to possess; or at least, not in the degree of which I now 
partook ; not that all the work seemed requisite to com- 
mence anew, for assuredly Christ had been raised in my 
heart, though until now, the government was not wholly on 
his shoulders ; but by this unreserved surrender to his pure 
guidance, the mystery of godliness was beginning to open 
in increasing light and power, and that spirituality which 
had been discovered, was now in a measure possessed. A 
yiew I had been affected with on my first convincement, 
now cleared. and appeared so near being realized, that my 
‘mind, almost without interruption, dwelt under so awful a 
covering, that even all conversation impressed me with fear, 
sand I was held in deep inward attention for, and to, the 
irevealings of life. In religious meetings I was for some 
time frequently affected, even to trembling, when matter 
‘would present to my mind, as though I must deliver it, 
though seldom more than a very litle ; notwithstanding, 
the love I felt was so universal, that I wanted all to be 
‘reached unto, but for this family, (the Society of Friends,) 
among whom I had tasted the soul sustaining bread, Oh! 
how did I long for them and their good.

of the revival of exercise ; and undoubtedly felt a sufficient
