Thus I went on, as my recollection serves, for about) 
seven years, after my first yielding to the reasonings before 
described ; and indeed just before being brought out of this 
horrible pit, I think the extremity never was so great, inso- 
much that I fainted in my spirit, and all hope was cut off, 
my language being, I shall die in the pit. In this state I 
attended a province, or quarterly meeting, in Cork, and after 
sitting two meetings for worship on the first day, in, I fear, 
wilful rebellion to the gentle intimations of duty, I went to 
Samuel Neale’s in a trying situation of mind and body, and 
his conduct towards me was like a tender father, saying, the: 
gift in thee must be stirred up. I got little rest that night; 
and next morning went in extreme distress to meeting, 
where I had not sat long before a serenity long withheld 
covering my mind, and I thought I itelligibly heard a 
language uttered, which exactly suited my own state; but i$ 
it so hung about me (as at my first appearance, though not 
any thing like the same clear command to express it,) that $ 
being lifted above all reasonings, before I was aware, I stood 
on my feet with it, and Oh! the rest I again felt, the pre- 
cious holy quiet! unequal in degree to what was at first my 
portion; but as though I was altogether a changed creature, 
so that to me there was no condemnation. Here was 
indeed a recompence even for years of suffering, but with 
this alloy, that I had long deprived myself of the precious 
privilege, by yielding to those reasonings which held me 
ina state of painful captivity. One might naturally suppose,

23rd. We called this morning, on an old man,

24th. In a little retirement this morning, light seemed

We got to Wisbaden the evening of the 26th, and met 
with an Englishman, who accompanied us to several bathing; 
houses, this place being famous for an extraordinary boiling, 
spring, of a sulphureous nature which is communicated byi 
pipes to the different houses. From thence we proceeded 
to Frankfort, a fine populous town, remarkable for the: 
liberties it possesses, being governed by its own magistrates, 
who are Lutherans; it is supposed to contain 20000. 
inhabitants, among them 3000 Jews.—No man pays more) 
than five pounds a year taxes, which commences on his: 
declaring himself worth one thousand five hundred pounds. 
This city being so privileged is a thriving one, and not 
obliged to take part in war, unless the empire be invaded! 
Here we met one called a Pietist, with whom we had some: 
religious conversation, to our mutual comfort. 


16th. We left St. Gilles and spent that night at Nismes. 


We travelled from Nismes in a tedious manner, drawn | 
by miles at the rate of about thirty miles a day, rising early) 
and late taking rest. The country abounds with vineyards, 
oliveyards, fig, and mulberry trees ; pomegranates growing | 
in the hedges like our white thorn, and the air in some) 
places rendered fragrant by aromatic herbs, springing up| 
spontaneously in rocky ground. ‘There is but little pasture | 
land in these parts; a rudeness in appearance, with the want

aborious life, in the service of her divine Lord and Master.

1821. Once upon retiring to bed in a very exhausted 
state, after an evening meeting in the city, (of London, 
where she then resided,) my dear -mother said with much 
tenderness of spirit, I long to be joined to the general 
assembly and church of the first born, yet, such is the love 
and concern I feel for the souls of the people, that my life 
scems of little consequence, and I could be satisfied to drop 
while declaring the mercy of God in Christ Jesus to a 
fallen race. 


On another occasion of the same kind she observed, © 
what a favour to have a good bed, but what a still greater 
mercy to have a good hope through grace, that after a few 
more fleeting days there will be a settlement in unmingled, 
everlasting rest, Iam so weaned from anxiety, that I seem 
to have nothing in the world to think of. 


On Ist day 16th, 3rd mo. she was largely exercised 
in the forenoon meeting, at Devonshire house, and in the 
evening had an appointed meeting for the inhabitants of 
that neighbourhood, wherein she was wonderfully sirength= 
ened to proclaim the important doctrines of the gospel. 
Whilst inviting those present to the consideration of their 
latter end, she mentioned how surprisingly her own life had 
been extended, and that having completed more than the 
three score and ten years, she could then look back upon. 
her existence as but a point, in comparison of eternity, 


The solemnity which prevailed at that season was 
remarked by many who attended it, and upon returning 
home in a very exhausted state of body, my beloved mother 
expressed the peace and satisfaction with which her mind 
was clothed. In the morning she also observed, that 
whenever she had awoke in the night the remembrance o 
that meeting was sweet and comforting to her, and that she 
loved to think of the feelings by which it had been marked. 


Thus with alacrity, and even cheerfulness, did this ` 
aged servant of the Lord prosecute the closing labours of 
her day, repeatedly observing, that although sometimes

weary in the work, she could honestly say she was not 
weary of it, but felt the service of her Lord and Master to 
constitute her meat and drink, in a spiritual sense. 


6th day, 25th. During that and the following day, 
she was frequently employed in a strain of heavenly rejoic- 
ing, and once observed, how little idea we can form of what 
will open upon the spirit when the incumbrance of mortality 
is laid down. I have not a wish to go, if I could proclaim 
to one more soul the rich mercy of God in Christ; but if 
it be the will of the Lord to take me, I hope my dear 
children you will be resigned, and preserved from all evil ; 
and may the Lord preserve your goings out and comings in 
from that day forth and for evermore. I have nothing to 
depend on, not a shred of my own, no good works to tell 
of; only mercy, that which visited me in the morning of 
the day, has supported me through life, and will support 
me in death ; unmerited, unbounded, and I trust, unchange- 
able mercy! I have loved the cause of my Redeemer, it 
was to draw to him, to attract and fix the attention of the 
mind on him alone, that I have been willing to proclaim his 


goodness.—Thy will be done, is the highest anthem ever 
“sung on earth or in heaven ; that will of God which is our 


sanctification. 


3rd day, 29th. She desired the xii. chap. of Hebrews

‘deriving peculiar comfort from that blessed record of divine 
‘doctrine and instruction; observing, it was part of that

bore testimony in London. Upon the last verse but one 
being read, “let us have grace whereby we may serve God 
| acceptably, with reverence and godly fear;’’ she audibly 
pronounced, Amen, Amen. 


_ Afterwards with much composure, and in a tone that 
bespoke the feeling of renewed thankfulness, she said I seem. 
-to have nothing to do but with the present moment, no 
looking back with pain or uneasiness. Oh, not to doubt 
the foundation is great mercy ; warn them, tell all, there

~The following is pari of a testimony of Southwark 
‘monthly meeting, concerning Mary Dudley deceased. 


~ This our beloved friend was born in the city of Bristol, 

‘the th of the 6th mo. 1750, of parents professing the 

rinciples of the Established Church,—In the 23rd year of 

er age, on the ground of settled conviction, she joined our 

teligious Society; about which period she felt herself 
Q 2 


176 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


constrained to speak in the line of ministry, from which 
her natural disposition exceedingly shrunk. After exercis- . 
ing the gift with which she was intrusted, the conflicts of! 
her spirit were so great that she gave way to reasonings) 
and doubts on the subject of her call to the sacred office, 
and thus became involved in unspeakable distress, from i 
which at times she could see no way to escape. 


In the year 1777, she was married to Robert Dudley, 
of Clonmel, in Ireland, but the society of an affectionate: 
husband, and an increase of domestic comforts, proved’ 
insufficient to afford that peace of which her exercised spirit! 
felt so much the want; and here she described her situation i 
as often miserable,—concluding that by disobedience she: 
had forfeited the divine favour, and should never again be! 
commissioned to proclaim her Lord’s goodness. But he! 
who had called her to his service, and designed to qualify) 
her for his work, brought her out of those perplexities and: 
close probations in which her mind had long been involved, 
to the comfort of many who had suffered with and for her, 
and to his own praise; enabling her again to bear public) 
testimony to his goodness. 


Ry) Fe e 


After the decease of her beloved husband, and two 
children who had arrived at maturity, trials which deeply; 
wounded her susceptible. feelings, she removed in the; 
year 1810, under an apprehension of duty, into the neigh- 
bourhood of London, and resided for the most part of the: 
remainder of her life within the compass of our monthly 
meeting.—She was a minister highly esteemed amongst us, | § 
sound in faith and doctrine, labouring diligently in gospel: 
love for the promotion of the cause of truth and righteousness. | 


In her last illness she was eminently favoured with 
the sensible enjoyment of the Lord’s presence, and often: 
testified of the support and consolation thus afforded her.’ 
I haye loyed the cause of my Redeemer, it was to draw toii 
him, and fix the attention of the mind upon him alone, that | 


MRS. MARY DUDLEY. 177 
I have been made willing to proclaim his goodness. 


During the last three weeks of her life, she suffered 
i much from the difficulty of breathing, and general bodily 
i uneasiness; her mind however was wonderfully supported 
so that to those around her she frequently appeared to be 
favoured with a foretaste of the rich enjoyment of perfect 
happiness and peace. 


She often seemed as if scarcely an inhabitant of earth. 

‘Her approaching dissolution was now apparent, and the 

following are some of her latest expressions. Grace has 

triumphed over nature’s feelings ; the Lord has fulfilled his 

| promise, he has given the victory through Jesus Christ, to 

whom be glory, and power, dominion, and strength, now 
and for ever, holy, holy, holy, 


Her departure was observable only by gradually ceasing 
to breathe, and her immortal and redeemed spirit we doubt 
not, ascended to the mansions of never ending rest and 
peace. She died at her house at Peckham, on the 24th of 
the 9th mo. 1823, in the 74th year of her age; a minister 
about 50 years; and her remains were interred in Friends’ 
burial ground, near Bunhill Fields.

Mis MARGARET WATSON. 


The subject of this Sketch is now living at Redcar * im 
the North Riding of Yorkshire, and is well worthy of being: 
recorded among the characters of holy and useful women. 
She was born of pious parents who were members of the: 
Methodist Society, who lived many years at Stockton upon! 
Tees, and have long since got to their eternal rest. Her 
father, Mr. George Watson, (generally styled Captain: 
Watson, his occupation being that of a sea captain.) 
experienced an happy exit out of time into eternity :—in: 


the full triumph of faith he entered the celestial haven of 


unspeakable rest and happiness, after having toiled for some: 
years on the changing ocean of time. He was savingly) 
brought to God under the ministry of the Rey. George. 
Whitfield. While that eminent servant of God was preach- - 
ing from those words of our Lord, “peace I leave with you, . 
my peace I give unto you; not as the world giveth, give [| 
unto you. Mr. Watson was so affected under the weighty 
truths advanced, that he wept bitterly on account of his- 
sins. Mr. Whitfield observing this, looked him full in the: 
face, and said, dry up thy tears thou blubbering creature; 
thou art the very person put-into the last wil! and testament 
of our Lord Jesus Christ. This personal and encouraging 


* Redcar is a small village in the parish of Marske; seven 
miles N. of Guisborough, and contains, by the returns of 1821—673 
inhabitants. Vormerfy this was only a small fishing village, composed 
principally of huts, but latterly it has risen into considerable emi- 
nence as a sea-bathing place. A neat methodist chapel, was the 
only place of worship here for many years, lately a new church has 
been erected, built principally by subscription from the inhabitants 
in the village and neighbourhood, and by donations from the visitors.

Mrs. MARY WILTSHAW, 


Her husband, Mr. Wiltshaw travelled in the Methodist’ 
connexion for about 20 years. His manners were some-- 
what singular, but his talents were acceptable. He retired’ 
from the work in the year 1809, and settled in his native; 
place, in the neighbourhood of Staffordshire, He bore his: 
last affliction with great patience and resignation, and died’ 
in peace, July 27th, 1818. Glory be to God” he uttered: 
with his expiring breath, 


The subject of this Memoir was born in the year 1763, 


either at Spalding or Holbeach in Lincolnshire, of respectable: 
parents who were Episcopalians, and that of the strictest) 
sect ; as they were very regular attendants on the service of | 
the Established Church, and as touching their outward: 
conduct they held themselves, and they were esteemed by, 
others blameless. Her maiden name was Chapman; it 
appears by certain documents now laying before me, and Bi: 
which were communicated by the family, that the Lord} 

graciously wrought upon her mind by his Holy Spirit while: 
but an infant, and by his enlightening and awakening, 


influences she was led to meditate and reflect upon the: § 


word and works of God, in a way that influenced her temper 
and conduct, which became very observable to her family: 
and companions, insomuch that she received by way of: 
opprobrium the appellation of Methodist; and that even! 
before she had any knowledge of such a people. There: 
were a few in that neighbourhood in that day, against whom | 
no accusation would be brought, except that in religious) 
matters they carried things too far, and became ‘‘ righteous 
over much;’’ even the father of this young woman!

sometimes expressed his fears by saying, I think our Mary 

i will’ be a Methodist.’” Mary not only knew from the word 
of God, and the dawnings of human reason that God was 
infinitely wise, and good, and powerful, but that he heard 
i and answered prayer when offered to him aright; but also 
i by happy and heartfelt experience. Hence secret prayer 
became an exercise in which she took great delight. She 
was much affected one day when at school in reading that 
« David prayed seven times a day.” She thought if it was 
needful for David to pray seven times a day, it must be 
‘equally needful and profitable for her; and she instantly 
sresolyed to follow his example, which practice she conti- 
nued for some time,—hence she was often missing, and 
‘retired for prayer into some private place. In these seasons 
she was often indulged with the most satisfactory evidence 
of the love and favour of God, by the freedom of access 
which she enjoyed and the strong consolations she felt. 


About the age of 22 she entered into the marriage state. 
‘But this union was but of short continuance, ere a very few 
years had come to an end she was left a widow, but as it 
pleased God, she had no fatherless children to care, or 
provide for. 


Soon after this she engaged herself as governess in a 
sgentleman’s family, this she considered asa providential 
‘opening, as his lady was a serious woman, and her husband 
being a captain in the navy, he was much from home. 
‘Here she enjoyed her religious privileges and became more 
decidedly pious, and was highly esteemed by her mistress, 
vas well as the younger branches of the family. But a 
circumstance very soon occurred which threatened to putan 
extinguisher upon all her prospects of enjoyment, in this 
‘domestic circle. The Captain received orders to sail for 
Gibraltar; and as the whole family was going to. go with 
him, the thought of parting with Mary seemed an heart 
Tending concern, to the captain’s lady ; and more especially 
to the children ; and Mary likewise suffered not a little at 
‘the thought either of leaving her country and friends ; or of 
being left behind. At length however, after repeated 


186 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


entreaties,—and having obtained the consent of her parents, 
she agreed to venture her all with them on the trackless 
ocean, to sail for this little Island, which is little but a barren 
rock in the midst of the sea. * Here she united with the: 
pious few that she found among the soldiers and inhabitants ; 
and God blest her, and made her a blessing. During they 
three years of her residence here, she was rendered useful 
to very many, It does not appear that there were any; 
missionaries stationed here, but there were some soldiers: 
truly alive to God,—and a pious sergeant who used to give! 
a word of exhortation, and occasionally preached to them, 
in which exercises they had full liberty by the superior 
officers. They had also regular meetings for public prayer: 
and christian communion, in all of which, the subject ofi 
this memoir took an active part. God blest her in her own: 
soul and she enjoyed sweet fellowship with the Father and’ 
the Son by the Holy Ghost. 


But upon receiving the painful intelligence of the death | 
of her father and mother, who died very shortly after each! 


* Gibraltar is a town of Andalusia, in Spain. It was taken from) 
the Spaniards by a combined fleet of English and Dutch ships, under 
the command of Sir George Rooke, in 1704, and this rather through | 
accident than any thing else. The Prince of Hesse, with 1800) 
men, landed on the Isthmus ; but an attack on that side was found 
to be impracticable, on account of the steepness of the rock. The» 
fleet fired 15000 shot, without making any impression on the works; 
so that the fortress seems to be equally impregnable, both to the: 
British and Spaniards, except by famine. At last a party of sailors, | 
having got merry with grog, rowed close under the New Mole in their 
boats; and as they saw that the garrison, which consisted of 100 | 
men, did not mind them, they were encouraged to attempt a landing; 
and having mounted the Mole, and hoisted a red jacket asa sig- 
nal of possession. This being immediately observed from by the 
fleet more boats and sailors were sent out, who, in like manner, 
having ascended the works, got possession of a battery, and soon 
obliged the town to surrender. After many fruitless attempts to 
recover it, it was confirmed to the English by the treaty of Utrecht, in | 
1713. There are upwards of 300 pieces of cannon mounted on the 
works. Gibraltar contains several streets, one of which is tolerably | 
Jarge and well paved. There is one English, and one Spanish church 
a Jews’ synagogue, and a Methodist chapel. “It is 25 miles N, of 
Ceuta, and 49 3. E. of Cadiz,

pious friend. She joyfully embraced the opportunity of

soul, and freedom of access to God. The. Lord heard-the

peace. The company then: began to entertain the highest

her arrival at home, her brother, who had resumed the:

with him, as his housekeeper ; until his marriage; when she!

union; not so much because Mr. Wiltshaw was a methodist, 
or on account of his piety; (for they were fully persuaded: 
that she would not unite herself with any one who was noti 
so ;) but they objected to an itinerant life. This important: 
step was made a matter of the most serious consideration, 
and earnest prayer by our departed friend. She had longi 
known that there is no pleasure that will bear reflection, 
except that which is found in true religion; and in the) 
worship and service of the living God. 


“Tis religion that must. give 
Solid comfort while we live ; 
Tis religion must supply 
Solid comfort when we die, 
And its heavenly joy shall be 
Lasting as eternity.” 


She had chosen God for her portion, and she longed for a 
more entire devotedness to his service. She thought in 
uniting herself to a zealous minister of the gospel of Christ,| 
this end would be most effectually answered ; inasmuch ası 
it would afford her a better opportunity, both of getting and: 
doing more good, hence they were united in the fear of the 
Lord, and walked in the light of his countenance. It was) 
at this time that she began more fully to occupy the talenti 
God had committed to her, by way of conversation, prayer, 
exhortation, and meeting classes. In these exercises God)

blessed her own soul, and made her a blessing to very many, 
| this encouraged her to proceed. 


_ She afterwards enlarged her sphere of action, and 
proportionable were her consolations, and usefulness increas- 
ed. She began to hold meetings in order to expound the 
word of God, and exhort sinners to turn to him for mercy 
i and salvation. God made her the instrument in the 
i conversion of very many ; and some very profligate charac- 
ters were turned: by her instrumentality from darkness to 
light, and from the power of satan to God, who were 
i afterwards bright ornaments to the cause of christianity, 
i and to this day Iam toldshe is held in grateful remembrance 
| by very many, in the various circuits in which they travelled. 
She used occasionally to supply the place of her husband, and 
| at other times assisted him in his work. She very frequently 
i visited the country villages, and invariably pursued that line 
_ of conduct which she believed the Lord marked out for her. 
Her views with respect to the plan of salvation were scriptural 
and exccedingly distinct and clear, and she had a very 
happy method of expressing her conceptions. 


The faithful minister will not confine his labours to 

| the pulpit, he will study the word of God and pray much in 
private that he may be able to bring out of God’s treasury 
things new and old. He will present the people before the 
Lord in private. He will not only plead with the people 

| for God, but will plead with God for the people. ‘This was 
i the apostle’s plan, Eph. ui. 14 to 19. Phil. i. 3, 4: 
This conduct was peculiarly exemplified in the character 
now before us, being raised by divine grace to a high state 
of moral rectitude, and knowing that divine grace could 
raise others who were equally fallen to as high, or even to 

i a higher state of holiness; and feeling constrained by the 
_ love of Christ thus instrumentally to bring others to experi- 
ence the same salvation, she laboured with all her might, 
in every possible way, and she was admirably fitted, and 
qualified by the great teacher himself, to instruct the 
ignorant, alarm the careless, to comfort them that mourned 
in Zion, and to lead forward and build up the christian

believers ; and great was her success, many, very many 

will be her crown of rejoicing in the day of the Lord Jesus, 

Her talents for preaching were very good, and her sermons | 
not only shewed that she had received a good education, 

but that she was in possession of that salvation which she 
recommended to others. She was well acquainted with the : 
scriptures, in the constant reading of which she took great | 
delight ; and to which she would refer at all times in support | 
of her arguments with the greatest propriety; but keeping | 
principally in view the essential doctrines of the christian 

religion. On one occasion she received a very unkind letter 

relative to her public work ; upon reading it she retired— 

like good Hezikiah, and laid it before the Lord, and appealed | 
to him for the purit of her motive and conduct—from 

whom she received an assurance of his approbation. 


Whatever opposition she met with in the discharge of 
her duty, she guarded against prejudice towards the persons 
who opposed her, always judging the most favourably of 
their motive. She was very careful in attending to the 
apostle’s exhortation, James, iv. 11, ‘ speak not evil one of 
another, brethren.” Ist. Evil speaking is against our 
character as members of the church of Christ. A citizen of 
Zion is thus described, Psalms, xv. 2, 3, “ he that walketh 
uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth 
in his heart. He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor 
doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against 
his neighbour.”? Tt was therefore worthy and becoming 
the apostolic character of James to caution the christians of 
his day, against any thing which might militate against their 
reputation as citizens of Zion. ` It is possible that the apostle 
may refer to some who had been more or less guilty, hence, 
he reasons the case with them, and exhorts them to a better 
conduct. 2nd. Evil speaking is against our character as 
brethren. The people of God are begotten by the same 
parent,—nursed in the same church,—fed at the same 
table, —united by the same bonds,—influenced by the same 
spirit,—travelling in the same road,—and journeying to 
same heaven. . As much as if the apostle had said,—shall 
the members of the mystical body of Christ,—children of

i another, God forbid! Mrs. Wiltshaw seems to have been 
peculiarly preserved from this snare of the devil, and that 
chiefly by constantly maintaining the true spirit of prayer 
and watchfulness ; her conduct herein, seems to have had 
a blessed influence, in preserving, or reclaiming others from

It pleased God severely to afflict her when in the 
‘Taunton Circuit; insomuch that her valuable life was 
despaired of, both by the physician and her friends, but it 
pleased God to raise her up once more to her weeping 
partner and children. One time during her affliction being 
had out of bed, it was expected she would expire while held 
in a chair at the window, the casement which faced the 
igarden being opened to let in a little fresh air. To all 
jappearance she was sinking into the arms of death. In 
this situation she appears to have had a vision of angels 
which she related as soon as she was able to converse. 
‘They appeared as in the garden under a tree, and looking at 
her ; when an intimation was given her, that she would be 
restored for a little season, in answer to the prayers of her 
husband and children. She expressed herself as being 
inexpressibly happy and longed to go with them ; and also 
a firm conviction resting upon her mind that she should 
‘recover, but this appeared at the time, too good news for 
iher friends to place any confidence in, especially considering 
iher present state of weakness and debility; but the fact is, 
‘she recovered from that time. 


All who knew her had an abiding conviction of her 
deep piety and habitual devotedness to God. It was her 
constant practice at least three times a day to retire for 
private prayer and communion with God, besides praying 
with her family at stated seasons, and more especially when 
iher husband was from home. 


When Mr. Wiltshaw became a supernumerary and set- 
tled at the place of his nativity he had regular preaching at his

own house, and whenever he was unable through increasing i 
infirmities or any other casuality to occupy the pulpit the; 
xeople were not suffered to go away without hearing from) 
kot an answer to the question what they must do toi 
be saved. 


As she drew near the close of her life and labours, she; 
evidently experienced a growing meetness for the inheritance} 
of the saints in light; and expressed the strong desires she: 
felt after the full enjoyment of the presence and smile of 
her Lord in heaven, Indeed no lover of Christ is fully, 
satisfied in his present state. 


“The full glories of the Lamb 
Adorn the heavenly plains.” 


They can endure the absence of their beloved and faithful 
friend for a season, especially while they have every assu- | 
rance of his love ; but they cannot endure the thought of a} 
final separation. A christian believer waits patiently, but) 
with a joyful blooming hope, of the eternal presence and J 


fruition of Christ in heaven. With pious Job he says, “Ti 
would not live here always,” and with holy Paul, ‘ for me to 
liveis Christ, but to die is gain.” With the royal psalmist he |

my sister if she did not hear the móst delightful music,

able for any gift in singing, would frequently break out in 
singing lines, and verses of different hymns, expressive of 
her views and feelings; as they occurred to her mind. 


For some time before she died she was speechless, but 
nearly the last words she was heard to utter were these, 


“ Though life sinks apace and death’s in my view, 
The word of thy grace will bring me safe through, 
Not fearing, not doubting with Christ on my side, 
I soon shall die shouting the Lord will provide.” 


Thus died this mother in our Israel, on wednesday, April 
the 28th, 1819. She filled up all the relations of a child, 
a wife, and a mother; as became a christian of the highest 
order. May her family imitate her excellences, and derive 
every possible advantage from her instructions, prayers, 
and example!

‘If the great design of the gospel ministry is to fit and: 
prepare the fallen spirit of man for the inheritance of the 
saints in light, that they may present those to whom they, 
minister, faultless before the throne of God; or as the 

apostle expresses it, ‘that we may present every man pers 
fect in Christ Jesus.” It is evident that a great work is) 
necessary to prepare the subject for this awful, and yet: 
glorious exhibition. Sinners must have their minds enlight- 
ened by divine truth, and by the holy Spirit of Godi 
awakened to a discovery of their sin and danger ; they musti 
be regenerated by divine grace. For this porpose, St.’ 
Paul was sent to the Gentiles, ‘to open their eyes, to turni 
them from darkness to light, and from the power of satan to: 
God, that they may receive the forgiveness of sins, and an! 
inheritance among the saints in light.” The business of) 
Christ’s embassadors is to espouse sinners to Christ, and) 
then to build them up in their most holy faith. ‘* To feed: 
the church of God which he has bought..with his blood; 

and supply them with that heavenly, spiritual, and suitable: 
food which Christ has provided in the gospel feast. They: 
must not be fed with the dry morsels of speculative divinity, 

or with heathen morality ; but with the genuine unadulter- - 
ated word of God; and not fed promiscuously, as if all were 

in the same state of grace, or of the same standing in "$ 
religious experience, but babes must be fed with milk, 7 
young men with meat, and fathers with the deep things of 
God. It must be the care of ministers to bring them all $ 
forward to the stature of a perfect man in Christ.

The subject of this memoir was born at Hotton, a 
village near Stokesley, in the North Riding of Yorkshire. 
Her parents by industry and economy brought up a family 
of eleven children, in a very respectable way and manner. 
They also endeavoured to train them up in the fear of God, 
and in the principles and practices of virtue and piety. Her 
si having long been an esteemed member of the Methodist 

ociety, and firmly attached to the doctrine and discipline 
of that religious community, he required his children to 
attend to the forms of religious worship at home, and in the 
house of God. * The methodist ministers being frequently 
entertained at the house, the children derived much advantage 
from their advice and prayers. 


= * It is an apostolic direction that children be brought “ up in the 
nurture and admonition of the Lord.” How well it is to begin early 
in life to discipline and instruct children in the fear of the Lord and 
in the forms of religious worship, more especially to the daily habits 
of private prayer. It seldom fails that speedy and visible effects are 
produced in the individuals thus favoured, and from them to others, 
the good effects produced are incalculable, and lasting as eternity 
as a case in proof of this, I record the following anecdote. 


< “When the Rey. George Whitfield, of happy memory, was 
preaching through America, God was pleased to bring to the know- 
ledge of himself one of a city, and two ofa family. A lady in New 
Eugland, experienced the power of religion, and, as a matter of course, 
became a praying christian. But she was alone; she could not per- 
suade any one to join with her in prayer; except her little daughter, 
i who was about nine years of age. This child she took with her into 
her closet from day to day, to witness her cries and tears. It pleased. 
| God, after some time, to touch the child’s heart, and after being made 
conscious of her sinful condition, she obtained a knowledge of salvation 
by the remission of her sins, and the witness of the Holy Spirit that 
| ghe'was adopted into God’s family. The child, who was then about 
eleven years of age, in a transport, addressed her mother, saying, 
«O mother, if all the world knew this! Pray mother, let me run to 
some of the neighbours, and tell them that they may be happy, and 
| love my Saviour too!” Ah! my dear child,” said the mother, 
“that would be needless, for I suppose that if you were to tell your 
experience, there is not one for many miles that would not laugh at 
you, and say that it is all a delusion.” “O mother,” said the child, 
“I think they would believe me; I must go over to that shoemaker 
and tell him ; he will believe me.” She ran over, and found him at 
work in his Shop. She began by telling him that he must die, and

Sarah in very early life was the subject of divine 
impressions, the thoughts of God,—of heaven and hell were 
much impressed upon. her soul, and the Holy Spirit of God 
enlightened, and comforted her tender mind. When about 
fifteen years of age she was deeply awakened to a sense of 
her guilt and danger as a sinner before God, The sudden 
death of one of the family was made the principal instru- 
ment in the hands of God of alarming her fears, and 
awakening her guilty conscience, ‘‘ For six months,” she 
observes, * I was constrained to say as the penitent psalmist, 
‘the sorrows of death compassed me about, the pains of 
hell gat hold upon me, I found trouble and sorrow.’’ My ery 
to the Lord was incessant. ‘* I watered my couch with my 
tears, and mingled my drink with my weeping.” But the 
Lord who is rich in mercy, towards them that call upon him, 
heard me in a day accepted, and in an hour of mercy suc- 
coured me. On the evening of new year’s day, 1802, whilst 
Mr. Wm. Warrener was renewing the covenant the Spirit 
descended, waving the olive branch of peace, and by the 
application of these words, “thy sins which are many are 
all forgiven thee, go in peace.” My warring passions were 
hushed into a settled calm, and I felt an assurance of the 
divine favour. From the time of my espousals to Christ, I 
saw and felt I must give the Lord my undivided heart, in 
order to enjoy that purity which the scriptures hold out as 
the privilege of believers. That holiness without whith no 
man can see the Lord, I sought in the diligent use of the 
means, using much fasting and self-denial. I think it was 
about ten years after my conversiun, and soon after I had 
received the evidence of sanctification that the Holy Spirit 
applied these words, ye are clean through the word which 
I have spoken, when I more particularly felt a travailing, 


in birth for souls; and these parts of scripture which were 


that he was a sinner, that she was a sinner too, but that her Saviour 
had heard her mother’s prayers, and had forgiven all her sins; and 
that now she was so happy, that she did not know how totell it! The. 
shoemaker was struck; his tears flowed like rain; he threw aside 
his work, and cried for mercy with prayer and supplication; the 
neighbourhood was alarmed, and in a few months from that time 
about fifty persons were brought to asaying knowledge of Christ.”

Was born in the parish of Mareham in the county of 
Cornwall, April 8th, 1792. Her mother appears to have 
been a woman who feared God, and endeavoured to discharge 
every personal and relative duty, so far as she had light. 
Hence she turned her attention towards the religious instruc- 
tion of her children, requiring them to attend the ordinances 
of religion, to read\ the word of God, and morning and 
evening to bow before him in secret prayer.’ This 
mode of proceeding, naturally led Elizabeth to the duty of 
meditation, reflection and prayer at other seasons, and when 
thus employed she felt the powerful operations of divine 
grace, and the Holy Spirit of God sometimes to alarm her 
fears, and at other seasons to soften her heart, and encourage 
and comfort her while engaged in his worship and service : 
insomuch that. her conscience became exceedingly tender, 
and when only about seven or eight years of age she used to 
enquire whether this or that was sinful, and if she was told 
it was she shunned it with all her strength ; on some occa- 
sions these operations. were so powerful that she was 
constrained to leave her companions and retire to weep and 
topray. She was much affected in reading or hearing of the 


202 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


sufferings of Christ. But although she was restrained frore 
outward sin, and strove to serve God and do his will, yet 
she was seeking salvation by the deeds of the law, not being 
sufficiently convinced of the depravity of her own nature, 
nor the exceeding sinfulness of sin, neither that justification 
before God is by faith alone. Indeed she did not discover 
this till about the age of eighteen; when vf a truth the com- 
mandment came home and she died to all hope of being 
saved by the deeds of the law. Now sin became exceeding] 
sinful and she partook largely of the wormwood and gall 
of genuine repentance. Here she probably suffered loss, in 
not uniting with the people of God, for although her mother 
attended the Methodist ministry and appeared well disposed, 
yet not being a member herself, neither any of the family, 
nor perhaps savingly converted to God, Elizabeth could not 
derive much assistance from them. 


In 1812 she joined the Methodist Society, and met in 
a class which was formed partly on her account in the 
village where she lived. She continued to seek the Lord 
diligently, till she found him to the joy of her heart. This 
happened as she was walking to a certain place, meditating: 
on her state of mind, and lifting up her heart to God in 
prayer, The Lord spoke with peace and power to her heart 
and those words were applied, “thy sins are all forgiven 
thee.” The Spirit’s evidence and witness remained. Alb 
guilt, condemnation, and tormenting fears were removed, and 
she felt unutterable joy and consolation through believing ; 
and for a considerable time felt nothing contrary to peace 
and joy ; but she afterwards found the risings of vain desire, 
pride, and other things in her heart, though they had not 
the dominion over her. But in reading and hearing the 
word of God she perceived that it was her privilege to be 
saved from all inward as well as outward sin. That * the 
blood of Christ cleanseth from all sin; that if we confess 
our sins God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to 
cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” Reading the life of 
Mrs. Ann Rogers was.a great help.to her in this matter, not 
only in informing her judgment, as it respected the privilege’ 
itself, but in pointing out thé way to sbtainit, She attended

November 17, 1818. Blessed be God who reigns on

Mis HANNAH PARROTT. 


Was born of pious parents, and resided with them 
many years at Radcliff, near Nottingham. Her father was | 
an acceptable and useful local preacher in the Methodist | 
connexion. But although she had the advantage of a reli- . 
gious education, and was brought early to the means of | 
grace, she continued many years in a careless and trifling ; 
state. She delighted in dress, and unprofitable conversation, 
more than in the things of God. This no doubt was a. 
source of grief to the mind of her pious father: Concerned 
for her salvation he at length with much entreaty and the - 
promise of a reward, prevailed upon her to go and hear 
Mr. Winfield, hoping that the word of that man of God | 
would be made a blessing to her soul, as it had been to 
many others. And no doubt the pious father would offer 
up fervent and importunate payer to the father of lights, | jj 
and the giver of all grace that the end for which he had ` 
prevailed upon his daughter to hear the word might be | 
answered. He well knew that nothing but the grace of 1 
God could change the heart, and give a new bias: to the 
disposition of the mind. No human effort can stop the | 
torrent or turn the channel of the propensity which isin | 
human nature to that which is evil. He knew by experience 
that it was divine grace alone, by which he had been made 
to differ from his former self, and from his fellow sinners, 
and he knew also that the same grace could change and 
renew the depraved heart of his child, and he had the 
happiness to know that the Lord had heard his prayer and 
given him the desire of his heart. The preacher took his 
text from Matthew viii. 11, 12, “ and I say unto you, that 
many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down

‘itself against the knowledge of God, and bring into captivity

Mrs. MARGARET FOX. 


Before we enter upon the character of this intrepid 
female, we will give a short) Sketch of her husband, Mr, 
George Fox. This will-be the: more acceptable as he was 
the founder of the Society of Friends. This extraordinary 
man was born in the year 1624, at Drayton in the Clay, in 
the county of Leicester.» His parents were’ members of the 
Church of England, moral in their conduct; and esteemed 
as religious characters. Their son George does hot appear 
to have had ‘the advantage of muchi learning, but was 
remarkably steady and thoughtful from a child. “He was 
put apprentice to a shoemaker; his master having also the 
occupation of a small farm, hence: he was frequently 
employed in agricultural engagements. When about twenty 
years of agé: he became» much concerned’ about the

ih dress, speech, atid behaviour, exposed him toa great

when he was reviled, reviled not again; but committed

the magistrates he exhorted Justice Bennett and others to 
tremble at the word of the Lord, upon which Bennett in 
contempt called him and his friends Quakers, by which 
name they have been distinguished to the present time. It 
appears that Margaret, the subject of the following Sketch, 
together with her former husband and most of the family 
were brought to the experimental knowledge of the truth 
through his instrumentality. 


After a life of indefatigable labour,—great sufferings,— 
and very extensive usefulness, this man of God died in 
London, November 13th, 1690, aged 67 years, and was 
buried in Bunhill fields, accompanied by several thousands 
of Friends and others. His writings were collected and 
published after his death in three folio volumes. One of 
his biographers says, he was valiant for the truth; bold in 
asserting it; patient in suffering for it; unweary in labour- 
ing in it; steady in his testimony to it; immoveable as a 
rock. Deep he was in divine knowledge ; clear in opening 
heavenly mysteries; plain and powerful in preaching; 
fervent ın prayer. He was richly endued with heavenly 
wisdom ; quick in discerning; sound in judgment; able 
and ready in giving ; discreet in keeping counsel; a lover 
of righteousness; an encourager of virtue, justice, temper- 
ance, meekness, purity, chastity, modesty, humility, charity, 
and self-denial in all; both by word and example, 
Graceful he was in countenance; manly in personage; 
grave in gesture; courteous in conversation; weighty in 
communication ; instructive in discourse ; free from affecta- 
tion in speech or carraige. A severe reprover of hard and 
obstinate sinners ; a mild and gentle admonisher. of such as 
were tender and sensible of their failings. Notapt to resent 
personal wrongs; easy to forgive injuries; but. zealously 
earnest where the honour of God, the prosperity of truth, or 
the peace of the church was. concerned. | Very tender, 
compassionate, and pitiful he was to all that were under any 
sort of affliction ; full of brotherly love ; full of fatherly care; 
for indeed the care of the churches of Christ was daily upon 
him, the prosperity and peace whereof he studiously sought. 
Beloved he was of God; beloved of God’s people; and,

MRS. MARGARET FOX, was the spouse: of the aboye 
Mr. George Fox. Some account of the wife ofthis great 
and extraordinary) man will be interesting to the pious 
feader. Itas taken from her writings which were collected 
and printed in.an octavo volume. 


Margaret Fox, widow of our ancient friend and elder, 
George Fox, was convinced of the principle of truth, on his 
first coming into that part of Lancashire where she dwelt, 
in 1652, being then wife of Thomas Fell, one of the Welsh 
judges ; a man much esteemed in his country for his wisdom, 
moderation, and mercy, being also a tender husband and 
loving father, and one who sought after God in the best 
Way it was made known unto him. He. frequently enter- 
tained those who were accounted serious and godly men ; 
and had often prayers and religious exercises in the family ; 
andin this manner also Margaret- was seeking after the 
tight way for, many years, though often afraid she was 
short of it. 


_' ‘She was born in the year 1614, her parents were of 
honourable repute in that country, and her father; John 
Askew, was of an ancient family. and estate, and a pious 
charitable man. It was in the seeking state before men- 
tiohed that it pleased divine wisdom to move the heart of 
George Fox, to visit the family of the judge, who was then 
in London, and to open unto them the eternal truth; by 
which means the minds of herself, children, and great part 
of the servants were convinced and turned.to God. . When 
the judge returned home, and found the anes change 
wrought on them, he was much surprised, and appeared to 
be troubled; but Richard Farnsworth, and some other 
Friends who came to the house soon after George Fox had 
been there, had some discourse with him, and he was still 
and quiet, and weighed things ; and George Fox. returned 
in the evening, and being admitted, spoke so powerfully 


216 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


and convincingly, that the judge was so far satisfied it was 
the truth, that he offered his own house as a meeting place, 
and was kind to Friends on every occasion, till the time of 
his decease; which was about the year 1658, being then 
60 years of age, 


His widow laboured to promote the cause of truth, 
applied frequently to the king, on behalf of her suffering 
friends, and visited them in various parts of the nation; 
sometimes accompanied by one of her daughters. About 
the year 1661, she was sent from her own house to 
Lancaster Castle, because she would not swear; was 
likewise premunired, and sentenced to forfeit her real and 
personal estate to the king, and to be imprisoned during 
life ; but after having been in prison about four years, she 
was set at liberty, by order of the king and council. Soon 
after this she was married to George Fox, but was again 
under the old premunire, taken from her house, and carried 
to prison; where she continued another year in a sickly 
state, till her husband obtained her discharge under the 
great seal. All these sufferings she endured with much 
patience, and neither fainted nor murmured ; but was kept 
so cheerful and easy under them, that her enemies were 
amazed to see it; and several of them that thus persecuted 
her, came to nothing; whilst she denied and despised the 
glory of this fading world for Christ’s and truth sake, God 
gave her honour and a name among the righteous; and 
gualifications many ways for considerable service in his 
church ; in which she shone as a morning star, being filled 
with zeal, wisdom, and understanding, for the propagation 
of truth, and righteousness ; of a clear discerning of spirits, 
and the working of the enemy, to draw from the life and 
power of truth, into a liberty that genders to bondage and 
to a separation and breach of unity among Friends ; appear- 
ing firm and zealous against the same. She was fervent 
and living in her ministry, and in supplication and prayers 
to Almighty God, to the edifying and building up many in 
that most precious truth, which gives victory over the world. 
She was not only a great and examplary sufferer for truth, 
but a visiter and sympathizer with the faithful in their

MRS. MARGARET FOX. 217 


sufferings, zealously interceeding with such as were in 
authority for their relief; as being afflicted, and mourning 
with those that mourned. She never spared herself in her 
manifold labours in truth’s account, both in her ministry 
abroad, in most places in this nation, and other services ; 
but approved herself as one that needeth not to be ashamed 
of her work and service of the Lord, which she performed 
with all sincerity, while God was pleased to give her 
strength and ability. She was preserved in a good under- 
standing to the last; and in the time of her sickness, was 
in a sweet frame of spirit. She uttered many heavenly 
expressions near her conclusion in this world, some of 
which are as follow. Come, come, says she, let us join to 
the Lord, and be of one spirit, let us join to the eternal God, 
and be of one spirit. A friend visiting her, who had been 
acquainted with her upwards of forty-five years, she said, 
the Lord is with me, and I am with the Lord, and in him 
only will I trust, and commit all the divine Providence of 
the Lord, both concerning my children, and all things they 
do enjoy from him, both in temporals and spirituals, who is 
the God -of all the mercies and blessings to his people 
throughout all generations; to him be glorious praises for 
ever, Amen. At another time she said, O,.my sweet Lord, 
into thy holy bosom do I commit myself freely, and not 
desiring to live in this troublesome, painful world, it is all 
nothing to me, for my Maker is my husband! At another 
time she said, come Lord, I am freely given up to thy will. 
Again she said, I freely forgive all people upon the face of 
the whole earth, for any wrong done to me, as freely as I 
desire to be forgiven ; and seeing those about her,sorrowful, 
she said, be quiet, for I am as comfortable in my spirit as 
ever I was. A little before she departed, she said to one by 
her, Rachel, take me in thy arms, I am in peace. 


She departed this life at Swarthmore-hall, the 23rd 
day of the 2nd mo. 1702, being near the 88th year of her 
age; and was buried in the burial ground at Simbrooke, 
belonging to Swarthmore, the 27th of the same, attended 
by many Friends and others.

Miss ANN THOM PSON, 
(Now Mrs, Coates.) 


She was born at Aysgarth, # in Wensleydale, but now 
resides at Reeth near Richmond, in the North Riding of” 
Yorkshire. ; 


At the age of about eighteen, she was savingly brought 
to God, under a sermon preached at Aysgarth by Miss Mary 
Barritt, (now Mrs. ‘Taft +) when she was powerfully 
awakened to a sight and sense of her sin and danger ; after 
the sermon, earnest and importunate prayer was made for 
her, yet, she did not then obtain comfort, but was increas- 


ingly distressed on account óf her past iniquities. 


* Aysgarth ísa small village, four miles E. S, E. of Askrigg, 
and contains æ population of 293. It is famous for its romantic 
situation on the banks of the river Ure. The church dedicated to 
St. Andrew is a handsome edifice. There is here a curious bridge, 
called Yore, which rises thirty-two feet, and spans twenty-one ; the 
concave of which is embellished with pendent petrifaction, and its 
airy battlements’ beautifully festooned with spreading ivy. The 
cataracts near this place also claim the attention of every traveller; 
so much so, that the learned Dr. Pocock, whose search after the 
sublime and marvellous brought him to Aysgarth, is said to have 
owned, with exultation, that these cataracts exceeded those so 
celebrated on the Nile. In addition to the parish church, there are 
two meeting houses, one for the Society of Friends, and another for 
the Methodists. Baines’? History and Dictionary of Yorkshire, 
Vol. 2. page 408.

MISS ANN THOMPSON. 219 


She begged the favour of sleeping with Miss B——, 
which was readily granted. After spending much time in 
prayer—they went to bed it is true—but to sleep was out 
of the question, Miss Thompson wept aloud, while her 
companion prayed and exhorted her to believe on the Lord 
Jesus Christ. Afterwards, when she was so enabled to 
believe, as to receive a satisfactory evidence that all her sins 
were forgiven, and herself reconciled to God through the 
blood of the cross;—her joy and consolation were as 
excessive as had been her trouble and sorrow. Some time 
after her conversion, she began to exercise in the public 


‘prayer meetings, and now and then, to give a word of 


exhortation. Finding that in proportion to her endeavours 
for the salvation of others her own happiness increased ;— 


‘and seeing that her labours were acceptable to the people 
and owned of God, she began to multiply her exertions, 


For a length of time, she publicly proclaimed the willingness 
and ability of Christ to save all them that come unto God 
by him ;—but of late years circumstances have obliged her 
to confine herself to a more limited spbere of action. The 


‘Lord has given her the cup of affliction to drink ;—but as 


it is prepared by him who is too wise to err and too good 
to be unkind, it will doubtless tend to the promotion of his 
glory, and the establishment of her own peace,—provided 
she continues to suffer the will of God in the spirit and 
temper of a faithful christian ; considering the weakness 
of her body, she feels satisfied in retiring from her work, and 
giving place to those whom the great Lord of the harvest may 
appoint to gather it in., When Jesus saw the multitudes, he 


‘was moved with compassion on them; because they fainted, 


and were scattered abroad as sheep having no shepherd. 
Then said he unto his disciples, the harvest truly is plen- 
teous, but the labourers are few; pray ye therefore the Lord 
of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his 
harvest. Matt. ix, 36,37, 38.

Mr. MARY LAWRANCE. 


r 


She is a native of Leicester, * and is now living there, . 
Her maiden name was Peet; her parents are at present | 
living at Bedford ;—and she has a brother a travelling : 
preacher in the Wesleyan connexion. She received her 
first good desires and religious impressions among the: 
Wesleyan Methodists, in connection with whom she was i 
converted to God ; and for some time lived in the enjoyment | 
of that peace which passeth all understanding; walking in 
all the commandments and ordinances of God blameless, . 
but being young in years, and much exposed to temptation | 
and the vanities of the world, lost her evidence,— forfeited her » 
peace, and again mingled with the world, and continued in 
a backsliding state for several years. It is true there was © 
no necessity for this, for St. John, in writing to the chris- - 
tian church, and addressing believers of diflerent degrees, 7 
standing, age, and experience, says, my little children these 
things write I unto you that ye sin not, which supposes that — 
they never need sin, otherwise the caution would have been 
useless ; this is also clear from God’s design in pardoning » 
us, Luke, 1. 74, 75, that he would grant unto us that we 
being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, mightserve -

he might serve God without (slavish) fear. How? in holi- 
ness and righteousness. How long ? all the days of his 
life.. When the Lord pardoned and delivered him, he 
did not mean him to come into bondage again, but to 
stand fast, to go forward perfecting holiness in the fear of 
the Lord. This is evident from the strength given to every 
little child in grace (in the use of the means) to restrain 
every inward bent to backslide, and to resist every outward 
attraction to sin by the power of pardoning grace. It is 


granted this strength is not inherent in ourselves. We are 


perfect weakness; neither is it given to us on the ground 


of merit, or for our prayers, morality, or good works, 


but through Christ, and by the exercise of faith, in all holy 
obedience. Isaiah, xlv. 24, surely shall one say in the 
Lord have I righteousness and strength. Phil. iv. 13, I can 
do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me. Thisis 
also clear from the promise, 2 Cor. xii. 9, my grace is 
sufficient for thee, for my strength is made perfect in 
weakness. This is a most precious promise, as it secures 
a sufficiency of grace to enable us to conquer every enemy, 
to perform every duty, however arduous, difficult, or painful, 
to endure every trial and affliction, whether in our persons, 
family, or circumstances, and to the end. And no doubt 
our young friend would have found it so, had she watched 
unto prayer, and continued to give her heart to God, but 
like too many, she forsook the fountain of living waters, 
and sought happiness and rest in broken cisterns, that 
could hold none, But during this time she was strictly moral 
in her outward conduct, frequently attended the preaching 
of God’s word, and sometimes felt painful convictions 
of the dangerous state in which she was living,—with- 
out God, and without hope in the world. She well 
knew that persons may be possessed of heathen morality,— 
the doing no harm,—mere negative goodness; yea, that 
they may have positive goodness too, so far as it respects 
their fellow creatures,—may help the needy, feed the 
hungry, cloathe the naked, subscribe to benevolent and reli- 
gious charities, and in addition to all this, attend all the 
outward forms of religious worship, and yet remain strangers 
to God’s work of grace in the heart,—the new birth,— 


992 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


pardon, peace, and holiness ; that with the form of godli- 
ness they may be destitute of the power thereof,—be mere 
painted sepulchres,—their religion but a farce; that all 
such are, as are wells without water, trees without fruit, 
bearers of lamps without oil, foolish virgins. She knew, 


both from the word of God, and her own experience, that 


a real christian is not as a mere picture. A picture may 


accurately resemble the original, but it wants substance and — 


life ;—it has eyes but it sees not, ears but it ears not, &c. 
A christian is not as a bust.or figure of a man. A 


sculptor may prepare materials, and form a figure of the 
human body, with all its various members, but it wants life.— 


Here she saw her own state and character, and was greatly 
alarmed at the sight. 


Our Lord hath declared,—except your righteousness 
shall exceed the righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees, 
ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven. 
Their righteousness though superior to that of some called 
christians, left them nevertheless in an unpardoned and 
unregenerate state,—consequently, destitute of that faith and 


love without which the life can exhibit before God no 
genuine fruits of righteousness. Without faith it is impos- 
sible to please God,—the faith by which the soul rests 
wholly and constantly upon the sacrifice and sufficiency of 
Christ, as its ground of acceptance with God, and as an 
inexhaustable source of light, life, consolation, and fruitful- 
ness. And love is the fulfilling of the law,—love to God 
and man, springing from faith in the Redeemer, and leading 
its possessor greatly to delight in the commandments of 
the Lord. i i 
She appears to have been brought back to God, under 
the ministry of Mr. R. Winfield, while preaching in one of 
the streets of Leicester, in the year 1818. She soon found 
peace with God, and her former comforts and enjoyments 
were restored unto her with an abundant increase for she 
obtained that perfect love of God which casteth out all 
tormenting fear; and enjoyed a present salvation. By 
grace are we saved, through faith,—justified, introduced

into the family of God, and receive the spirit of adoption. 
As christians we are saved from the present evil world, from 
the sinful love of its riches, pleasures, honours, and froin 
the powers of darkness,—discerning them under every form, 
suppressing every evil desire, and repelling every assault of 
the enemy ; saved by grace, we have the promise of eternal 
salvation; there remaineth therefore a rest for the people 
of God. Heaven is promised to us, we have a title to, and 
a growing meekness for it, yea a pledge, foretaste, and ear- 
nest of future glory. Such became the happy experience 
of this pious female, and such was the constrainmg influence 
of the love Christ shed abroad in her heart, that she was 
sweetly constrained to say to others, come hither all ye that 
fear the Lord, and I will tell you what he hath done for my 
soul; and then, to invite them also to come to the gospel 
feast, that they might taste and see that the Lord is gracious. 
She soon became the leader ofa class among the Revivalists, 
and thinking that it was her duty (after repeated trials,) to 
call sinners to repentance, (the people also concurring in 
this opinion) she was put upon the printed plan asa 
preacher. She is a woman of great gifts, speaks with 
propriety, has an astonishing flow of words, and is some- 
times remarkably eloquent. She is methodistical in her 
sentiments, and preaches a free, full, and present salvation 
with great effect and success. She has been sent for to 
open a great number of chapels and places of worship in 
the connexion of R. Winfield. She has since united in 
connexion with the Ranters, or (as they call themselves, 
Primitive Methodists,) This step she took (if Iam correctly 
informed,) in consequence of considerable uneasiness among 
the leading friends of the society with whom she was 
connected. At the time when this rupture in Robert 
Winfield’s society happened, our sister Lawrance felt very 
desirous to have come back to the Wesleyan Methodist 
Connexion, through whom she first received good to her 
soul, and for whom she ever after felta strong regard, she even 
intimated her desire for a re-union with the Methodists, but 
the difficulty was here, she could only be received amongst 
them upon trial, and then afterwards as a private member ; 
and until she had received a ticket, she would not have been 
U2 


224 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


permitted to act officially or publicly in any capacity in 
that Society. The members of her classes, with herself, 
must have been committed to the care of other leaders, and 
received.in the same way, on trial, This was very painful 
to her; for although she could have submitted to all this, 
as it respected herself, yet the members of her classes, for 
whose welfare as a spiritual mother she was much concerned, 
were not willing to be separated from her. She felt her 
responsibility, and trembled at the thought of any of them 
being scattered and lost; to prevent which she and the 
applied to, and were received by the Ranters as they stood, 
viz. as members, leaders, or local preachers ; notwithstand- 
ing all this, it does not appear that there has been any 
change in her views of scripture truth, or that she has 
suffered any; declension in her zeal for, and purity towards 
God. The souls committed to her care still continue to 
meet with her in class, and she still occupies the talents God 
has given to her for the good of souls. She preaches with — 
great acceptance, and continues to have fruit. May she 
increase with all the increase of God !

MRS. HAINSWORTH. 


Christ, very early in life. Her convictions for sin, and the 


i sorrow she felt on account of it, were truly of a godly sort. 


A true penitent, whose spirit is deeply wounded for sin, feels 


i pungent grief, and overwhelming sorrow ; the flinty heart 
i melts into tenderness before the Lord, and the eyes overflow 
with floods oftears. What anxious thoughts,—what cutting 
reflections !—what painful forebodings are now felt, when 


the foundations of the great deep are broken up within ! what 
agonies ring the soul. O, says the sinner, I have rebelled 
against that God, whom angels adore! J have broken his 
righteous law, defied hisawful judgments, and despised all 
his mercies! I have neglected the salvation of my soul for 
many years! Ihave trampled under foot the blood of the 
covenant, and turned a deaf ear to the voice of the charmer ! 
O, wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the 
body of this death? Such were the views and feelings of 
Mrs. Hainsworth when the Lord by his Spirit set her sins in 
battle array before her. But though heaviness continued for 
a night, joy sprung up in the morning ;—and it wasa 
morning without clouds and darkness, when the Lord spoke 
peace to her soul. She could then sing, 


“ My God is reconcil’d, 

His pardoning voice I hear; 

He owns me for ‘his child, 

I can no longer fear; 

With confidence I now draw nigh, 
And Father, Abba, Father, cry.” 


Through Christ Jesus, she received pardon of sin, peace 
with God, adoption into the family of heaven, a title to the 
inheritance of the saints in light, and a divine and heavenly 
nature. Old things were passed away, and behold, all 
things are become new. Soon after this, she felt an earnest 
desire that others might be brought into the same liberty, 
and enjoy the same salvation. For this purpose she prayed 
in private and in public, and likewise exhorted her neigh- 
bours and acquaintances to turn to the Lord, and seek his 
mercy and love. Encouraged by some little fruit; she 
ventured to enlarge her sphere of action. In this she was 
sensibly favoured with the approbation of God and her own 


226 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


conscience. She had laboured in the word and doctrine 
several years before her union with Mr. Hainsworth took 
place. After their marriage, she continted to preach and | 
exhort, as opportunities occurred. She very frequently 
accompanied him to the country places, and during these 
visits, generally spoke to the people after he had preached. 
This novelty in their proceedings never failed to excite 
considerable attention, insomuch that the places of worship — 
were generally crowded, especially by the time she had to 
occupy her husband’s place. These labours of love were 
acceptable to God, and well pleasing and profitable to the 
people. Good was done, and some fruit remains to this day. 
She has occasionally exercised in public since the death of 
her husband, and now and then paid a visit to some distant 
places, with much satisfaction to the people, and to the 
profit of precious souls. Her manner of address is very 
pleasing ; her voice melodious ; her views of scripture truth 
very clear: and her. ministrations are often attended with 
much of the divine unction and power. But her work in’ 
the Lord’s vineyard, is nearly finished; she seems ripening 
apace to join her husband, and the innumerable company 


before the throne, where all the mysteries of providence 
shall be unfolded, * 


“Where all the ship’s company meet, 
Who sail’d with their Saviour beneath.” 


There to see Jesus her King, the God and Saviour in his 
beauty, brighter than the sun, sitting on the throne of his 
glory. It is impossible to describe the happiness of the 
heavenly inhabitants. But if the promises be so precious 
to the truly pious, what will thefulfilment be? If the drops 
of divine love be so sweet, what will the ocean be? If a 
small ray, a beam from the divine effulgence be so glori- 
ous and transforming, how glorious must saints and angels 
be, that bask in his presence. There is fulness of joy, and 
at his right hand pleasures for evermore. Eye hath not 
seen nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of 
man to conceive what God hath laid up for them that love 
him, We read in the Revelations, he that overcometh

She is the daughter of Mr. Francis Wilson, of Wharton 
Lodge, near Wetherby, in Yorkshire,—and niece to the late 
Miss Isabella Wilson * of Sinnethwaite. Eliza, the sub- 
ject of this memoir, had the honour to be born of pious 
parents, and the unspeakable advantage of a religious 
education, She also from early life enjoyed the society, 
the counsel, conversation, and prayers of the faithful 
ministers of the gospel, and other pious friends, who were 
frequently and very hospitably entertained under her father’s 
roof. It is not therefore to be wondered at, that through 
the divine blessing upon such means and instruments, s 
should in very early life be drawn over to the side of virtue 
and piety. Not indeed without many struggles with, and 
against the natural depravity of her own heart, and the 
various suggestions of the enemy of her soul’s salvation, 
which if yielded to, would have led her to neglect the 
concerns of her soul. But as her understanding received 
increasing light, her soul became alive to her state and 
danger, her convictions increased, which led her to the 
throne of mercy and of grace, for help and salvation. She 
soon experienced the truth of that divine assertion, ask and 
ye shall receive, seek and ye shall find, She sought the 
Lord, and found him to the joy of her soul. After enjoy- 
ing the safety and comfort of religion for herself she felt 
desirous that others would come and taste, and see that the 
Lord is gracious, and she not only felt desirous and anxious 
on their account, but soon found that it was become a duty 
incumbent upon her to invite them to come to the gospel

man is now given to they public. It is written by Mr. Pipe, 
and may be had of Mr. Mason, at the Methodist Book Room, 
London. It is a well written book, the materials being both 
abundant and excellent. It will be read with peculiar interest 
and feeling by her relatives and friends, and indeed by all who 
love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity, and not the less so, 
because, the pious and benevolent author pledges himself to 
devote any profits that may arise from its publication to the

Mrs. JANE PEARSON. 


This eminent female was a member of the Society of 
Friends, commonly called Quakers, and for many years was 
an acceptable and useful speaker in that community. She 
appears very early in life to have had her mind embued 
with divine grace, or the strivings of the Holy Spirit of God, 
which she stifled and resisted, giving place to guiety, trifling 

company, and lightsome conversation. But soon after her 
marriage, and when about 23 years of age, she was more 
‘ully and deeply awakened to a sense of her depravity and 
danger.—These discoveries and convictions brought her to 
the throne of grace, and to the footstool of divine mercy for 
salvage, which she shortly obtained, and soon after felt 
earnestly concerned for the salvation of others, and believing 
it to be her indispensible duty to speak in public for 
their edification and comfort; she with much fear and 
trembling entered upon the important work ; in which she 
continued till far advanced in life. As her conduct and 
conversation corresponded with her-holy profession, and as

_ The following Sketch of her religious experience and 
public labours, is taken from *¢ Sketches of Piety in the Life 
and religious experiences of Jane Pearson, extracted from 
her own memorandums, Second. Edition.” —Printed at 
York, 1818. 


% 

“It has long remained with weight upon my mind, to 
leave a few remarks respecting the Lord’s dealings, when he 
iwas pleased to lay his hand in judgment upon me, for my 
backslidings; hoping it may be of service to sdme poor, 
tossed, afflicted, disconsolate, tempted, bewildered mind; 
for I believe it would have been of service to me, in my 
painful moments, to have beheld the footsteps of others. 


I was born at Newton, near Carlisle, of sober, religious 
parents. My father dying when I was young, I had more 
experience of my mother’s religious care in our tuition. 


Tt pleased the Lord by his good Spirit, to work in my 
heart, in my young years; which brought a godly sorrow 
over me, anda fear lest I should be taken away in my 
childish follies. When the bell. used’ to’ toll for those of 
other persuasions, Oh! the awe and inward fear attendant 
on these occasions ! 


-I loved to read the scriptures, especially the New 
Testament; and when I read the passage where our blessed 
Lord is described as having suffered.so much from the high 
professors, who despitefully treated him,- and crucified him, 
my heart became melted and tendered under a sense of it. 


About this time it pleased the Lord to:send Mary Kirby, 
of Norfolk ; and she beingalone, requested me to accompany 
ner. My mother gave me up, and it wasa time of reaping 
some advantage; for when I returned home, I felt my 
heart, in a good measure, cleansed and emptied of the old 


234 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


inhabitants; my stiff will being measurably subdued; and 
loving retirement, I was drawn from my old companions. 


I then witnessed a state of deep poverty of spirit, which! 
caused me thus to address the Almighty, ‘Lord, what 
wouldest thou have me to do?’ 


I was sitting in our womens’ meeting for discipline, ati 
Carlisle, when it appeared clear to me, that if I continued! 
thus inward with God, I should soon have to speak to others. . 
This intimation was so far from humbling me, that I did: 
not even desire to be excused, or pray the divine Master to: 
have patience with me; but I resolutely said, * I never will. 
do so.’ I started aside like a broken bow, and I believe: 
went into greater alienation from the life, than I had ever: 
done before ; and just it would have been, if infinite wisdom: 
had cut me off in my disobedience. 


At the age of between one and two and twenty, I was: 
married to John Pearson, a sober, religious young man. 
About a year after my marriage, my false rest was broken; 
though I was rightly married, and, I trust, in best wisdom. 
United to a choice haba I was swimming as in an ocean | 
of pleasure; but I witnessed, instead of peace on earth, a) 
heart-piercing sword. My undone condition was present’ 
with me day and night, when awake. Indeed I slept but 
little ; sleep departed from my eyes, and slumber from my i 
eye-lids; so that when night came, I wished for morning. i 
And though preserved from gross evils, so heavy was the | 


Lord’s hand in judgment against the sinful, impure part in J) | 


me, that there was sufficient work for his heart-piercing | 
sword, which divides betwixt the precious and the vile, that f; 
which serves him, and that which serves him not. 


My case now, in my own view, was exceedingly | 
er 


deplorable ; so that I neither eat nor slept much, which f 
occasioned a visible decline in my health. Indeed I was: 
just a wonder to behold; the people wondering what had i 
befallen me. The enemy followed me closely with most | 
besetments ; things that my very soul loathed. 


MRS. JANE PEARSON. 235 


I ate my bread with weeping, and mingled my drink 
with my tears.x—Oh ! that my troubles were written with 
an iron pen, and lead in the rock for ever! For surely a 
hundredth part is far beyond my power of description. 


About this time I was much drawn inward in prayer ; 
and for a time, I believe I prayed without ceasing: and yet, 
‘the Lord knew what I needed, to fit me for his work and 
‘Service.—At length I witnessed the truth of that declaration ; 
“when thy judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants will 
learn righteousness ;’” for truly I did experience inward 
purity of heart and cleanness of hands; and in the Lord’s 
own time he gave access to his throne; and the spirit of 
prayer and supplication was poured out upon me. I then 
felt a holy sense of this truth, ‘the Lord liveth;” and 
* because he lives, I live also.” 


-~ This was a day of close trial ; for I was brought to 
the test, whether I would keep my covenant that I had 
made with the Lord, which was, that if he would set me 
clear of the enemy, command what he pleased, I would 
obey. Frequently in assembling with the Lord’s people, 
our meetings were often favoured with lively testimonies. 
On such occasions, scripture sentences would impress my 
‘mind with some degree of life and power, and I felt some 
“concern of mind to declare itin theaudience. I had a hope 
‘which as an anchor stayed my soul, and raised a holy 
belief, that he who was my confidence, would unfold the 
mysteries of his kingdom, and give an undoubted evidence, 
with unsullied clearness, that it was his will that the candle 
he had lighted, should be set on the candlestick, to give 
light to those around; and thanks be to his ever worthy 
name, for he fulfilled it. 


I then in great fear, went to our little meeting at 
Graysouthern. A few words presented lively, and I well 
‘remember the subject.—Oh ! the peace that I felt that night, 
after that short testimony. It would have been acceptable 
to have been dissolved, and to have been with Christ, which 
is far better,

And now I had great peace of mind, so that instead of 
my heart being a place for dragons, for owls, and for 
screech owls; for cormorants, and for bitterns; there be 
to be a melody in my heart, as it were the voice of the Son 
of God, whose countenance is comely; and the myrtle, box, 
and pine sprang up in that heart which had been a breeding- 
place for nettles. This is the change that is wrought in 
man, by being born again of the incorruptible seed and 
word of God. This was the change that was wrought 
in me. 


I had now frequently to speak in meetings, and had 
satisfaction in so doing; and friends did not discountenance 
me in my childlike movings ; but approved, though with a 
godly care.” 


As the author’s design is only to publish Biographical 
Sketches of the lives and ministry, experience and labours 
of holy women, he must pass over much excellent matter, 
contained in the journal of the exercises and afflictions of | 
this holy woman. She seems to have waded through deep 
waters in the afflictions, and bereavement of her husband 
and children, These feelings are sometimes touchingly 
represented in poetic strains of eloquence, and feeling.
