3rd mo. 28th, 1797. Iwas favoured once more to 
altend our quarterly meeting at Carlisle, very near the place 
of my nativity, and the meeting I belonged to for many 
years. The meeting of ministers and elders was a favoured 
season; I had the evidence of peace in my little labours ; 
and indeed all the. meetings were more or less owned with 
the heart solacing presence of Zion’s king. It was like 
taking my leave ; and I was helped to be faithful; so that 
in my return, for many miles, my cup ran over, and I 
seemed anointed with the oil of gladness. Great. was my 


238 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


peace ; such a full foretaste of heavenly joy, as I have not 
before experienced, except when I first opened my mouth 
in testimony. There seemed nothing betwixt my soul and 
its blessed Redeemer. At that time my joy was so full, that: 
I did long to be dissolved, feeling nothing but purity and 
holiness about me; or at least, I had the sense of full 
acceptance with the Father, in my endeavours to obey. 


6th mo. 30, 1802,—I was at our week-day meeting, 
and was favoured with a solemn silence, resembling that in 
heaven, where angels and archangels adore in profound 
silence. Oh! I saw into the joys thereof; a place where 
sorrow cannot come; none of the inhabitants have any 
affliction. I was this day favoured to partake of the most 
substantial sustenance of divine good, that perhaps I ever 
experienced ; the heavenly bread was handed to my scul in 
no sparing portion, with, ** take, eat, this is my body. 


12th mo. 23rd day, 1804. First day I was at our 
meeting, in which I had an open time, much to my own 
satisfaction; and I hope to that of others. Indeed truth 
rose in dominion. In leaving the meeting a sense of accept- 
ance was given me; measurably receiving the sentence of 
well done, in my own particular; with a secret hope, that 
if I continued thus to steer my course carefully, eyeing my 
guide ; in simplicity and godly sincerity, dealing out to the 
people, as immediately given; pursuing the thread of m 
testimony in the power, depending wholly upon the Lord, 
he would be mouth and wisdom, tongue and utterance. 


3rd of 12th mo. 1806. In our week-day meeting, I 
was engaged ¢o set forth the necessity of not only receiving 
the seed of the kingdom, but with all readiness of allowing 
its growth; as the work of truth in the heart of man, is 
described by our great master, to be progressive; first the 
blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear. JI had 
peace in returning to my habitation, and this language 
presented to me: ‘* Ever since thou wast born, my love 
has been to thee.” This melted me; may I be worthy of 
such a favour.

4th of 5th mo. 1807. Fourth day I was at meeting. 
A solemn time it was to me; for T was much engaged in 
mental breathings; the spirit helping my infirmities 


inwardly to pray. A large portion of heavenly bread was 


handed to me, without much wrestling, or having it to set 
before others; and although our souls’ enemies may be 
numerous, a language livingly opened, “the Lord shall fight 
for you, and you shall hold your peace.” It applied to 
myself, as I had no commission to divulgeit. I had strong 
consolation in God. 


Sth mo. 6th, 1810. I have been surprised that the 
older and more infirm I grow, the more I am enlarged in 
mind, and the more illuminated in regard to scripture sen- 
tences. Oh! how the watch word when it comes, brightens 
upon my mind, and inwardly gives me to expatiate 
thereupon. It is the Lord’s doing, and marvellous indeed in 
my eyes. Lord what am I, that thou continuest thus to 
acknowledge me, and that thou thus expandest my heart in 
old age, when the keepers of the frail building tremble 
exceedingly. 


14th of 1lth mo. 1810. This day we had a very 
confirming season, in our silent week-day meeting. I 
thought I should never more doubt being under the notice 
of heaven, the evidence was so strong, and my love seemed 
perfectly godward ; so that it cast out all fear. I neither 
feared death, hell, nor the grave. The armies of the aliens, 
for the present, were entirely put to flight. My faith was 
strong respecting my own well being; and even I had faith 
for those who that day gathered with me. We seemed 
indeed come to Zion, the city of the living God, and 
gathered in spirit with an innumerable company of angels. 


Previous to this precious season, I had very great 
Openings into divine things, pertaining to another life ; 
things’so sacred as not to be medled with; which brought 
me to think I should soon be gathered; and in looking at 
the ministry I had been gifted with, and how I had been 
moved under the openings I had been favoured with,

eternally. Amen!

MRS. JANE PEARSON. 241 


About the 18th year of her age, she accompanied 
through this county, a female friend, then upon a visit to 
the meetings of friends in these parts. 


In the year 1757, being then about 22 years of age, 
she was married to John Pearson, of Graysouthern, within 
the limits of this meeting, a religious young man. In the 
course of several succeeding years, she passed through 
various deep baptisms, and refining operations; and thus 
becoming obedient to the forming hand, she received a gift 
in the ministry. She came forth very acceptably in public 
testimony, about the year 1773. 


In the year'1777, she visited generally the meetings of 
friends in Westmoreland and Lancashire ; in 1779 those of 
Westmoreland, Lancashire, and Yorkshire; and in 1787, 
those of Lancashire, Cheshire; Shropshire, Worcestershire, 
Warwickshire, Somersetshire, Devonshire, and Cornwall. 
Her gospel labours in these visits were, we believe, very 
acceptable, yielding’ to herself the consoling reward 
of peace. 


About this time she removed to Whitehaven, at which 
place she has since resided. 


She was diligent and exemplary in the attendance of 
meetings. Her ministry was sound, lively, and edifying ; 
and though her appearances were frequent, and sometimes 
large, she was particularly careful not to go beyond the 
pure openings of the Holy Spirit. In prayer she was 
remarkably powerful and fervent. She was a truly affec- 
tionate parent and friend ; tenderly sympathizing with the 
afflicted. In conversation lively, ‘affable, and instructive ; 


being endowed with an excellent understanding. She 


retained her natural cheerfulness even to advanced years, 
and her mental faculties unimpaired to the. last. 


Sometimes. she intimated the serenity of her prospects, 
when the. trials and exercises attendant upon humanity, 
should. terminate. 


942 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


Not many weeks prior to her decease, and upon a 


friend’s taking leave of her, she seemed affected, and said, . 


“ though I drop tears, I am not left comfortless. No; we 
have not followed cunningly devised fables. I think what 
I feel, might convince the whole world. Oh! it is 
marvelous! it is marvelous ! ’” 


Her remains were interred in Friends’ burial ground, 
in Whitehaven, on the 25th of 3rd mo. 1816, after a large 
and solemn meeting. She was about 81 years of age, and 
a minister about 42 years.

and in early life was brought to an experimental knowledge 
of the truth ; evidencing the reality of the change which 
divine grace had wrought in her heart by a very exemplary

life. Her self-denial, spirituality of mind, profitable 
conversation ; unwearied zeal, diligence and Jabour in pro- 
toting the best interests of mankind, both at home and 
abroad, raised her very high in the esteem of those who had 
the privilege of a personal acquaintance with her; and 
many who have known her only by reading the records of 
her religious experience and labours, will have abundant 
cause to praise God for the abundant grace which was 
manifested to her. The following Sketch of her life and 
ministry is taken from,—‘some account of the life and 
‘religious exercises of Mary Neale, formerly Mary Peisley, 
principally compiled from her own writing, Second Edition, 
published at Dublin, 1795.” 


* Mary Neale, otherwise Peisley, daughter of Peter 
and Rachel Peisley, was born in the year 1717, near 
Mountrath in the Queens country, and educated in the Soci- 
ety of the people called Quakers; but a disposition to keep 
company unrestrained by the cross of Christ, led her from 
truth’s simplicity in manners and behaviour, whereof she 
thus expresses herself. 


[count it an infinite mercy and high favour, that the 
omnipotent God suffered not the thread of my life to be cut, 
during the many years that I lived in disobedience to his 
holy will; and though often by the operation of his grace 
inwardly touched and convicted of my errors, and the vail 
so far rent from off my understanding, as to let me see that 
I stood on the brink of ruin, yet did I as often suffer the 
enemy and adversary of my soul again to darken my under- 
standing and benumb my spiritual feeling. 


T have to remember, as an inexpressible favour and 
mercy to my soul, that in the height of all my vanity, and 
Stupidity, I was not suffered to run into the gross enormities 
of the world, I was kept from those loud, crying, hardening, 
black crimes which, had I run into, mightso highly provoke 
my creator, as to have caused him to say in his wrath; 
‘thou shalt not enter into my rest.’

244 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES, 


A short time before -my conversion, I had a fall from 
my horse, by which I was apparently in danger of having 
my neck disjointed, anda sudden end put to my life; as 
soon as I rose on my feet, and recovered my senses, the 
Lord by his grace, and good spirit shewed me clearly that 
I was not in a fit condition to meet him, the just and holy 
judge of heaven and earth, and caused me solidly to con- 
sider the dismal consequence of being hurried off the stage 
of mortality, in an unprepared state, the impression of which 
never left my mind, till God by his grace had made me more 
fit for his kingdom, the glory of which be given to his ever- 
lasting name.” 


About this time it appears from her journal, that two 
ministers paid a religious visit to the place and neighbour- 
hood where she then resided, whose conversation and | 
powerful ministry was made an everlasting blessing to her- 
soul, she had felt the sorrow of a wounded spirit, but was 
a stranger to the comforts and consolations arising from 
peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ; she had 
heard of these by the hearing of the ear, but she now 
waited, and sought, and prayed that she might be made a 
happy partaker of the joys of salvation, and she did not 
wait and seek in vain, From this time she appears to have 
continued a vessel of honour fitted for the master’s use. 


« Her entrance into the work of the ministry was 
ahout the beginning of the year 1744, near which time she 
had unexpected domestic trials, which brought her very | 
low in mind, from a sense of the singularity of her situation, 1 
but her trust being in the Lord, she was eminently 
supported.’’ 


“J am resolved,” says she, ** by the blessed assistance 
of Israel’s God, not to bury that talent that he has given 
me, in the earth, nor to quit the occupying of it for any | 
outward occupation ; better would it be for me to wander 
as the prophets formeily did; destitute, distressed, and 
naked, than to sell an unfading inheritance, for any prospect 
of advantage here.

both publicly and privately ; so that I have no condemnation 
on that account, nor have I repented leaving all to answer his 
holy requirings, but humbly thank him, that he enabled me 
so to do; and were crowns and diadems laid at my feet, I 
would not give his approbation for them. 


I have many times thought a soul rightly influenced 
and affected with the love of God, is like the needle touched 
with the loadstone, that which ever way it be turned, rests 
not, nor settles, till it comes to its true centre, that is, while 
it retains the virtue of the loadstone. Thus it is with the 
soul that has been quickened and renewed by that efficacious 
power, which has been extended, to draw our souls from 
earth to heaven, for certain it is they have a natural ten- 
dency to sink into the earth, or earthly enjoyments, but 
unless we renewedly witness the visitations of that warming, 
heart melting love of God, which keeps the soul alive to 
him, and brings into that holy fellowship which is with the 
Father, and his Son Christ Jesus, by livingly feeling him 
to be in us, and we in him, all religion is but dead form 


and empty shew; as the branch cannot bring forth fruit of © 


itself, except it abide in the vine, no more can we, except 
we abide in him.” 


«c In the latter part of this journey, I was seized with 
a violent intermitting fever, which illness detained me 
several weeks, and caused me to travel in great bodily 
weakness, yet the Lord was graciously pleased at times to 
strengthen me for the service he had called me to, beyond 
my own and others expectation. I waited near a month 
for a passage, which seemed tedious to me, some of the 
time at a public house at Parkgate, destitute of friends or 
acquaintance, but dared not repine at the will of providence.

MRS. MARY NEALE. 249 


In this journey J rode about five thousand miles, and 
attended five hundred and twenty five meetings. I landed 
at Dublin the 9th mo. 1750, being about two years and nine 
months absent; had the company of my esteemed friend, 
Samuel Fothergill. We had a rough but swift passage, 
and were in danger of driving upon the Welch coast, but 
the Lord was our preserver. My friends rejoiced to see 
me, as I did them, some were concerned at the state of my 
visibly impaired health.” 


Several years after this we find her in America, where 
she writes, ‘‘In this province we met with many difficulties 
both of body and mind, the former by long journeys, in a 
very thinly inhabited, country, through unbeaten paths in the 
woods, dangerous swamps and creeks, with wild and venom- 
ous creatures around us, and with such food and lodging 
as we had never been accustomed to; yet the Lord our God 
was pleased to make it up to us, by his comfortable presence, 
and good spirit. 


At Nuce in North Carolina, we had a large and com- 


fortable meeting, in which I thought it might be truly said, 
the Lord’s power was over all, and that even devilish spirits 
were made subject to that power, by which we were 
assisted to speak. 


One thing which friends here, as well as in North 
Carolina, Maryland, and some parts of America were in the 
practice of, gave us considerabie pain, and we apprehended 
was the cause of truth’s not prospering amongst them, as 
otherwise it would, that is, buying and keeping of slaves, 
which we could not reconcile with the golden rule of doing 
unto all men as we would they should do unto us.” 

4 

This excellent woman appears to have returned from 
America in the year 1756, and after visiting the friends, 
and holding a number of meetings in different parts of her 
own country, she sweetly fell asleep in Jesus, in the 
year 1757.

The grace of God received and improved, makes a 
glorious change in the hearts and lives of men. This is 
evident from scripture, experience, and observation. This 
change is so great that it is sometimes called a new creation, 
a new birth, and a resurrection from the dead, St. Paul 
informs the Romans of the great change which the grace of 
God had made in their hearts and lives; in their present 
and future state. ‘For when ye were the servants of sin, 
ye were free from righteousness ; what fruit had ye then in 
those things whereof ye are now ashamed ? for the end of 
those things is death; but now being made free from sin, 
and become the servants of God, ye have your fruit unto 
holiness, and the end everlasting life.” Rom. vi. 20, 24. 
If we pay any attention to matters of fact, we have heard 
of thousands, and have known many who were enemies to 
all righteousness, and lived in the practice of all kinds of 
iniquity, being brought by divine grace to love and serve 
God; and who have been hereafter eminent for piety, 
holiness, and usefulness. And others who were gay and 
trifling, giddy and thoughtless, have become serious and 
humble, holy and useful. Among the latter class we find 
the subject of this Memoir, who is now a pious, holy, and 
useful individual. She is a native of Breastone, im the 
county of Derby, where she chiefly resides, except when 
for religious purposes she visits the different churches 
belonging to the people with whom she is united in chnis- 
tian fellowship. She isa member of the New Methodigt 
Connexion, and has been preaching the gospel im man 

large towns and country villages in this kingdom, for the 
last twenty years. The Lord has taken away her naturaj

sight, but he has continued her spiritual’ vision, so that she 
clearly sees’ the things that belong for her peace, and is 
likewise eridued with gifts and talents to preach, to edifica- 


tion, exhortation, and to comfort, before any community of 


christians. 


She was steady, circumspect, and modest from a child, 


yet, her convictions for sin were very deep and protracted! 


Many have unhappily deceived themselves in the opinion 
that nothing’ but’ positive, and prestmptuous acts of rebellion 


against God will subject them to punishment hereafter. They 
place much confidence in what is called a harmless, inoffen- 


sive life, as if it were virtuous enough not to. be’ abandoned 
to vice. Notso, the subject of this Memoir, whea the 
divine commandment came home to her heart, and by the 
illuminating and’ awakening spirit of God, she saw the 
exceeding’ breadth of the divine law, and felt the exceeding 
sinfülness of sin, she died to all hope of being saved by the 
deeds of the law; she felt the sentence of death in herself, 
and was driven out of every refuge, and stripped of every 
plea, except that of the poor publican, «God be merciful 
to me a sinner.” But believing that God had opened a 
way for the exercise of mercy to the chief of sinners, she 
prostrated herself at the footstool of Jehovah, and on the 
ground of the alone sacrifice of him who died for sinners, 
pleaded with sueh a degree of confidence and faith as met 
with divine aeceptance. She found light and liberty, peace 
and joy, through believing, and experienced, — 


“The o’erwhelming power of saving grace, 
The sight that veils the seraph’s face, 

The speechless awe that dares not move, 
And all the silent heaven of love.” 


From that time her delight was to converse about the things 
of God, and to hear the preaching of the gospel by the 
ambassadors of Jesus Christ. And as she increased in 
spirituality and heavenly mindedness, in love to God, and 
conformity to him, her love to souls increased, and she 
secame earnestly desirous of their salvation. She saw 


2b2 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


herself surrounded by those who were evidently thronging 
the way to eternal ruin, and her feeling heart was melted 
into sympathy at the affecting sight. Her soul recoiled at 
the idea of so many of her fellow creatures perishing, when 
such abundant provision was made for their everlasting 
happiness. She looked at the infinite virtue and eternal 
efficacy of the Redeemer’s blood,—at the freeness and the 
sufficiency of divine grace,—at the indiscribable horrors of 
damnation,—and the unspeakable felicities of the skies, 
and by these views was moved from time to time to speak 
to them on the things that pertained to their peace. Her 
talents and gifts increased by being occupied, and as evident 
good was done, her field of usefulness and labour became 
very extensive. 


She has been in Lancashire, Cheshire, Yorkshire, 
Derbyshire, Staffordshire, and Nottinghamshire, preaching 
the unsearchable riches of Christ,—endeavouring to per- 
suade the children of men to be reconciled to God. She 
has preached in various respectable chapels, to the astonish- 
ment of hundreds, and it is said she has been made the 
honoured instrument in the conversion of very many. 


Lam thankful to hear that some pious friends have 
engaged to supply her temporal necessities; and that from 
their firm conviction of her exalted piety and great usefulness. 
Surely such an act of christian benevolence will meet with 
an abundant recompence of reward, in that day when the 
judge of the human race shall say, “ well done thou good 
and faithful servant,” &c. ‘ Whosoever shall give you a 
cup of water to drink in my name, because ye belong to 
Christ, verily I say unto you, he shall not lose his 
reward.” Mark ix. 41.

Mis MARGARET ADAMS. 


Margaret was converted to God through the instrumen- 
tality of the Arminian Bible Christians, and lived and died 
a member of that community. The following Sketch of her 
character is taken from their Monthly Magazine for January, 
1825, page 20. 


« A short account of the experience of Margaret Adams: 


It is cause of regret that our beloved sister hath left behind 
her so little of her experience. She has writtena little, and but 
a little. Perhaps one cause of this neglect was the mean 
views which she had of herself. Most likely many from 
this consideration have buried many things that might have 
been useful to others, had they been recorded. May those 
who come after, learn by the errors of those who are 
gone before. 


The following was found in her own hand writing. 


«‘ The Lord was pleased to meet me in the way of 
mercy. Glory be to God for his redeeming grace, and his 
ten thousand times ten thousand mercies towards me,—l, 
who fell on the brink of ruin; glory be to God, I am 
out of hell. 


I believe, if ever any one had reason to praise God it 
is 1; for I was a despiser of all good; and the people of 
God were a people that I held in great derision. I even 
looked on them with scorn and contempt, and particularly 
on W, O’ B’s people.

After the Lord was pleased to send up W. O’ B. from 
West of the North of Cornwall, there was much talk about 
him. Some saying there never was such a man in that 
part before. Iheard of his coming into our parish of 
Moorwinstow, and it was published for him to preach at 
Brownspit, on Tuesday, the 13th of February, 1816. 1 
then was ready to go and hear, or to see what kind of man 
this was, whom the people made so much ado about, 


My mother was not agreeable to my going to hear any 
people that went by the name of Methodists; but some of 
my old companions called on me, and my brother Thomas 
and I went with them. We went, but what did we go for?

-had to say. I recollect he preached in a barn, and stood 
on a threshing machine. We stood just at the door, so 
that we could see the man that was called such a wonder, 
As for myself I do not know that ever I felt so much against 
a man that I knew nothing about. I was so exasperated 
against him, that I thought I should be glad to hear he was 
confined. I recollected there was a lad with him that 
exhorted after W. ©’ B. had preached, who, we were 
informed, was'S. Thorne; and he intreated the people to 
leave the city of destruction, and become travellers to 
Mount Sion. Iwas so ignorant, I did not know that T

homewards, I asked of the people whether they did know 
the way to Sion, or whether there was such a place or not ? 
None could tell me where, or what this place was; so we 
still remained in ‘darkness, and continued to mock those 
people.—Soon after we heard of- W. ʻO’ B. coming to 
Goosham ; this being near, my father, mother, and all the

once a month. In the time of their coming there, by some

house to inquire. Hearing some one knock at the door, 
1 opened the inside door, and looked through the passage 
and saw who it was; I fastened the door again, and said, 
it is the old (Bryan. However my mother went and

February 16th, 1817. M. A. 


Written from her mouth by Brother Reed. 


{ was born at Cory, in the parish of Moorwinstow, and 
county of Cornwall, February 27th, 1799. My parents’ 
names were John and Ann Adams. They were professed 
members of the establishment, and regularly attended the 
Church of England; but they were strangers to vital godli- 
ness, destitute of an experimental knowledge of God, and 
lived after the course of this world. Seeing no greater 
concern for salvation in them, I did not see any néed of it 
for myself, and not having any spiritual instructor, I followed 
the maxims and customs of the world with greediness. 
When W. O’ Bryan first came into our neighbourhood to 
preach, I was one of his hearers, and became a very great 
persecutor, both of him and the doctrine taught by him. I 
felt a greater hatred to him, than to any other man I ever 
saw; but for what reason I cannot tell, any other than this, 
he was extolled as a wonderful man, and | was afraid that 
he would be the means of putting down dancing &c. which 
I much liked. 


After some time, my mother invited him to our house 
to preach; but I was exasperated against it, thinking that 
if he came to preach, we should have no more dancing 
meetings there; so my brother Thomas and I consulted 
together how to prevent it, and agreed to persuade our 
father against it; and prevailed with him; so the meeting 
was prevented. 


Notwithstanding my enmity against the truth, I conti- 
nued to attend the preaching; and one night under the 
word felt powerfully wrought upon, and saw the need of 
prayer. I returned home, and changed my lodging room, 
for the sake of being alone, in order to pray, for I was 
ashamed to let any one see me upon my knees. On being

asked why I changed rooms? I refused to tell, being: 
ashamed to let them know the cause. After I got into the: 
room, I locked and bolted the door, and put something, 
before it. So astonishing was my shame of every christian 
duty, through the carnal mind which I then had, which is; 
at enmity with God.. And as was my love of pleasure, and! 
my shame of the cross of Christ, so was my love of gaiety.. 
Some time after being dressed 'to go to preaching, I looked! 
into the glass and thought, should I be converted and! 
obliged to take down ‘my curls! such was the pride of my) 
heart, that I should feel something within saying, I would |

and keep my curls too, I should be glad of it. 


After some time I was invited to attend a watch-night, ,

I then thought, should this be the Spirit of God I now feel,

than what the preacher hath now described me, what shall 
Ido then? I then gave myself up to God, to work as he 
pleased with me. Ithen felt a weakness anda sighing in- 
wardly take hold on me, and I fell to the ground, not being 
able to stand any more than an infant. When I fell to the 
ground, I saw hell open to receive me, and nothing but the 
mercy of God, and tne thread of life kept me from falling 
in. [then was constrained to cry aloud for mercy, so that 
the preacher could not proceed. At that time I wore false 
plaiting under my bonnet, and I felt as if that and my curls

Soon after Margaret was convinced of sin, she was 
converted to God ; and witnessed her change of heart by a 
change in her deportment. She could not remain quiet and 
satisfied with the enjoyment of the love of God in her own 
soul; she felt a desire to invite others to come also, and 
‘taste and see that the Lord is gracious, About christmas, 
1817, she began to speak in public ; she was well received, 
and her word was accompanied with divine energy. About 
lady-day, she removed to the parish of North-hill, which lay 
in Neot Circuit ;, but there she was not satisfied, feeling her 


258 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES, 


heart affected with a sense of the misery and danger of 
mankind, she ventured all on Christ, and about midsummer 
became an Itinerant: She travelled awhile in Luzxillian, 
Truro, Canworthy Water, and Dock Circuits. In 1821, she 
felt a difficulty in pursuing her line of duty, through a 
scrofula which affected her throat. Atthe Conference 1821, 
she was still numbered among-the travelling preachers; but 
had no appointment. She was kindly entertained in. the 
houses of several friends, and means used for her recovery; 
but to no purpose, she still grew ‘worse. In the spring of 
1822, her uncle Adams, of Hartland, took her to his house, 
where a doctor attended her; but all means proved alike 
ineffectual. She still grew weaker and weaker; but strong 
in faith giving glory.to God. She was very happy during 
her illness,—then she fully proved the reality of that gospel 
which she had preached to others, as may be seen by the 
following letter sent me (the Editor,) from her uncle, with 
whom she died. ai 


My dear Friend, | W: 


I take up my pen.to let you know of dear 
Margaret’s death, which took place on the 26th. I may 
well add she died a happy and composed saint in the Lord. 
She has borne her affliction with christian fortitude and 
resignation, and in patience she possessed her soul. 


The night before she died, she was exhorting all ‘that 
she saw to prepare to meet her at the right hand of God. 
She felt a bright evidence that she should land safe home in 
glory. She will be buried at Edystone Chapel. *

As nothing has been written concerning the truly

comes within my knowledge, Ifyou think them worth

hoping this, with them, will prove a blessing to your

Margaret Adams was the first female preacher that 
came to this neighbourhood. She was instrumental, under 
God, of laying thé foundation of a church in Chilbrook, 
and several other places in Roach, and its vicinity. No 
sooner did she blow the gospel trumpet in these 
places, than multitudes flocked to hear the joyful sound. 
Nor did. they hear in- vain, Many were pricked to the 
heart. It was no uncommon thing, while our Sister was 
exhorting the people to flee from the wrath to come, to. see 
five, or ten, at once, crying out for mercy to that God 
against whom they had sinned; and a great number were 

rhs ag 


260 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


brought from darkness unto light, and from the power 
of sin and satan unto God. We have had many glorious 
meetings with our departed Sister, at Chilbrook. While 
sinners of almost every description, have been convinced 
and converted, believers have been built up in their 
most holy faith, and encouraged to persevere in the ways 
of the Lord; so that the name of our Sister is still dear to 
many in this neighbourhood, and many, we trust, will have 
to bless God to all eternity, for sending such a character 
among us. 


Sister Adams, had every appearance of a woman of 
eminent piety. She was amiable and loving in her dispo- 
sition, and of a meek and lowly mind and temper. The 
simplicity and modesty, she constantly maintained, con- 
strained every one who knew her, to love and admire her. 
She ever manifested somewhat of the spirit of her divine 
Lord and Master; and always endeavoured to strike at the 
root of pride. She had always very low thoughts of herself; 
and perhaps on that account, little or nothing has been left 
behind her of her christian experience. It was evident to 
all who knew her, that, in all her preaching, exhorting, 
praying, and conversation, she aimed at the glory of God, 
and the good of souls. It was conspicuous in her general 
demeanour, that she had Christ put on. Too much cannot 
be said in praise of her excellent spirit, zealous concern for 
the salvation of souls, and constant aim to glorify God in 
her life, and conduct. But lest any one should think I had 
magnified her character beyond its bounds, I conclude b 
saying, let me die her death, and let my last end be like hers.

MRS. MARY PRIDEAUX, 


Mrs. MARY PRIDEAUX. 


(From Piety Promoted.) 


‘Mary Pridéaux, wife of William Prideaux, of the 
County of Cornwall, was a pattern of meekness and piety ; 
and as she grew in years, she grew in grace, and the know- 
ledge of our Lord Jesus Christ; and had a part of the 
ministry committed to her, in which she was a faithful 
steward, and a bright example to others, not being forward 
to appear in ministry, as well knowing that true silence 
never shames the gospel ; but when under the constraining 


power of truth, her ministry was with the demonstration of 


the spirit, and with power, greatly to the refreshment and 
strength of the honest hearted ; and when she felt the draw- 
ings of truth, she was ready to leave her near connections 
in life. She visited some parts of the west when her name 
was Mary Davies; and after her marriage several times, 
and not long before the close of her life, she found a con- 
cern to visit some of the midland counties, which service 
seemed near to accomplish her day’s work, having soon 
after her return, publicly to declare, happy would it be for 
all in the conclusion of their time, to have to say with the 
apostle, “ I have fought the good fight, I have finished my 
course, I have kept the faith, henceforth is laid up for me 
the crown of righteousness, which the Lord the righteous 
judge, shall give me at that day ; and not to meonly, but to 
all those also that love his appearing.” 


A short time after, she was taken ill with a fever, 
which continued about four weeks, during which she 


264 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


behaved with patience, meekness, and yet with christian 
fortitude ; and many heavenly expressions dropt from her, 
at a meeting in her own house. She had to commemorate 
the goodness of the Lord, to all those who put their trust in 
him, and humbly petitioned, that he would be with them to 
the end; that they that lived in his fear, might die in his 
favour ; requesting his protection in every trying season; 
with fervent desire that all who were present might know 
a thorough resignation of will; for the Lord our God 
requires obedience from all his servants; and the same 
evening she signified, that she thought her time was near 
a conclusion. Some days after she said, ‘humility is 
a qualification I desire my children may be endued with ;” 
and signified to them her hope, that her advice in times 
past might be remembered, saying, ‘I hope it may be as 
bread cast on the waters that may return after many days ; 
I have endeavoured to do my duty by you.? Her dis- 
order increased, she desired she might endeavour to bear 
it; and that those in health would improve their time, 
whilst health and strength were afforded, saying, “ I cando 
but little now ; it would indeed be bad if L had my peace to 
make with the Lord; I had dedicated my health and 
strength to his service, according to my ability.” Finding 
herself growing weaker, she desired that her family might 
be resigned. to the will of Providence, adding, that she 
enjoyed great peace and tranquillity. of mind, for which she 
was. thankful; and further added, “< Oh, this is favour 
indeed, to enjoy such tranquillity !. All seems serene, and 
the streams of life flow. freely,.the river. seems clear as 
crystal! Oh, that none may put of repentance till con- 
fined to a sick bed!” On seeing one of her daughters 
she said, ‘« Oh! be good, be good and fear the Lord my 
dear child ;”’ and again said, ‘4 Then. shall ye know, if 
you follow on to know the Lord, his going forth to be 
as the morning, he shall come unto. us as the rain, as 
the latter and former. rains upon the earth. O4 the 
cunning foxes have holes and lodging places, but the 
dear Son of God hath not where to lay his head. 
Lamentable indeed, where, where this is the case.”

OF the Ann Mercy Bell, of the city of York, was born in 
$, but the London. She had her education in Friend’s school, and 
his had I workhouse, being admitted soon after its establishment, and 
case,” she afterwards continued there as a schoolmistress for 


many years. Being early favoured with divine visitations, 
She was not only preserved from the gross pollutions of the 


266 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


world; but was in a good degree, enabled to renounce 
vain. and youthful pleasures and amusements, which 
she frequently expressed with humble thankfulness and 
gratitude. 


In the year 1731, she married Nathaniel Bell, of 
York, and became a member of that meeting. and while 
in a private capacity, was well,esteemed asa friend of cir- 
cumspect life and conversation, a pattern of plainness, and 
therein, as well as in other respects, a good example. 
At length, steadily adhering to the divine teacher in her 
heart, and under the influence of the spirit of truth, she 
had, from a well grounded experience, to declare to others 
the way of life and salvation. In this service she faith- 
fully laboured, according to ability received, at home and 
in adjacent parts; and in the course thereof, found drawings, 
in the love of the gospel, to visit various other parts of 
this nation; also, when engaged in family visits, she found 
it her concern not to overlook those, who by misconduct 
had incurred the censure of friends. 


Her labours were not confined to those of the Society 
of Friends, but in the course of her travels, she had com- 
passionately to call and direct people of other denominatons, 
to the unweary teacher in themselves; and had meetings 
among them in divers places where no Friends were 
settled. 


In the year 1753, she found a concern to visit Friends 
in London; and during her stay in that city, under the 
influence of love to mankind, had to exhort the inhabitants 
thereof, in the streets, markets, and many places in and 
about London, Westminster, and Southwark ; calling them 
to repentance and amendment of life. In this service she 
was signally furnished with ability to labour, to the ten- 
dering many of their minds, and acknowledgment of her 
good will to them; and such was the ardour of her mind, 
and the flowing forth of love to them, that she frequently 
preached three or four times a day, in different parts. On 
her return home she had to acknowledge that she was

Mrs. ELIZABETH HOLME. 


(From Piety Promoted.) 


Elizabeth Holme, of Newcastle upon Tyne, was the 
daughter of Anthony and Dorothy Wilson, and born at 
Highway, near Hawkshead, in Lancashire. She was favoured 
with a religious education, and ia her youth her mind was 
impressed with the fear of God. She was often drawn into 

“retirement, and a watchful state of mind, thus she attained 

“a growth in religious experience, and about the 34th year 

‘of her age, was concerned to bear testimony to the efficacy 
PATS 


268 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


of that divine principle which she herself had felt ; in which 
service she grew, and in company with Lydia Lancaster, 
visited the meetings of Friends in Ireland and Scotland. 


After her marriage with Reginald Holme, she visited 
various parts of this nation; and in her station of a wife, 
she conducted herself with prudence and propriety; and 
being preserved in watchfulness, suffered not her temporal 
concerns to hinder her services in the church. -Her last 
illness was short, scarcely ten days, most of which time she 
kept her bed, appearing to be under great bodily weakness, 
ha not much pain, and bright in her understanding to 
the last. 


To a friend who came to see her, at parting, she said, 
“remember me affectionately to thy husband, and Jet him 
remember me when he draws near the throne of grace that 
I may pass through the valley of the shadow of death, and 


be enabled to put of the robe of mortality and put on — 


immortality, full of glory; and, I trust, to enjoy a part of 
that portion that is laid up for the faithful ; for such I have 
endeavoured to be, according to the ability given; I have 
nothing stands before me. Ido not clearly see this in the 
finishing stroke, but every stroke draws nearer and nearer ; 
but in this I have no will, but stand ready, and in patience 
wait till his own time.” 


Her daughter sitting by her, she said, “Oh, sweet 
peace, what an enjoyment it is in this weakness; I have 
discharged my duty to God and his people in this place. 


A near friend called to see her, he said, “thou hast 
laboured faithfully amongst us, and we shall have a great 
want of thy company.” She said, ‘‘ I have so; I hope it 
may be as bread cast on the waters, that may arise many 
days hence.’”? At another time she said, “ I thought I had 
been going, but it seems as ifthe people held me, not so 
willing to let nie go as Lam myself. Oh, that every link 
of this chain was broke, that I might lie down in peace 
for evermore.” .

The morning before she died, being 5th day, her 
daughter sitting by her she said, “I may say with king 
Hezekiah, the hand of the Lord is upon me, I am waiting for 
my change.” And after asking, ‘‘is thy husband gone to 
meeting ’” she added, ‘* I wish it may be-a refreshing sea- 
son to him, and all the living members assembled this day, 
with whom my spirit unites, and craves the canopy of 
divine love may overshadow their minds, and strengthen 
them for the works’ sake.” After a pause, she said to her 
daughter, “my dear, thy company is precious to me in this 
affliction, and thy husband, which I dearly love. O Lord, 
let us taste of thy goodness, that we may be refreshed. 


She quietly departed this life the 9th of the 2nd mo. 


1781, and was interred on the the 12th, in Friends’ burial 
ground in Newcastle; aged near 78, a minister 44 years.

family, and being only in low circumstances, she firml

service; and for change of air, she went into her native 
county, which gave her an opportunity of visiting her near

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


Mis MARY GURNEY. 


(From Piety Promoted) 


Mary Gurney, of Norwich, was the daughter of Edmund 
and Mary Gurney of that city; Friends well esteemed, and 
religiously concerned to educate their children in the way 
of truth ; and their care herein was the means of her being, 
in a good degree, preserved from the vanities of the world, 
in the time of her youth. 


About the 33rd year of her age she was favoured with 
a close, humbling visitation of divine love, under which 
she was concerned to bear testimony thereto, by way of 
public ministry, in which, Friends had unity with her; 
and though she did not travel much abroad, she visited some 
of the meetings in her own, and some adjacent counties. 
But in the year 1788, she visited the meetings of Friends 
in Bristol, Worcestershire, and divers other places, in which 
her public ministry, and religious services in Friends families 
where her lot was cast, were to the comfort and satisfaction 
of many. 


In the close of her visit, she staid a short time in 
London, and attended some meeting there; and having 
visited the week-day meeting, at Plaistow, and had accept- 
able service therein, she was soon after taken ill; and was 
conveyed to the house of Joseph Cockfield, at Upton, where 
her indisposition rapidly increased, she said that she hoped 
she should be favoured with patience to bear itall. The 
following day, her disorder continued to gain ground, anda 
person being present saying she might still live to do further

Mrs. SARAH BROWN. 


The following Sketch is taken from a Collection of 
Testimonies concerning several ministers of the gospel, 
amongst the people called Quakers, ip 


« Some account of Sarah Brown, of Pickering, with 
some acount of her dying sayings, as near as can be remem- 
bered ; from the monthly meeting of Malton, in Yorkshire, 


She was carefully educated by her parents in the 
principles of truth; and when very young, she fell under a 
concern of heart, that she might come to be acquainted with 
the Lord for herself ; and in order thereto, as she in the time 
of her last illness declared, she was made willing to seek out 
private places to pour forth her supplications to the Lord; 
beseeching him, to make the way of truth more fully known 
to her ; and also to enable her to walk therein ; which concern 
he was pleased to regard, in his own time, to his praise, and 
to her growth and encouragement in the truth, for about the 
22nd year of her age, a part in the ministry was committed to 
her, which became a very close concern upon her,jbeing such 
a cross, that she said, she had rather have parted with her 
natural life; but could find no peace without answering the 
Lord’s requirings ; and therefore she resolved, thr ough his 
divine assistance, to be obedient unto him, though all sorts 

of people might hiss at her. 


She travelled in the service of the ministry, in this and 
several of the neighbouring counties, and was well received, 
she being of a grave, modest and exemplary behaviour, as 
became her vocation, and our holy profession ; and the Lord

MRS. SARAH BROWN. 277 


was pleased to favour her with christian courage to the last ; 
for in the time of her late illness, she signified, that she 
had freely given up herself, and all that was near to her to 
the Lord; and in great sweetness of spirit, very frequently 
expressed her earnest desire for the preservation of her 
husband and children in the truth. She often bewailed the 
loose professors of our own society, and also the blindness 
and profanity of many in other professions, expressing her 
desire for the good of all people ; and said that she had no 
cause to distrust the Lord, for he had been wonderfully kina. 
And near her end she had many sick fits, yet often broke 
forth in great sweetness saying, ‘glory be to the eternal God, 
whom she felt to be near to her in that the time of her great 
affliction of body.’ 


About an hour before her departure, she seemed to 
have a hard struggle with death and spake not much more 
to us; buta few minutes before she drew her last breath, 
she appeared easy, and very sweetly cried out, ‘ glory be to 


the eternal God!’ And so long as she could speak, in 


sweetness of spirit, gave glory to God. And although she 
hath finished her course in this world, her memory is sweet 
to us that are left behind, 


She died the 18th of the 4th mo. 1729, in the 33rd 
year of her age, and was buried at Pickering aforesaid.

« This our dear friend was born at Warterstow, in they 
county of West Meath, in the year 1694; the names of her: 
parents were Jacob and Jane Fuller, who being honest and: 
religious persons, carefully educated their children in thes 
way of truth; and she was dutiful to them to the end of 
their days. . 


Andas she grew in years, she had religious inclinations, . 
and thereby came sensibly to know the want of an inward $ 
acquaintance with the Lord in spirit, which education of 
itself could not give her. Thus the Lord began to prepare: 
her, by his word and power in her heart, for future service. 
And her love increasing in the pure holy fear, she was! 
preserved out of the vanity and folly, which too much’ 
abound in somé of the youth of our day. She loved! 
retirement, and often, with a tender, humble and broken » 
spirit, waited for a further manifestation of the pure, holy) 
principle of light and grace, and in those inward exercises ' 
she frequently witnessed the comfort of divine love. .

Wilson, who frequently gave her up tc answer such services 
as were required of her; and as she by faithfulness had obtain- 
ed to a good degree of advancement in the truth, she was not 
hasty, nor forward to offer her gift, but waited in the pure 
silence, to be endued with power from on high, which is 


the true qualification of all whoare called into that weighty 


work of the ministry; whereby she became skilful in divid- 
ing the word suitably tothe states of the people. And 
although she seldom appeared large in testimony at home, 
yet when she did appear, what she delivered was sound 


and weighty, often being as glad tidings of life and salvation 


by Jesus Christ, to the true mourners in Zion, and consola- 
tion to the needy soul. This seemed to be her particular 
gift; yet at times, the power and dread that she appeared 
in, did strike at the very root and mystery of iniquity, that 


“works, and too much prevails in the children of disobedience; 
hating the appearance of evil in any, but greatly concerned 


that peace and unity might be maintained amongst Friends, 
and that the ancient testimony and discipline, settled 


amongst us, might be kept up ; and was serviceable therein, 
through her zeal for the prosperity of truth. 


She was a diligent attender of meetings, when at home ; 
also our quarterly and national meetings. She sometimes 
visited Friends both in the north and south of this nation ; 
and also in company with our dear friend Elizabeth Pease, 
visited Friends in Scotland, and some parts of the North of 
England. And inthe 7th mo. 1729, she with her dear 
companion Jane Gee, having had a concern upon their 
minds for some time to visit Friends in Wales and some 
parts of England, in full unity they left us. And fora 
further account of her labours and service in that country 
we refer to the following postscript, wrote by her compa- 
nion ; and have ground for hope, that she is entered into 
that rest prepared for the righteous. She was a minister 
about 1] years.”

MRS. DEBORAH WARDELL. 


Mr. DEBORAH WARDELL. 


A testimony from the e's meeting of Newcastle 
upon Tyne, concerning Deborah Wardell. 


There remains in our hearts a short testimony to give 

for our dear friend and sister, Deborah Wardell, who died 

iin the 70th year of her age. She was even like a shock of 

i corn fully ripe, gathered in its due season, and we doubt 

i not but the Lord has received her soul into the mansions of 

i glory, where the wicked cease from troubling, and the 
faithful are at rest. ; 


Her ministry was very lively ; she was sound in word 
and doctrine, and very edifying; preaching the coming of 
our Lord Jesus Christin his spiritual appearance ; frequently 
opening the scriptures and the mysteries of life and salvation ; 
with fervent exhortations to serve the Lord in righteousness 
and true holiness. 


Her christianity did shew itself by her meet and 
peaceable spirit. She was many times fervent in prayer 
to the Lord, for the rising generation, that they might come 
up in the places of the faithful who are gone before. 


In the time of her last illness, which continued above 
three months, she oftentimes was in a sweet frame of mind 
and frequently used to say the thoughts of death were no 
terror to her; but was entirely resigned to the will of the 
Lord; and often expressed the hope she had in her 
latter end.

Two days before she died, wna a very sick fit, upon 
her being a little recovered of it, she desired to see her 
children, and expressed herself to them after this manner ; 
I did not think I should have been alive till now. I hope 
it will bea happy hour for me. I pray God bless you in all 
your undertakings, and that he may be with you, as he has 
been with me, to the end of your days. 


Lancelot Wardell’s testimony concerning his dear 
departed wife, Deborah Wardell, who died the 7th of the 
10th mo. 1732. 


She was descended from honourable parents, viz. John - 
and Margaret Walton, of Bishop-Aukland, who were early 
convinced, in the morning of the day, wherein truth was — 
published by George Fox and others. They kept an open 
door for travellers who were sent abroad in the service of 
truth, to promote the gospel of our Lord and Saviour Jesus 
Christ; as, since their death, did most of their children ; 
who are all gone to their rest, as shocks of corn gatheredin 
due season, of which she was the last. 


She was a true yoke-fellow, an affectionate wife, a 
tender mother, and a faithful labourer in the vineyard of 
the Lord ; and where her lot was cast, of good service both 
as to her ministry and in meetings of business ; having been 
an approved mother in our spiritual Israel, for her care, 
conduct, and advice. 


Some years since, being visited with sickness, she ~ 
ordered her children to be brought, into her chamber; at 


which time, it-was her concern to admonish them to be — 


faithful to the Lord’s requirings, that they might obtain a 
crown of life. In order thereto, she said her desire 
was, that they might live in the fear of the Lord, and keep 
near to his preserving power, that they might witness his 
peace, when tlie time of dissolution came; which would — 


be of more value to them than all the world; for what 


would all the world signify to her now, if she wanted that ? 
“If this be the time of my dissolution,” said she, “I am

MRS. JANE GEE. 283 


not afraid to pass through the vale of death, being fully

Mrs. JANE GEE. 


A testimony from the national half-years’ meeting, in 
Dublin, concerning Jane Gee. 


She was descended from honest parents, and religiously 
inclined in her young years; of a free and affable disposi- 
tion, courteous and solid deportment, and often expressed 
the satisfaction she had in the company and conversation of 
honest friends. 


In the year 1714, she joined in’ marriage with our 
friend John Gee; was a tender and affectionate wife, 
charitable to the poor, and by her prudent and religious 
conduct gained a good report. à

In or about the year 1721, she received a gift in the 
ministry, which, through the cross, she gave up to; having 
first known, in a good measure, the work and power of 
truth in her own heart, to sanctify, fit, and prepare her for 
service ; and having the prosperity of truth in view, she 
joined with Friends in several services of the Church, being 
gifted also for the discipline thereof, particularly for that of 
visiting families ; wherein she was well accepted. She 


frequently recommended inward retirement, to wait upon 
the Lord. 


She was diligent in attending meetings for worship, 
and, when of ability, travelled through various parts of this 
nation in the service of truth. In the year 1729, having a 
concern to visit the meetings of Friends in Wales, and some 
parts of England, she went, with the concurrence of her 
friends here, in company with her dear friend and compa- 
nion Elizabeth Wilson. They travelled through Wales, 
and divers parts of England; and on her return at Man- 
chester, her dear companion was removed from her by 
death, which sorrowfully affected her; yet she patiently 
submitted to the Lord’s will; and soon after returned 
home, to the comfort and satisfaction of her husband 
and friends. 


She afterwards visited most, or all the meetings of 
Friends in this nation, Her mild and innocent conversation 
and deportment, corresponded with the doctrine she 
preached, and engaged Friends’ love greatly, self being of no 
reputation with her. t 


The indisposition of body which occasioned her death, 
was of long continuance, and attended with great pains at 
times, which she bore patiently, and seemed resigned to 
the will of God, whether to live or die. And as she 
drew near her conclusion, was frequent and fervent in 
prayer and praises to the Lord. under a sense of his gracious 
and merciful dealings with her.

MRS. ELIZABETH RAWLINSON 285 


visit her, she sat up in bed, though very weak, and in a 
fresh and lively sense of divine favour, expressed her sat-

sensible to the last; and we doubt not is entered into that 
eternal rest which is prepared for the righteous.

MISS ANN CARR. 287 


- Our dear friend Elizabeth Rawlinson, before mentioned, 
was in a wonderful manner filled with inward strength and 
comfort, and brake forth saying, “death is no terror to me. 
It is no. surprise to me. My heart is full of the joy of 
God’s salvation ; yea, full of the comforts of the Holy 
Ghost. _ The Lord visited my soul when I was very young, 
preparing me for that work which he shewed me was to be 
required at my hand ; telling me if I was faithful I should 
be a mouth for him, and now I can say come Lord Jesus, 
thy servant isiready. I have fought the good fight of faith, 
I have finished my course, my day’s work is done; hence- 
forth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness; yea, 
I feel it sure to me. Oh! the height and length and 
breadth of the comfort and joy that flows in my soul! My 
tongue is too short to set forth one half of the goodness of 
my God,” 


Mis ANN CARR. 


The subject of this short Sketch, is a person well 
known in this part of the country, and I am persuaded from 
my own personal acquaintance with her, and from all, I 
have heard from those who have a more intimate knowledge 
of her, that she is distinguished for piety, zeal, and useful- 
ness ; and is generally respected. Indeed wherever there 
is genuine piety, and intimate fellowship with the divine 
being, such persons must be known in order to be valued 
and loved. And the more intimately we are acquainted 
with such, the more highly we appreciate their excellencies, 
and value their worth. 


When men and women are converted to Gad, and are

spared to evidence their change of heart by a suitable 
conduct for a length of time; they become eminent in the 
church of God,—their praise is in the whole church, perhaps 
in many churches. And not only so, but they have a good 
character in the esteem of those that are without; at least 
they have a character for sincerity, honesty, integrity, 


industry, and faithfulness; so that even wicked people 


sometimes have them in reverence, and although while in 
health and strength they may at times slander the pious, yet 
in this they frequently speak contrary to their better judg- 
ment, and against the remonstrances of their own conscience, 
and that merely to countenance themselves in a course of 
wickedness and sin, and as a proof of this, if sickness seizes 
them, and death and eternity stare them in the face, they 
will send for such to talk to them, and pray with them. 
« They that honour me,” saith God, “I will honour.” 


This eminent female was born in the neighbourhood of 
Market Raisin, in the county of Lincoln, about the year 
1781. She was converted to God when about 17 or 18 
years of age, under the ministry of the Methodist preachers. 
The writer of this short account then travelled in Grimsby 
circuit, which then included what is now called Market 
Raisin circuit. During my stay in that neighbourhood, 
Ann Carr was deeply awakened to a sense of her guilt aad 
danger as a sinner before God; she returned to the Lord 
with penitential sorrow, and a broken heart. In this state 
of mind she united with the people of God. {gave her, 


her first society ticket. She soon found the Lord was- 


« merciful and gracious, long suffering and abundant in 
goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving 
iniquity transgression and sin.” No sooner had she 
obtained mercy and forgiveness at the hand of God, but she 
proclaimed the loving kindness of God in the language of 


the psalmist, “ come hither all ye that fear the Lord and T 


will tell you what he hath done for my soul.” To God her 
heart and mouth were filled with increasing praise and 
thanksgiving, ‘‘O Lord I will praise thee, though thou wast 
angry with me thine anger is turned away, and now thou 
comfortest me,” ‘Thou hast brought me up also out of

MISS ANN CARR 289 


an horrible pit, and out of the miry clay, and hast set my 
foot upon a rock and hast established my goings, and hast 
put a new song into my mouth, even of praise and thanks- 
giving to God; many shall see it and fear and trust in the 
Lord.” And indeed many did see it, and feared, and 
trusted in the Lord. Many saw by signs following the 
grace of God that was in her, and many wicked persons 
began to think if Ann Carr is right I am wrong, if she is in 
the way to heaven I am in the way to hell; these slavish 
tormenting fears, in some, wrought conviction for sin, and 
extorted the inquiry ‘* what must I do to be saved ;” being 
encouraged, they also began to trust in the Lord. So that 
the Lord having planted her in his vineyard, employed her 
as a labourer, and succeeded her labours with his blessing. 
Many thought highly of her piety, and admired her zeal ; 
but not all! Some thought her too obstrusive, talkative, 
and zealous. The former of these encouraged her in all 
her efforts to do good, but had she been influenced by the 
conduct and conversation of the latter, the exercise of those 
talents which the great head of the church had committed 
to her for public usefulness, would have been perverted, and 
rendered a curse instead of a blessing.—In the midst of 
conflicting passions and varied sentiments, she however 
kept close to her divine teacher, and were enabled by the 
constant exercise of faith, watchfulness, and prayer, to keep 
up an uninterrupted intercourse with the divine being, 
through the eternal spirit. 


She thought if God be for me, no matter who is 
against me. If he requires and approves of my efforts to do 
ood, it is better to obey God rather than man. Of the 
first of these she was fully assured by the peace and happi- 
ness which she felt in her own soul, and by the effects 
produced upon others. Her public labours were increased, 
the field opened wider and wider, and this without any 
efforts of her own ; so that she could not attend to the 
invitations and appointments which she received, without 
giving herself wholly up to the work of the Lord. This 
was contrary to her design. Indeed if she could have 
maintained her confidence in God, and enjoyed peace with 


290 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


him, she would have declined all publicity; but being 
persuaded that necessity was laid upon her, to publish 
salvation by Jesus Christ, she so far obeyed as to do this 
occasionally, and in the neighbourhood where she lived. 


Some time after this, she thought it her imperious 
duty to give herself more fully to the Lord and to his work. 


She has preached the unsearchable riches of Christ, 
through a great part of Lincolnshire, Yorkshire, Notting- 
hamshire, Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Cleveland, and 
Durham, and if I am correctly informed, the Lord has 
given her many souls wherever she has laboured. A very 
valuable correspondent in the Methodist Connexion speaking 
of Ann Carr, says, ‘‘ her labours and usefulness have been 
very extensive. From my knowledge of her for 
six or eight years, I can indeed say, I never knew 
a more consistent character; too much cannot be 
said of her usefulness.” She now resides chiefly in Leeds, 
with Martha Williams and * some others, and visits in 
regular rotation with her companions, a number of villages 
which forms a kind of circuit. They have in connection 
with them several other preachers, both male and female, 
and also a good chapel in that part of Leeds called Leylands, 
which will probably contain six or seven hundred persons, 
and which I understand is well attended. They have also 
a chapel at Brewery Field, Holbeck, and have about 18 or 
20 preachers and exhorters, whose names and appointments 
are printed on a regular plan, entitled <“ A Sabbath-day 
Pian, for the Female Revivalist Preachers in the Leeds 
Cireuit.’” They have also their regular quarterly meetings, 
and other meetings for worship and discipline, similar to 
those of the Wesleyan Connexion. The Lord is carrying 
on a gracious work among them Many sinners, and not 
a few of the basest kiad, have been deeply awakened to a 
sense of their sin and danger, and have been enabled to 
evidence by their subsequent conduct, that they were brought

Mrs. CATHERINE PHILLIPS. 


This greatly gifted and eminently holy and useful 
woman, appears to have been one of the most celebrated 
female preachers ever raised up among the Friends, or 
people called Quakers. Very early in life she was favoured 
with very peculiar and extraordinary manifestations of 
divine grace and mercy, by which she was fitted and quali- 
fied to move in that extensive field of labour and usefulness 
to which she appears to have been called by divine provi- 
dence. About the age of 16 she became a decided 
character ; being fully convinced that no exterior, whether 
of dress, language, or deportment would answer the purposes 
of divine mercy in the redemption of man, or secure the 
peace, and safety of the soul; that nothing but a change of 
heart, and personal holiness would be of any avail in a 
dying hour, and at the awful day of final discrimination 
and decision. She therefore sought and obtained the ines- 


timable treasure of salvation. 


About the age of 22 she entered upon the great and 
2c 


292 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


important work of calling sinners to repentance, a work to 
which she believed herself ‘moved by the Holy Ghost,” and 
continued in it till within a short period of the time when the 
‘< weary wheels of life stood still,” which was at the age of 
68. During which period she travelled through the greatest 
part of England, Ireland, Wales, Scotland, Holland, and 
many parts of the vast continent of America. Her maiden 
name was Payton. She entered into the marriage state 
when about 44 years of age, with a person to whom her 
early ministry was rendered of especial profit; and there 
is something very interesting in the providential occurrences 
which brought them together, and something very much to 
admire in the manner in which they conducted themselves 
towards each other. 


Her praise seems to have been in all the churches in 
connexion with the people with whom she was united. A 
large octavo volume, containing near 400 pages, chiefly 
written by her own hand, has since her decease been pub- 
lished, from which a few extracts will be made. 


‘* As the dealings of the Almighty with me from my 
youth have been singular, and are worthy to be retained in 
remembrance with thankfulness, I have committed to 
writing some remarkable circumstances of my life; tending 
to awaken future thanksgiving and watchfulness in myself 
ind, considering how wonderfully the divine arm has been 
manifested for my help, to encourage me to a steady trust 
therein, and perseverence in submission thereto; and in 
order to leave to my surviving relations some memorials of 
the various exercises and dangers which I have passed 
through, and of the merciful support and preservation 
vouchsafed from the Lord therein. 


I cannot date the first dawn of divine light upon my 
soul; for with humble thankfulness I may. say, that early in 
the morning of life I knew the Lord to be a God nigh at 
hand; convincing of evil, and raising breathings after the 
saving knowledge of his divine love and power. Friends

MRS. CATHERINE PHILLIPS. 


house. I loved their company when but very young, and

I could read well when very young, and spending 
much time with my afflicted father, I read much to him ; 
and the experience and sufferings of faithful martyrs, and of

being often tendered thereby, and my love of virtue and 
piety strengthened. But even in my childhood I experi- 
enced many conflicts, and my convictions for evil were 
strong; so that at times my heart was sorrowful, and my 
pillow watered with my tears, although my countenance 
and deportment were mostly cheerful. Once having 
yielded to temptation, my sense of guilt was such, that I 
concluded I had sinned against the Holy Ghost; and that, 
agreeable to Christ’s testimony, I‘ should never be forgiven.’ 
This so affected my tender mind with sorrow and unutter~ 
able distress, that it could not be entirely concealed from 
the family ; although I was enabled, even in childhood, to 
keep my exercises of mind much to myself. I think I must 
have been eight or nine years of age when it was thus 
with me. . 


My natural disposition was very volatile, my appre- 
hension quick; and as my faculties opened, I delighted 
much in books of a very contrary nature and tendency to 
those which had engaged my attention in my childhood. [ 
also read history, was fond of poetry, and had a taste for 
philosophy; so that I wasin the way to embellish my 
understanding, (as is the common phrase,) and become 
accomplished to shine in conversation. But the Lord in 
his wisdom more fully opened my understanding, I saw that 
I must desist from these amusing publications and studies, 
and pursue the one necessary business, viz. working out the 
salvation of my immortal soul. My wanderings from the 
chief shepherd of Israel, were brought to my remembrance, 
and my sins set in order before me; which wrought great 
humiliation and brokenness of heart, with strong ‘cries to 


294 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 

him, that he would graciously pass by my transgressions, 
and receive me into covenant with himself. And although 
this dispensation was not agreeable to degenerate nature, 
which, like Adam when he had transgressed, seeks to evade 
the condemnation ; yet, because of the glory which I was 
favoured to discover beyond it, and the divine love which I 
saw therein, I said, in the secret of my soul, ‘it is good for 
me to be under it; and I was made willing patiently to 
abide the judgments of the Lord for sin, in order that I 
might witness remission thereof through the baptism of 
repentance, and the sanctifying life or spirit of his Son Jesus 
Christ. And this mercy, in the appointed season of infinite 
wisdom, I experienced; so that my transgressions were 
blotted out of the book of remembrance. 


* * *& © 


The adversary here transformed himself as into an 
angel of light, and, under the specious appearance of righ- 
teousness, represented the way, so strait, that it was 
impossible to walk therein and act as a rational being ; 


thereby endeavouring to‘discourage me, or prevent my. 


attaining to the true gospel liberty in the use of the 
creatures ; some of those religious principles which I had 
received by education, were called in question ; and I was 
left without any foundation in certainty respecting them ; 
nor could I attain to it by the testimony of others or the 
writings of such as had vindicated them to the world ; being 
to receive my convincement of them, from the deep ground 
of divine revelation. All which I have seen was necessary 
to fit me for the service which was appointed me; that the 
foundation of my faith might be laid in certainty, and that 
I might be able to testify with boldness, that I had experi- 
enced what I asserted to be the truth; and be also suitably 
qualified to sympathize with, and minister to such as were in 
the like states. I saw early for what station I was designed 
in Christ’s church. 


Having now entered the lists of public combatants in 
the Lamb’s army, I pretty soon became concerned to travel

for the promotion of truth and righteousness; and for more 
than twenty years, had but little intermission from gospel

In the 5 mo. 1749. I left home, in order to visit some 
part of Wales; in which journey my dear friend Lucy 
Bradely was made willing to accompany me, with whom I 
travelled in sweet unity.—In this journey the principal, 
share of public service fell to my lot; wherein the Lord 
was evidently with me, strengthening for the work of 
the day, to the honour of his own name. And I had 
ground to hope that our labour was not entirely in vain ; 
some persons being powerfully affected, who, I hope, long 
retained a sense of that visitation; particularly William 
Phillips * from Cornwall, who was then upon a visit to 
his relations at Swansea.. 


A concern for the west continuing and increasing,—l 
sought for a companion, but could hear of none suitable. 
This added to my exercise ; for it seemed very dangerous 
for such a child as I, to travel alone ; but after waiting as 
jong as I durst, I laid my concern before Friends of our 
monthly meeting, and requested their certificate, + but told 
them that I knew of no companion ; and if they had not been 
free to let me go alone, I believe I should have been easy 
to have waited longer; but they gave me a certificate ; and 
in the 11 mo. 1749, I left home in great humility and fear. 
I proceeded to Bristol, and from thence, through part of 
the counties of Wilts, Somerset, Dorset, and Devon, to 
Penzance in Cornwall. And although I went from home 
alone, I was not much without a suitable companion, the 
Almighty putting it into the heart of one or other of his

I visited the meetings of Friends pretty generally, some 
of which were attended by many people of other societies ; 
before whom the Lord gave me boldness to testify of his 
truth with good authority, and to lay open the false and 
dangerous opinions of some professing christians, partieu- 
larly that of unconditional election and reprobation ; which 
dark principle was then likely to gain ground in these 
parts. 


The Bristol quarterly meeting ended satisfactorily, many 
valuable ministers attended it, and the testimony of truth 
was measurably exalted, It had pleased the Lordin the several 
times I had been in this city, to favour me with consider- 
able liberty in the exercise of my gift, whereby a door was 
opened to me in the minds of Friends there ; which favour 
I hope I receive with due thankfulness. I proceeded to 
London, attending several meetings in the way, appointed 
by Rachel Wilson; at one of which we met with our 
valuable friend Daniel Stanton, from America, with whom 
we went in Company to London; where we were affection- 
ately received by many Friends, and I had good ground to 
believe my coming to that city, was in the will and wisdom 
of the Almighty, though greatly contrary to my own.”

Colonies; and many friends have given up large posses-

* The reader may form some idea of the condition of negroes 
in Lousiana by the following regulations. 
CITY COUNCIL OF NEW ORLFANS. 
“An ordinance in relation to Slaves in the city and suburbs 
of New Orleans, as also in the Neighbourhood thereof, and to no 
other person herein mentioned.—The Council ordains as follows : 


Art. I. No Slave or Slaves shall have, hold, occupy, reside, 
or sleep in any house, out-houses, building, or inclosure, other 
than his or her owner’s representatives, or of the person whom 
he is or they are serving for hire, without first obtaining a ticket 
or tickets from his, her, or their owner or owners, and every slave 
without permission shall be committed to gaol by any officer of 
police, or any other white person, those to receive twenty lashes, &c. 


Art. VI. The assembly of slaves for the purpose of dancing 
or other merriments, shall take place only on Sundays, and solely 
in such open or public places as shall be appointed by the mayor; 
and no such assembly shall continue later than sunset, &c.—And 
all slaves offending against this statue shall be imprisoned and 
receive from 10 to 25 lashes. 


Art. VII. No person giving a ball to free people of colour 
shall on any pretext admit or suffer to be admitted to said ball 
any slave, on penalty of a fine from 10 to 50 dollars; and any 
slave admitted to any such ball shall receive 15 lashes. 


ArT. VIII. Every slave, except such as may be blind or infirm 
who shall walk in any street or open place with a cane, club, or 
other stick, shall be carried to the police goal where he shall 
receive 25 lashes, and shall moreover forfeit every such cane  &ce. 
to any white person seizing the same. 


Art. IX. If any slave shall be guilty of whooping or hallooing

The 20th, we left Peedee River, accompanied by John 
and Charles Moreman, and the two friends who came with 
us from the Wateree. We rode that day about 40 miles 
through the woods, without seeing any house ; and at night 
took up our lodging in the woods, by the side of a swamp, 
which afforded plenty of canes for our horses. Our friends 
made us a little shed of the branches of pine-trees, on a 
rising sandy ground, which abounded with lofty pines. 
We made a large fire, and it being a calm, fair moon-light 
night, we spent it cheerfully, though we slept but little. 
Our saddles were our pillows. In the morning we pursued 
our journey about 45 miles; and at night took up our

What a disgrace to the republic of America that with all its 
boasted freedom and equal rights, that out of 20 states there 
are ll in which slavery is a part of their political constitution, 
and that in those states in which it is not allowed, the conditions 
of blacks and coloured persons are in a condition but little 
removed from slavery. New York for instance is called a free 
state, yet even here white people will not worship God in the same 
place, nor will they so much as have their hair cut, or be shaved 
by the same person who performs these offices for the blacks. And 
in the public papers both men and women are frequently advertised 
for sale, or to be let out for hire. Whata noble pattern have the 
Friends in America set to other religious bodies in that country; 
may they make haste and delay not to follow their example. Ep.

_ The 7th we set out for Carvers Creek, a journey of 
about 160 miles, through an almost uninhabited country. 
At one place where we lodged, the room wherein we lay 
was exposed to the weather on almost every side, and it 
being a wet night, the rain beat in upon us in bed; but my 
mind was preserved in sweet peace, under a sense of divine 
favour. Another night we lay in the woods with tolerable 
comfort, though the weather was cold, and the ground 
damp. About two hours before we stopped, as I was 
attempting to cross a swamp I fell into it, although I 
mounted my horse immediately after putting ona dry pair 
of stockings, rode in my wet clothes, and lay down in them, 
I was preserved from taking cold. In the night two of our 
horses * strayed away from us, and our guides were obliged 
to leave us and go in quest of them; so that we were 
several hours by ourselves in this wilderness, surrounded, for 
ought we knew, by bears, wolves, and panthers. Before 
we pitched our tent, I had been intimidated by an account 
which had been given me respecting the panthers infesting 
that quarter ; one of which it was said had killed a person, 
not very far distant from this spot ; but when we were thus left 
all fear was removed, and we spent the time of our friends’ 
absence cheerfully. Į went without the shelter of our shed, 
and renewed our fire with some wood our friends had 
gathered. The fire, under Providence, was probably our 
preservation from those ferocious animals. It was a fine 
moon-light night, our friends tracked our horses’ footsteps 
in the sand for about three miles in the way we had come, 
and found them feeding on some luxuriant canes. As we 
proceeded on our journey, some of our company discovered 
the tract of a wild beast in the sand, which gave room to

We breakfasted at a miserable inn, about 8 miles on 
our way; where we met such a wicked set of company, who 
had spent the night there, that we concluded it providential 
that we did not press forward to lodge there. 


The 26th of the 3rd mo. 1754, we left the province of 
North Carolina, and came into Virginia, and the Lord was 
pleased to cause his peace to rest upon our spirits, that we 
were renewedly convinced that there were movings in his 
counsel. We had travelled upwards of a thousand miles in 
North Carolina, and being preserved from various jeopardies 
and trials, to the praise of his adorable name. 


The 27th we had our first meeting in Virginia, 
wherein the testimony of truth was borne in a close 
manner by both of us against a dull inactive spirit, and 
appeared to have some present effect. 


After having laboured among them (in America) two 
years and seven months, we took a solemn leave in the 
love of the gospel on the 5th of the 6th mo. 1756. The 
10th of 7th mo., we landed at Dublin, having travelled 
upon the continent and islands, upwards of 8750 miles.

most of them of the offspring of Friends, with whom we had
