In our public meeting at this place, I was more at 
liberty in the exercise of my gift, than had been usual with 
me in Holland; at which I afterward admired, being told 
that my interpreter was uncommonly defective in rendering 
what I said into Dutch. This circumstance sometimes 
revolved in my remembrance, accompanied with some kind 
of doubt respecting my being so much at liberty to speak, 
when what I delivered was not well interpreted to the peo- 
ple; but after some years, a friend at Norwich told me, that 
there was at that meeting a sensible Jew, who understood 
the English tongue well, who told him that he had attended 
the meeting, and that my interpreter did not do me justice ; 
but, continued he, ‘it was no matter, as all she said was 
directed to me ;’ and my friend added, that itso affected him, 
that he believed he would freely interpret for me, should I 
ever want his assistance. This relation removed my before 
mentioned doubt, for the word preached found its way to 
one mind, for which in divine wisdom it was appointed. 


On coming to Helvoetsluys, we found that the wind 
was against our sailing for England, and that the inn was 
full of company, many of whom were waiting for their pas- 
sage to England; for the landlord put us in a house which 
was ready furnished, and we became a family to ourselves, 
being furnished with provisions from the inn. The wind 
continuing contrary until the Ist day of the week, and there 
being in the place many people of divers nations and 
stations, who could speak English ; with the concurrence 
and assistance of our landlord and company, we got our 
dining room well seated; and on the Ist day morning held 


‘a meeting in it, whereto the strangers pretty generally came. 


I was favoured to declare the truth among them, to the 
relief of my own spirit, and I believe to the comfort and 
satisfaction of my companions; but the labour was hard, 
through the unpreparedness of the hearts of some to receives 
and perhaps the want of a sufficient knowledge of the 
language in others to understand the doctrines delivered. 


302 BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES. 


The 15th of the 10th mo. I got home, to the mutual 
satisfaction of myself and relations; and notwithstanding 
my great fatigue, in a rather better state of health than 
when I left it; and found my dear aged mother well; and 
here I also met my dear friend Lucy Bradley, who was 
returning home from her visit to Friends in Ireland, and 
our rejoicing one in another was mutual.’’ 


In passing over her travels and labours for upwards 
of 20 years, we find her in the year 1783 labouring in 
her own country, concerning which she writes, 


I had some public meetings in this journey to my 
satisfaction, and I hope to the edification of many peo- 
ple attending them. One of them was held at Cambridge; 
which I hope was serviceable, although I was not favoured 
to rise in the exercise of the divine gift bestowed upon 
me, to that height I did when in that town many years 
ago. ‘That was indeed a singular time, and answered a singu- 
ar end, viz. to convince a man who had contemned women’s 
ministry in Christ's church, of its weight, efficacy, and 
consistency with the gospel dispensation. The same man, 
who did not live in the town, was invited to attend this 
meeting, and he might therein hear gospel truths pub- 
lished, and treated upon in a more argumentative way, 
than it was common for me to be engaged in. The all- 
wise employer of true gospel ministers knows how to 
direct his servants, both as to the matter and the manner 
wherein he intends it should be communicated to the 
people. And I have admired his wisdom and condes- 
cension therein, when without forethought my speech 
has been accommodated to the capacities of those to whom 
it was directed. To such as were illiterate and ignorant, 
i have spoken in very low terms; and to those of more 
understanding, in such as answered its level; while to 
the learned, and those of superior natural abilities, I 
might say with the prophet, ‘the Lord God hath given 
me the tongue of the learned.’ I have not wanted elo- 
quence of speech, or strength of argument, wherein to 
conyey and enforce the doctrines given me to preach;

of which I could say, as my Lord and Master did, «my 
doctrines are not mine, but his who sent me ;’ and his love 
life, and power, hath accompanied them, to the stopping of 
the mouths of gainsayers, and convincing of the understand- 
ings of many, of the rectitude and efficacy of ‘the truth as 
it is in Jesus.” Those who are accoutred for the service of 
him ‘ who spake as never man spake,’ must be educated in 
his school, and disciplined by his wisdom; whereby they 
are made able ministers of the New Testament, not of the 
letter but of the spirit; for the letter killeth, but the spirit 
hat life. Thus have I, with many of my fellow-labourers, 

een assisted to minister in the gospel of Christ; and now 
in the close of a laborious day’s work, I may commemorate 
the mercy, power, and wisdom of him who chuseth whom 
he pleaseth for the various offices in his church. He 
appoints, of both male and female, ‘some apostles, some 
prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers ; 
for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry,” 
&c. Thus from early youth, have I travelled and laboured, 
that the saving knowledge of God may increase, through 
experience of the prevalence of the power of his Son; 
whereby the true believers in him become crucified to the 
world, and the world unto them. Freely I have received 
the knowledge of salvation through the sanctifying opera- 
tion of the spirit of Christ; and freely I have testified 
thereof, and of God’s universal love through his Son to 
mankind ; for he would have none to perish, but that all 
should be saved, and attain to the knowledge of his 
truth.” 


A testimony from the monthly meeting of Friends, for 
the western division of Cornwall, held at Falmouth, the 
6th of the 4 mo. 1795, concerning our late valued friend, 
Catherine Phillips, formerly Payton. 


«Tt appears from accounts received, that she was born 
at Dudley, in Worcestershire, the 16th of the Ist mo. 
1726—7, Old Style. Her parents, Henry and Ann Payton, 
were honourable Friends; and he an approved minister, 
who, when in health, was much from home in the discharge

of his religious duties; but for many of the latter years of 
his life was confined to his chamber by a paralytic disorder ; 
so that the care of a large young family devolved mostly 
upon his wife, a woman of eminent piety and prudence, 
whose anxious solicitude for, and watchful attention to her 
children, they have often commemorated with filial tender- 
ness. Thus instructed by example and precept, our beloved 
friend was early engaged ‘ to seek the Lord for her portion, 
and to know the God of her fathers to be the lot of her 
inheritance.’ And being much the companion of her 
afflicted father, she was probably thereby preserved from 
many levities incident to youth, as well as edified by his 
conversation and virtues. In this allotment she had also 
opportunity to cultivate a disposition for retirement, so 
favourable to the growth of that good seed which the

extended to Ireland, Scotland, Holland, and the continent 
of America; in the course of which, according to accounts 
received, her labours amongst Friends and others were bles- 
sed to the convincement, edification, and comfort of many. 


In the year 1772, she entered upon the marriage state 
with our late valued friend, William Phillips, and removed 
into Cornwall; where she was much engaged in religious 
labour, as well for the spreading of the testimonies of truth 
among strangers, as in repairing the waste places in the 
Society ; being often zealously concerned for the support of 
our christian discipline. 


Some time before her decease, she thus expressed 
herself, ‘I am going where the wicked cease from troubling, 
and the weary are at rest. Oh, these-souls of ours! that 
we should be willing to run the risk of losing them for any 
of the enjoyments of this life. {may say to you follow me 
as I have followed Christ. Beware of pride, and of the 
very ground of pride.’ When under the pressure of great 
bodily suffering, she said, ‘this is a trial; Lord God 
Almighty sanctify it to my soul,’ again, ‘I am thankful I 
feel no cloud ;? and making a short pause, added, ‘I have 
recompense at the Lord’s hand for sin ;’.soon after which, 
the fits which attended her in this illness returned and 
continued till about half an hour before she expired, during 
which space she lay very quiet, and drew her breath shorter 
and shorter to the last. 


She died the 16th of the 8th mo. 1794, in the 68th 
year of her age, and 46th of her ministry; and; after a 
meeting of Friends and others of the neighbourhood, held 
on the occasion, she was decently interred at Kea.

BIOGRAPHICAL SKETCHES, 


Mis ANN BURROWS. 


This eminent femalé was born at Nottingham, of very 
industrious and respectable parents.“ Her mother has been 
a member of the Methodist Society for many years; her 
father has lately been removed by death. 


The subject of this Memoir, like most other youre 
people, sought happiness in the world ;—in the PN 
visible and terrestrial. Happiness is the ptirsuit of all, 
though our pursuits after it are as various as our views of it: 
All unregenerate petsons ate seeking it in the world, yet, 
they seek itin vain, because they seek it where it is not to 
be found,—they seek the living among the dead. The 
gratifications of sense, and the things of the world, seem to 
promise them peace, happiness, and satisfaction ;—they 
believe its promises, pursue the shadow, and grasp at its 
phantom, but it eludes the touch, it dances before them, 
and still appears at a distance, though not far off..—But 
could it have been found in the world, surely Solomon 
would have found it, but he stamps vanity and vexation of 
spirit upon all created good ;—indeed 


“The spider’s most attenuated thread 
Is cord—is cable 

To man’s tender tie on earthly bliss, 
That breaks at every breeze.” 


It is not to be found out of God ;—he being the true 
centre of happiness and the rest for the soul. The psalmist 
was convinced of this, when he said, * return unto thy rest 
O my soul, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee :”

MISS ANN BURROWS. 307 


and so was Ann Burrows when she became deeply 
awakened to a sense of her lost and helpless state as a 
sinner before God. And she sought and found peace 
and salvation through believing in our Lord Jesus Christ. 
She has for some tıme been a member and preacher among 


the Revivalists. She is deeply pious, and much devoted to 


God-and to his work. She began to exercise in public 
when about 17 years of age, and is now about 25. She 
has preached at Birmingham, and through the greatest part 
of Warwickshire, in Leicestershire, and in London. In 
consequence of ill health, she has desisted in a great mea- 
sure from her public work, and resides with her mother, in 
Nottingham, still doing what she can. She is truly pious, 
and has been enabled in all her travels t conduct herself 
with prudence and circumspection. It is said that the 
cause of God never suffered on her account. By prayer 
she lived near to the fountain of all blessedness, and through 
faith kept open the intercourse between her soul and God, 
and was preserved by his mighty power as in the hollow of 
his hand. “He shall keep the feet of his saints,” has been 
peculiarly exemplified in the experience of this eminent 
female. She is rather low in stature, but comely in her 
apearance, and of an amiable disposition. Her talents are 
acceptable, and she has been very useful. May the Lord 
strengthen and preserve her useful life if it seem good in 
his sight ; and if otherwise, prepare her for his everlasting 
kingdom. <‘ The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, 
and he that winneth souls is wise.”
